    Get Started

    Start Here: Deployment Roadmap¶

    This page gives the order in which to set up Splunk for SAP LogServ for the first time, from the request to SAP to working dashboards. Work through the steps in order: each one names the page with the details and ends with a check that tells you the step is done.

    Decide before the data flows

    The Data TA works at index time. Sourcetype routing, the filters and the cloud_provider stamp are applied when an event is indexed, and the event keeps what it was indexed with. Make the decisions of steps 6 to 8 before you save the Data TA’s Configuration page (step 9), so that a Deployment Server’s first push carries them, and in every case before any input starts (step 10). Whatever SAP’s queue holds when the input starts is indexed with the settings in place at that moment.

    The Steps at a Glance¶

    The steps are grouped as in the Get Started menu, with three exceptions: step 8 uses a page from 1. Plan (Capacity Planning and First Start), step 12 is on the Configure and Operate tab (AWS S3 Direct), and step 15 is on the AI Assistant and Enterprise Security Integration tabs.

    1. Plan

    1. Request from SAP and prepare your cloud
    2. Pick your topology
    3. Prepare the forwarding tier

    2. Install the Data TA

    1. Create the indexes and set their retention
    2. Install the Data TA
    3. Choose cloud attribution
    4. Decide filtering
    5. Decide on the first-start queue backlog
    6. Distribute the Data TA (gate: the Data TA is on every heavy forwarder)

    3. Connect Your Cloud

    1. Connect your cloud

    4. Verify Your Data

    1. Verify your data

    Configure and Operate (AWS S3 Direct)

    1. Load history

    5. Install the LogServ App

    1. Install the LogServ App and its search-head add-ons
    2. Run Diagnostics, then backfill the dashboards

    Optional

    1. The AI Assistant and the Enterprise Security content


    1. Request from SAP and Prepare Your Cloud¶

    Start here: SAP does this work on its side, and most later steps need its results. Plan and Prerequisites lists what to ask for, per cloud. SAP’s turnaround can be the longest wait of the whole setup, so send every request to SAP on day one and carry on with steps 2 to 9 while you wait.

    • AWS. Pick your scenario on Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario. AWS Remote S3 Connect is the default; choose AWS Remote S3 Filter now if your forwarders’ load or the first-start backlog (step 8) must be cut, because the scenario decides which template you deploy. Then do the AWS side of your scenario’s guide now, in your own AWS account (the guides’ Secondary account): get the ARNs of the S3 bucket and the SQS queue in your SAP ECS account and their AWS Region, deploy the CloudFormation template, and send SAP LogServ support the request to apply the queue and bucket policies for the role the template creates. In the Connect guide these are steps 1 to 3; in the Filter and Copy guides, steps 1 to 4, which also create the bucket for the Lambda code. If you will load history with AWS S3 Direct (step 12), which reads SAP’s bucket, ask in the same request for s3:ListBucket for that role in SAP’s bucket policy. Nothing reads SAP’s queue yet: the input comes in step 10, and the Filter and Copy templates create no Lambda trigger.
    • Azure. Get the storage account name, the queue name and an account SAS with ss=bq, srt=o and sp=rp (plus a if you configure a dead-letter queue). Ask when the SAS expires (its se= value) and how SAP renews it: the input stops reading when the SAS expires. See Parameters to obtain from SAP and What the SAP-provided SAS must cover.
    • GCP. Create a service account in a GCP project of your own and give its email address to SAP. SAP grants it access to the LogServ subscription and bucket, and gives you the project ID and the subscription name. Check your organization’s policy on service-account keys before install day, and decide how you will rotate the key. See The onboarding sequence, What SAP must grant your service account and Parameters for the input.
    • Every cloud. Ask SAP how long its queue keeps a message and how old the oldest waiting message is. You need both in step 8 (First Start: The Queue Backlog).

    Done when: you hold the values your cloud’s guide asks for (AWS: the two ARNs, the Region, a deployed CloudFormation stack, and SAP’s confirmation that both policies are applied; Azure: the account, the queue, the SAS and its expiry; GCP: the project ID, the subscription and SAP’s confirmation of its grants), and you know how long SAP’s queue keeps messages. Steps 2 to 9 can run while you wait for SAP; step 10 cannot start until this step is done.


    2. Pick Your Topology¶

    Pick the row that matches your Splunk deployment. The steps below refer to these names. The exact placement of every package is on Where Each Package Goes.

    Topology What it means for the steps below
    Single instance One Splunk Enterprise instance indexes, searches and runs the inputs, and every package goes on it. There is no distribution: in step 9 you save the Data TA’s Configuration page on the instance itself.
    DS + HFs + on-premises search head Heavy forwarders run the inputs and parse the data, your Deployment Server pushes the Data TA to them, the indexers hold the indexes, and the LogServ App goes on the search head. Every step applies.
    DS + HFs + Splunk Cloud As above, but the heavy forwarders send to Splunk Cloud, you create the indexes in Splunk Cloud, and the LogServ App goes on the Splunk Cloud search head. The Deployment Server is your own, on premises: Splunk Cloud does not host one.
    HFs without a DS (Splunk Cloud or on-premises search head) You install the Data TA directly on each heavy forwarder and save its Configuration page on each one, with the same values: nothing copies them between forwarders. The indexes go on your indexer tier or the Splunk Cloud stack.
    Splunk Cloud only Supported: not blocked, but a heavy forwarder is strongly recommended. The Data TA, the cloud add-on and the LogServ App go on the Splunk Cloud search head, and the inputs run there, so ingest competes with your users’ searches. The LogServ Azure and GCP add-ons declare the search-head workload, but their installation on a Splunk Cloud search head has not been tested yet.

    Clustered tiers: an indexer cluster gets the two indexes from an index-only app on its manager node (step 4); a search head cluster gets the LogServ App and its add-ons from its deployer.

    Read Plan and Prerequisites for every topology, Splunk Cloud Considerations if you use Splunk Cloud, and Capacity Planning and First Start to size the heavy forwarders.

    Done when: you know which instance gets which package, and how many heavy forwarders you need.


    3. Prepare the Forwarding Tier¶

    These items apply to each heavy forwarder, or on a single instance to that instance. With Splunk Cloud only, the add-on and role items apply to the Splunk Cloud search head.

    • Deployment client (topologies with a DS). Point each heavy forwarder at your Deployment Server and check that it phones home.
    • Splunk Cloud (heavy forwarders that send to Splunk Cloud). Install your stack’s universal forwarder credentials app on each heavy forwarder.
    • Network. Allow HTTPS (port 443) from each heavy forwarder to your cloud. AWS: the AWS STS endpoint (the Splunk Add-on for AWS assumes the role splunk-logserv-ta-role through it), and the SQS and S3 endpoints of the Region that holds SAP’s queue and bucket. Azure: <account>.blob.core.windows.net and <account>.queue.core.windows.net. GCP: oauth2.googleapis.com, pubsub.googleapis.com and storage.googleapis.com. If the forwarders reach the internet through a proxy, see Plan and Prerequisites → Heavy Forwarders.
    • AWS only: the Splunk Add-on for AWS (Splunkbase 1876) on each heavy forwarder that will run an input. Version 8.2.2 or later is recommended (SVD-2026-1005). Install it directly on the heavy forwarder, not through a Deployment Server: the add-on keeps its accounts and inputs in its local/ folder, which a Deployment Server push replaces, and for an add-on the Deployment Server manages, the AWS S3 Direct screen offers only its Apply this as an administrator view, which generates the configuration but creates nothing.
    • Who does the setup. Creating, editing or deleting an Azure or GCP input, and the Create backfill button on the AWS S3 Direct screen, need a role with the admin_all_objects capability on the instance where you do it, on Splunk Enterprise and Splunk Cloud alike. The LogServ App treats only roles named exactly admin, sc_admin or sc_subadmin as admins. See Roles and Access, and on Splunk Cloud the role notes on Splunk Cloud Considerations.

    Done when: each heavy forwarder is listed in Forwarder Management (Agent Management in Splunk 10.0 and later) on your Deployment Server; with Splunk Cloud, each heavy forwarder’s _internal events can be searched from the Splunk Cloud search head; on AWS, Apps → Manage Apps on each heavy forwarder shows the Splunk Add-on for AWS; and you know which account will create the inputs.


    4. Create the Indexes and Set Their Retention¶

    The solution uses two indexes: sap_logserv_logs for the data and logserv_ai_assistant_audit for the AI Assistant’s audit trail. Keep these names unless you have a reason to change them; renaming takes the procedure on Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA.

    • Single instance. The Data TA creates both indexes when you install it in step 5. Set their retention afterwards.
    • Standalone indexer. Create both under Settings → Indexes, or with a small indexes.conf.
    • Indexer cluster. Put both stanzas in an index-only app under the manager node’s manager-apps/, with repFactor = auto on each, and push it as the configuration bundle. Without repFactor = auto the indexes are not replicated.
    • Splunk Cloud. Create both yourself under Settings → Indexes, or with the Admin Config Service (ACS), before any data arrives.

    Retention. The Data TA sets none for sap_logserv_logs, so Splunk’s default applies unless you set one; it keeps the audit index for 90 days. Choose the retention you need when you create the indexes. Events older than an index’s retention can be removed soon after they are indexed, which matters when you load history in step 12.

    Who can search the data. Every role that will use the dashboards must be able to search sap_logserv_logs. Roles that may search all non-internal indexes (*, as Splunk’s built-in roles do) already can. Add the index only to roles with a narrowed list (Settings → Roles → role → Indexes, on Splunk Cloud too). Grant the audit index only as Restricting who can read the audit index describes.

    See Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA.

    Done when: Settings → Indexes on each indexer, or on Splunk Cloud, lists both indexes with the retention you chose (on a single instance, after step 5).


    5. Install the Data TA¶

    • Topologies with a DS. Install it on the Deployment Server only. Do not install it on the heavy forwarders by hand: the Deployment Server’s push replaces each forwarder’s copy, local/ included (step 9).
    • HFs without a DS. Install it on each heavy forwarder.
    • Single instance. Install it on the instance.
    • Splunk Cloud only. Install it on the Splunk Cloud search head as a private app. On Splunk Cloud it is needed only where the inputs run on the search head.
    • Indexers and search heads that run no inputs do not need it.

    See Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA. Leave its Configuration page unsaved until step 9.

    Done when: Apps → Manage Apps shows Splunk TA for SAP LogServ at version 0.1.2, and its Configuration page opens with the Filters and Cloud Provider tabs.


    6. Choose Cloud Attribution¶

    Each event can carry an indexed cloud_provider field that says which cloud it came from. The recommended setup is the same for every fleet: leave the Data TA’s Cloud Provider dropdown at Not set (its default). The Azure and GCP inputs stamp their own events, and AWS S3 Direct stamps the inputs it creates. On AWS you add _meta = cloud_provider::aws to each SQS-Based S3 input as soon as you create it in step 10, following Add the _meta line to an AWS input: create the input, disable it at once, add the line, restart, enable it again. On Splunk Cloud with no heavy forwarder, where you cannot edit the file, see Splunk Cloud Without a Heavy Forwarder. Setting the dropdown as well adds a second stamp next to an input’s own. See Choose Cloud Attribution.

    Done when: you have written down the dropdown value, and on AWS you have planned the _meta line for each input.


    7. Decide Filtering¶

    Filtering is off by default. Decide whether to turn it on and with which values:

    • Folders and sources to include or exclude.
    • Days in the Past (default 7; 0 turns it off). It applies only while filtering is on. It also leaves out of an AWS S3 Direct backfill the days older than its cutoff, so if you will load history (step 12), set it to cover that history.
    • The daily refresh. With filtering on and Days in the Past above 0, a daily job moves the cutoff; on a Deployment Server it also reloads the server class, and each heavy forwarder restarts about once a day to apply it.
    • Azure: the Unix command output. SAP delivers some Azure data in a folder named undefined/undefined: Unix command output, about 0.7 million events and 125 MB a day on the reference system, which stays under the base sap_logserv_logs sourcetype. Unless you need it, drop it with Exclude Sources ps, top, netstat, iostat, vmstat, df, cpu, interfaces, bandwidth, openPorts, nfsiostat, Unix:ListeningPorts. Folder patterns cannot reach it (Data Delivered Without Folder Fields). If you keep it, restrict who can search it: a ps row can carry the arguments a process was started with, passwords and tokens included.

    See Decide Filtering.

    Done when: you have written down Enable Filtering, the include and exclude values and Days in the Past.


    8. Decide on the First-Start Queue Backlog¶

    SAP’s queue keeps a notification for each new object until a consumer takes it or it expires, so a new input can start with days or weeks of notifications waiting, on Azure even months. The input works through them on top of the live feed. Decide now, before the first Save in step 9, how to handle them:

    • Let it drain. Estimate how long the catch-up takes and size the heavy forwarders for it.
    • Ask SAP to purge the older messages, shortly before you start the input in step 10 (in the AWS Filter and Copy scenarios, before you create the Lambda’s trigger). On AWS you can load those days later with AWS S3 Direct (step 12). On Azure and GCP nothing in this solution can load them later.
    • AWS Remote S3 Filter: its Lambda passes on only objects with events newer than its DaysInThePast setting, a parameter of the template you deployed in step 1. To change it, update the stack before you create the Lambda’s trigger.
    • Keep old events out of the index with Days in the Past (step 7). The forwarders still download and parse them, so the catch-up takes as long.

    If your choice changes the filter values of step 7, enter the changed values in step 9. See First Start: The Queue Backlog.

    Done when: you have chosen how to handle the backlog (if a purge, SAP has agreed to do it shortly before your input starts; otherwise you have accepted the catch-up time), and your filter values reflect that choice.


    9. Distribute the Data TA¶

    • Topologies with a DS. On the Deployment Server, open the Data TA’s Configuration page, enter the values from steps 6 to 8 and Save, whether filtering is on or off. The Save stages the Data TA for the heavy forwarders and creates the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class, disabled. In Forwarder Management, edit that server class’s agent assignment and name your heavy forwarders by host name or IP address. Never use *: it sends the Data TA, with a restart, to every deployment client, search heads included. Then click Deploy to Forwarders. Each heavy forwarder picks the Data TA up at its next phone-home and restarts; allow 5 minutes or more.
    • HFs without a DS, single instance, Splunk Cloud only. Save the Configuration page with the values from steps 6 to 8 on each instance that holds the Data TA (Without a Deployment Server).

    See Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders.

    Gate: the Data TA must be on every heavy forwarder before any input is created

    An event that arrives before the Data TA keeps the base sourcetype sap_logserv_logs, its folder fields are never set and its routing never happens, permanently.

    Done when: the Version Check on each heavy forwarder shows the Data TA at version 0.1.2 with its build, and, with a Deployment Server, Forwarder Management shows each heavy forwarder as Ok under SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders.


    10. Connect Your Cloud¶

    Follow your cloud’s guide, on each heavy forwarder that runs an input (single instance: the instance; Splunk Cloud only: the Splunk Cloud search head): Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario leads to the AWS Remote S3 Connect, Filter or Copy guide, the Azure Setup Guide or the GCP Setup Guide. If you chose a purge in step 8, have SAP do it shortly before you create the input (Filter and Copy: before you create the Lambda’s trigger).

    • AWS. You did the AWS side in step 1, so pick up your guide at its access-key step: step 4 of the Connect guide, step 5 of the Filter and Copy guides. Add _meta = cloud_provider::aws to each SQS-Based S3 input as soon as you create it, following Add the _meta line to an AWS input (create, disable at once, add the line, restart, enable); on Splunk Cloud with no heavy forwarder, see Splunk Cloud Without a Heavy Forwarder. In the Filter scenario, create the Lambda’s trigger only once SAP has confirmed both policies: the Lambda discards a notification whose object it cannot read.
    • Azure and GCP. Run one input per queue or subscription, on one heavy forwarder. Each input keeps its own record of what it has read, so a second input on the same queue or subscription can index a message twice (Azure, GCP).
    • Credential renewals. Put the renewal dates in your calendar: the Azure SAS expiry, the GCP service-account key and the AWS access key. Replacing a SAS or key in an Azure or GCP input needs admin_all_objects too. See Rotate credentials in the Azure and GCP guides, and Rotate the Access Key in your AWS guide (Connect, Filter, Copy).

    Done when: the input reads without errors (Azure and GCP: its log line done: messages=N ... events=N shows events; AWS: the Splunk Add-on for AWS logs no errors in _internal), and the first events appear in index=sap_logserv_logs.


    11. Verify Your Data¶

    Run the searches on Verify Your Data. Use the index name, not the sap_logserv_idx_macro macro: a search head that has neither the Data TA nor the LogServ App does not know the macro yet.

    Done when: every event carries splunk_solution=splunk_for_sap_logserv, the sourcetypes match what SAP delivers to you (Supported Log Types), each event indexed since its input got its _meta line has one cloud_provider value (a few AWS events read in the minutes between creating an input and adding the line carry none, which is expected), and no folder that the Data TA routes by folder alone stays under sap_logserv_logs.


    12. Load History¶

    The inputs read only what SAP’s queue holds. To load older days:

    • AWS. Use the Data TA’s AWS S3 Direct screen on the heavy forwarder (or Splunk Cloud search head) that has the Splunk Add-on for AWS. Its Create backfill button needs admin_all_objects; without it, the screen shows the configuration for an administrator to apply. The role needs s3:ListBucket on the bucket, and for SAP’s bucket SAP’s bucket policy must also allow it (step 1). With filtering on, Days in the Past must cover the days you load, and the index’s retention must cover them too. See AWS S3 Direct: Backfill and Recovery.
    • Azure and GCP. The product has no history load. Contact your Splunk team.

    Done when: on AWS, the two check searches the AWS S3 Direct screen gives under each backfill show its scan finished and the events of its days in the index.


    13. Install the LogServ App and Its Search-Head Add-ons¶

    On the search head (search head cluster: through its deployer; Splunk Cloud: the Splunk Cloud search head; single instance: the instance), install the Splunk Common Information Model add-on (Splunk_SA_CIM, Splunkbase 1621) 5.0.0 or later, the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (742) and the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (833), then the LogServ App. Without the Windows add-on, the panels that need Windows event fields stay empty. If you renamed the data index, update the index macro. See LogServ App Prerequisites and Install the App and Seed the Dashboards.

    Done when: the LogServ App opens, and the Summary of its Diagnostics page lists Splunk_SA_CIM, Splunk_TA_windows and Splunk_TA_nix as present and names your data index under Index (from the app macro).


    14. Run Diagnostics, Then Backfill the Dashboards¶

    The dashboards read hourly rollups, so until you backfill them they show only the hours since the LogServ App was installed.

    1. Open the LogServ App’s Diagnostics page (Data Doctor) and check which sourcetypes it finds.
    2. As an admin (a role named admin, sc_admin or sc_subadmin), open Settings → Dashboard Data. Under Backfill window, pick a window that covers the history in your index, including what you loaded in step 12, up to 365 days back: 30 days by default, 60, 90, 180 or 365 days, or a custom range of UTC days.
    3. Click Run backfill, and keep the page open until every row has finished: the Environment Topology (graph) row is written only after the page has collected its results.

    Start a long backfill so that it does not run during the nightly retention window (00:34 to 02:36 in the search head’s time zone): rows written into a collection while its retention runs can be lost until you run the backfill again.

    See Backfilling on first install.

    Done when: the Dashboard Data tab reports Backfill complete, and the dashboards show your history.


    15. Optional: the AI Assistant and the Enterprise Security Content¶

    • AI Assistant. It ships turned off. To use it, install the Splunk MCP Server on the search head, grant its mcp_tool_execute capability to the roles that will use the AI Assistant (the MCP Server grants it only to admin and sc_admin, so analysts and sc_subadmin need it added: step 2 of Set Up the AI Assistant), decide who is audited (a user’s role needs edit_log_alert_event or edit_tcp), then have an admin turn it on and answer both acknowledgements. See Set Up the AI Assistant.
    • Enterprise Security content. It ships enabled. With ES on its own search head (as on Splunk Cloud), install the LogServ App there as well (Enterprise Security Integration: Prerequisites). On a search head without Enterprise Security, turn it off. The AI Assistant’s Security prompts run 13 of these searches, and a disabled search makes its prompt fail, so if you use those prompts, stop only the schedule of those 13 and disable the rest (Disabling or tuning the ES content).

    Done when: the AI Assistant button appears in the LogServ App’s top bar (if you turned it on), and the ES searches run on a schedule only where Enterprise Security does.


    Next Steps¶

    • Configuring Filters: change the filters later.
    • Application Settings: the LogServ App’s settings.
    • Troubleshooting: find the section for a symptom.
    • Upgrading to This Release: when a new build comes out.
    • Removing the Solution: to uninstall.

    1. Plan

    Architecture¶

    This page shows how Splunk for SAP LogServ moves SAP LogServ data from your cloud into Splunk, and what each package does on the way. Read it while you plan; which package goes on which Splunk instance is on Where Each Package Goes.

    The Packages¶

    Splunk for SAP LogServ is four packages of its own, plus the Splunk Add-on for AWS when your SAP ECS data is in AWS:

    Package Splunk Web label App ID What it does
    Data TA Splunk TA for SAP LogServ splunk_ta_sap_logserv Index-time parsing, sourcetype routing and the optional filters for the data your ingest add-on collects. It has no data inputs of its own: its two scripted inputs are maintenance jobs that write to _internal. It also carries the Configuration page (Filters, Cloud Provider), the Deployment Server automation, the AWS S3 Direct backfill screen, and the definitions of the two indexes, sap_logserv_logs (SAP data) and logserv_ai_assistant_audit (AI Assistant audit log).
    LogServ App Splunk App for SAP LogServ splunk_app_sap_logserv Dashboards, search-time field extractions, macros, the scheduled searches that fill the dashboards’ KV Store rollups, Environment Topology, the Enterprise Security content and the AI Assistant (ships disabled). It contains no Python and no inputs.
    Splunk Add-on for AWS Splunk Add-on for AWS Splunk_TA_aws (Splunkbase 1876) Collects from AWS S3: its SQS-Based S3 inputs read the notifications of new LogServ objects and download the objects. The AWS S3 Direct screen creates Generic S3 inputs in it for backfill.
    LogServ Azure add-on Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on Azure splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure Collects from Azure Blob Storage: its sap_logserv_azure_queue input reads the Storage Queue that Event Grid fills with BlobCreated notifications and fetches each blob with a SAS. See the Azure Setup Guide.
    LogServ GCP add-on Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on GCP splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp Collects from Google Cloud Storage: its sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub input pulls a Pub/Sub subscription fed by the bucket’s OBJECT_FINALIZE notifications and fetches each object with a service-account key. See the GCP Setup Guide.

    Each NDJSON line of a LogServ object becomes one event with sourcetype sap_logserv_logs (on AWS you set it on the SQS-Based S3 input, and it must be exactly sap_logserv_logs: the Data TA parses and routes only events that arrive with that sourcetype; the Azure and GCP inputs always use it). The Azure and GCP inputs also stamp cloud_provider on their events. From there the Data TA handles every cloud the same way.

    The Data TA works where the data is parsed: on the heavy forwarders that run the ingest inputs, or on a single instance. A heavy forwarder parses each event before it forwards it, so the indexers receive finished events and the Data TA’s index-time settings do nothing there. The indexers only need the two indexes; in a distributed deployment you create them on the indexer tier. A Deployment Server, if you use one, holds the Data TA to distribute it to the heavy forwarders. The logserv_ai_assistant_audit index is where the AI Assistant writes its audit events; without it they have nowhere to go.

    The LogServ App works at search time on the search head (or the single instance). It finds the SAP data through the macro sap_logserv_idx_macro and the audit events through sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro, so a renamed index needs the macros changed rather than the App; see Renaming an index.

    Why separate packages?

    Index-time work and search-time work run on different Splunk tiers. Keeping them apart means the forwarders carry no dashboards, search-time extractions or AI Assistant code, and the search head carries no ingest logic. On a single instance both packages are installed on the same instance and Splunk merges their configuration.

    Install Matrix¶

    Where you install each package depends on your topology: single instance, Deployment Server with heavy forwarders, Splunk Cloud with or without your own heavy forwarders, search head and indexer clusters. All of them are in one table on Where Each Package Goes.

    Data Flow¶

    AWS¶

    SAP writes your LogServ objects to an S3 bucket in the SAP ECS account, and the bucket sends a notification for each new object to an SQS queue there. How the notifications reach Splunk depends on the scenario you deploy in your own Secondary AWS account (see Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario):

      SAP ECS account (managed by SAP)
  +-------------------------------------------------------------+
  |  SAP LogServ S3 bucket  --(new object)-->  SAP SQS queue    |
  +-------------------------------------------------------------+
          |                       |                       |
       Connect                 Filter                   Copy
          |                       |                       |
          |              Lambda in your account   Lambda in your account
          |              reads SAP's queue and    reads SAP's queue and
          |              forwards the             copies each new object
          |              notifications that       to a bucket in your
          |              pass its filters to a    account; that bucket
          |              queue in your account    notifies a queue in
          |                       |               your account
          |                       |                       |
          v                       v                       v
  Input reads SAP's       Input reads your        Input reads your queue
  queue and downloads     queue and downloads     and downloads from your
  from SAP's bucket       from SAP's bucket       bucket
          |                       |                       |
          +-----------------------+-----------------------+
                                  |
                                  v
            Heavy Forwarder: Splunk Add-on for AWS, SQS-Based S3 input
            (signs in through the IAM role splunk-logserv-ta-role in your
            account; cross-account for Connect and Filter)
    • Connect deploys only an IAM user and a cross-account IAM role in your account.
    • Filter also deploys a Lambda, a queue and a dead-letter queue; the objects are still downloaded from SAP’s bucket.
    • Copy also deploys a Lambda, a bucket, a queue and a dead-letter queue.
    • Filter and Copy need an S3 bucket of your own for the Lambda code.

    Backfill and recovery use a fourth channel with no queue: a Generic S3 input in the Splunk Add-on for AWS that reads a bucket prefix directly. The Data TA’s AWS S3 Direct screen creates these inputs; see AWS S3 Direct: Backfill and Recovery.

    Azure¶

      SAP LogServ Blob Storage (managed by SAP)
        |
        v  (BlobCreated notifications via Event Grid --> Storage Queue)
  LogServ Azure add-on: sap_logserv_azure_queue input on a Heavy Forwarder
  (add-on installed on each Heavy Forwarder that may run an input)
        |   fetches each blob with a SAS; emits sourcetype = sap_logserv_logs
        v
  Same Data TA filtering + routing --> Indexers --> Search Head

    Run one input for each queue. See the Azure Setup Guide.

    Google Cloud¶

      SAP LogServ GCS bucket (managed by SAP)
        |
        v  (OBJECT_FINALIZE notifications via Pub/Sub topic --> PULL subscription)
  LogServ GCP add-on: sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub input on a Heavy Forwarder
  (add-on installed on each Heavy Forwarder that may run an input)
        |   fetches each object with a service-account key; emits sourcetype = sap_logserv_logs
        v
  Same Data TA filtering + routing --> Indexers --> Search Head

    The service account is yours: you create it in a GCP account of your own, give its email address to SAP support, and SAP grants it read access to the LogServ subscription and bucket (the GCP counterpart of the AWS cross-account IAM role). Run one input for each subscription. See the GCP Setup Guide.

    From the Heavy Forwarder to the Dashboards¶

    Whatever the cloud, each event then goes through the same steps:

      Heavy Forwarder (or single instance): the Data TA at index time
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
  |  0. The input reads each object; every NDJSON line becomes   |
  |     one event (sourcetype sap_logserv_logs)                  |
  |  1. Filters, only when Enable Filtering is on (nullQueue)    |
  |  2. Set host, source, clz_dir and clz_subdir                 |
  |  3. Route to the final sourcetype                            |
  |  4. Stamp splunk_solution (and cloud_provider when set)      |
  |  5. Keep only the "_raw" text as the event                   |
  |  6. Forward to the indexers                                  |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
        |
        v
  Indexers: sap_logserv_logs
        |
        v
  Search Head: LogServ App (search-time fields, rollups, dashboards)

    Steps 1 to 5 are TRANSFORMS- classes of the [sap_logserv_logs] stanza, and Splunk runs them in the order of their names. The filter class, TRANSFORMS-00-filter, is written to the Data TA’s local/props.conf when you save the filters, and sorts before the shipped classes 01 (host, source and folder fields), 02 to 09 (routes), 50 and 51 (stamps) and 99 (unwrap _raw). The filters have to run before step 5, because they match the envelope keys that the unwrap removes. An event the filters drop still passes through the later steps, so filtering saves license and storage, not forwarder CPU (see Capacity Planning and First Start).

    Index-Time Filtering¶

    The Data TA’s filters decide at index time which LogServ events are indexed. They run on the parsing tier (the heavy forwarders, or the single instance) and send the events they drop to nullQueue, so those events are never indexed and do not count toward ingest-based licensing:

    • Include Filters / Exclude Filters: folder patterns on clz_dir/clz_subdir, for example linux/* or linux/cron.
    • Include Sources / Exclude Sources: patterns on the event’s source (the log file’s path), optionally limited to one folder, for example linux/linux_secure=/var/log/zypper.log.
    • Days in the Past: drops events whose own _time (the epoch in the raw NDJSON) is older than midnight UTC N days ago. It keys on the event’s timestamp, not on the storage object’s path date. Default 7.

    Enable Filtering is off by default, and none of these settings applies until it is checked. You save the filters on the Data TA’s Configuration page:

    • With a Deployment Server managing your heavy forwarders, save them on the Deployment Server. They reach the forwarders when you click Deploy to Forwarders; with Days in the Past above 0, the daily refresh pushes its new cutoff by itself.
    • Without a Deployment Server, save them on each heavy forwarder (or the single instance); they apply there without a restart.

    Filters work at index time: what is indexed before you set them stays indexed. Decide them before the inputs start; see Decide Filtering and, for every setting, Configuring Filters.

    Sourcetype Routing¶

    During index-time parsing the Data TA reads each event’s envelope (the NDJSON keys around _raw) and assigns its final sourcetype with regex rules in transforms.conf. It keys on one of three things, depending on the log type:

    • The source path: Linux (/var/log/messages, /var/log/cron, …), ISC BIND (/var/lib/named/log/named/...), Squid (/var/log/squid/access.log, …), Windows (WinEventLog:...) and the SAP Web Dispatcher access log (.../log/http_access_log).
    • clz_subdir alone: for example HANA audit (hanaaudit), the ABAP gateway, dispatcher, enqueue server, event, message server and work process logs, the SAP Host Agent and SAP Router.
    • clz_dir and clz_subdir together, where the same folder name exists under more than one clz_dir (for example audit under both abap/ and scc/): ABAP audit, ICM and sapstartsrv, HANA trace, the SAP Cloud Connector logs and sap/sapstartsrv.

    HANA trace files delivered without folder fields are routed by their source path instead. The route classes run in order (02 to 09) and a later match replaces an earlier one: /var/log/messages lines in the sap/saprouter folder first match the Linux route, then become sap:saprouter.

    For every log type and its sourcetype, see Supported Log Types.

    The LogServ App and the AI Assistant¶

    The AI Assistant ships disabled. When an admin turns it on, its predefined prompts run the App’s saved searches through the Splunk MCP Server with no LLM involved; for free-form prompts the LLM vendor receives the question and, for each search, a summary whose content the privacy tier sets, never the raw event rows. See Privacy Tiers.

    How the LogServ App, the AI Assistant and the Environment Topology view are built is described in LogServ App and AI Assistant Internals.

    Next Steps¶

    • Supported Log Types: what SAP delivers and how each log type is parsed.
    • Where Each Package Goes: the placement table for every topology.
    • Plan and Prerequisites: what to request from SAP and prepare on each tier.

    Supported Log Types¶

    Overview¶

    SAP ECS environment logs are not a singular data source but a collection of OS-specific, SAP environment, database, and other application logs.

    Due to the nature of this solution, the SAP LogServ packages are not standalone integrations. To take full advantage of their capabilities (like CIM mapping), install the search-tier add-ons listed in LogServ App Prerequisites.

    For a streamlined data ingestion process, all selected logs are ingested under one sourcetype: sap_logserv_logs. The Data TA then assigns each event its final sourcetype during index-time parsing on the heavy forwarder (or the single instance). SAP application logs (HANA audit and trace, ABAP, Cloud Connector, SAP host services) are routed by their clz_dir / clz_subdir folder fields. Linux, ISC BIND (DNS), Squid (proxy), Windows and SAP Web Dispatcher access logs are routed by their source path, and so are HANA trace files delivered without folder fields. When both kinds of route match, the later one wins: /var/log/messages lines in the sap/saprouter folder become sap:saprouter.

    All events are in NDJSON format with metadata (like _time, host, source, etc.) and the _raw field containing the event contents. To limit index size, only the _raw field is ingested from each event – metadata fields are either mapped to Splunk’s native metadata fields or dropped. However clz_dir and clz_subdir fields are preserved to maintain backtracking capabilities. These fields correspond to the directory tree of the original data in object storage.

    The Data TA also stamps splunk_solution (always splunk_for_sap_logserv, identifying events that flowed through this solution) at index time on every routed event. Events can also carry an indexed cloud_provider field (aws, azure, or gcp, identifying the cloud the data was ingested from). The Azure and GCP ingest add-ons set it on every input. For AWS, add _meta = cloud_provider::aws to each SQS-Based S3 input (the inputs the AWS S3 Direct screen creates get it automatically). The Data TA’s Configuration → Cloud Provider dropdown ships as Not set; see Choose Cloud Attribution for when to change it.

    Ingest channel: AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, or Google Cloud Storage

    The sourcetype mappings below apply identically to all three ingest channels — AWS S3 (via the Splunk Add-on for AWS), Azure Blob Storage (via the LogServ Azure add-on), and Google Cloud Storage (via the LogServ GCP add-on). The Data TA’s index-time routing transforms key on the clz_dir / clz_subdir fields carried inside each NDJSON event (and, for the Linux, DNS, proxy, Windows and Web Dispatcher access types and for HANA trace files delivered without folder fields, on the event’s source path), which the SAP LogServ collector writes the same way regardless of object-storage destination. AWS S3 setup is covered in Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario and its AWS guides; see the Azure Setup Guide and the GCP Setup Guide for the other clouds. Azure- and GCP-ingested events carry an indexed cloud_provider field automatically (stamped per input by their add-on); AWS-ingested events carry it once _meta = cloud_provider::aws is on each AWS S3 input — see Choose Cloud Attribution.

    LogServ Object Storage Path Structure¶

    The log files in the SAP LogServ object storage location (AWS S3 bucket, Azure Blob Storage container, or GCS bucket) follow this path pattern (the leading container/prefix segment is environment-specific — logserv/ here; some landscapes use e.g. clzlogserv/):

    <prefix>/<clz_dir>/<clz_subdir>/<YYYY>/<MM>/<DD>/<filename>.json.gz

    For example:

    logserv/linux/messages/2025/09/15/messages-abc123.json.gz
logserv/hana/hanaaudit/2025/10/01/hana-xyz789.json.gz
logserv/dns/binddns/2025/11/20/dns-def456.json.gz

    The clz_dir/clz_subdir values are used by the index-time filter to match include/exclude patterns. The filter’s Include Sources and Exclude Sources fields match the event’s source value instead — the log file’s path, such as /var/log/zypper.log — which is how log files that share a folder are told apart. See Configuring Filters for details. Some Azure data sits in a folder named undefined/undefined and its events carry no folder fields; see Data Delivered Without Folder Fields.

    Primary Supported Log Types¶

    These log types have dedicated parsing logic — index-time routing to a specific final sourcetype, plus search-time field extractions — to provide the most accurate parsing. The tables below show the sourcetype mapping for each.

    SAP HANA Audit (LogServ App)¶

    The LogServ App provides rich search-time field extractions for SAP HANA audit events — the full audit-record field set (service, host, SID, user, action, status, SQL statement, and the derived risk/criticality fields) plus CIM field aliases.

    Source field value Sourcetype assigned Filter path
    hana audit log sap:hana:audit hana/hanaaudit

    SAP Web Dispatcher (LogServ App)¶

    The LogServ App provides search-time field extractions for SAP Web Dispatcher access logs — client/method/status/URI, four-stage timing, TLS posture, and derived response-time / error fields, plus CIM field aliases. Like the ABAP sourcetypes, it also extracts sap_sid and sap_instance from the source metadata field (/usr/sap/<SID>/<instance>/...): a path with no /usr/sap/<SID>/ directory (three upper-case letters or digits) gets no sap_sid, and one with no instance directory (upper-case letters followed by digits, such as W00) right below /usr/sap/<dir>/ gets no sap_instance.

    Source field value Sourcetype assigned Filter path
    web dispatcher access log sap:webdispatcher:access webdispatcher/accesslog

    SAP ABAP Application Logs (LogServ App)¶

    The LogServ App provides search-time field extractions for 9 SAP ABAP application log types. Each sourcetype includes sap_sid and sap_instance extraction from the source metadata field, plus type-specific field extractions.

    Source field value Sourcetype assigned Filter path
    ABAP security audit log sap:abap:audit abap/audit
    ABAP dispatcher log † sap:abap:dispatcher abap/dispatcher
    ABAP enqueue server log sap:abap:enqueueserver abap/enqueueserver
    ABAP event log † sap:abap:event abap/event
    ABAP gateway log sap:abap:gateway abap/gateway
    ABAP ICM (Internet Communication Manager) log sap:abap:icm abap/icm
    ABAP message server log sap:abap:messageserver abap/messageserver
    ABAP sapstartsrv log sap:abap:sapstartsrv abap/sapstartsrv
    ABAP work process log † sap:abap:workprocess abap/workprocess

    The ICM log (dev_icm) gives the request type, session ID, SAP client (sap_client), user and terminal of each session-list entry, the direction, addresses and protocol of each connection, and the class of the ICM’s own messages (icm_severity: ERROR or WARNING). It records no HTTP status code. The Data TA gives this sourcetype to the abap/icm folder only. Data TA builds up to 1791935359 (2026-10-13) gave it to every LogServ folder named icm, so a Web Dispatcher’s own ICM log (webdispatcher/icm) indexed by them is sap:abap:icm, with the Web Dispatcher’s sap_sid and sap_instance; from build 1792189743 (2026-10-16) it keeps sap_logserv_logs, like the Web Dispatcher’s other secondary folders.

    † Discontinued from LogServ scope — effective April 2026

    SAP discontinued three of the ABAP log types above from LogServ delivery effective April 2026:

    • ABAP work process log — sap:abap:workprocess
    • ABAP dispatcher log — sap:abap:dispatcher
    • ABAP event log (external events) — sap:abap:event

    LogServ no longer delivers new events for these sourcetypes. The LogServ App retains their parsing logic and dashboards, and any data already ingested remains fully searchable — but no new events will arrive through LogServ going forward.

    SAP also discontinued the ABAP transport log (abap/transport, /usr/sap/trans/log) in the same April 2026 change; LogServ never routed it to a dedicated sourcetype, so it does not appear in the tables on this page.

    If you require continued collection of these logs, please contact SAP directly to discuss the options available for your environment.

    SAP HANA Trace Logs (LogServ App)¶

    The LogServ App provides search-time field extractions for HANA trace logs, including SID/instance extraction from the source path.

    Source field value Sourcetype assigned Filter path
    HANA trace log sap:hana:tracelogs hana/tracelogs
    HANA trace log delivered without folder fields: a .trc file or backup.log in /usr/sap/<SID>/HDB<nn>/<host>/trace/ or its DB_<tenant>/ subfolder sap:hana:tracelogs none — Include Sources or Exclude Sources /usr/sap/*/HDB??/*/trace/*

    Real Azure deliveries can send the HANA trace directory without clz_dir and clz_subdir (see Data Delivered Without Folder Fields); on the reference system all of the real HANA trace data arrived that way. The Data TA routes these events by their source path instead, and only when the event has no folder fields; an event that has them is routed by its folder as before. Other files in the trace directory, such as backint.log or compressed .trc.gz files, and files in deeper subfolders keep the base sap_logserv_logs sourcetype, and so do HANA trace events indexed by an earlier Data TA build. Routing does not add folder fields, so a folder pattern such as hana/tracelogs never matches these files: in Include Filters it does not keep them (an allow-list drops them), and in Exclude Filters it does not drop them. Use the source pattern in the table.

    SAP Cloud Connector (LogServ App)¶

    The LogServ App provides search-time field extractions for SAP Cloud Connector audit and HTTP access logs.

    Source field value Sourcetype assigned Filter path
    SCC audit log (CSV format) sap:scc:audit scc/audit
    SCC HTTP access log sap:scc:http_access scc/tracelogs

    SAP Service Logs (LogServ App)¶

    The LogServ App provides search-time field extractions for SAP host-level service logs. These are infrastructure services that run at the host control level (/usr/sap/hostctrl/) rather than within a specific SAP instance.

    Source field value Sourcetype assigned Filter path
    SAP Start Service log (auth, SSL/TLS) sap:sapstartsrv sap/sapstartsrv
    SAP Host Agent execution log sap:saphostexec sap/saphostexec
    SAP Router connection and trace log sap:saprouter sap/saprouter

    SAP Service Log Details

    • sap:sapstartsrv includes fields for OS authentication failures, SSL/TLS negotiation errors (protocol version, cipher suite, peer addresses), and webmethod invocation failures.
    • sap:saprouter covers both .log files (CONNECT/DISCONNECT/INVAL DATA events with connection IDs and host addresses) and .trc files (NiBuf/NiI error traces with peer/local addresses and return codes) as a single sourcetype.
    • On GCP the router’s records can also arrive as /var/log/messages lines in the sap/saprouter folder. These lines get sap:saprouter too. On the reference system at least 70% of them, in the one hour measured, were the router’s own connection and trace records, and the rest the router container’s wrapper output and other text; every line had the same tagged syslog form, and the newest lines carry the router container’s tag. They are router data, so do not drop them with an entry such as sap/saprouter=/var/log/messages.

    Linux OS logs¶

    The LogServ App parses linux:cron, linux:warn, linux:sudolog, linux:slapd, lastlog, who and linux_messages_syslog itself; the first four are LogServ-App-owned names, deliberately distinct from the pretrained names of the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux. The App ships no extraction for linux_secure: its firewall and kernel panels parse those events inline, and their CIM fields come from the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux on the search tier.

    Source field value Sourcetype assigned Filter path
    /lastlog lastlog linux/linux_secure
    /var/log/cron linux:cron linux/cron
    /var/log/firewall linux_secure linux/linux_secure
    /var/log/kernel linux_secure linux/linux_secure
    /var/log/localmessages linux_messages_syslog linux/localmessages
    /var/log/messages linux_messages_syslog linux/messages, linux/proxy
    /var/log/pacemaker/pacemaker.log linux:slapd linux/pacemaker, linux/slapd
    /var/log/slapd.log linux:slapd linux/slapd
    /var/log/sssd/sssd* linux_secure linux/linux_secure
    /var/log/sudolog linux:sudolog linux/sudolog
    /var/log/warn linux:warn linux/warn
    /who who linux/linux_secure

    On /var/log/pacemaker/pacemaker.log lines the App extracts resource_agent and cluster_resource from resource-agent lines and pacemaker_daemon and pacemaker_function from daemon lines. slapd.log lines name no user.

    Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows¶

    Source field value Sourcetype assigned Filter path
    WinEventLog:Application XmlWinEventLog windows/WinEventLog:Application
    WinEventLog:(*.)Operational XmlWinEventLog windows/WinEventLog:Powershell
    WinEventLog:Security XmlWinEventLog windows/WinEventLog:Security
    WinEventLog:System XmlWinEventLog windows/WinEventLog:System

    The LogServ App ships no XmlWinEventLog extraction: fields such as EventCode, severity and signature come from the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (742) on the search head.

    Squid Proxy (squid:access, squid:cache, squid:store)¶

    Parsing of Squid’s native format is absorbed into the LogServ App (from the archived Splunk Add-on for Squid Proxy v2.1.0 — no longer required as a separate install), and the App parses the logformat=splunk_recommended_squid key=value format SAP LogServ proxy logs use with its own transforms. Each file has its own sourcetype: access.log holds the requests, cache.log the daemon’s own messages and store.log the object-store journal. Data indexed by an earlier Data TA carries all three as squid:access, so the dashboards count only access.log lines as requests.

    Source field value Sourcetype assigned Filter path
    /var/log/squid/access.log squid:access proxy/squid, linux/proxy
    /var/log/squid/cache.log squid:cache proxy/squid, linux/proxy
    /var/log/squid/store.log squid:store proxy/squid, linux/proxy

    Real LogServ deliveries do not all use one folder layout. The AWS bucket files Squid under proxy/squid; Azure delivers it under linux/proxy; GCP delivers pacemaker.log under linux/pacemaker and a proxy VM’s /var/log/messages under linux/proxy. The Filter path columns list every path seen, and the Data TA declares all of them, so a filter rule meant to cover a log type on every cloud names each of its paths — proxy/squid, linux/proxy for Squid. To exclude Squid, keep in mind that linux/proxy also carries a proxy VM’s /var/log/messages: Exclude Filters proxy/squid with Exclude Sources linux/proxy=/var/log/squid/* drops the Squid files of both layouts and keeps those lines.

    ISC BIND (isc:bind:*)¶

    Parsing is absorbed natively into the LogServ App (from the archived Splunk Add-on for ISC BIND v2.0.0 — no longer required as a separate install).

    Source field value Sourcetype assigned Filter path
    /var/lib/named/log/named/default.log isc:bind:query dns/binddns
    /var/lib/named/log/named/general.log isc:bind:network dns/binddns
    /var/lib/named/log/named/lame-servers.log isc:bind:lameserver dns/binddns
    /var/lib/named/log/named/network.log isc:bind:network dns/binddns
    /var/lib/named/log/named/notify.log isc:bind:transfer dns/binddns
    /var/lib/named/log/named/queries.log isc:bind:query dns/binddns
    /var/lib/named/log/named/resolver.log isc:bind:network dns/binddns
    /var/lib/named/log/named/update.log isc:bind:transfer dns/binddns
    /var/lib/named/log/named/xfer-out.log isc:bind:transfer dns/binddns

    Filter Path Column

    The Filter path column shows the clz_dir/clz_subdir value used in the index-time filter include/exclude patterns. See Configuring Filters for details.

    Source Field Value Column

    In the Linux, Windows, Squid and ISC BIND tables the Source field value column shows the source values that the filter’s Include Sources and Exclude Sources fields match; the SAP tables describe the log instead. Some rows are shorthand rather than literal values: /var/log/sssd/sssd* stands for every sssd file, rotated copies such as /var/log/sssd/sssd.log-20260913 included, and WinEventLog:(*.)Operational for the Operational channels. Real deliveries on the reference system carry lastlog and who without the leading / that the table shows (the routing accepts both forms). A source pattern must match the whole value and is case-sensitive, so list the values your own deliveries carry before writing one — see Source Pattern Syntax.

    Secondary Supported Log Types¶

    The log types below are within LogServ’s scope and are ingested and fully searchable once SAP has activated them for your landscape (Network and WAF/F5 logs are activated only on request, and WAF/F5 applies only if your RISE package includes WAF or F5), but they do not have the dedicated index-time routing and search-time field extractions that the Primary types above have. They remain under the base sap_logserv_logs sourcetype in raw form; detailed, per-type parsing may be added in a future release.

    These data sources are drawn from Section 2 (“Data sources”) of the SAP LogServ service description and are the sources not covered by a Primary parser above. Each entry ends with how to keep it out of the index with the Data TA’s filters (Configuration → Filters, Enable Filtering checked; see Configuring Filters for complete recipes).

    • Network / Flow logs — VPC/VNET network-traffic flow logs (source/destination IPs, ports, protocols, and traffic statistics). Category-level in the source document; no dedicated clz_dir/clz_subdir; activated on request. Filter: the folder is not known, so only an Include Filters allow-list drops it; once you know its folder or source values, name them in Exclude Filters or Exclude Sources.
    • WAF / F5 logs — Web Application Firewall / F5 traffic and firewall system events (successful and failed connection attempts). Category-level; no dedicated clz_dir/clz_subdir; activated on request. Filter: as for Network / Flow — an Include Filters allow-list, or an exclude once the folder or source is known.
    • SAP ABAP — transport + HTTP access — the ABAP transport log (abap/transport — discontinued by SAP from LogServ scope effective April 2026) and the ABAP HTTP access log (abap/httpaccess, newly added to LogServ scope). Filter: Exclude Filters abap/transport, abap/httpaccess; an allow-list must name the Primary ABAP folders one by one, since abap/* keeps both.
    • SAP Web Dispatcher — process / sapstartsrv / dev_icm traces — webdispatcher/process, webdispatcher/sapstartsrv, webdispatcher/devicm; only webdispatcher/accesslog has a Primary parser. The Web Dispatcher’s ICM log (webdispatcher/icm) is raw as well; Data TA builds up to 1791935359 (2026-10-13) typed it sap:abap:icm (see the ICM paragraph above). Filter: Exclude Filters webdispatcher/process, webdispatcher/icm, webdispatcher/sapstartsrv, webdispatcher/devicm, or webdispatcher/accesslog (not webdispatcher/*) in an allow-list.
    • Additional Linux system logs — /var/log/zypper.log, /var/log/YaST2 (linux/linux_secure), and /var/log/cluster/corosync.log (linux/pacemaker). Filter: these share their folders with Primary log types — linux/linux_secure also holds the firewall, kernel, sssd, lastlog and who logs, and linux/pacemaker the Pacemaker cluster log — so a folder pattern cannot drop them without dropping those too. Drop them by source with Exclude Sources: /var/log/zypper.log*, /var/log/YaST2/* for zypper and YaST2 (real deliveries carry /var/log/zypper.log, /var/log/YaST2/mkinitrd.log and /var/log/YaST2/config_diff_<date>.log), and /var/log/cluster/corosync.log* for corosync. corosync.log has not been observed in real data on the reference system; the path is the one the service description names, so confirm the source value your deliveries carry before relying on the pattern. See Recipe 3.
    • Database — SAP ASE (Sybase) — ASE error log, Backup Server log, and Job scheduler error log (sybase/install). Filter: Exclude Filters sybase/*.
    • Database — Microsoft SQL Server — MSSQL database audit logs (MSSQLDBAudit). Filter: no folder is known, so only an Include Filters allow-list drops them; once you know their folder or source values, exclude those.
    • SAP NetWeaver Java — deploy, JSMON, JStart, server, ICM, security, and general trace/log files (java/*). Filter: Exclude Filters java/*.
    • SAP BusinessObjects (BOBJ — BI / BODS / IPS) — BI/IPS, BODS and Jobserver, Webapp, Tomcat, and SAC Agent logs (bobj_bi/*, bobj_bods/*, bobj_sacagent/*). Filter: Exclude Filters bobj_bi/*, bobj_bods/*, bobj_sacagent/*.
    • DP Agent (Data Provisioning Agent) — framework alert and trace logs (dpagent/alert, dpagent/trace). Filter: Exclude Filters dpagent/*.

    Check the folders and files your own deliveries use

    The folder names above come from the service description; none of these Secondary folders has appeared in the reference system’s real deliveries, while the zypper and YaST2 files have. Before relying on a rule, list what your deliveries carry under the base sourcetype:

    | tstats count where `sap_logserv_idx_macro` sourcetype=sap_logserv_logs by clz_dir, clz_subdir, source

    Some events carry no folder fields at all and do not appear in that list — see Data Delivered Without Folder Fields below. An Include Filters allow-list drops them unless Include Sources keeps them.

    Out of scope

    Per the LogServ service description, DB2 and MaxDB database logs are not in LogServ scope, and are therefore not listed above.

    Data Delivered Without Folder Fields¶

    SAP files some Azure data in a storage folder named undefined/undefined (<prefix>/undefined/undefined/<YYYY>/<MM>/<DD>/), and its events carry no clz_dir or clz_subdir. In about four weeks of real Azure deliveries on the reference system it was about 19.9 million events of two kinds, each from a single host:

    • Unix command output — about 19.4 million events, with source values ps, netstat, iostat, cpu, nfsiostat, top, openPorts, interfaces, df, bandwidth, vmstat and Unix:ListeningPorts; ps alone is about 80%. Together that is about 0.7 million events and roughly 125 MB of text a day. This output is not among the data sources the LogServ service description lists. They stay under the base sap_logserv_logs sourcetype and are not parsed: each event holds one table row, a header line on its own, or a table whose line breaks are written as the two characters \n.
    • HANA trace files — about 566,000 events, the .trc files and backup.log of /usr/sap/<SID>/HDB<nn>/<host>/trace/. The Data TA routes them to sap:hana:tracelogs by their source path (see SAP HANA Trace Logs).

    Folder patterns cannot reach either kind: an Include Filters allow-list drops them all, hana/tracelogs in Include Filters does not keep the trace files, and no Exclude Filters entry drops them. Use Include Sources and Exclude Sources, which match the source value.

    Drop the Unix command output unless you need it

    If you do not use this output, drop it with Exclude Sources ps, top, netstat, iostat, vmstat, df, cpu, interfaces, bandwidth, openPorts, nfsiostat, Unix:ListeningPorts. If you keep it, review who can search it: a ps row can carry the arguments a process was started with — up to 34% of the real ps rows checked on the reference system did — and process arguments can contain passwords, keys or tokens. See Configuring Filters → Events Without Folder Fields.

    Where Each Package Goes¶

    This page is the one place that says which Splunk instance gets which package, for every supported topology. Use it to plan your install; the install steps are on the pages it links to.

    Package Matrix¶

    SH = the search tier: the search head, the Splunk Cloud search head, or every member of a search head cluster (through the deployer). IDX = indexers. HFs = heavy forwarders. DS = Deployment Server. On a single instance, install every required package on that instance.

    Package Get it from Required? SH IDX HFs DS
    Data TA (splunk_ta_sap_logserv) GitHub release_binaries required only where the search head runs the inputs — (create the indexes) ✓ (from the DS, or installed directly) ✓ (holds it to distribute it)
    LogServ App (splunk_app_sap_logserv) GitHub release_binaries required ✓ — — —
    Splunk Common Information Model (Splunk_SA_CIM) Splunkbase 1621, 5.0.0 or later required (the App’s declared dependency) ✓ — — —
    Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows Splunkbase 742 required for the Windows dashboard ✓ — — —
    Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux Splunkbase 833 required for CIM / ES coverage of linux_secure ✓ — — —
    Splunk Add-on for AWS Splunkbase 1876: no minimum enforced; 8.2.2 or later recommended (SVD-2026-1005, third-party package fixes); docs verified on 8.3.1; the AWS S3 Direct screen warns below 8.1.0 required if your SAP ECS data is in AWS only where the search head runs the inputs (see the Splunk Cloud only row) — ✓ (installed directly, not by the DS) —
    LogServ Azure add-on (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure) GitHub release_binaries required if your SAP ECS data is in Azure only where the search head runs the inputs (see the Splunk Cloud only row) — ✓ (installed directly, not by the DS) —
    LogServ GCP add-on (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp) GitHub release_binaries required if your SAP ECS data is in Google Cloud only where the search head runs the inputs (see the Splunk Cloud only row) — ✓ (installed directly, not by the DS) —
    Splunk MCP Server Splunkbase 7931: 1.1.0 or later; 1.2.1 or later recommended (SVD-2026-1004) only for the AI Assistant ✓ — — —
    Splunk AI Assistant Splunkbase 7245 optional; recommended companion to the MCP Server ✓ — — —

    The four LogServ packages are the 0.1.2 tarballs in the release_binaries/ folder of the GitHub repository: splunk_ta_sap_logserv-0.1.2.tar.gz, splunk_app_sap_logserv-0.1.2.tar.gz, splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure-0.1.2.tar.gz and splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp-0.1.2.tar.gz, with their AppInspect reports and a README that lists each file’s md5 and size.
