    Topology Data TA LogServ App and search-tier add-ons Ingest add-on (AWS, Azure or GCP) The two indexes
    Single instance The instance The instance The instance Created by the Data TA when it first loads; set the retention of sap_logserv_logs yourself (Splunk’s default applies until you do)
    DS + HFs + on-prem search head The DS, which pushes it to each HF The search head Each HF, installed directly On the indexer tier: see the indexer rows below
    DS + HFs + Splunk Cloud The DS, which pushes it to each HF The Splunk Cloud search head Each HF, installed directly On the Splunk Cloud stack: Settings > Indexes or ACS
    HFs without a DS (Splunk Cloud or on-prem) Each HF, installed directly; save its Configuration tabs on each HF The search head (or the Splunk Cloud search head) Each HF, installed directly On the indexer tier, or on the Splunk Cloud stack
    Splunk Cloud only, no heavy forwarder: supported (not blocked); a heavy forwarder is strongly recommended The Splunk Cloud search head, which runs the inputs The Splunk Cloud search head The Splunk Cloud search head; the inputs run there (the LogServ Azure and GCP add-ons have not been installed on a Splunk Cloud search head by the project) On the Splunk Cloud stack: Settings > Indexes or ACS
    Search head cluster Not on the members (ingest stays on the HFs) Every member, from the deployer Not on the members On the indexer tier
    Standalone indexer Not needed (allowed: its index definitions then create the indexes; its parsing settings never run there, though its two maintenance scripts still run, every 10 minutes and daily) — — On the indexer: Settings > Indexes, or a small indexes.conf
    Indexer cluster Not needed on the peers (allowed: its parsing settings never run there, though its two maintenance scripts still run on every peer) — — An index-only app with both index stanzas and repFactor = auto, in the manager node’s manager-apps/, pushed as the configuration bundle

    The index settings and the steps for each case are on Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA.

    Notes¶

    • The rule behind the table. The Data TA goes where the data is parsed: the heavy forwarders that run the ingest inputs, or the single instance. The Deployment Server holds it to distribute it. The indexes are created on the indexer tier: a heavy forwarder parses each event before forwarding it, so the indexers need only the two index definitions.
    • Deployment Server: optional. With one, install the Data TA on the Deployment Server only, never also directly on the heavy forwarders it manages: a push replaces the forwarder’s copy of the app, local/ included. Nothing reaches the forwarders on its own. They must be deployment clients, and the Data TA arrives after its Configuration page is saved on the Deployment Server, the forwarders are added to the server class, and Deploy to Forwarders is clicked; each forwarder restarts when it arrives. See Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders. A Splunk Cloud stack is never a Deployment Server: run your own, or install the Data TA directly on each heavy forwarder.
    • Ingest add-ons are installed directly on each instance that runs an input, never through a Deployment Server. Their credentials and inputs live in their own local/, which a push would replace. When a Deployment Server manages the Splunk Add-on for AWS on an instance, the AWS S3 Direct screen there only generates the configuration for an administrator to apply. Install the Azure or GCP add-on on each heavy forwarder that may run an input, but run one input for each queue or subscription: every input keeps its own record of what it has read, so a second input on the same queue can index a redelivered message twice. For Google Cloud, use the LogServ GCP add-on, not the general-purpose Splunk Add-on for Google Cloud Platform (Splunkbase 3088), which cannot decompress the gzipped LogServ objects. One heavy forwarder can run the add-ons of several clouds; see More Than One Cloud.
    • AWS inputs. The SQS-Based S3 inputs read the queue of your scenario (SAP’s queue for Connect, the queue in your Secondary account for Filter or Copy) and download each object from the bucket its notification names (SAP’s bucket for Connect and Filter, your copy bucket for Copy). The index = sap_logserv_logs setting that sends the events to the right index is on these inputs, not in the Data TA.
    • Search heads. We strongly recommend against the Data TA and the ingest add-ons on a search head, Splunk Cloud included: ingest belongs on the heavy forwarders. Nothing blocks it, and a search head that runs the inputs itself (the “Splunk Cloud only” row) needs the Data TA there; see Running the TAs on a search head. On the Splunk Cloud Victoria Experience, installing the Data TA and the LogServ App on the search head and opening the AWS S3 Direct screen there have been checked; creating and running inputs on a Splunk Cloud search head has not been tested by the project, and the LogServ Azure and GCP add-ons have not been installed on one. On the Classic Experience, inputs run on an Inputs Data Manager (IDM). The Data TA’s app.manifest does not list the forwarder workload (_forwarders); whether Splunk Cloud installs it on an IDM has not been tested, and neither has this path.
    • Search-tier add-ons go on the search tier only. For LogServ data, CIM (1621), Windows (742) and Unix/Linux (833) provide search-time content only: the Data TA parses every event as sap_logserv_logs and only then routes it to XmlWinEventLog, linux_secure and the other sourcetypes, so these add-ons’ parse-time settings never apply. No LogServ package extracts XmlWinEventLog fields, so without 742 the Windows dashboard’s Event Code, Severity and Service panels stay empty. The App parses its other Linux sourcetypes itself; 833 provides the CIM fields of linux_secure. If you use one of these add-ons’ own inputs for other data, follow that add-on’s placement guidance for them.
    • Enterprise Security. The App’s ES content does its work only where ES runs, so install the LogServ App and its search-tier add-ons on the search head that runs ES too. On Splunk Cloud, ES has its own search head, separate from the one your users open for other apps (Enterprise Security Integration: Prerequisites).
    • No standalone Squid Proxy or ISC BIND add-ons. Their parsing is built into the LogServ App. If either is installed beside it, both parse the same events, and the App’s home view shows a banner recommending you remove the standalone add-on.
    • Splunk Cloud indexes. Create both indexes yourself, in Settings > Indexes or with the Admin Config Service (ACS), with the retention you want, before any data arrives. Do this also when the Data TA is installed on the Cloud stack: Splunk does not document that a private app’s index definitions create the indexes there.
    • The AI Assistant ships disabled. It needs the Splunk MCP Server 1.1.0 or later on the same search head as the LogServ App: the predefined prompts use its Run Saved Search tool, which first shipped in 1.1.0. The App’s health check blocks only versions below 1.0.3 (the CVE-2026-20205 fix) and sets no upper bound; the newest version verified is 2.0.0. See Set Up the AI Assistant.

    Next Steps¶

    • Plan and Prerequisites: what to request from SAP and prepare on each tier.
    • Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA.
    • LogServ App Prerequisites: the search tier in detail.

    Plan and Prerequisites¶

    Use this page before you install anything: it lists what to request from SAP, what each Splunk tier needs, and the access, volume and retention decisions to make first. Which package goes on which instance is on Where Each Package Goes; the order of the whole deployment is on the Deployment Roadmap.

    Splunk Platform Requirements¶

    • Splunk Enterprise 9.4.3 or later, or Splunk Cloud Platform. 9.4.3 is the minimum supported version: it is the platform this release is tested on. Nothing in the packages enforces it at install, and the LogServ App does not depend on Splunk’s own UI components (it bundles its own React and @splunk UI libraries).
    • Splunk Cloud Platform: checked on Victoria Experience stacks running Splunk Cloud Platform 10.x, most recently 10.5.2605.10 (2026-10-21). No test on the Classic Experience is recorded.
    • Heavy forwarders, not universal forwarders, for the ingest tier: the Data TA does its work while the data is parsed, and the ingest add-ons run as inputs on a full Splunk Enterprise instance.

    The Packages¶

    A deployment of Splunk for SAP LogServ uses three kinds of package:

    • the Data TA (splunk_ta_sap_logserv): index-time parsing, sourcetype routing and filtering of the data your ingest add-on collects; it has no data inputs of its own;
    • the LogServ App (splunk_app_sap_logserv): dashboards and search-time content on the search head;
    • one ingest add-on for your cloud: the Splunk Add-on for AWS, the LogServ Azure add-on (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure) or the LogServ GCP add-on (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp).

    Architecture explains what each does.

    Request from SAP and Prepare Your Cloud Account¶

    SAP LogServ is an optional SAP ECS service: confirm with SAP that it is enabled for your SAP ECS landscape before you request anything below.

    Start these first: they wait on SAP support and on your own cloud administrators, and nothing can be ingested until they are done. Each cloud’s setup guide has the details.

    SAP ECS on AWS¶

    Choose your AWS scenario first (Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario). Connect is the default. Filter is for when the forwarder load or the first-start backlog has to be cut. Copy keeps your own copy of new objects from the time it starts (plus what is still waiting in SAP’s queue); it cannot load older history, and it stores the objects decompressed. History is loaded with AWS S3 Direct in every scenario.

    From SAP LogServ support:

    1. The ARNs of the S3 bucket that holds your LogServ data in the SAP ECS account and of the SQS queue that receives its notifications, and their AWS Region.
    2. After you deploy the scenario’s CloudFormation template in your Secondary account: the two access policies, one on SAP’s queue and one on SAP’s bucket, that give your role splunk-logserv-ta-role access. The example policies are in the repository’s aws_assets/sap_ecs_account_policies/ folder.
    3. If you will load history with AWS S3 Direct (in any scenario: data from before your inputs started is only in SAP’s bucket): s3:ListBucket on the bucket ARN in SAP’s bucket policy. The example policy includes it, but SQS-based ingest never needs it, so confirm that SAP kept it.

    In your own AWS account:

    • A Secondary AWS account, separate from the SAP ECS account, in which you can deploy CloudFormation stacks and create IAM users and roles. Deploy the stack in the Region of SAP’s bucket and queue.
    • Filter and Copy: an S3 bucket for the Lambda code, with a name of your own (bucket names are global), in the stack’s Region.
    • The IAM user’s access key that the setup guides create: plan how you will rotate it (Rotate the Access Key in the Connect, Filter or Copy guide).

    SAP ECS on Azure¶

    SAP provisions the storage account, the container, the Storage Queue and the Event Grid subscription in the SAP ECS Azure account; you create nothing in Azure. From SAP support:

    1. The storage account name and the Storage Queue name.
    2. An account SAS with ss=bq, srt=o and sp=rp (blob read and queue process), plus a if you will configure a dead-letter queue. See What the SAP-provided SAS must cover.
    3. The SAS expiry date (its se= value) and how SAP renews it. When the SAS expires, the input stops reading until you enter a new one. Put the date in your calendar; see Rotate credentials.

    See Parameters to obtain from SAP.

    SAP ECS on Google Cloud¶

    SAP provisions the bucket, its notification, the Pub/Sub topic and the subscription in the SAP-managed project. The one resource you create is the service account:

    1. In a GCP project of your own, separate from the SAP-managed project, create a service account. It needs no roles in your project.
    2. Enable the Cloud Pub/Sub API and the Cloud Storage API in that project.
    3. Check before install day whether the organization policy iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation applies to the project: it blocks the JSON key the input needs.
    4. Give the service account’s email address to SAP support. SAP grants it roles/pubsub.subscriber on the LogServ subscription and roles/storage.objectViewer on the bucket, and returns the project ID and the subscription name for the input. Ask also for the subscription’s acknowledgement deadline.
    5. Plan how you will rotate the service account’s key: it is yours, and nothing renews it for you. See Rotate credentials.

    See The onboarding sequence, What SAP must grant your service account and Parameters for the input.

    Every Cloud: the Queue Backlog¶

    Ask SAP how long its queue keeps a message and how old its oldest message is. A new input starts with every notification still waiting, which can be days or weeks of data, and on Azure even months. Decide before the input starts whether SAP purges the older messages or you filter them. On AWS, purged days can be loaded later with AWS S3 Direct; on Azure and Google Cloud, nothing in this solution can load a purged day. See First Start: The Queue Backlog.

    Deployment Server¶

    A Deployment Server is optional. Use one to manage the Data TA on several heavy forwarders; without one, you install and configure the Data TA on each heavy forwarder.

    • It is a Splunk Enterprise instance you run. A Splunk Cloud stack is never a Deployment Server; your Splunk Cloud subscription includes a license for one you run yourself (request it from Splunk Support).
    • The heavy forwarders must be its deployment clients (deploymentclient.conf) before you distribute the Data TA.
    • Deploy to Forwarders needs the edit_deployment_server capability, which Splunk’s admin role has.
    • Add only the heavy forwarders that collect LogServ data to the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class, never *: * would push the Data TA, with a restart, to every deployment client, search heads included.
    • Keep the ingest add-ons out of its server classes; see Heavy Forwarders.

    See Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders.

    Heavy Forwarders¶

    • Forwarding: each heavy forwarder forwards to your indexers. For Splunk Cloud, install on it the universal forwarder credentials app that your Splunk Cloud stack provides.
    • The Data TA: from your Deployment Server, or installed directly when no Deployment Server manages it.
    • The ingest add-on for your cloud, installed directly on each heavy forwarder that may run an input, never through a Deployment Server. Its credentials and inputs live in its own local/, which a push would replace. A heavy forwarder is strongly recommended over a search head; a search head is not blocked (see Running the TAs on a search head).
      • AWS: the Splunk Add-on for AWS (Splunkbase 1876). No minimum version is enforced; 8.2.2 or later is recommended (Splunk advisory SVD-2026-1005, third-party package fixes). These pages were checked with 8.3.1, and the AWS S3 Direct screen warns about versions below 8.1.0. Install it now and configure it with your AWS setup guide (add-on documentation). Its SQS-Based S3 inputs may share one queue across inputs and forwarders; see Add Heavy Forwarders on the Same Queue.
      • Azure: the LogServ Azure add-on; see Install the Azure add-on. Run one input for each queue: each input keeps its own record of what it has read, so a second input on the same queue can index a redelivered message twice.
      • Google Cloud: the LogServ GCP add-on; see the GCP Setup Guide. Run one input for each subscription, for the same reason.
    • Network egress (HTTPS, port 443):
      • AWS: the AWS STS endpoint, and the SQS and S3 endpoints of the Region that holds SAP’s queue and bucket.
      • Azure: <account>.queue.core.windows.net, and the blob endpoint each notification names, normally <account>.blob.core.windows.net.
      • Google Cloud: oauth2.googleapis.com, pubsub.googleapis.com and storage.googleapis.com.
    • Outbound proxy:
      • The Splunk Add-on for AWS has its own setting, on its Configuration > Proxy tab (checked in version 8.3.1).
      • The LogServ Azure and GCP add-ons have no proxy setting. They use Python’s standard HTTP client, which takes its proxy from HTTPS_PROXY in splunkd’s environment. This comes from reading their code and has not been tested in the lab.
      • Whenever splunkd runs with HTTP_PROXY or HTTPS_PROXY set, also set NO_PROXY=127.0.0.1,localhost (plus the host name in mgmtHostPort, if it is not a loopback address). Otherwise calls to splunkd’s own management port, with their session key, go to the proxy.
    • The admin_all_objects capability, on any platform, for creating, editing or deleting an Azure or GCP input, which includes entering a new SAS or key: the add-ons save the input through Splunk’s REST interface as the signed-in user, and Splunk allows that write only with this capability. The Create backfill button of the AWS S3 Direct screen needs it too; without it the screen only generates the configuration for an administrator to apply. Find a role that holds it on each instance where you will do this.
    • Capacity: the Data TA’s work per event decides how many heavy forwarders your volume needs; see Capacity Planning and First Start.

    Indexers¶

    Create sap_logserv_logs and logserv_ai_assistant_audit on the indexer tier before any data arrives:

    • Single instance: the Data TA creates both when it first loads.
    • Standalone indexer: Settings > Indexes, or a small indexes.conf.
    • Indexer cluster: an index-only app with both stanzas and repFactor = auto, in the manager node’s manager-apps/, pushed as the configuration bundle. Without repFactor = auto the indexes are not replicated.
    • Splunk Cloud: Settings > Indexes, or the Admin Config Service (ACS).

    Separate indexers do not need the Data TA itself. The settings to use are on Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA. Both index names can be changed: the LogServ App finds them through the macros sap_logserv_idx_macro and sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro; see Renaming an index.

    Search Head: the LogServ App and Its Add-ons¶

    On the search tier (the search head, the Splunk Cloud search head, or every member of a search head cluster), install:

    • the LogServ App;
    • Splunk_SA_CIM (Splunkbase 1621) 5.0.0 or later, the App’s declared dependency;
    • the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (742), which the Windows dashboard needs;
    • the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (833), for the CIM fields of linux_secure;
    • only for the AI Assistant: the Splunk MCP Server (7931) and, optionally, the Splunk AI Assistant (7245).

    These add-ons go on the search tier only, not on the Deployment Server, the heavy forwarders or the indexers. Do not install the standalone Squid Proxy or ISC BIND add-ons: the LogServ App has their parsing built in. KV Store must be enabled on the search head. See LogServ App Prerequisites.

    Capacity, Volume and Retention¶

    • Daily volume and license. Every event the filters keep is indexed into sap_logserv_logs and counts toward your Splunk license; events the filters drop do not. Measure the log-type mix and the forwarder load with Measure Your Own Heavy Forwarder.
    • Azure Unix command output. On Azure, SAP also delivers Unix command output (ps, top, netstat and others) in a folder named undefined/undefined: on the reference system about 0.7 million events and 125 MB of text a day, which the Data TA indexes unparsed. Decide whether to drop it before the input starts; see Data Delivered Without Folder Fields and Decide Filtering.
    • Retention. The Data TA sets no retention or size limit for sap_logserv_logs, so Splunk’s defaults apply until you set your own; it gives logserv_ai_assistant_audit 90 days (frozenTimePeriodInSecs = 7776000). Where you create the indexes yourself, set both. Make the retention of sap_logserv_logs cover the oldest data you will load: events older than an index’s retention are removed soon after they are indexed.

    Roles and Access¶

    Check these before users open the dashboards:

    • Every role that uses the dashboards can search sap_logserv_logs. On Splunk Enterprise the default user role allows *, which matches every index whose name does not start with _, so it and the roles that import it (such as power) can already search the index. Add the index to any role with a narrowed list (Settings > Roles > role > Indexes). On Splunk Cloud, check each role’s Indexes tab the same way.
    • The audit index is granted only as Restricting who can read the audit index describes.
    • App admins. The LogServ App treats only roles named exactly admin, sc_admin or sc_subadmin as admins. Only they can open its Settings page and clear or backfill the dashboard data. Give the people who run the App one of these roles; see LogServ App Prerequisites.

    Splunk Cloud¶

    • Roles. sc_admin is the customer’s administrator role. Splunk uses the admin role and the system roles to run the stack. sc_subadmin is not a standard role; some stacks create a delegated-admin role with that name.
    • Installs are private-app installs on your stack (on the Victoria Experience: Install app from file, or ACS), which run Splunk’s app vetting.
    • Indexes: create both yourself, as above, with the retention you want.
    • No Deployment Server: the Data TA’s Deploy to Forwarders button never appears on a Splunk Cloud stack. Use a Deployment Server of your own, or install the Data TA directly on each heavy forwarder.
    • admin_all_objects: the gates above apply on Splunk Cloud too, and whether your admin role holds the capability depends on your stack; check it under Settings > Roles. See Capability-gated REST endpoints.

    See Splunk Cloud Considerations.

    Next Steps¶

    • Splunk Cloud Considerations, if you use Splunk Cloud.
    • Capacity Planning and First Start: how many heavy forwarders, and the first-start backlog.
    • Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA.

    Splunk Cloud Considerations¶

    Read this page before you install Splunk for SAP LogServ where the search tier, or the whole deployment, is Splunk Cloud Platform. It covers where each package goes, how to install a private app, which Splunk Cloud roles can configure the packages, and the capability checks that can refuse a write.

    Splunk assigns each Splunk Cloud Platform stack one of two Experiences, Victoria or Classic; an Experience is not a version. To find yours, in Splunk Web click Support & Services → About. These notes were checked on one Splunk Cloud Platform 10.x stack, most recently on 10.5.2605.10 (2026-10-21). That stack is taken to be on the Victoria Experience, but its Experience was not read from Support & Services → About. No test on a stack known to be on the Classic Experience is recorded.

    Splunk Enterprise: what still applies¶

    If you run Splunk Enterprise and your admins use Splunk’s stock admin role, which holds admin_all_objects, nothing on this page needs a workaround. These items still apply on Splunk Enterprise:

    • The audit capability. A user’s AI Assistant activity is audited only when their role holds edit_tcp or edit_log_alert_event (the /receivers/simple row below). Splunk Enterprise’s default admin role holds both, power holds edit_log_alert_event, and user holds neither.
    • admin_all_objects for Azure and GCP inputs and AWS S3 Direct backfills: creating, editing or deleting a LogServ Azure or GCP input (replacing its SAS or service-account key included), and Create backfill on the AWS S3 Direct screen, which without it offers only the Apply this as an administrator view: it generates the configuration but creates nothing. A hardened admin role that lacks the capability is refused these too.
    • The filesystem fallback for Data TA Configuration saves, which serves any role in the write list that lacks admin_all_objects, a hardened admin role included.
    • The edit_deployment_server check on Deploy to Forwarders, on your own Deployment Server (below).
    • The admin-tier write lists on the LogServ App’s KV Store collections. They apply on every platform (Application Settings).

    Where the packages go with Splunk Cloud¶

    The full matrix is Where Each Package Goes. With Splunk Cloud:

    Where What to install
    Splunk Cloud search head The LogServ App and its search-tier add-ons (LogServ App Prerequisites).
    Splunk Cloud indexes Create sap_logserv_logs and logserv_ai_assistant_audit yourself, with the retention you want, before any data arrives: Settings → Indexes → New Index, or the Admin Config Service (ACS). See Create the indexes.
    Your heavy forwarders (Splunk Enterprise instances you run) The Data TA and the ingest add-on for your cloud: the Splunk Add-on for AWS, the LogServ Azure add-on or the LogServ GCP add-on. They send to the stack with its universal forwarder credentials app. If a Deployment Server manages the forwarders, install the Data TA on the Deployment Server only and push it from there (Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders); without one, install it directly on each forwarder. Install the Azure and GCP add-ons directly on the forwarders that run their inputs, never through the Deployment Server.

    Notes:

    • Retention counts from each event’s time. Splunk freezes a bucket when its newest event is older than the index’s retention, so history you load later with AWS S3 Direct is removed soon after indexing if the index keeps less than its age. Set Searchable retention (days) to cover the oldest day you will load.
    • The Data TA on the Cloud stack is allowed, and needed only where the inputs run on the search head.
    • Splunk Cloud with no heavy forwarder is supported: it is not blocked, but a heavy forwarder is strongly recommended. On the stack these notes were checked on, installing the Data TA and the LogServ App on the search head and opening the AWS S3 Direct screen there have been checked; creating and running inputs there has not been tested. On the Classic Experience, inputs run on an Inputs Data Manager (IDM) rather than the search head; that path has not been tested (Where Each Package Goes). On Victoria the LogServ App, the Data TA and the ingest add-on all go on the Cloud search head, and the inputs run there, so the search tier your users search on also carries the ingest load, including the first-start backlog. The LogServ Azure and GCP add-ons declare search-head support, but running them on a Splunk Cloud search head has not been tested. See Running the TAs on a search head.

    Installing the packages on Splunk Cloud¶

    The Splunk Add-on for AWS and the search-tier add-ons are on Splunkbase. The LogServ App, the Data TA and the LogServ Azure and GCP add-ons are private apps: download their tarballs from the repository’s release_binaries/ and upload them.

    • Victoria Experience: in Splunk Web, Apps → Manage Apps → Install app from file, or install with ACS. Splunk vets each upload before it installs it. Splunk’s steps: Install a private app on Victoria Experience.
    • Classic Experience: follow Install a private app on Classic Experience.

    Each LogServ package passes AppInspect’s Cloud checks (--mode precert --included-tags cloud) with no errors and no failures; the reports are beside the tarballs in release_binaries/. To update, upload the newer tarball the same way: a newer build with the same version number (0.1.2) installs over the installed one (checked on Splunk Cloud Platform 10.5.2605.10).

    You cannot edit files under an app’s local/ on Splunk Cloud. Use these Splunk Web screens instead of the local/ edits other pages describe:

    Setting Where in Splunk Web
    Indexes and their retention Settings → Indexes
    Which indexes a role can search Settings → Roles → role → Indexes
    Filters and the Cloud Provider value (where the Data TA runs on the search head) Apps → Splunk TA for SAP LogServ → Configuration
    History loads from AWS Apps → Splunk TA for SAP LogServ → AWS S3 Direct (AWS S3 Direct)
    The data index macro after a rename Settings → Advanced search → Search macros, sap_logserv_idx_macro, in each LogServ app that has it (Renaming an Index)
    Disabling or re-scheduling the LogServ App’s scheduled searches Settings → Searches, reports, and alerts
    AI Assistant and Dashboard Data settings the LogServ App’s Settings pages (Application Settings)

    One setting has no Splunk Web field: the _meta = cloud_provider::aws line on a Splunk Add-on for AWS SQS-Based S3 input that runs on the Cloud search head (the add-on’s SQS-Based S3 form has no field for it; checked on version 8.3.1). Without file access, set it with a REST write that needs admin_all_objects; see Splunk Cloud Without a Heavy Forwarder.

    Splunk Cloud roles¶

    Role Who has it What it means for LogServ
    sc_admin The customer’s administrator role on Splunk Cloud Platform. Splunk gives it the capabilities to install apps, manage indexes, and manage users and passwords. The role you normally install and configure LogServ with.
    admin and the system-user roles Splunk, which uses them to monitor and maintain the stack. Do not change or delete them.
    sc_subadmin (only where your stack has one) Not a Splunk-supplied role. Some stacks create a delegated-admin role with this name. LogServ grants it write access by name and the App treats it as an admin. Its capabilities, admin_all_objects included, are whatever your stack gave it.
    power, user Standard roles. Search and view dashboards; cannot install or configure apps.

    Check your role. In Settings → Users, look at the roles on your account. If you hold sc_admin, you are the stack administrator. If you hold a delegated-admin role (such as sc_subadmin), open it under Settings → Roles → role → Capabilities and check for admin_all_objects, edit_storage_passwords, and edit_tcp or edit_log_alert_event. The table below says what each one controls.

    Only three role names count as admin

    The LogServ App treats a user as an admin only when they hold a role named exactly admin, sc_admin or sc_subadmin, and the packages’ write lists in metadata/default.meta name only those three roles. A user whose delegated-admin role has any other name gets no Settings entry in the App’s menu, and opening the page shows 403 — Admin access required, so that user cannot change the AI Assistant settings or run Dashboard Data Clear and Backfill. Give such users one of the three roles itself; whether a role that only imports one of them is enough has not been tested. See Who Can Open the Page.

    The AI Assistant also needs the Splunk MCP Server’s mcp_tool_execute capability, which the MCP Server grants by default only to admin and sc_admin. Add it to a delegated-admin role such as sc_subadmin and to every analyst role that will use the AI Assistant (Roles and Capabilities).

    Capability-gated REST endpoints¶

    Splunk’s REST framework enforces some capability requirements server-side, independent of any per-object access control list. These gates decide what an admin role without admin_all_objects (a delegated admin on Splunk Cloud, or a hardened admin on Splunk Enterprise) can do with the LogServ packages; the /receivers/simple gate also decides whether each AI Assistant user is audited:

    REST endpoint Gate LogServ usage
    /storage/passwords edit_storage_passwords HEC audit-forwarder tokens, MCP bearer tokens, and LLM provider credentials where the free-form path is used
    /storage/collections/data/<collection> None — collection-level metadata ACL only AI Assistant settings + acks, topology layouts, dashboard refresh preferences
    /configs/conf-<name>/... admin_all_objects (splunkd refuses the write with requires capability: admin_all_objects even when the app’s metadata gives the role write access) The Data TA’s Configuration tabs, which fall back to a direct file write on a 403 (below). The LogServ App keeps its AI Assistant settings in KV Store instead, to avoid this gate.
    /data/inputs/<service> admin_all_objects Creating, editing or deleting a LogServ Azure or GCP input on the add-on’s Inputs page, replacing its SAS or service-account key included. The input handler writes the input to data/inputs/<kind> as the signed-in user, and splunkd refuses that write to a role without the capability, so the save fails with HTTP 403 (“This operation is forbidden”), on any platform. The passSystemAuth = true line each add-on carries on its [admin_external:*] stanza has no effect: Splunk defines that setting only for [script:*] handlers. Create these inputs on a heavy forwarder (recommended), with a role that holds the capability.
    The Splunk Add-on for AWS input endpoint (/servicesNS/nobody/Splunk_TA_aws/splunk_ta_aws_aws_s3), and the Data TA’s s3_direct_meta handler, which writes configs/conf-inputs and disables and enables the new input through data/inputs/aws_s3 admin_all_objects: the screen checks for it before it offers Create backfill, and the handler’s configs/conf-inputs write is behind the /configs/conf-* gate above The Data TA’s AWS S3 Direct screen. Its writes run as the signed-in user, with no system-context bypass, by design. Without the capability the screen shows Apply this as an administrator with the generated configuration and creates nothing. On Splunk Cloud, sign in with an account that holds the capability and create the backfill on the screen; do not apply the generated configuration by hand. See AWS S3 Direct.
    /receivers/simple edit_tcp or edit_log_alert_event (on Splunk Enterprise the default admin role holds both, power holds edit_log_alert_event and user neither; on Splunk Cloud, check your roles as described above) AI Assistant audit events: the browser writes each one as the signed-in user, so a user without either capability is not audited and sees an Audit events are not being written warning in the AI Assistant panel. edit_log_alert_event is the narrower one to grant; either lets the role write events to any index, and edit_tcp also lets it change TCP data inputs — see Who Can Write Audit Events

    The takeaway: write access in an app’s metadata does not get past these gates; a role without the capability gets 403. The LogServ packages avoid the gates where they can (the App keeps its settings in KV Store) or work around them (the Data TA’s Configuration saves fall back to a direct file write). Three actions they neither avoid nor bypass, on Splunk Cloud and Splunk Enterprise alike:

    • creating, editing or deleting a LogServ Azure or GCP input: admin_all_objects;
    • Create backfill on the AWS S3 Direct screen: admin_all_objects;
    • writing AI Assistant audit events on /receivers/simple: edit_tcp or edit_log_alert_event, checked for each user, so whether a user’s activity is audited depends on that user’s role.

    What the LogServ packages do for admin roles¶

    These are in the shipped packages and need no configuration.

    sc_subadmin in metadata/default.meta write ACL¶

    Every LogServ package (the App, the Data TA, and the Azure and GCP add-ons) ships this global rule in metadata/default.meta: access = read : [ * ], write : [ admin, sc_admin, sc_subadmin ]. It gives the three roles write access to every knowledge object in the app (saved searches, macros, lookups, eventtypes, tags, etc.) at the metadata layer. The packages do not create sc_subadmin; they name it for stacks that have a delegated-admin role of that name. The App’s KV Store collections use the same three-role write list, apart from six that every user writes: four per-user preference collections and two Data Doctor collections. The App keeps the AI Assistant’s settings and legal acknowledgements in KV Store, which needs no admin_all_objects, and opens its Application Settings page only to the three role names; both are described in Application Settings.

    If you rebuild the Data TA from source, the build step that keeps sc_subadmin in this list is described in Data TA Internals.

    Data TA Configuration saves fall back to the filesystem¶

    The Data TA’s Configuration → Filters and Cloud Provider tabs write their settings through splunktaucclib’s REST persist. If that write returns 403 (“This operation is forbidden” — the admin_all_objects gate on /configs/conf-*), the handler falls back to writing local/splunk_ta_sap_logserv_settings.conf directly on the filesystem, so Save succeeds for a role in the write list without admin_all_objects: a delegated admin role on Splunk Cloud, or a hardened admin role on Splunk Enterprise. Note passSystemAuth is not honoured for UCC [admin_external:*] settings handlers — the filesystem fallback is what actually carries these saves. The LogServ Azure and GCP add-ons have no such fallback (the /data/inputs/<service> row above).

    Deploy to Forwarders does not apply on Splunk Cloud¶

    The Data TA’s Deploy to Forwarders button (Configuration → Filters and Cloud Provider) appears only on a Deployment Server, and a Splunk Cloud stack is never one. So the button does not appear on Splunk Cloud, for any role, and Splunk Cloud needs no capability for it. A Deployment Server for your heavy forwarders is a Splunk Enterprise instance you run yourself; your Splunk Cloud subscription includes a Deployment Server license, which you request from Splunk Support. See Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders.

    On that Deployment Server, the button and the check that decides whether to show it need the edit_deployment_server capability, not admin_all_objects. Splunk Enterprise’s admin role holds it; a custom Deployment Server operator role needs it added, or the button does not appear.

    Splunk Cloud Support tickets you may need to file¶

    Symptom Ticket request
    AI Assistant SETUP REQUIRED banner; MCP requests return Invalid token audience: <X> Ask Splunk Cloud Support to set the stack’s MCP audience to mcp (Splunk MCP Setup)
    Your admin role cannot install private apps, or private-app vetting rejects one Standard Splunk Cloud private-app submission flow; out of scope for this guide
    Your delegated admin role needs admin_all_objects: the AWS S3 Direct screen shows Apply this as an administrator, or an Azure or GCP input save returns 403 Sign in with an account that holds admin_all_objects, or ask your stack’s administrator or Splunk Cloud Support whether your role can be given it

    Next Steps¶

    • Capacity Planning and First Start: size the instances that parse LogServ data, and plan for the backlog a new input finds in its queue.
    • Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA.

    Capacity Planning and First Start¶

    Use this page before you install, to size the instances that parse LogServ data and to plan for the backlog a new input finds in its queue.

    The Data TA does its work where LogServ data is parsed: on the heavy forwarders in a distributed deployment, or on the single instance. There every LogServ event passes through the same chain of index-time rules, so the CPU those rules spend per event decides how many events a heavy forwarder can take. This page explains what the Data TA does with each event, what is known of its cost, how to size heavy forwarders from a measurement on your own, what does and does not add capacity, when to give each cloud its own forwarders, and how to handle the first-start backlog.

    Upgrading from an earlier build? Update the Data TA to build 1792189743 or later before you size or add hardware; see Upgrading to This Release and Version Check.


    What the Data TA Does With Each Event¶

    A Splunk instance handles each event in a fixed series of pipelines, linked by queues. Each pipeline runs on one thread. One parsing, merging, typing and index pipeline together form a pipeline set; a heavy forwarder has one pipeline set unless parallelIngestionPipelines says otherwise. The slowest pipeline sets the pace of the whole set: when it cannot keep up, its queue fills and the queues in front of it fill after it.

      LogServ object in S3, Azure Blob Storage or Google Cloud Storage
  (gzipped NDJSON, one event per line)
    |
    v
  Input                 Splunk Add-on for AWS (SQS-Based S3), or the LogServ
    |                   Azure / GCP add-on: read the notification, download the
    |                   object, decompress it, hand its lines to Splunk
    v
  [parsingQueue]
    |
    v
  Parsing pipeline      split into lines (LINE_BREAKER), keep lines of up to
    |                   100,000 bytes whole (TRUNCATE)
    v
  [aggQueue]
    |
    v
  Merging pipeline      read the timestamp from the "_time" key
    |
    v
  [typingQueue]
    |
    v
  Typing pipeline       the Data TA's index-time transforms, in order:
    |                   filters (only with Filtering on), host / source /
    |                   folder fields, 34 sourcetype routes, splunk_solution /
    |                   cloud_provider, unwrap "_raw"
    v
  [indexQueue]
    |
    v
  Index pipeline        on a Heavy Forwarder: send the event to the indexers
                        or Splunk Cloud (tcpout); on a single instance: index it

    The typing pipeline is where the Data TA’s rules run, in the regexreplacement processor. Splunk tries every rule of the chain on every event, so a route that does not match an event still costs its search:

    Step Rules What it does How its cost grows
    Filters up to 6, only with Filtering on keep or drop the event (Configuring Filters) with the line length
    Metadata 3 set host and source; write the clz_dir and clz_subdir fields with the line length
    Sourcetype routes 34 give the event its sourcetype: 26 routes look for one key and value, such as "clz_subdir":"dispatcher" or "source":"/var/log/cron"; 1 checks the source path of events without folder fields; 7 look for two folder keys, such as "clz_dir":"abap" and "clz_subdir":"audit" with the line length
    Stamps 2 write splunk_solution and cloud_provider small
    Unwrap 1 keep only the "_raw" text of the envelope with the line length

    The routes and the metadata rules read up to 100,000 characters of a line (LOOKAHEAD = 100000), like the filters and the unwrap. A line of up to 4,096 characters costs each rule no more than with a narrower window; a longer line costs each rule a read to its end, in proportion to its length.

    The seven two-key routes, for abap/audit, abap/icm, abap/sapstartsrv, hana/tracelogs, scc/audit, scc/tracelogs and sap/sapstartsrv, use the shape of the filter rules, which stays linear in the line length at the 100,000-character window. Older Data TA builds carried six of them in a form whose cost grows with the square of the line length; Version Check shows which form a forwarder runs, and the release notes describe the changes (build 1791935359, build 1792189743).


    Measured Cost¶

    No index-time figure has been measured for the current routing yet. The only index-time figures come from Data TA builds before 1791935359, in which the cost of the two-key routes grows with the square of the line length; they are kept, with a search-time comparison of the route forms, in Reference Measurements at the end of this page. Until a measured figure is published here, size from your own measurement; one busy hour is enough (Measure Your Own Heavy Forwarder).


    Sizing Method¶

    Size from the busiest pipeline’s cost per event and your peak arrival rate. For LogServ data the busiest pipeline is normally the typing pipeline; search 1 shows whether it is on your forwarder.

    1. Peak arrival rate. Take the busiest hour of LogServ events and divide by 3,600 to get events a second (search 5, or search 6 before you have a forwarder).
    2. Cost per event. Measure the busiest pipeline’s CPU per LogServ event at the 90th percentile, in microseconds (search 3).
    3. Ceiling per pipeline set = 1,000,000 / cost per event, in events a second.
    4. Plan rate per pipeline set = half the ceiling. The other half absorbs bursts, because the input fetches objects in batches and the rate within an hour is uneven, and the catch-up after an outage or a delivery delay, when the backlog arrives at once. A first start can bring a backlog of weeks or more; see First Start: The Queue Backlog.
    5. Plan rate per heavy forwarder = plan rate per pipeline set x pipeline sets: one, or two on a forwarder with spare cores (Add a Second Pipeline Set).
    6. Heavy forwarders needed = peak arrival rate / plan rate per heavy forwarder, rounded up. Add one if a forwarder must be able to fail without the others falling behind.

    Worked with the lab figures measured before the update (Reference Measurements):

      cost per event (typing pipeline, p90)   2,944 microseconds
  ceiling per pipeline set                1,000,000 / 2,944  =  340 events/s
  plan rate per pipeline set              340 / 2            =  170 events/s  (about 0.6 million an hour)
  plan rate per HF, 1 pipeline set                              170 events/s
  plan rate per HF, 2 pipeline sets                             340 events/s  (about 1.2 million an hour)

    At that cost per event, a feed whose busiest hour carries 12 million events (3,333 events a second) would need 10 heavy forwarders with two pipeline sets each. That is why the update comes first.

    Data TA Cost per event (90th percentile) Ceiling per pipeline set Plan rate per pipeline set Plan rate per HF, 1 set Plan rate per HF, 2 sets
    Before build 1791935359, lab feed (short events: 84 bytes of event text) 2.94 ms 340 events/s 170 events/s 170 events/s 340 events/s
    Before build 1791935359, longer lines higher, with the square of the line length lower lower lower lower
    Build 1791935359 or later measure (search 3) 1,000,000 / cost half the ceiling plan rate per set 2 x plan rate per set

    Your log-type mix and line lengths differ from the lab feed, so measure on your own forwarder, and measure again when the mix changes, for example when log types with long lines are added.

    The typing pipeline is not the only limit. The input itself uses CPU outside the pipelines to download and decompress the objects, and the output to the indexers or Splunk Cloud needs network bandwidth. Leave room on the forwarder for the input and the operating system as well.

    On a single instance the same chain runs on the instance that also indexes and searches, so the same method applies to its typing pipeline, with less spare CPU around it.


    Adding Capacity¶

    Update the Data TA¶

    Install Data TA build 1792189743 or later on every instance that parses LogServ data, then measure again (search 3) before you add hardware:

    • Heavy forwarders managed by a Deployment Server: install it on the Deployment Server, in both etc/apps/ and etc/deployment-apps/, and push it to the forwarders (Upgrading to This Release). Do not also install it directly on those forwarders: the push replaces their copy, local/ included. A Save on the Filters or Cloud Provider tab copies the Data TA into deployment-apps/ only when no copy is there yet or when the copy’s [launcher] version in default/app.conf differs from the one in etc/apps/, so it does not copy a newer build with the same version number, such as a later 0.1.2 build.
    • Heavy forwarders that no Deployment Server manages: install it directly on each one.
    • A single instance: install it directly.
    • A Splunk Cloud search head that runs the inputs: upload the newer tarball as a private app (Splunk Cloud Considerations).

    Version Check shows the build each forwarder runs after the update.

    Add a Second Pipeline Set¶

    Each input sends its data through one pipeline set, so a second pipeline set gets work only from a second input. Both are needed:

    1. On the heavy forwarder, add to $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/system/local/server.conf (or a small app of your own) and restart Splunk:

      [general]
parallelIngestionPipelines = 2

    2. Add a second input that reads the same queue:

      • AWS: a second SQS-Based S3 input with the same settings as the first, including the same SQS queue URL and Source Type sap_logserv_logs (step 7 of the AWS Remote S3 Connect Setup Guide). The queue hands each message to one input at a time, so the two inputs share the work.
      • Azure and GCP: see Multiple landscapes / fleets in the Azure Setup Guide and the GCP Setup Guide, including the at-least-once trade-off of several inputs on one queue or subscription. Those notes are about how fast the input fetches objects: for typical volumes they find one input enough, and suggest a larger batch_size or max_blobs_per_fire / max_objects_per_fire, or a shorter interval, before a second input. On a forwarder whose typing pipeline is the limit (search 1) those settings do not help (What Does Not Add Capacity); the second pipeline set gets work only from a second input.

    Splunk’s guidance is to add a second pipeline set only on a forwarder that is significantly under-utilized, and not to go beyond two without Splunk Professional Services (Manage pipeline sets). A pipeline set keeps several threads busy, so check the forwarder’s CPU and search 1 first. server.conf is not part of the Data TA, so a Deployment Server push of the Data TA does not change it.

    Add Heavy Forwarders on the Same Queue¶

    Forwarders that read the same queue share its messages, so adding a forwarder adds a full set of pipelines. The Splunk Add-on for AWS documents scaling SQS-Based S3 inputs this way (SQS-Based S3 input). Give each new forwarder the Data TA (through your Deployment Server’s server class, or installed directly where no Deployment Server manages the forwarders), the ingest add-on, and the same input or inputs as the first.

                                  +--> Heavy Forwarder 1
                              |      input A  --> pipeline set 0
                              |      input B  --> pipeline set 1
  one queue  -----------------+
  (SQS queue, Azure Storage   |
   Queue or Pub/Sub           +--> Heavy Forwarder 2
   subscription)                     input A  --> pipeline set 0
                                     input B  --> pipeline set 1

    Azure and GCP: more inputs on one queue are at-least-once

    Each LogServ Azure or GCP input keeps its own record of the objects it has ingested, in a file on the forwarder that runs it. No other input shares that record: not a second input on the same forwarder, and not an input on another forwarder. The queue or subscription normally hands a message to one input at a time, but when a message comes back (its lease or acknowledgement deadline ran out, a delete or acknowledgement failed, or the process stopped first; Pub/Sub can also, rarely, redeliver a message after it was acknowledged), another input can ingest the same object a second time. So run one input per queue or subscription by default, and add inputs or forwarders on it only for throughput or to catch up a backlog, accepting possible duplicates. See Multiple landscapes / fleets in the Azure Setup Guide and the GCP Setup Guide.


    What Does Not Add Capacity¶

    • The Data TA’s own filters. The Filters tab saves license and indexing, not forwarder CPU. Its rules run in the typing pipeline as the first steps of the same chain, and the keep-or-drop decision goes to the last filter step that matched, so a dropped event is downloaded, split into lines, timestamped and run through the transforms like any other event before it is discarded. The filters also add rules of their own to the chain (Configuring Filters).
    • More inputs on one pipeline set. They download in parallel, but every event still passes through the same typing pipeline thread.
    • More cores alone. A pipeline is one thread. If the typing pipeline already uses one full core, more cores help only through a second pipeline set or another forwarder.
    • The input’s batch size or interval. They change how fast objects are fetched, not how fast their events are parsed. The Azure and GCP setup guides suggest them before a second input; that advice is for an input that falls behind on fetching, not for a forwarder whose typing pipeline is busy.
    • A smaller LOOKAHEAD on the routing rules. It saves CPU only on lines longer than 4,096 characters, and on AWS those lines would lose their host, source, folder fields and sourcetype.


    What Reduces the Load¶

    Data that never reaches the forwarder costs nothing to parse:

    • AWS: the Lambda pre-filter. The Lambda drops the notifications of folders you do not want, so the forwarder never downloads those objects and its load falls with the volume. See the AWS Remote S3 Filter Setup Guide and Configuring Filters: AWS Lambda-Based Filtering.
    • Azure and GCP: the input’s include_filters / exclude_filters. They match the object path before the download (Azure Setup Guide, GCP Setup Guide).
    • Log types you do not use, left out at the source. Where your SAP LogServ subscription lets you choose the log types delivered, leave out the ones you do not need. Search 7 shows which log types make up your volume.


    More Than One Cloud¶

    A heavy forwarder can run the Splunk Add-on for AWS, the LogServ Azure add-on and the LogServ GCP add-on together. Their inputs are of different kinds (aws_sqs_based_s3, sap_logserv_azure_queue, sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub), each add-on keeps its credentials in its own local/, and the Azure and GCP add-ons call their clouds’ REST APIs without a cloud SDK. Every event goes through the same Data TA chain, so size the forwarder for all its feeds together (Sizing Method). Each input runs through one pipeline set, so with parallelIngestionPipelines = 2 the inputs of two clouds can be spread over the two pipeline sets (Add a Second Pipeline Set).

    Give each cloud its own forwarders when:

    • The feeds together are more than one forwarder takes. You need more forwarders anyway: one set per cloud is one way to add them, more forwarders on the same queues is the other (Add Heavy Forwarders on the Same Queue).
    • One cloud must not hold up the other. Inputs on one forwarder share its pipelines, so a backlog, a burst or an outage on one queue delays the other cloud’s data too, and so does a restart to update one add-on. A first start is the common case (First Start: The Queue Backlog).
    • Your security policy wants one cloud per host. A shared forwarder holds the credentials of both clouds, for example an AWS access key and a GCP service-account key, and needs network access to both.

    Separate forwarders do not change how events are attributed to their cloud. With a Deployment Server, the Data TA’s Cloud Provider dropdown has one value for every forwarder in the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class, including those that read another cloud. Whenever you ingest from more than one cloud, leave it at Not set and add _meta = cloud_provider::aws to each SQS-Based S3 input; the Azure and GCP inputs label their own events (Choose Cloud Attribution).


    First Start: The Queue Backlog¶

    SAP’s queue receives a notification for every new LogServ object from the day SAP sets it up, which can be well before your input first reads it. The queue keeps each notification until a consumer takes it or it expires, so a new input can start with days or weeks of notifications waiting, and on Azure even months. The input works through them on top of the live feed, at the pace of the busiest pipeline. Wherever the input runs, on a heavy forwarder, a single instance or a Splunk Cloud search head, that pipeline runs at full load until the backlog is gone and new data can reach Splunk late in the meantime; on an instance that also serves searches, the catch-up competes with them.

    How far back the backlog can reach depends on how long the queue keeps a message, which SAP sets:

    Cloud Queue How long it keeps a message
    AWS SQS queue 4 days by default, at most 14 (Amazon SQS message quotas); the queues the Remote S3 Copy and Filter templates create in your Secondary account keep messages 14 days
    Azure Storage Queue, fed by Event Grid 7 days by default; Event Grid can also send messages that never expire (Event Grid delivery properties)
    GCP Pub/Sub subscription 7 days by default, at most 31 (Subscription message retention)

    A notification that expires before it is read is gone, but the object it names stays in the bucket.

    Estimate the Catch-Up¶

    The backlog holds about the live rate times the time it covers. It drains at what the forwarders can parse beyond the live feed: the ceiling per pipeline set (search 3) times the pipeline sets, minus the live arrival rate (search 5, or search 6 before you have a forwarder). Worked with the lab figures before the update, for a feed of 0.5 million events an hour, a 14-day backlog and one forwarder with one pipeline set:

      backlog     14 days x 0.5 million events an hour  =  168,000,000 events
  ceiling     one pipeline set, lab cost per event  =  340 events/s
  live feed   0.5 million events an hour            =  139 events/s
  to spare    340 - 139                             =  201 events/s
  catch-up    168,000,000 / 201                     =  835,821 s, about 9.7 days

    Forwarders sized by the Sizing Method have at least the peak live rate to spare, so they need at most as long as the backlog covers: up to two weeks for a 14-day backlog, with the busiest pipeline at full load and nothing left for bursts. Before you start the input, ask your SAP representative how long the queue keeps messages and how old its oldest message is.

    Before You Start the Input¶

    • Ask SAP to purge the older messages. One way to avoid the initial load is to contact your SAP representative and ask them to purge the older messages from the queue before you start the input. A purge removes only the notifications; the objects stay in the bucket. On AWS you can load the days you want afterwards, at a pace you choose, with AWS S3 Direct. On Azure and GCP the add-ons have no backfill: a purged day stays in the bucket, but nothing in this solution will load it (see Historical backfill in the Azure and GCP setup guides). If you will need those days, agree with your Splunk team how to load them before you ask SAP to purge. The purge of an SQS queue or an Azure Storage Queue removes every message in it (PurgeQueue, Clear Messages), so time it shortly before you start the input. A Pub/Sub subscription can instead be moved forward to a point in time, which acknowledges only the messages published before it (Replay and purge messages with seek). Those messages can be replayed later only if SAP’s subscription keeps acknowledged messages or its topic keeps messages; ask SAP before the seek. With the AWS Remote S3 Copy or Filter approach, the Lambda starts taking SAP’s messages as soon as its SQS trigger is active (step 9 of those guides), so ask before that step.
    • AWS Remote S3 Filter: let the Lambda leave the older objects out. The Filter approach’s Lambda passes an object’s notification on only when at least one of the object’s events is newer than DaysInThePast days and in a folder that IncludeFilters includes and ExcludeFilters does not exclude (steps 3.g to 3.i of the AWS Remote S3 Filter Setup Guide), so the rest of the backlog never reaches the forwarder. The setting applies to every later object as well.

    While It Drains¶

    • Add capacity for the catch-up. A second pipeline set with a second input, or another forwarder on the same queue, drains the backlog faster (Adding Capacity). Remove the extra input or forwarder once the backlog is gone. On Azure and GCP, while the extra input runs, a message that comes back to the queue or subscription can be ingested twice, because each input keeps its own record of what it has ingested (Add Heavy Forwarders on the Same Queue).
    • Or slow the input down (Azure and GCP). A lower max_blobs_per_fire / max_objects_per_fire, or a longer interval, limits how many objects the input takes a minute (Azure, GCP). The catch-up takes longer, but leaves CPU for the rest of the instance: other inputs, and searches on a single instance or a search head. The input’s log line (done: messages=N blobs=N events=N ..., objects=N on GCP) shows how many events an object carries; at 2,000 events an object, 6 objects a firing at the default 60-second interval come to about 200 events a second. Keep that rate above the live rate, or the backlog never shrinks, and the catch-up shorter than the time the oldest notifications have left, or they expire unread.
    • Days in the Past keeps old events out of the index, not off the forwarder. The Data TA’s filter saves license and indexing, but the forwarder downloads and parses each event before it drops it, so the catch-up takes just as long (Days in the Past, What Does Not Add Capacity).

    To follow the catch-up: while the backlog lasts, search 1 shows the busiest pipeline near 1.0 and search 2 the queues in front of it full, and the forwarders’ LogServ events an hour stay well above the live level:

    index=_internal source=*metrics.log* group=per_index_thruput series=sap_logserv_logs host IN (<HF1>, <HF2>)
| timechart span=1h sum(ev) as events

    On Azure and GCP, a firing that takes the full max_blobs_per_fire / max_objects_per_fire means more may be waiting. Ask SAP how many messages its queue still holds; the depth of the queue in your Secondary account (AWS Remote S3 Copy and Filter) is in its CloudWatch metrics ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible and ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage.

    Afterwards¶

    • Rebuild the dashboards for the backlog’s days. The LogServ App’s dashboards read hourly rollups, and an event that arrives more than about an hour after its hour is missing from them until its days are rebuilt (Late-arriving data). Settings → Dashboard Data lists such days of the last 30 under Late-arriving data, with a backfill of exactly those days. For older days, or on a new install, run the backfill once the backlog is in, with a window that covers it (Backfilling on first install).
    • Load what never arrived. Notifications that SAP purged, or that expired before they were read, never reach the input. On AWS, load the days you want from the bucket with AWS S3 Direct. On Azure and GCP the shipped add-ons cannot load them (see Ask SAP to purge the older messages above).


    Measure Your Own Heavy Forwarder¶

    Run these searches from a search head that sees the forwarder’s _internal data; forwarders send it by default. Replace <HF> with the forwarder’s host name as it appears in _internal, and sap_logserv_logs with your index name if you renamed it. Use a time range with busy LogServ hours: one busy hour for searches 1, 2, 4 and 9, the last 7 days for searches 3 and 5. _internal usually keeps about 30 days. All of them are read-only.

    1. Which Pipeline Is Busiest¶

    CPU per pipeline thread, in cores, in 5-minute steps. A pipeline near 1.0 is saturated, however many cores the forwarder has.

    index=_internal host=<HF> source=*metrics.log* group=pipeline
| eval pipeline=name.":".coalesce(ingest_pipe, "0")
| timechart span=5m per_second(cpu_seconds) by pipeline

    The number after the colon is the pipeline set: typing:0, typing:1 and so on.

    2. Which Queue Fills¶

    index=_internal host=<HF> source=*metrics.log* group=queue
| eval fill_pct=round(100*coalesce(current_size_kb/max_size_kb, current_size/max_size), 1)
| timechart span=5m perc90(fill_pct) by name

    The pipeline queues report their size in KB and the output queue in bytes; the coalesce covers both, so the output queue gets a column too.

    Events flow parsingqueue, aggqueue, typingqueue, indexqueue, then the output queue (tcpout_*). The bottleneck is the last queue in that order that is full. A full typingqueue with a mostly empty indexqueue points at the index-time transforms; a full indexqueue or output queue points at the output to the indexers or Splunk Cloud.

    3. Cost per Event and Capacity per Pipeline Set¶

    The CPU of the typing pipeline (and of its regexreplacement processor, which runs the Data TA’s rules) per LogServ event, over the hours with at least 10,000 LogServ events, and the rates of the Sizing Method from it:

    index=_internal host=<HF> source=*metrics.log*
    ((group=per_index_thruput series=sap_logserv_logs) OR (group=pipeline name=typing))
| bin _time span=1h
| eval typing_cpu=if(group="pipeline", cpu_seconds, null()),
       regex_cpu=if(group="pipeline" AND processor="regexreplacement", cpu_seconds, null()),
       logserv_ev=if(group="per_index_thruput", ev, null())
| stats sum(typing_cpu) as typing_cpu_s, sum(regex_cpu) as regex_cpu_s, sum(logserv_ev) as logserv_events by _time
| where logserv_events>=10000
| eval typing_us=typing_cpu_s*1000000/logserv_events, regex_us=regex_cpu_s*1000000/logserv_events
| stats count as busy_hours, sum(logserv_events) as logserv_events,
        median(regex_us) as regex_median_us, perc90(regex_us) as regex_p90_us,
        median(typing_us) as typing_median_us, perc90(typing_us) as typing_p90_us,
        max(typing_cpu_s) as typing_peak_cpu_s_in_an_hour
| eval ceiling_eps_per_set=round(1000000/typing_p90_us, 0), plan_eps_per_set=round(500000/typing_p90_us, 0),
       typing_peak_pct_of_one_core=round(100*typing_peak_cpu_s_in_an_hour/3600, 1)
| foreach *_us [ eval <<FIELD>>=round('<<FIELD>>', 1) ]
    • typing_p90_us is the cost per event of step 2 of the sizing method; ceiling_eps_per_set and plan_eps_per_set are steps 3 and 4.
    • regex_median_us and regex_p90_us are the figures in the lab table under Reference Measurements.
    • On a forwarder that also parses other data, the CPU includes that data, so the cost per LogServ event is an upper bound.
    • Splunk writes per_index_thruput (and per_sourcetype_regex_cpu, search 9) only for the busiest series of each metrics sample: maxseries in the [metrics] stanza of limits.conf, 10 by default. On a forwarder that writes to many indexes, a sample that leaves out sap_logserv_logs makes the search count too few LogServ events, and so overstate the cost per event.
    • With two pipeline sets the search adds up both sets. The cost per event stays right; typing_peak_pct_of_one_core is then for both sets together.
    • If search 1 shows another pipeline as the busiest, replace name=typing with its name.
    • After an update of the Data TA, run it once over hours before the update and once over hours after it, and compare.

    4. Where the CPU Goes, by Processor¶

    index=_internal host=<HF> source=*metrics.log* group=pipeline
| stats sum(cpu_seconds) as cpu_s by name processor
| addinfo
| eval avg_cores=round(cpu_s/(info_max_time-info_min_time), 3)
| sort - cpu_s
| head 15

    Run it over a fixed time range, such as one busy hour. name=typing processor=regexreplacement is the Data TA’s rules; name=merging processor=aggregator is the timestamp; name=parsing processor=linebreaker is the line breaking.

    5. Peak Arrival Rate at the Forwarders¶

    index=_internal source=*metrics.log* group=per_index_thruput series=sap_logserv_logs host IN (<HF1>, <HF2>)
| bin _time span=1h
| stats sum(ev) as events by _time
| stats max(events) as peak_events_hour, median(events) as median_events_hour
| eval peak_events_per_s=round(peak_events_hour/3600, 0), median_events_per_s=round(median_events_hour/3600, 0)

    List every forwarder that reads LogServ data. The median counts only hours with LogServ data. The same top-series limit as in search 3 applies: on a forwarder with many indexes the counts can come out low.

    6. Peak Rate Before You Have a Forwarder¶

    If the data already arrives somewhere, for example on a test forwarder or under another sourcetype, count it by hour in the index instead (replace the macro with index=<your index> if the data is in another index):

    | tstats count where `sap_logserv_idx_macro` earliest=-7d@h latest=@h by _time span=1h
| stats max(count) as peak_events_hour, median(count) as median_events_hour
| eval peak_events_per_s=round(peak_events_hour/3600, 0)

    This counts by event time, not arrival time, so it smooths out delivery bursts; keep the headroom of step 4.

    7. Log-Type Mix¶

    | tstats fillnull_value="(none)" count where `sap_logserv_idx_macro` earliest=-24h by sourcetype, clz_dir, clz_subdir
| sort - count
| head 20

    The folders with the most events are the first to consider for the Lambda pre-filter or for leaving out at the source. The folder fields exist on data the Data TA has parsed; events without them show as (none).

    8. Parsing Warnings and Errors¶

    index=_internal host=<HF> sourcetype=splunkd (log_level=WARN OR log_level=ERROR)
    (component=DateParserVerbose OR component=LineBreakingProcessor OR component=AggregatorMiningProcessor OR component=regexExtractionProcessor OR component=Regex)
| timechart span=15m count by component

    Each warning is CPU and log volume too. PCRE_ERROR_DEPTHLIMIT errors, or lines truncated at 10,000 bytes, mean a Data TA without the long-line fix of 0.1.2 (release notes).

    9. Regex CPU per Sourcetype (Optional)¶

    index=_internal host=<HF> source=*metrics.log* group=per_sourcetype_regex_cpu
| stats sum(cpu) as cpu_ms, sum(ev) as events by series
| eval ms_per_event=round(cpu_ms/events, 2)
| sort - cpu_ms

    Splunk reports cpu in milliseconds; across all series it comes to about the regexreplacement CPU of search 4. Events count under the sourcetype they end up with, so add up sap_logserv_logs and the sourcetypes the Data TA routes to. This group, too, lists only the busiest series of each sample (maxseries, 10 by default), so its totals can fall short of search 3: in the lab’s busiest hour its LogServ sourcetypes added up to 394,452 events, against 423,531 in per_index_thruput, about 7% fewer. Splunk reports this group only where regex_cpu_profiling is on; the lab’s Splunk 9.4.3 forwarders report it with nothing set in limits.conf. If it returns nothing, use search 3.


    Version Check¶

    The current Data TA is version 0.1.2, build 1792598960 (Download the Packages). Every forwarder should show the build you installed on the Deployment Server, or on the forwarder itself where no Deployment Server manages it. The table shows the form of the two-key routes in each build:

    Data TA The two-key routes
    0.1.2 build 1792189743 and later seven, in the filter generator’s shape with a 100,000-character window: linear, the whole line
    0.1.2 build 1791935359 six, anchored with (?s)^: tried once per event, first 4,096 characters
    0.1.2 builds before 1791935359, 0.1.1, 0.0.6, 0.0.5.x, 0.0.4.2 unanchored: tried at every character
    0.0.4.1 five of them, unanchored
    0.0.3.x none

    Check on each heavy forwarder, or on the single instance, not only on the Deployment Server: the forwarders are where the rules run.

    The installed version and build:

    grep -E "^(version|build)" $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/default/app.conf

    The routing-cost fix is in place with version = 0.1.2 and build = 1791935359 or higher, the 100,000-character window with build = 1792189743 or higher. In Splunk Web on the forwarder, the same from a search:

    | rest /services/apps/local splunk_server=local
| search title=splunk_ta_sap_logserv
| table title version build

    The rules in effect, including any local/ override:

    $SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk btool transforms list | grep -cF '(?=.*"clz_dir"'
$SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk btool transforms list set_srctype_abap_icm | grep -E '^(REGEX|LOOKAHEAD)'

    The first command prints the number of routes still in an older two-key form, (?s)^(?=.*...) or unanchored: 0 after the update to build 1792189743. The second shows the ICM route in the generator’s shape and LOOKAHEAD = 100000.

    Remove a local override of the routes before you update

    If you added the six anchored routes ((?s)^(?=.*...)(?=.*...)) to the Data TA’s local/transforms.conf as a test, remove them, and restart Splunk, before you install build 1792189743. local/ wins over default/ key by key, so the old REGEX would stay in effect together with the build’s new LOOKAHEAD = 100000, and on lines near 100,000 characters that combination exceeds Splunk’s regex match limit. The first command above prints 0 when no such override is left.


    Reference Measurements¶

    These measurements predate the current routing. The index-time figures were taken on the lab heavy forwarder with Data TA builds before 1791935359, whose six two-key routes were tried at every character of an event: they show what those builds cost, not a figure for build 1791935359 or later. The Sizing Method and Estimate the Catch-Up use them as worked examples.

    Lab heavy forwarder, before build 1791935359 (index time)

    These are lab numbers from one heavy forwarder and one feed: Splunk 9.4.3, 2 vCPUs, one pipeline set, real SAP LogServ data delivered through Azure Blob Storage and read by the LogServ Azure add-on’s queue input, and Data TA builds with the six old routes. The cost per event is CPU time from Splunk’s metrics.log divided by the LogServ events the forwarder passed on in the same hour, over every hour with at least 10,000 LogServ events.

    Lab heavy forwarder
    Hours measured 418 hours between 2026-09-14 and 2026-10-01
    LogServ events 80.0 million, with 84 bytes of event text on average in Splunk’s throughput metrics; those count after the unwrap, so the lines the routes read were longer (see the note The events were short below)
    Regex CPU per LogServ event (regexreplacement, the Data TA’s rules) median 2.42 ms, 10th percentile 2.02 ms, 90th percentile 2.93 ms
    Typing pipeline CPU per LogServ event (all its processors) median 2.44 ms, 90th percentile 2.94 ms
    Busiest hour by regex CPU 1,298 CPU seconds, 36% of one core, at 118 events a second
    Busiest hour by events 470,869 events (131 a second), 1,102 CPU seconds
    Regex CPU in hours without LogServ data 0.37 CPU seconds an hour (median)

    Both CPU figures count everything the processor or pipeline did in the hour, divided by the LogServ events. On a forwarder that also parses other data with index-time transforms, they are an upper bound for LogServ.

    In the busiest hour the typing pipeline used 1,304 CPU seconds, 1,298 of them in regexreplacement; the merging pipeline used 28, the index pipeline 6 and the parsing pipeline 2. The Data TA’s rules were nearly all of the CPU in the forwarder’s pipelines.

    At the typing pipeline’s median of 2.44 ms per event, one pipeline set runs out of time at about 410 events a second (1 second / 2.44 ms), or about 340 at its 90th-percentile cost of 2.94 ms. That ceiling is arithmetic: averaged over an hour, the lab forwarder’s typing pipeline used at most 36% of one core. Over shorter spans it came closer. In the busiest hour it used 0.81 of a core over 5 minutes, and the queues in front of it (typingqueue, aggqueue, parsingqueue) were at times full while the index queue stayed empty (search 1, search 2). The data arrives in bursts, which is why the Sizing Method plans for half the ceiling.

    The cost per event depends on the log type. Splunk’s regex CPU per sourcetype (search 9) for the same busiest hour, for the LogServ sourcetypes with more than 1,000 events:

    Sourcetype after routing Events Regex CPU per event
    sap_logserv_logs (no route matched) 334,510 2.4 ms
    linux_messages_syslog 32,062 6.4 ms
    isc:bind:query 18,026 5.0 ms
    sap:sapstartsrv 3,722 3.6 ms
    linux:cron 2,056 15 ms
    linux_secure 1,936 21 ms
    linux:warn 1,378 62 ms

    In the same hour the cost per event differed by a factor of about 25 between log types, so the mix matters as much as the volume.

    The events were short. The 84 bytes is the event text after the unwrap, which is what Splunk’s throughput metrics count. The routes read the whole NDJSON line, which also carries the envelope keys around "_raw" (_time, host, source, clz_dir, clz_subdir and others); in LogServ sample data they add about 150 characters a line. With the old routes the cost rises steeply with line length. One hour on a second lab heavy forwarder, 845 events with 566 bytes of event text on average, came to about 50 ms per event; that is a single hour, so treat it as an indication only. At search time (Search Time, Splunk’s Own Regex Library), the six old routes alone took 5.8 ms per event on whole lines of about 460 characters and 442 ms on lines of about 4,160. Byte sizes from the throughput metrics do not give the line length the routes read, so measure your forwarder’s cost per event with search 3 or search 9 rather than scaling the lab figure by event size.

    Build 1791935359 and Later (Index Time)¶

    No index-time figure has been measured for build 1791935359 or later. What is known:

    • Without LogServ data, the lab forwarders’ regex CPU did not change with the update: a median of 0.36 and 0.38 CPU seconds an hour on the two forwarders, against 0.35 and 0.37 before it (measured on build 1791935359).
    • At search time, on the same regex library, the six two-key routes anchored at the start of the line are 179 to 1,778 times faster than the old form (Search Time, Splunk’s Own Regex Library; measured with ^, and the build-1791935359 (?s)^ form measured no slower at about 4,160 characters). Build 1792189743 and later use the filter generator’s form with LOOKAHEAD = 100000 instead, which is not measured here.

    How much of the 2.42 ms measured on the older builds the update removes on a forwarder has not been measured.

    Search Time, Splunk’s Own Regex Library¶

    Splunk 9.4.3 uses the same PCRE2 library (10.40) for index-time transforms and for regex and match() at search time. Measured at search time on generated LogServ events, the six routes cost per event:

    Line length (characters) Six old routes Six anchored routes Anchored routes are faster by
    about 460 5.8 ms 0.032 ms 179 times
    about 1,160 35 ms 0.073 ms 485 times
    about 2,660 181 ms 0.162 ms 1,120 times
    about 4,160 442 ms 0.249 ms 1,778 times

    The anchored routes in this table start with ^; the build-1791935359 (?s)^ form measured no slower (0.185 ms per event at about 4,160 characters). Build 1792189743 and later use the filter generator’s form with LOOKAHEAD = 100000, which this table does not measure. Every event got the same result from the old and the anchored routes. Search time is not index time: the table shows the direction and how the cost depends on line length, not what the routes cost on your forwarder.
