    2. Install the Data TA

    Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA¶

    This page creates the two indexes the solution writes to and installs the Data TA (splunk_ta_sap_logserv, shown in Splunk Web as Splunk TA for SAP LogServ). Use it after you have planned your topology (Where Each Package Goes, Plan and Prerequisites) and before you connect your cloud. For the LogServ App, see Installing the LogServ App.

    High Level Steps¶

    Follow the steps in order:

    1. Decide where the Data TA goes.
    2. Create the two indexes on the indexer tier, with the retention you want, before any data arrives.
    3. Download the packages.
    4. Install the Data TA (Splunk Enterprise or Splunk Cloud).
    5. Before you distribute it: choose cloud attribution and decide filtering.
    6. Distribute the Data TA to the heavy forwarders.
    7. Check the build on each heavy forwarder.

    Less common tasks (renaming an index, running the add-ons on a search head, macros on the Deployment Server) are under Advanced at the bottom of this page.


    1. Where to Install¶

    The Data TA goes where LogServ data is parsed: on the heavy forwarders that run the ingest inputs, or on the single instance. A Deployment Server holds it in order to distribute it. The indexes are created on the indexer tier (step 2). Which instance gets which package, for every topology, is on Where Each Package Goes (the matrix, and By Topology). For the Data TA, that means one of these:

    • Single instance: that instance.
    • Heavy forwarders managed by a Deployment Server: the Deployment Server only; it pushes the Data TA to the heavy forwarders (Distribute the Data TA). This holds with Splunk Cloud too.
    • Heavy forwarders without a Deployment Server: each heavy forwarder that runs a LogServ input, installed directly.
    • Splunk Cloud with no heavy forwarder: the Splunk Cloud search head, because the inputs run there. This is not blocked, but we strongly recommend a heavy forwarder; see Running the TAs on a search head.

    Indexers and search heads that run no LogServ inputs do not need it: create the two indexes on the indexer tier instead (step 2; installing the Data TA on an indexer is allowed but adds nothing beyond its index definitions), and the LogServ App carries the search-time content.

    The Data TA parses every LogServ event on the heavy forwarders (or the single instance), so its cost per event decides how many heavy forwarders your volume needs; see Capacity Planning and First Start.

    With a Deployment Server, install the Data TA on the Deployment Server only

    When a Deployment Server manages your heavy forwarders, do not also install the Data TA directly on those forwarders. A push from the Deployment Server replaces the forwarder’s copy of the app, its local/ folder included, so local settings on the forwarder are lost. The Data TA does not reach the forwarders by itself either: the forwarders must be deployment clients, you save the Configuration page on the Deployment Server, assign the forwarders to the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class and click Deploy to Forwarders. Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders gives the steps.

    Why not the Inputs Data Manager (IDM)?

    On the Splunk Cloud Classic Experience, inputs run on an Inputs Data Manager (IDM). The Data TA’s app.manifest declares the workloads _search_heads and _indexers only; it does not declare _forwarders. Whether Splunk Cloud installs such an app on an IDM is not documented, and this path has not been tested. Use a heavy forwarder you manage yourself. With no heavy forwarder on the Victoria Experience, the inputs run on the search head, and the Data TA goes there too. (The LogServ Azure and GCP add-ons declare _forwarders, and also _search_heads, so a search head is an allowed target for them too, although a heavy forwarder is strongly recommended; installing them on a Splunk Cloud search head has not been tested.)


    2. Create the Indexes¶

    The solution uses two indexes:

    Index Purpose Default name Macro
    SAP data index Receives every LogServ event (logs ingested from AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage or Google Cloud Storage and routed to their sourcetypes) sap_logserv_logs sap_logserv_idx_macro
    AI Assistant audit index Receives every audit event the AI Assistant writes: predefined-prompt dispatches, free-form vendor calls (when the LLM path is enabled), security blocks, privacy-tier elevations, legal acknowledgements logserv_ai_assistant_audit sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro

    Create both on the indexer tier before any data arrives. An event sent to an index that does not exist on the indexers is dropped (unless your indexers set lastChanceIndex), and an index created later does not get those events back.

    Retention. The Data TA sets no retention for sap_logserv_logs, so the platform default applies unless you set one. It sets 90 days for the audit index (frozenTimePeriodInSecs = 7776000). Set the retention of sap_logserv_logs to cover the oldest data you will load, including any history you load later with AWS S3 Direct.

    How you create them depends on your topology:

    • Single instance — nothing to do. The Data TA ships default/indexes.conf with both indexes, and that one instance is the indexer, so installing the Data TA creates them. To give sap_logserv_logs a retention other than the default, add frozenTimePeriodInSecs = <seconds> under [sap_logserv_logs] in the Data TA’s local/indexes.conf and restart Splunkd.
    • Standalone indexer, indexer cluster or Splunk Cloud — create them yourself, as described in Creating the indexes on a separate indexer tier below.

    Why the indexer needs the index definitions

    Events are stored on the indexer tier, so both indexes must be defined there. The Data TA does its parsing on the heavy forwarders (or the single instance), and a heavy forwarder parses each event before it forwards it, so on an indexer the only part of the Data TA that would do anything is its indexes.conf. That is why the indexes are created on the indexer tier by the tier’s own method rather than by installing the Data TA there. If you do install the Data TA on a standalone indexer, its default/indexes.conf creates the indexes there, and its two scheduled scripts (the filter upgrade check every 10 minutes and the daily filter refresh) still run on it, doing nothing useful. On the Deployment Server and the heavy forwarders, which store no LogServ events, the index definitions do no harm.

    Creating the Indexes on a Separate Indexer Tier¶

    Use the same settings the Data TA’s default/indexes.conf uses, so paths and retention match:

    [sap_logserv_logs]
homePath   = $SPLUNK_DB/sap_logserv_logs/db
coldPath   = $SPLUNK_DB/sap_logserv_logs/colddb
thawedPath = $SPLUNK_DB/sap_logserv_logs/thaweddb

[logserv_ai_assistant_audit]
homePath               = $SPLUNK_DB/logserv_ai_assistant_audit/db
coldPath               = $SPLUNK_DB/logserv_ai_assistant_audit/colddb
thawedPath             = $SPLUNK_DB/logserv_ai_assistant_audit/thaweddb
frozenTimePeriodInSecs = 7776000

    Add frozenTimePeriodInSecs to [sap_logserv_logs] to set its retention. Then pick the method that matches how your indexer tier is managed.

    Standalone indexer (Splunk Enterprise). Either:

    • Splunk Web: Settings → Indexes → New Index. Create sap_logserv_logs, then logserv_ai_assistant_audit, leaving the default paths. Then set their retention with frozenTimePeriodInSecs in indexes.conf (Splunk Web writes each new index to the local/indexes.conf of the app chosen in the form’s App field): 7776000 seconds (about 90 days) for the audit index, to match the bundled default, and the value you want for sap_logserv_logs. Restart Splunkd. Or
    • Config file: add the stanzas above to $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/system/local/indexes.conf (or to a small index-definition app of your own) on the indexer and restart Splunkd.

    Indexer cluster. Put the stanzas in an index-only app under the cluster manager, $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/manager-apps/<your_index_app>/local/indexes.conf, and add repFactor = auto to both stanzas. Without repFactor = auto an index is not replicated across the peers. Then push the configuration bundle from the manager node: splunk apply cluster-bundle on its command line, or the bundle actions on its Settings → Indexer Clustering page in Splunk Web. Every peer receives the index definitions. The peers need nothing else from the Data TA. Putting the whole Data TA in the bundle is allowed but unnecessary; if you do, remove its inputs.conf first, as Splunk recommends for add-ons on indexer clusters.

    Splunk Cloud. Create both indexes yourself, with the retention you want, before any data arrives: in the Splunk Cloud console (Settings → Indexes → New Index, where the retention is the Searchable retention) or with the Admin Config Service (ACS). When you install the Data TA on a Victoria Experience stack as a private app, Splunk also installs its indexing-related default/ files, indexes.conf among them, on the Cloud indexers (its local/ files do not go there), but Splunk does not document that this creates the indexes, so do not rely on it.

    Check Who Can Search the Indexes¶

    Each role that uses the LogServ App’s dashboards must be able to search sap_logserv_logs. On Splunk Enterprise the default user role allows *, which matches every index whose name does not start with _, so roles that keep * (or import such a role) already can. Check your roles in Settings → Roles → role → Indexes, on Splunk Cloud too, and add the index to any role with a narrowed list. Give access to the audit index only as Audit Log → Restricting who can read the audit index describes.

    Both index names can be changed; see Renaming an index.


    3. Download the Packages¶

    All four packages of this release, their AppInspect reports and a README with the release details are in the release_binaries folder of the GitHub repository:

    File Package Version Build md5
    splunk_ta_sap_logserv-0.1.2.tar.gz Data TA (Splunk TA for SAP LogServ) 0.1.2 1792598960 41a04986683c5d33014d8ab2fdb832f6
    splunk_app_sap_logserv-0.1.2.tar.gz LogServ App (Splunk App for SAP LogServ) 0.1.2 394 1d82a2ac049391b2d7b2fb347d112649
    splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure-0.1.2.tar.gz LogServ Azure add-on (Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on Azure) 0.1.2 1792558069 5a5b0cfcd5f77dfa1e22dcc3545c8306
    splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp-0.1.2.tar.gz LogServ GCP add-on (Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on GCP) 0.1.2 1792558072 42713371e1ba1042b1149065cc1c59a9

    This page installs the Data TA. The LogServ App goes on the search tier (Installing the LogServ App); the Azure and GCP add-ons are installed later, per heavy forwarder, in the Azure and GCP setup guides. The Splunk Add-on for AWS comes from Splunkbase (app 1876) and is not part of this release.

    To check a download, compare its md5 with the table: md5sum <file> on Linux, md5 <file> on macOS, certutil -hashfile <file> MD5 on Windows.


    4. Install the Data TA¶

    Install it on each instance that step 1 names: the Deployment Server, each heavy forwarder without a Deployment Server, the single instance, or the Splunk Cloud search head that runs the inputs.

    Splunk Enterprise¶

    Your Deployment Server, heavy forwarders and single instance run Splunk Enterprise, also when your search tier is Splunk Cloud.

    4.a From the Splunk Web home screen, click the gear icon next to Apps.

    4.b Click Install app from file.

    4.c Locate the downloaded splunk_ta_sap_logserv-0.1.2.tar.gz file and click Upload.

    4.d If Splunk Enterprise prompts you to restart, do so.

    4.e Verify that the add-on appears in the list of apps and add-ons. You can also find it on the server at $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv.

    On a Deployment Server this installs the Data TA in etc/apps/ only. It is copied into etc/deployment-apps/ for the forwarders when you first save its Configuration page there (Distribute the Data TA).

    If splunkd runs with a proxy variable, exempt its own management port

    The add-on’s configuration pages (and the Azure and GCP add-ons’ inputs) talk to the local splunkd management port, by default 127.0.0.1:8089, through Splunk’s Python HTTP client, which honours the HTTP_PROXY / HTTPS_PROXY environment variables. If the environment splunkd runs in sets either of them, for example in splunk-launch.conf or the systemd unit, also set NO_PROXY=127.0.0.1,localhost (plus the host name in mgmtHostPort, if it is not a loopback address). Otherwise those calls, with their session key, are sent to the proxy instead of to splunkd.

    Splunk Cloud¶

    Install the Data TA on your Splunk Cloud stack only when the inputs run on the Cloud search head (Splunk Cloud with no heavy forwarder). With your own heavy forwarders, install it there with the Splunk Enterprise steps above instead; the Splunk Cloud stack does not need it (installing it there is allowed).

    The app installation workflow depends on your Splunk Cloud Platform Experience, Victoria or Classic. To find yours, in Splunk Web click Support & Services > About.

    • Installation instructions for Victoria Experience
    • Installation instructions for Classic Experience

    Create the indexes yourself either way (step 2). For what differs when the inputs run on a search head, see Running the TAs on a search head and Splunk Cloud Considerations.


    5. Before You Distribute: Two Index-Time Decisions¶

    The Data TA attributes each event to its cloud and applies your filters at index time, so whatever is indexed before you decide stays as it was indexed. Decide both before the first Save on the Deployment Server, and before any input starts:

    1. Choose Cloud Attribution: the Cloud Provider value (normally Not set) and the per-input _meta line for AWS.
    2. Decide Filtering: whether to turn filtering on, and with which values.


    6. Distribute to the Heavy Forwarders¶

    • With a Deployment Server: follow Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders. The forwarders receive the Data TA only after those steps.
    • Without a Deployment Server: the Data TA is already on each heavy forwarder (step 4). Enter the same Configuration values and click Save on each one; see Without a Deployment Server.
    • Single instance, or the Splunk Cloud search head that runs the inputs: nothing to distribute. Enter your Configuration values there and click Save.


    7. Check the Build on Each Heavy Forwarder¶

    Before you create any input, check on each heavy forwarder (or the single instance) that it runs this Data TA build: see Version Check. The routing runs where the data is parsed, so a forwarder that has not received the Data TA yet indexes every event under the base sap_logserv_logs sourcetype, permanently.


    Advanced¶

    Renaming an Index¶

    Both indexes are macro-configurable, so you can use other names (for example, to follow a corporate naming convention) without changing the apps: you create the index, update the macros, and point the writers at the new name.

    Note

    Both the Data TA and the LogServ App include a macro named sap_logserv_idx_macro that resolves to index="sap_logserv_logs". The LogServ App also includes sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro for the audit index.

    To Rename the SAP Data Index¶

    A rename touches three places: the indexer tier, every ingest input (normally on the heavy forwarders), and the search head. The Deployment Server is not involved. On a single instance all three are the same instance.

    1. Pick a new name (for example myorg_sap_logs).
    2. Create the index on the indexer tier under that name, with the methods in Creating the indexes on a separate indexer tier (on a single instance: Settings → Indexes → New Index, or a stanza in the Data TA’s local/indexes.conf). On Splunk Cloud, use Settings → Indexes or ACS: a local/indexes.conf does not reach the Cloud indexers. See the Splunk docs for Splunk Cloud or Splunk Enterprise.

    3. Update the macro in every app on the search head that ships it. Open Settings → Advanced search → Search macros, set App to All, and filter on sap_logserv_idx_macro. Edit the row whose app is splunk_app_sap_logserv and change the definition from index="sap_logserv_logs" to index="myorg_sap_logs". Where the Data TA is also installed on this search head (a single instance, or a search head that runs the inputs), edit the row whose app is splunk_ta_sap_logserv too. Each edit is saved in that app’s local/macros.conf. Both are needed: the scheduled rollups and the Settings → Dashboard Data backfill run in the LogServ App and use its copy, while the live dashboard panels run in each user’s default app, where Splunk ranks the Data TA’s copy above the App’s (other apps are ranked in reverse alphabetical order). Check the result:

      | rest /servicesNS/-/-/configs/conf-macros splunk_server=local
| search title=sap_logserv_idx_macro
| table eai:acl.app definition

      Then run `sap_logserv_idx_macro` | stats count in the Search app once data arrives in the new index.

    4. Point every ingest input at the new index. The destination index is set by each input’s index field, in the ingest add-on for your cloud, not in this Data TA: for AWS, each SQS-Based S3 input in the Splunk Add-on for AWS (see the AWS Remote S3 Connect Setup Guide), and the Index field of every later backfill on the AWS S3 Direct screen; for Azure, each sap_logserv_azure_queue input’s index field (Azure Setup Guide); for GCP, each sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub input’s index field (GCP Setup Guide). These inputs normally run on the heavy forwarders. The AWS S3 Direct screen offers only the indexes defined on the instance it runs on, so to pick the new name there, define the index on that forwarder too, for example with Settings → Indexes on it. (On a forwarder the Deployment Server manages, do not put it in the Data TA’s local/: the next push replaces that folder.)

    The Data TA still ships its own [sap_logserv_logs] stanza in default/indexes.conf, and a local/indexes.conf cannot remove it: Splunk merges the two files setting by setting, so local/ can only override values. An unused, empty sap_logserv_logs index does no harm. If you do not want it, disable it once every ingest input points at the new index: on each instance where the Data TA defines it and events are stored (a single instance, or an indexer you installed the Data TA on), add the following to the Data TA’s local/indexes.conf (or use Settings → Indexes → Disable), then restart Splunkd. Do not edit or delete the Data TA’s default/indexes.conf; an upgrade replaces it and brings the stanza back.

    [sap_logserv_logs]
disabled = true

    The AI Assistant and a renamed data index

    After sap_logserv_idx_macro is changed, the AI Assistant refuses free-form queries that start with the macro: its query guard compares the macro with the shipped definition index="sap_logserv_logs" (The SPL Guard).

    To Rename the AI Assistant Audit Index¶

    1. Pick a new name. Do not start it with an underscore: _-prefixed index names are reserved for Splunk’s internal indexes, AppInspect rejects them for custom apps, and Splunk Cloud will not accept them (the shipped index was itself renamed off an underscore prefix for these reasons).
    2. Create the index on the indexer tier under that name, with the same methods as above.
    3. Update the macro definition. Open Settings → Advanced search → Search macros, find sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro (only the LogServ App ships it), and change the definition from index="logserv_ai_assistant_audit" to index="<your_new_name>". This controls READS: the in-app Audit Log viewer and any user-written queries resolve the macro to your renamed index.
    4. Update the LogServ App config. Open Settings → AI Assistant → General → Audit & Telemetry, set the Audit index name field to your renamed index, and Save Defaults. This controls WRITES: the App posts audit events to the configured index name.

    The config field controls writes; the macro controls reads. They MUST point at the same index, but Splunk does not keep them in step for you: keep them aligned whenever you rename.


    Running the TAs on a search head¶

    We strongly recommend against installing the Data TA, the LogServ Azure add-on or the LogServ GCP add-on on a search head, Splunk Cloud included: ingest belongs on the heavy forwarders, and inputs on a search head put that load on the tier your users search on. Nothing blocks it, though. On a search head that runs the inputs itself (with the Splunk Add-on for AWS, or with the Azure or GCP add-on), the Data TA parses and filters there as it does on a heavy forwarder, and the AWS S3 Direct screen works there too; on Splunk Cloud, and on an instance with no enabled AWS input, it shows a warning that recommends a heavy forwarder. Two things work differently there:

    • Search head clusters. A search head cluster does not replicate inputs, so an input created on a member (on the Azure or GCP add-on’s Inputs page, or on the AWS S3 Direct screen) runs only on that member. An input the deployer pushes to every member runs on every member: a Generic S3 input then reads every object on each member, so each object is indexed once per member; the Azure and GCP add-ons share their queue or subscription between the members, and a message goes to one member, but each member keeps its own dedup record, so a redelivered message can be indexed twice. The filter rules and the Cloud Provider stamp that the Data TA’s Configuration page generates are written only on the member where you save them. The saved Filters settings normally reach the other members (not when the save falls back to writing the settings file, as it does for an account without admin_all_objects), and another member rebuilds its rules from them at its own daily filter refresh, but only while Enable Filtering is checked and Days in the Past is greater than 0: turning filtering off, and rules saved with Days in the Past at 0, never reach the other members. Save the Filters and Cloud Provider tabs on every member that runs inputs.
    • Deployment clients. On a search head that is a deployment client for other apps but holds the Data TA directly, the daily filter refresh runs as it does on a single instance. It is skipped only where the Deployment Server delivers the Data TA, or where the instance’s record of what its Deployment Server sent ($SPLUNK_HOME/var/run/serverclass.xml) is missing, unreadable or lists no app. The same rule applies to a heavy forwarder that holds the Data TA directly; see Heavy Forwarder without a Deployment Server.


    Macros and the Deployment Server¶

    When the Deployment Server pushes the Data TA to the heavy forwarders, its macros.conf travels with it, but heavy forwarders run no user searches, so a macro there has no effect. Macros matter on the search tier. Where the Data TA is also installed on a search head (a single instance, or a search head that runs the inputs), its copy of sap_logserv_idx_macro is the one the live dashboard panels use, ranked above the LogServ App’s copy; see step 3 of To Rename the SAP Data Index.

    What this means in practice:

    Scenario Where the change happens Deployment Server involved?
    You rename the data index Indexer tier: create the new index. Ingest inputs (normally on the heavy forwarders): set index to the new name on every SQS-Based S3 input, sap_logserv_azure_queue input and sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub input, and on later AWS S3 Direct backfills (WRITE). Search head: override sap_logserv_idx_macro in each app that ships it there (READ). See Renaming an index. No: none of these is pushed by the Deployment Server, and the Data TA routes by sourcetype, not by index
    You rename the audit index Indexer tier: create the new index. Search head: Settings → AI Assistant → General → Audit index name (WRITE), plus sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro in the LogServ App (READ). See Renaming an index. No
    You want a custom diagnostic macro on every heavy forwarder Add it to etc/deployment-apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/local/macros.conf on the Deployment Server, then Deploy to Forwarders; the forwarders pull it at their next phone-home. Operational effect: none, because forwarders do not resolve macros. Keep a copy in etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/local/macros.conf as well: when the Data TA’s version changes, the next Configuration save, or the next daily filter refresh, replaces the whole deployment-apps copy, hand edits included, with a copy of etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/. Yes (cosmetic)

    What the Deployment Server does push usefully from this Data TA: the filter rules and the Cloud Provider stamp, managed on the Data TA’s Configuration page on the Deployment Server. See Configuring Filters and Choose Cloud Attribution.


    Next Steps¶

    1. Choose Cloud Attribution, then Decide Filtering: both before the first Save on the Deployment Server.
    2. Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders, if a Deployment Server manages them.
    3. Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario to connect your cloud.

    Choose Cloud Attribution¶

    This page decides how each LogServ event records the cloud it came from, in the indexed field cloud_provider. Decide before the first Save on the Deployment Server’s Configuration page and before any input first runs: the value is written at index time, and every event keeps the value it was indexed with, the first-start backlog included.

    In short: leave the Data TA’s Cloud Provider dropdown at Not set (the default) on every fleet, and add _meta = cloud_provider::aws to each AWS SQS-Based S3 input. The Azure and GCP inputs, and the AWS S3 Direct backfills, stamp their events themselves.


    What Gets Stamped¶

    The Data TA’s Configuration page has two tabs: Filters (Configuring Filters) and Cloud Provider. The Data TA stamps two indexed fields at index time on the sap_logserv_logs sourcetype every LogServ event arrives with, with the same WRITE_META mechanism it uses for clz_dir and clz_subdir:

    Indexed field Value How it’s set Configurable
    splunk_solution splunk_for_sap_logserv Always stamped on every event No: ships active, no UI control
    cloud_provider aws / azure / gcp / (none) By the input’s own _meta line, and by the Cloud Provider dropdown when it is set Yes: per input, and Configuration → Cloud Provider

    Both fields are written on the instance that parses the data (the heavy forwarder, or the single instance), so they are available as indexed fields for tstats, accelerated searches and raw-event filtering.

    splunk_solution (always on). Every event indexed through the Data TA carries splunk_solution = splunk_for_sap_logserv. There is nothing to configure. It identifies events that flowed through the Splunk for SAP LogServ pipeline, which helps when the same index or Splunk instance also receives data from other solutions.

    splunk_solution is distinct from vendor_product

    The LogServ App also defines a per-sourcetype vendor_product search-time field (for example SAP HANA, SAP NetWeaver ABAP, SAP Web Dispatcher, ISC:Bind) that dashboards and CIM mapping rely on. That field describes which product produced a given event. splunk_solution is a separate, coarser stamp identifying the solution that ingested it. The two coexist and do not collide.

    cloud_provider comes from two places:

    • The input’s _meta line. The LogServ Azure add-on’s sap_logserv_azure_queue input always carries _meta = cloud_provider::azure (the add-on writes it into its input stanza), and the LogServ GCP add-on’s sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub input always carries _meta = cloud_provider::gcp. Every input the AWS S3 Direct screen creates is stamped _meta = cloud_provider::aws straight after it is created. The Splunk Add-on for AWS’s SQS-Based S3 inputs carry no _meta unless you add it; the add-on’s form has no field for it.
    • The Cloud Provider dropdown on the Data TA’s Configuration page:
    Selection Effect
    Not set (default) The Data TA adds no cloud_provider value of its own.
    AWS Every event the Data TA processes on that instance is stamped cloud_provider = aws.
    Microsoft Azure Every event the Data TA processes on that instance is stamped cloud_provider = azure. Not needed with the LogServ Azure add-on, whose input already stamps this value.
    Google Cloud Platform Every event the Data TA processes on that instance is stamped cloud_provider = gcp. Not needed with the LogServ GCP add-on, whose input already stamps this value.

    The dropdown does not replace an input’s _meta; it adds a second value beside it. An Azure event under dropdown = AWS carries both azure and aws (seen in the lab), so mvcount(cloud_provider) is 2 and the event can be counted under both clouds. A repeated value is expected to stay as well, according to Splunk’s description of _meta, so an Azure event under dropdown = Microsoft Azure can carry azure twice; this same-value case has not been reproduced in the lab. That is why the dropdown stays at Not set wherever an input stamps its own events.


    Recommended: Not Set Plus Per-Input _meta¶

    Use this on every fleet, AWS-only fleets included:

    1. Leave the Cloud Provider dropdown at Not set on every instance that runs the Data TA. With a Deployment Server, that is the value it pushes.
    2. Azure and GCP: nothing to do. Their inputs stamp their own events.
    3. AWS SQS-Based S3 inputs: add _meta = cloud_provider::aws to each input’s stanza before the input first runs, as described in Add the _meta line to an AWS input.
    4. AWS S3 Direct backfills: nothing to do. The screen stamps each input it creates.

    Adding a second cloud later changes nothing: each input keeps labelling its own events.

    Add the _meta Line to an AWS Input¶

    On each heavy forwarder (or the single instance) that runs an SQS-Based S3 input for LogServ:

    1. Create the SQS-Based S3 input in the Splunk Add-on for AWS, as your AWS setup guide describes.
    2. Right away, set the input to disabled on the add-on’s Inputs page, so that it reads as little as possible before the line is in place.

    3. Open $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/Splunk_TA_aws/local/inputs.conf, find the input’s stanza, [aws_sqs_based_s3://<input name>], and add the line:

      _meta = cloud_provider::aws

    4. Restart Splunkd.

    5. Enable the input again on the add-on’s Inputs page.

    The line is per instance: the Deployment Server does not manage the Splunk Add-on for AWS, so it neither pushes nor removes it. Events the input read before the line was in place keep no cloud_provider; inside the LogServ App’s dashboards they count as aws anyway (Events without a stamp).

    What has been tested

    In the lab, adding this line to existing SQS-Based S3 stanzas and restarting Splunkd worked: the events read afterwards carried a single aws. The full create, disable, edit, restart, enable sequence has not been run end to end on Splunk Add-on for AWS 8.3.1, and whether a later edit of the input in the add-on’s form keeps a hand-added _meta line is not known. Check the stanza after any edit of the input, and check the result with the search in Check the Result.


    Alternative for AWS-Only Fleets: the Dropdown Set to AWS¶

    On a fleet that ingests only from AWS and never uses the AWS S3 Direct screen, you can instead set the dropdown to AWS and leave the SQS-Based S3 inputs without _meta. The Data TA then stamps aws on every event it processes.

    Not with AWS S3 Direct, and not with a second cloud

    • AWS S3 Direct stamps every backfill input _meta = cloud_provider::aws, without checking the dropdown, so with the dropdown on AWS a backfilled event gets aws from both, and can carry it twice (mvcount(cloud_provider) = 2), as described in What Gets Stamped; this same-value case has not been reproduced in the lab.
    • Before you add another cloud or load history with AWS S3 Direct, switch to the recommended setup: set the dropdown to Not set and add the _meta line to every SQS-Based S3 input. Events indexed earlier under the dropdown keep their single aws.
    • Never set the dropdown to Microsoft Azure or Google Cloud Platform where the LogServ Azure or GCP add-on runs.


    With a Deployment Server¶

    The dropdown’s value is written into the Data TA’s local/transforms.conf, which the Deployment Server pushes to every forwarder in the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class, so one value applies to all of them. To change it, Save the Cloud Provider tab on the Deployment Server, then click Deploy to Forwarders, as on the Filters tab (Distribute the Data TA). The per-input _meta lines are per heavy forwarder and are not touched by the push.

    On a single instance, or a heavy forwarder without a Deployment Server, the Save takes effect on that instance at once.

    More than one cloud

    The Cloud Provider dropdown is a Data-TA-wide setting: it stamps the same value on every event that instance’s Data TA processes. If a single heavy forwarder ingests from more than one cloud (any mix of AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage and Google Cloud Storage), the dropdown cannot tell the channels apart, and because the sap_logserv_azure_queue and sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub inputs already carry their own _meta values, a dropdown value would tag their events with both values. Leave the dropdown at Not set and attribute per input: set _meta = cloud_provider::aws on the Splunk Add-on for AWS SQS-Based S3 inputs; the Azure and GCP inputs already attribute their own events. With the dropdown at Not set the Data TA adds no cloud_provider value of its own, so each input’s _meta value is the only one written.

    This applies when each cloud has its own forwarders too. With a Deployment Server, every forwarder in the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class receives the same dropdown value, so AWS would also be stamped on the events of a forwarder that reads only Azure or GCP. See Capacity Planning → More Than One Cloud for when to give each cloud its own forwarders.


    Splunk Cloud Without a Heavy Forwarder¶

    When the inputs run on the Splunk Cloud search head, you cannot edit Splunk_TA_aws/local/inputs.conf. The per-input route there is a REST write to the input’s stanza through configs/conf-inputs, the same call the AWS S3 Direct screen makes for its own inputs. It needs a role with the admin_all_objects capability, which splunkd requires for configs/conf-* writes, and REST access to your stack’s search head API on port 8089. Splunk Cloud opens that port only to the subnets on your stack’s search-api IP allow list, which is closed by default; add your address with the Admin Config Service (ACS), for example acs ip-allowlist create search-api --subnets "<your address>/32". Then:

    curl -u <admin_user> \
  "https://<your-stack>.splunkcloud.com:8089/servicesNS/nobody/Splunk_TA_aws/configs/conf-inputs/aws_sqs_based_s3%3A%2F%2F<input_name>" \
  -d "_meta=cloud_provider::aws"

    Then disable the input and enable it again on the add-on’s Inputs page, so it starts again from the stanza as written. The same configs/conf-inputs write stamps the AWS S3 Direct screen’s Generic S3 inputs, and that has been checked on a heavy forwarder with Splunk Add-on for AWS 8.3.1; this route for an SQS-Based S3 input, and on Splunk Cloud, has not been tested. Without it, and with the dropdown at Not set, the SQS-Based S3 events carry no cloud_provider: the LogServ App’s dashboards still count them as aws, but your own searches do not (Events without a stamp). See Splunk Cloud Considerations for the capability.


    Events Without a Stamp¶

    The LogServ App ships a search-time macro, sap_logserv_cloud_provider_default_macro, defined as:

    eval cloud_provider=coalesce(cloud_provider, "aws")

    The App’s dashboards count events that have no cloud_provider as aws: their rollups apply the same coalesce, and the global Cloud filter treats a missing value as AWS. This covers events indexed before the field existed, and AWS events from inputs without _meta, in dashboards such as Multi-Cloud Overview.

    It is not a global default. Outside the App’s dashboards (your own searches, Enterprise Security content, a cloud_provider=aws filter) an unstamped event has no cloud_provider value at all, and tstats ... by cloud_provider leaves such events out unless you give it a fillnull_value (before the count). Stamping at index time, as recommended above, makes the field usable everywhere.


    Check the Result¶

    After the first events arrive, check that every event carries exactly one provider, using the index name (the App’s macros may not exist yet on your search head):

    | tstats fillnull_value="(none)" count where index=sap_logserv_logs earliest=-24h by cloud_provider, sourcetype

    index=sap_logserv_logs earliest=-30d _index_earliest=-15m
| eval cloud_provider_values=mvcount(cloud_provider)
| fillnull value=0 cloud_provider_values
| stats count by cloud_provider_values

    (none) in the first search means an input without _meta (and the dropdown at Not set). The second counts the events indexed in the last 15 minutes, whatever their event time, so it also works while an input drains a backlog (Verify Your Data, check 3): 0 is an event without a stamp, and any 2 means the dropdown is set while inputs carry their own _meta: set the dropdown to Not set and deploy. Events already indexed keep their values.


    Next Steps¶

    1. Decide Filtering: the other index-time choice to make before the first Save.
    2. Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders, if a Deployment Server manages them.

    Decide Filtering¶

    This page helps you decide whether the Data TA should filter LogServ data, and with which values, before you distribute it. It is a decision page: Configuring Filters is the reference for every field and rule.

    Decide before the first Save on the Deployment Server’s Configuration page, and at the latest before any input starts. The Data TA’s filters run at index time, on the heavy forwarders or the single instance: anything indexed before you decide stays as it was indexed. With a Deployment Server, the first push carries your choice to the forwarders, and each forwarder restarts once when the Data TA arrives.

    Write your values down as you go (Your Values at the end), then enter them on Configuration → Filters in the next step.


    1. Turn Filtering On, or Leave It Off¶

    Enable Filtering is off by default: every LogServ event is indexed, and the other fields on the Filters tab have no effect until you check it.

    • Leave it off if you want all the data SAP delivers, or want to decide later for new data only.
    • Turn it on to drop folders, files or old events before they are indexed. Dropped events use no license and no index space; the forwarder still downloads and parses them (Configuring Filters).

    With a Deployment Server, filtering on means a restart a day

    While Enable Filtering is checked and Days in the Past is above 0, the Data TA’s daily refresh moves the time cutoff, the Deployment Server pushes the new rules, and each heavy forwarder in the server class restarts about once a day to apply them. With Days in the Past at 0 the refresh changes nothing and no daily restart follows, so you can filter by folder or file without it. See Days in the Past.


    2. Days in the Past¶

    Days in the Past drops events whose own _time is older than midnight UTC that many days ago. It applies only while Enable Filtering is checked.

    • Default 7. Set 0 (or leave the field empty) to keep events of any age. The range is 0 to 3650.
    • The first-start backlog. A new input can start with days or weeks of notifications waiting in SAP’s queue (First Start: The Queue Backlog). Days in the Past drops the older events of that backlog at index time; the forwarder still downloads and parses them, so it does not make the catch-up shorter.
    • Loading history later. On AWS, history is loaded with AWS S3 Direct. With filtering on, that screen leaves out every day older than the cutoff, because their events would be dropped on arrival. Before a history load, raise Days in the Past to cover the oldest day you will load, or set it to 0.


    3. Azure: the Unix Command Output¶

    On Azure, SAP files some data in a storage folder named undefined/undefined, and its events carry no clz_dir or clz_subdir. Almost all of it is the output of Unix commands (source values such as ps, netstat, iostat, top): about 0.7 million events and 125 MB of text a day on the reference system, about 80% of it ps. It stays under the base sap_logserv_logs sourcetype, and the LogServ App does not parse it; it only counts it in its volume dashboards. See Data Delivered Without Folder Fields.

    • To drop it, which we recommend unless you use it: turn filtering on and set Exclude Sources to ps, top, netstat, iostat, vmstat, df, cpu, interfaces, bandwidth, openPorts, nfsiostat, Unix:ListeningPorts. Folder patterns cannot reach these events, so Exclude Filters cannot drop them. If you turn filtering on only for this, also set Days in the Past to 0: with the default 7, older events are dropped too and, with a Deployment Server, each forwarder restarts about once a day (see 1 and 2).
    • If you keep it, restrict who can search it: a ps row can carry the arguments a process was started with, and arguments can contain passwords, keys or tokens.
    • An Include Filters allow-list drops it too, together with the HANA trace files that arrive in the same folder without folder fields, unless an Include Sources entry keeps them (Events Without Folder Fields).


    4. Which Folders and Files to Keep¶

    With Include Filters at */* (the default) every folder is kept, and you drop what you do not want with Exclude Filters (folders) and Exclude Sources (files). With an allow-list in Include Filters, only the folders you list are kept. Filter Recipes has ready-made settings for both, and How the Rules Combine gives the order the rules run in.


    5. AWS Remote S3 Filter: the Lambda Is a Separate Filter¶

    If you use the AWS Remote S3 Filter scenario, its Lambda filters notifications in AWS before the forwarder sees them, with settings of its own that you enter in the CloudFormation template. It is not the Filters tab and behaves differently: it reads every object, its time cutoff is a rolling now minus N days, * in its patterns also matches across /, an empty include list drops everything, and it drops notifications it cannot process. See AWS Lambda-Based Filtering and the AWS Remote S3 Filter Setup Guide.


    Your Values¶

    Field on Configuration → Filters Default Your value
    Enable Filtering unchecked
    Include Filters */*
    Exclude Filters empty
    Include Sources empty
    Exclude Sources empty (on Azure, consider the twelve Unix command names above)
    Days in the Past 7 (applies only with filtering on)

    You can change them later; a change applies to events parsed after the forwarders receive it (Updating Filters on a Deployment Server).


    Next Steps¶

    1. First Start: The Queue Backlog: decide how to handle the notifications already waiting in SAP’s queue. Your choice can change Days in the Past.
    2. Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders: enter these values there in step 2. On a single instance, or a heavy forwarder without a Deployment Server, enter them on Configuration → Filters and click Save.
    3. Then Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario to connect your cloud.

    Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders¶

    When a Deployment Server manages your heavy forwarders, the Data TA reaches them only after the one-time steps on this page: nothing is distributed automatically when you install it. Use this page after you have installed the Data TA on the Deployment Server and made the two index-time decisions. Without a Deployment Server, see Without a Deployment Server at the end.


    0. Before the First Save¶

    The first push carries your Configuration values to every forwarder, and each forwarder restarts when the Data TA arrives. Have these ready:

    • The filter values (Decide Filtering), including, for Azure, whether to drop the Unix command output with Exclude Sources.
    • The Cloud Provider value (Choose Cloud Attribution): normally Not set.
    • What to do about the first-start backlog (First Start: The Queue Backlog): ask SAP to purge it (on AWS you can load the purged days later with AWS S3 Direct; on Azure and GCP nothing in this solution can load them), or filter it.


    1. Make the Heavy Forwarders Deployment Clients¶

    On each heavy forwarder that will run a LogServ input, point it at the Deployment Server and restart it:

    $SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk set deploy-poll <deployment-server>:8089
$SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk restart

    Or put the same in $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/system/local/deploymentclient.conf:

    [deployment-client]

[target-broker:deploymentServer]
targetUri = <deployment-server>:8089

    Then check on the Deployment Server, in Settings → Forwarder Management (named Agent Management in newer Splunk Enterprise versions), that each forwarder is listed. Do this first: the Data TA recognises a Deployment Server by a server class it already has or by forwarders that phone home to it, and a Save on an instance it does not recognise as one does none of the steps below. To check from the Deployment Server’s command line:

    curl -sk -u <admin_user> \
  "https://localhost:8089/services/deployment/server/clients?output_mode=json&count=1"

    An empty entry list means no forwarder has phoned home yet.

    Keep the Splunk Add-on for AWS and the LogServ Azure and GCP add-ons out of the LogServ server class: they are installed on each forwarder directly, and a push replaces an app’s local/ folder, where their credentials and inputs live.


    2. Save the Configuration Page on the Deployment Server¶

    On the Deployment Server, open the Splunk TA for SAP LogServ app, go to Configuration, enter your values on the Filters tab (or leave Enable Filtering unchecked) and click Save. Save the Cloud Provider tab too if you set it to anything other than Not set. Save even if you do not want filtering: the first Save is what prepares the distribution.

    On a Deployment Server, a Save on either tab:

    1. Copies the whole Data TA from etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/ to etc/deployment-apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/, its local/ folder included, if that copy does not exist yet or its version ([launcher] version in default/app.conf) differs. Otherwise it copies nothing; see Later Builds With the Same Version.
    2. Creates the server class SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders, if it does not exist: disabled, with no forwarders assigned, and with the Data TA mapped to it with restartSplunkd = true, so each forwarder restarts when it receives the app.
    3. Copies the generated local/transforms.conf and local/props.conf (the filter rules and the Cloud Provider stamp) into the deployment-apps copy.

    After the Save, the Filters tab shows a Deployment Server Detected banner, a Server Class Setup Required notice while the server class is disabled (or Client Targeting Needed if the class is enabled but has no forwarders assigned) and a Deploy to Forwarders button.

    Example

    The button, and the check that decides whether to show it, need the edit_deployment_server capability. Splunk Enterprise’s admin role has it; a custom Deployment Server operator role needs it added, or the button does not appear.


    3. Assign the Heavy Forwarders to the Server Class¶

    1. Go to Settings → Forwarder Management (or Agent Management), Groups / Server Classes.
    2. Find the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class.
    3. Click the three-dot menu → Edit agent assignment.
    4. Under Include, enter your heavy forwarders’ IP addresses or host names, separated by commas. Click Preview and check that exactly your LogServ forwarders match.
    5. Click Save.

    Never use * here

    * assigns the class to every deployment client of this Deployment Server, search heads and unrelated forwarders included. Each of them would receive the Data TA and restart (restartSplunkd = true). Name the heavy forwarders.

    Example

    Client Targeting

    Splunk matches each entry against the forwarder’s IP address, host name, DNS name, client name or GUID (instance ID), not against the Instance Name column. IP addresses are the simplest to get right.

    In the lab, saving the assignment also enabled the server class. Return to the Filters tab and refresh the page: the setup notice should be gone. If it still says the class is disabled, enable the class in Forwarder Management. If it shows Client Targeting Needed, the class has no agent assignment yet: repeat this step.

    Example


    4. Deploy to Forwarders¶

    1. On the Filters tab, click Deploy to Forwarders and confirm. The banner confirms that the deployment reload has started.

      Example

    2. Each forwarder picks up the Data TA at its next phone-home (phoneHomeIntervalInSecs in deploymentclient.conf, 60 seconds by default) and then restarts.

    3. Check Settings → Forwarder Management: the forwarders should show Ok under the server class. Allow 5 minutes or more for the status to change from Pending to Ok.
    Example

    Deploy to Forwarders reloads the whole Deployment Server

    The button reloads every server class on this Deployment Server, not only SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders: if another server class has changes waiting, its clients receive them at their next phone-home too. (Saving an edit in Forwarder Management also reloads the Deployment Server, so the forwarders may start receiving the Data TA as soon as you save the assignment in step 3.) The Data TA’s own daily filter refresh reloads only its own server class.


    5. Check the Build on Each Heavy Forwarder¶

    On each heavy forwarder, check that it runs the Data TA build you installed on the Deployment Server: see Version Check. Create no input before every forwarder shows the build. Events a forwarder indexes before it has the Data TA keep the base sap_logserv_logs sourcetype and are neither routed nor filtered, permanently.

    To see which filter a forwarder applies, read its local/transforms.conf, not its filter_settings REST endpoint, which can show older settings (Reading the Active Filter Configuration).


    Later Builds With the Same Version¶

    The Save copies the whole Data TA into deployment-apps/ only the first time and when the version changes. Every 0.1.2 build has the version 0.1.2, so a newer 0.1.2 build that you install in etc/apps/ on the Deployment Server is not copied, and the forwarders keep the older build. Install the new build into etc/deployment-apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/ as well, keeping its local/ folder, then click Deploy to Forwarders. The commands are in Upgrading to This Release → Updating the Data TA.

    While Enable Filtering is checked and Days in the Past is above 0, the Data TA’s daily filter refresh makes the same version-change copy (it also runs when splunkd starts) and then reloads the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class. After a version upgrade on the Deployment Server, the forwarders can therefore receive the new version and restart without a Save or Deploy to Forwarders. Plan the upgrade for that.

    A copy made because the version changed, by a Save or by the daily filter refresh, replaces the whole deployment-apps copy, including anything you added by hand under etc/deployment-apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/local/, with a copy of etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/. Keep hand edits in etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/local/ too.


    Changing Settings Later¶

    Change the Filters or Cloud Provider tab on the Deployment Server, click Save, then Deploy to Forwarders: see Updating Filters on a Deployment Server. A change applies to events parsed after the forwarders receive it.

    While filtering is on and Days in the Past is above 0, the Data TA’s daily refresh pushes a new time cutoff by itself, and each forwarder in the server class restarts about once a day (Days in the Past).


    Without a Deployment Server¶

    A Deployment Server is optional, Splunk Cloud included: Splunk Cloud is never a Deployment Server (the Deploy to Forwarders button never appears there), and your Splunk Cloud subscription includes a deployment server license for one you run yourself (you request it from Splunk Support).

    Without one:

    1. Install the Data TA directly on each heavy forwarder that runs a LogServ input (Install the Data TA).
    2. On each forwarder, enter your values on Configuration → Filters (and Cloud Provider, if you set it) and click Save. The Save writes the rules on that forwarder and applies them at once, with no restart; no Deploy to Forwarders button appears.
    3. With several forwarders, enter the same values on each one: nothing copies them between forwarders.
    4. Check the build on each forwarder (Version Check).

    Do not install the Data TA directly on a forwarder that a Deployment Server also pushes it to: the push replaces the forwarder’s copy, its local/ settings included. A forwarder that a Deployment Server manages for other apps only can hold the Data TA directly; see Heavy Forwarder without a Deployment Server for how its daily refresh behaves.


    Next Steps¶

    1. Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario, then follow the setup guide for your cloud to create the inputs.
    2. Verify Your Data once events arrive.

    3. Connect Your Cloud

    Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario¶

    Use this page to pick the setup guide for the cloud your SAP ECS (RISE) environment runs in and, on AWS, the deployment scenario. You read it twice:

    • While planning (step 1 of the Deployment Roadmap): pick your guide and, on AWS, the scenario, because the scenario decides which template you deploy. Then start the cloud side of the guide, which needs nothing in Splunk.
    • Before you create the inputs (step 10 of the Deployment Roadmap), once:
      • the prerequisites are met;
      • the Data TA is installed (Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA) and has reached the instances that will run your inputs (Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders);
      • you have made the two index-time decisions, cloud attribution and filtering.

    Both decisions apply only to what is indexed after you save them, so the first events your inputs deliver get whatever is in place when they start.

    Which setup guide?

    1. Choose the cloud first. It is the cloud SAP runs your SAP ECS environment in: Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure or Google Cloud Platform. Azure and GCP each have one setup guide; AWS has three scenarios.
    2. On AWS, use AWS Remote S3 Connect unless you have a reason not to. It deploys only an IAM user and a role in your own account, and the Splunk Add-on for AWS reads SAP’s queue and bucket directly. The Data TA’s own filters work with it.
    3. Choose AWS Remote S3 Filter when the load on your forwarders, or the backlog of notifications waiting in SAP’s queue at the first start, needs cutting before it reaches Splunk. A Lambda in your account drops the notifications of the objects you do not want, so the forwarder never downloads them.
    4. Choose AWS Remote S3 Copy only if you want your own copy of new log files in a bucket in your account. It copies the objects whose notifications are still waiting in SAP’s queue when you activate its trigger, then every new object, so it cannot load history, and it stores gzipped files decompressed.
    5. History comes from AWS S3 Direct in every case. No AWS scenario loads objects older than the notifications still waiting in SAP’s queue when your input or Lambda first reads it (4 days by default, at most 14; SAP sets the retention). Load older days with AWS S3 Direct once the setup works.

    Where These Steps Run¶

    Each setup guide has a cloud side, done in your cloud’s console and with SAP, and a Splunk side. The Splunk side runs on the instance that holds the input, because an input collects data on the instance it is defined on:

    Your topology Ingest add-on, its account or credential, and its input The Data TA (must be there before the input starts)
    Single instance The instance The instance
    Heavy forwarders, with or without a Deployment Server Each heavy forwarder that runs an input, configured directly on it, not through the Deployment Server Each heavy forwarder: pushed by the Deployment Server, or installed directly where there is none
    Splunk Cloud with no heavy forwarder The Splunk Cloud search head. Not blocked, but a heavy forwarder is strongly recommended The Splunk Cloud search head
    • The ingest add-on is the Splunk Add-on for AWS, the LogServ Azure add-on or the LogServ GCP add-on. The LogServ Azure and GCP add-ons declare search heads as an allowed target, but neither has been tested on a Splunk Cloud search head.
    • Routing to the LogServ sourcetypes happens at index time, on the instance where the input runs. Events that arrive before the Data TA is there keep the sourcetype sap_logserv_logs for good, so check the Data TA build on each heavy forwarder first (Version Check).
    • Creating an AWS S3 Direct backfill needs the admin_all_objects capability. The Azure and GCP guides say what their inputs need.

    Amazon Web Services (AWS)¶

    All AWS deployment scenarios ingest the same LogServ logs into Splunk, with some differences in what they deploy and what they add. All of them involve two distinct AWS accounts.

    All deployment scenarios for AWS require the use of an AWS Secondary account (a different AWS account than the one SAP ECS is running in) due to the requirement from SAP for a cross-account IAM Role to access the AWS SAP ECS account where the LogServ logs reside. See the diagram below for reference.

    For brevity and clarity, the AWS account at the top of the diagram will be referred to as the SAP ECS account and the second AWS account on the bottom of the diagram will be referred to as the Secondary account from this point onward.

    The table below lists the AWS Resources required for each deployment scenario:

    AWS Resources AWS Remote S3 Connect Setup AWS Remote S3 Filter Setup AWS Remote S3 Copy Setup
    S3 Bucket (SAP ECS account) ✅ Required ✅ Required ✅ Required
    SQS Queue (SAP ECS account) ✅ Required ✅ Required ✅ Required
    S3 Bucket for the Lambda code (Secondary account, you create it) ❌ Not Required ✅ Required ✅ Required
    S3 Bucket for the log copies (Secondary account, the template creates it) ❌ Not Required ❌ Not Required ✅ Required
    SQS Queue (Secondary account) ❌ Not Required ✅ Required ✅ Required
    SQS Queue DLQ (Secondary account) ❌ Not Required ✅ Required ✅ Required
    IAM Policy (Secondary account) ✅ Required ✅ Required ✅ Required
    IAM Role (Secondary account) ✅ Required ✅ Required ✅ Required
    IAM User (Secondary account) ✅ Required ✅ Required ✅ Required
    Lambda Function (Secondary account) ❌ Not Required ✅ Required ✅ Required
    Lambda Log Group (Secondary account) ❌ Not Required ✅ Required ✅ Required

    Under Connect, the Splunk Add-on for AWS reads SAP’s queue and downloads each object from SAP’s bucket. Under Filter, a Lambda reads SAP’s queue and passes the notifications it keeps to the queue in your account; the add-on reads that queue and still downloads each object from SAP’s bucket. Under Copy, a Lambda copies each new object into the bucket in your account, which notifies the queue in your account; the add-on reads that queue and that bucket. Filter and Copy also need a bucket of your own to hold the Lambda’s code.

    If you want your own copy of the LogServ logs, in a bucket in your Secondary account, AWS Remote S3 Copy Setup provides one. Its Lambda copies the object of every notification it receives from SAP’s queue: the notifications still waiting there when you activate the Lambda’s trigger, then every new object. It never lists SAP’s bucket, so objects that were there before are not copied. Gzipped objects are stored decompressed, under the same key without .gz, so the copy takes more storage than SAP’s bucket.

    The table below lists the different features supported by each deployment scenario:

    Feature AWS Remote S3 Connect Setup AWS Remote S3 Filter Setup AWS Remote S3 Copy Setup
    Your own copy of the logs ❌ Not Supported ❌ Not Supported ✅ Supported, for the notifications in SAP’s queue at trigger activation and every new object after that
    Loads history from SAP’s bucket ❌ Not Supported ❌ Not Supported ❌ Not Supported
    Cuts the forwarder’s load before download ❌ Not Supported ✅ Supported ❌ Not Supported
    AWS Lambda-based Filtering ❌ Not Supported ✅ Supported ❌ Not Supported
    Native TA Index-Time Filtering ✅ Supported ✅ Supported ✅ Supported

    To load history in any scenario, use AWS S3 Direct.

    Native TA Filtering vs. AWS Lambda-based Filtering

    The Data TA’s native index-time filtering works with every scenario and every cloud. It runs inside Splunk, on the heavy forwarders or the single instance, and is configured in Splunk Web. Dropped events cost no license or index storage, but the forwarder still downloads and parses them before it drops them.

    The AWS Lambda-based filtering of the S3 Filter Setup runs in your AWS account, before Splunk. The forwarder never downloads the objects it drops. The Lambda itself reads every new object once to decide, so S3 GET requests rise rather than fall, and the Lambda and the queue in your account add AWS cost. It decides per object: when any one record in an object passes, the whole object is passed on. Its patterns and its day cutoff do not behave exactly like the Data TA’s; see AWS Lambda-Based Filtering.

    The two can be used together. See Configuring Filters for the native filtering.

           AWS Remote S3 Connect Setup Guide¶

    Note

    This deployment scenario uses an IAM User with a configured Access Key and a cross-account IAM Role to directly access LogServ resources in the AWS SAP ECS account where the LogServ logs reside without the need to copy logs to a secondary S3 bucket. It is the default AWS scenario.

    • No S3 Bucket or SQS Queue in your Secondary account
    • The input reads SAP’s SQS Queue and downloads from SAP’s S3 Bucket
    • CloudFormation Template provided

           AWS Remote S3 Filter Setup Guide¶

    Note

    This deployment scenario uses an IAM User with a configured Access Key and a cross-account IAM Role to directly access LogServ resources in the AWS SAP ECS account where the LogServ logs reside without the need to copy logs to a secondary S3 bucket. A Lambda function filters the notifications by the age and the folder (clz_dir/clz_subdir) of each object’s records, set through parameters on the Lambda function.

    • An S3 Bucket you create for the Lambda code; no bucket for log copies
    • Secondary SQS Queue needed; the input reads it and downloads from SAP’s S3 Bucket
    • Log filtering options supported
    • CloudFormation Template provided

           AWS Remote S3 Copy Setup Guide¶

    Note

    This deployment scenario uses an IAM User with a configured Access Key and a cross-account IAM Role along with a secondary S3 bucket and SQS queue. Use this deployment scenario only if you want your own copy of the new LogServ log files in your own S3 Bucket; it does not copy history.

    • Your own copy of new log files, stored decompressed, under your own retention
    • Requires an S3 Bucket you create for the Lambda code, plus the bucket for the copies that the template creates
    • Requires secondary SQS Queue
    • CloudFormation Template provided

           AWS S3 Direct: Backfill and Recovery¶

    Note

    Not a deployment scenario in its own right — a second channel that complements any of the three above. It uses the Splunk Add-on for AWS’s Generic S3 input to read a bucket prefix directly, with no queue in the path.

    • For loading history (days older than the notifications in SAP’s queue), and for recovering a window whose notifications expired, were purged or were discarded
    • Created from the Data TA’s AWS S3 Direct screen (Splunk Web → Splunk TA for SAP LogServ → AWS S3 Direct), or by hand over REST or inputs.conf. Not from the add-on’s own Generic S3 form: its bucket list needs an AWS permission that cannot be scoped to one bucket
    • Run it for a specific job, then disable it — SQS-Based S3 remains the steady-state path

    Microsoft Azure¶

    When your SAP ECS environment runs in Microsoft Azure, LogServ logs land in an Azure Blob Storage container instead of Amazon S3. Ingest is handled by the first-party LogServ Azure add-on (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure, shown in Splunk Web as Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on Azure), the Azure counterpart to the Splunk Add-on for AWS. Install it directly on the instance that runs its input, not through the Deployment Server, since its SAS credential lives in the add-on’s own local/: a heavy forwarder is strongly recommended, and a search head is not blocked. Its sap_logserv_azure_queue modular input consumes Azure Event Grid → Storage Queue BlobCreated notifications and fetches each blob over a SAS, emitting sourcetype = sap_logserv_logs into the same downstream pipeline (routing, filtering, dashboards, ES integration) as the AWS path.

    In a RISE / SAP ECS deployment, SAP provisions and manages the Azure storage account, Storage Queue, Event Grid subscription, and SAS in the SAP-managed Azure account — you create nothing in Azure; you install the add-on and configure one input with the values SAP provides.

           Azure Setup Guide¶

    Note

    Queue-based Azure Blob ingest — the Azure equivalent of the AWS SQS-Based S3 Connect scenario.

    • Install the LogServ Azure add-on directly on the instance that runs the input, a heavy forwarder where you have one (not via the Deployment Server)
    • Configure one sap_logserv_azure_queue input for the Storage Queue, with the storage account, queue name, and SAS values SAP provides
    • No AWS-style secondary account or cross-account IAM role — SAP provides one account SAS that covers both the Storage Queue and the blobs; the Azure Setup Guide lists the permissions it must include (What the SAP-provided SAS must cover)

    Google Cloud Platform (GCP)¶

    When your SAP ECS environment runs in Google Cloud Platform, LogServ logs land in a Google Cloud Storage (GCS) bucket instead of Amazon S3. Ingest is handled by the first-party LogServ GCP add-on (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp, shown in Splunk Web as Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on GCP), the GCP counterpart to the Splunk Add-on for AWS. Install it directly on the instance that runs its input, not through the Deployment Server, since its service-account key lives in the add-on’s own local/: a heavy forwarder is strongly recommended, and a search head is not blocked. Its sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub modular input pulls a Pub/Sub subscription fed by the bucket’s OBJECT_FINALIZE notifications and fetches each object with a service-account key, emitting sourcetype = sap_logserv_logs into the same downstream pipeline (routing, filtering, dashboards, ES integration) as the AWS path.

    In a RISE / SAP ECS deployment, SAP provisions and manages the GCS bucket, bucket notification, Pub/Sub topic, and subscription in the SAP-managed GCP project. The one GCP resource you create is the service account: in a GCP account of your own (a secondary account, separate from the RISE project), create a service account, hand its email address to your SAP support contact, and SAP grants it read access to the LogServ subscription + bucket (roles/pubsub.subscriber + roles/storage.objectViewer) — the GCP analogue of the AWS path’s customer-account cross-account IAM role. You then mint the account’s JSON key, install the add-on, and configure one input with the project ID + subscription name SAP provides plus your key.

           GCP Setup Guide¶

    Note

    Notification-driven GCS ingest — the GCP equivalent of the AWS SQS-Based S3 Connect scenario.

    • Create a service account in your own GCP account and hand its email to SAP support, who grant it roles/pubsub.subscriber + roles/storage.objectViewer on the LogServ resources
    • Install the LogServ GCP add-on directly on the instance that runs the input, a heavy forwarder where you have one (not via the Deployment Server)
    • Configure one sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub input for the subscription, with the project ID + subscription name SAP provides and your service account’s JSON key
    • Like the AWS Connect scenario’s secondary account, the identity is customer-homed — SAP binds cross-project grants to it; no infrastructure lands in your project

    Next Steps¶

    1. Follow the setup guide for your cloud and, on AWS, your scenario.
    2. Verify Your Data before you go further.
    3. On AWS, load the history you need with AWS S3 Direct.
    4. Install the LogServ App.

    AWS

    AWS Remote S3 Connect Setup Guide¶

    Introduction¶

    This guide connects the Splunk Add-on for AWS directly to the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket that SAP LogServ manages for you. It is the default AWS scenario; Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario compares it with the other two.

    The deployment diagram below shows two different AWS accounts. For brevity and clarity, the AWS account at the top of the diagram will be referred to as the SAP ECS account and the second AWS account in the middle of the diagram will be referred to as the Secondary account from this point onward.

    Your SAP ECS LogServ subscription for AWS (e.g. in your SAP ECS account) should have one S3 Bucket in that account where LogServ will store your LogServ logs. It should also have one SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account that receives notifications when new logs are added to the S3 Bucket in that account.

    You will need to obtain the AWS ARN for the SQS Queue and the S3 Bucket that resides in your SAP ECS account prior to performing the steps in this setup guide.

    Take note of the AWS Region in your SAP ECS account where the S3 Bucket and SQS Queue are located as you will need to deploy the CloudFormation template provided in that same region in your Secondary account.

    No AWS scenario loads history on its own

    The input reads only the notifications in SAP’s SQS Queue, which reach back only as far as that queue keeps messages: 4 days by default, at most 14, as SAP sets it. To load older days, use AWS S3 Direct once this setup works. The AWS Remote S3 Copy Setup does not copy history either: choose it only if you want your own copy of new log files.

    If you run the Copy scenario today and switch to this one, deactivate the Copy Lambda’s SQS trigger before you enable the input in step 7. Both read SAP’s SQS Queue, and each message goes to only one of them.


    High Level Steps¶

    Below are the high level steps for this setup process listed in the order they should be followed.

    Please ensure the user you log in with in your AWS Secondary account has the appropriate permissions to perform all the steps outlined below.

    • Before you begin: check where each step runs, and install the Splunk Add-on for AWS on each instance that will run the input (see Before You Begin)
    1. Obtain the ARNs for the SQS Queue and the S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account
    2. Deploy the AWS CloudFormation Template provided for this remote S3 connect deployment approach in your Secondary account
    3. Contact SAP LogServ support and request an update to the access policies for the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket residing in your SAP ECS account, and wait for SAP to confirm that both are applied
    4. Create an Access Key for the new IAM User that was created with the CloudFormation template in your Secondary account
    5. Configure your AWS Secondary account in the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS)
    6. Configure the new cross-account IAM Role from your AWS Secondary account in the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS).
    7. Once SAP has confirmed both policies, configure a new SQS-Based S3 Input in the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS), and give it the _meta = cloud_provider::aws line.
    8. Confirm that LogServ logs are being ingested into Splunk


    Before You Begin¶

    Where These Steps Run¶

    Steps Where
    1 to 4 The AWS console of your Secondary account, and a request to SAP LogServ Support
    Install the Splunk Add-on for AWS (below), 5 to 7 Splunk Web on each instance that will run the input: each heavy forwarder (recommended), the single instance, or, with no heavy forwarder, your Splunk Cloud search head. Configure each heavy forwarder directly, not through a Deployment Server
    8 A search head that can search the LogServ data index

    Several heavy forwarders can read the same SQS Queue: the queue hands each message to one of them, so they share the work. Give each one the same account, IAM role and input. See Adding Capacity in Capacity Planning and First Start.

    Check These First¶

    Steps 1 to 3 need nothing in Splunk, so do them on day one (step 1 of the Deployment Roadmap). Check the items below before you go on with step 4.

    • The prerequisites are met and the Data TA is on each of those instances (Plan and Prerequisites, Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA). On heavy forwarders, check its build with Version Check. Routing to the LogServ sourcetypes happens at index time, so events indexed before the Data TA arrives keep the sourcetype sap_logserv_logs for good.
    • You have decided cloud attribution and filtering. Both apply at index time, to what is indexed after you save them.
    • You have planned the first start. The input starts with every notification already waiting in SAP’s queue. Read First Start: The Queue Backlog before step 7, including whether to ask SAP to purge the older messages.

    Install the Splunk Add-on for AWS¶

    Install the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS) (Splunkbase app 1876) on each instance from the table above. It runs the SQS-Based S3 input and holds the AWS account and IAM role you configure in steps 5 to 7; the LogServ dashboards do not need it on the search head. See the add-on’s installation documentation.

    • Version: 8.2.2 or later is recommended. Splunk advisory SVD-2026-1005 (fixes in third-party packages) says to upgrade to 8.2.2 or higher. The solution enforces no minimum version; these guides were checked on 8.3.1, and the AWS S3 Direct screen shows a warning below 8.1.0.
    • Install it directly on each heavy forwarder. Do not add it to the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class, and do not distribute it with a Deployment Server: a push replaces an app’s local/ folder on the forwarder, which is where Splunk Web saves the account, the IAM role and the input you create in steps 5 to 7.
    • Just install it now; steps 5 to 7 configure it.


    1. Obtain ARNs from SAP ECS Account¶

    Before you can deploy the CloudFormation template in your Secondary account, you need to obtain the AWS ARN for two resources that reside in your SAP ECS account:

    • The S3 Bucket that stores your LogServ logs
    • The SQS Queue that receives notifications when new logs are added to the S3 Bucket

    You will also need to note the AWS Region where these resources are located, because the CloudFormation template in the next section must be deployed into that same region in your Secondary account.

    What does an ARN look like?

    AWS Amazon Resource Names (ARNs) follow a predictable format. Examples:

    • S3 Bucket ARN: arn:aws:s3:::sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd
    • SQS Queue ARN: arn:aws:sqs:ap-south-1:121212121212:sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd-logserv

    How to obtain the ARNs:

    1.a If you do not have console access to your SAP ECS account, contact SAP LogServ Support to obtain the ARN for the S3 Bucket, the ARN for the SQS Queue, and the AWS Region where these resources reside.

    1.b If you do have console access to your SAP ECS account, obtain the ARNs yourself:

    • For the S3 Bucket: navigate to the S3 console, find the bucket used for LogServ logs, click on the bucket name, and copy the ARN from the Properties tab.
    • For the SQS Queue: navigate to the SQS console, find the queue that receives S3 notifications, click on the queue name, and copy the ARN from the Details section.

    1.c Save both ARNs and the AWS Region in a secure location — you will reference them during the next section (Deploy CloudFormation Template) and again when configuring the SQS-Based S3 Input.


    2. Deploy CloudFormation Template¶

    Before you deploy the CloudFormation template, take note of the AWS Region in your SAP ECS account where the S3 Bucket and SQS Queue are located as you will need to deploy the CloudFormation template provided in that same region in your Secondary account.

    What does the CloudFormation template do?

    Creates the following resources:

    • An IAM User - Default name is splunk_logserv_user
    • An IAM Policy named splunk-logserv-ta-policy
    • An IAM Role named splunk-logserv-ta-role
    • An Inline IAM Policy on the IAM User to assume the IAM Role created above

    It creates no S3 Bucket, no SQS Queue and no access key: the input reads SAP’s resources through the IAM Role, and you create the access key in step 4.

    2.a Navigate to the CloudFormation console (ensure the region you are in matches the region in your SAP ECS account)

    2.b Click on the Create stack button and select With new resources (standard)

    Example

    2.e Enter just the name (not the ARN) of the S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account in the CrossAccountS3Bucket parameter - If your ARN looks like this arn:aws:s3:::sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd then just use the name like this sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd

    Example

    2.f Enter the complete ARN of the SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account in the CrossAccountSQSQueueArn parameter
