    3. Contact SAP LogServ Support¶

    Once the deployment of the CloudFormation templates completes successfully, you will need to provide SAP LogServ Support with the ARN of the IAM Role named splunk-logserv-ta-role that was created by the template.

    The ARN for the IAM Role should look like the one below but with your 12-digit AWS account Id of your Secondary account.

    arn:aws:iam::secondary-account-id:role/splunk-logserv-ta-role

    Example access policies for the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket residing in your SAP ECS account are provided as a reference to provide clarity on the specific permissions that need to be applied by the SAP LogServ Support team.

    • Example SQS Queue Access Policy
    • Example S3 Bucket Access Policy

    Ask SAP to keep s3:ListBucket on the bucket itself (arn:aws:s3:::<bucket-name>) in the S3 Bucket policy, as the example does. The SQS-Based S3 input does not need it, but AWS S3 Direct, which loads history and recovers outages, does: for a bucket in SAP’s account, AWS requires both your IAM Role’s policy and SAP’s bucket policy to allow it. The template already grants it on your side.

    Wait until SAP LogServ Support confirms that both policies are applied before you create the input in step 7. Steps 4 to 6 can be done in the meantime.


    4. Create Access Key for IAM User¶

    The CloudFormation template creates the IAM User but no access key for it, so you create one here (AWS: To create an access key for an IAM user).

    4.a Navigate to the IAM console in your Secondary account and search for the IAM User name you used when deploying the CloudFormation template. Click on the name of the IAM User to see the user details.

    Example

    4.b Click on the Security credentials tab in the middle of the screen. Scroll down and click on the Create access key button.

    Example

    4.c Select the Local code use case, check the Confirmation checkbox and click on the Next button.

    Example

    4.d Enter a description tag value if desired and click on the Create access key button.

    Example

    4.e Copy the values for both the Access key and the Secret access key and save them in a secure place as you will need them in the upcoming steps. Now click on the Done button.

    Example


    5. Configure Secondary Account (AWS Add-on)¶

    Please ensure the user you log in with in your Splunk instance has the appropriate permissions to perform all the steps outlined below. Do steps 5 to 7 on each instance that will run the input (Where These Steps Run).

    5.a Login to your Splunk console then find and open the Splunk Add-on for AWS App

    Example

    5.b Click on the Configuration tab, then click on the Account tab, then click on the Add button

    Example

    5.c Choose and enter a descriptive name for the account in the Name field. Enter the access key ID you created for the IAM User in the Key ID field and its secret in the Secret Key field. Leave the Region Category set to Global. Click on the Add button.

    Example


    6. Configure IAM Role (AWS Add-on)¶

    6.a Click on the IAM Role tab to the right of the Account tab, then click on the Add button

    Example

    6.b Choose and enter a descriptive name for the role in the Name field. Enter the IAM Role ARN in the IAM Role ARN field, then click the Add button. The ARN for the IAM Role should look like the one below but with your 12-digit AWS account Id of your Secondary account.

    • arn:aws:iam::secondary-account-id:role/splunk-logserv-ta-role

    7. Configure SQS-Based S3 Input (AWS Add-on)¶

    Create the input only after SAP LogServ Support has confirmed that both policies from step 3 are applied, and after the Data TA is on this instance (Check These First).

    Once added, the input starts with every notification already waiting in the SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account (up to 14 days of them), on top of the live feed. Before you add it, see First Start: The Queue Backlog, which includes asking SAP to purge the older messages.

    7.a Click on the Inputs tab. Click on the Create New Input button. Select the Custom Data Type option at the bottom of the drop-down, then select the SQS-Based S3 (Recommended) option.

    Example

    7.b Fill out the first three fields in the SQS-Based S3 Input (Name, AWS Account, Assume Role)

    • Choose and enter a descriptive name for the input
    • Select the AWS Account you configured previously
    • Select the IAM Role you configured previously
    Example

    7.c Fill out the next three fields in the SQS-Based S3 Input (Force using DLQ, AWS Region, Use Private Endpoints)

    • Leave the Force using DLQ (Recommended) checkbox checked
    • Select the AWS Region where you deployed the CloudFormation template previously
    • Leave the Use Private Endpoints checkbox unchecked
    Example

    7.d Fill out the next three fields in the SQS-Based S3 Input (SQS Queue Name, SQS Batch Size, S3 File Decoder)

    • Enter the URL of the SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account, not the ARN or just the name
      • If the ARN for your SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account looks like this:
        • arn:aws:sqs:ap-south-1:121212121212:sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd-logserv
      • Then format it as a URL like this:
        • https://sqs.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/121212121212/sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd-logserv
    • Leave the SQS Batch Size set to 10
    • Leave the S3 File Decoder set to Custom Logs
    Example

    7.e Fill out the next three fields in the SQS-Based S3 Input (Signature Validate All Events, Source Type, Index)

    • Uncheck the Signature Validate All Events checkbox (sqs_sns_validation = 0 in inputs.conf). SAP’s queue receives the S3 notifications directly, not through SNS, so they carry no SNS signature; with the box checked, the add-on logs that a message has no valid SNS signature and does not process it.
    • Enter the value of sap_logserv_logs in the Source Type field
    • Enter sap_logserv_logs in the Index field: the LogServ data index, or the name you gave it if you renamed it (Renaming an Index)
    • Click on the Add button
    Example

    7.f Add the cloud attribution to the input. Leave the Data TA’s Cloud Provider dropdown at Not set, and give this input its own stamp instead (Choose Cloud Attribution). The form has no field for it, and the input starts reading as soon as you click Add, so:

    • On the Inputs tab, disable the new input straight away.
    • Add this line to the input’s stanza, [aws_sqs_based_s3://<input name>], in $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/Splunk_TA_aws/local/inputs.conf:
    _meta = cloud_provider::aws
    • Restart Splunk, then enable the input on the Inputs tab.
    • After any later edit of this input in the form, check that the line is still there.

    This is the procedure in Add the _meta Line to an AWS Input. It has not yet been run end to end on Splunk Add-on for AWS 8.3.1, and whether a later edit of the input in the form keeps the line is not known. After you enable the input, check the result with the search in Check the Result.

    Events the input reads without the line carry no cloud_provider field: the LogServ App’s dashboards count them as AWS, but searches of the raw events do not see it. On Splunk Cloud, where you cannot edit the file, see Splunk Cloud Without a Heavy Forwarder.

    One SQS-Based S3 input on one heavy forwarder parses its events through one pipeline set, which limits how many events a second it can take. For high LogServ volumes, see Capacity Planning and First Start before you add inputs or forwarders.


    8. Confirm LogServ Logs are Being Ingested¶

    After completing all the previous steps, verify that LogServ logs are successfully being ingested into Splunk.

    The first events typically appear within 5-10 minutes of completing the SQS-Based S3 Input configuration. The input polls the SQS Queue at the configured interval (default 300 seconds, under the input’s Advanced Settings), so allow a short lag before the first events arrive.

    8.a Log in to Splunk Web on a search head that can search the LogServ data index and open the Search & Reporting app.

    8.b Search with the index name itself (sap_logserv_logs, or the name you gave it). The sap_logserv_idx_macro macro is defined only where the LogServ App or the Data TA is installed, which a search head may not have yet.

    index=sap_logserv_logs earliest=-1h | stats count by sourcetype, host

    8.c You should see the LogServ sourcetypes your SAP LogServ subscription delivers, from several hosts; Supported Log Types lists them. Log types without a route of their own keep the sourcetype sap_logserv_logs. Verify Your Data has the full set of checks, including the routing and attribution searches.

    8.d If no events appear after 15-20 minutes, troubleshoot as follows:

    • SQS Queue has no messages – Verify the SAP LogServ Support team has applied the updated access policies (from Section 3) to the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account. Without those policies, your Secondary account cannot receive SQS notifications or read from the S3 Bucket.
    • Authentication or permission errors – In the Splunk Add-on for AWS, check the logs for errors: run index=_internal source=*aws* level IN (ERROR,WARNING) earliest=-1h | head 50. Common causes are a mis-copied Access Key/Secret Key (Section 4), an incorrect IAM Role ARN (Section 6), or the IAM Role not yet propagated through AWS (wait 5 minutes after initial setup).
    • SQS URL format – Double-check the SQS Queue Name field in the SQS-Based S3 Input (Section 7) is the full URL (https://sqs.<region>.amazonaws.com/<account-id>/<queue-name>), not the ARN or bare queue name.
    • Wrong AWS Region – The CloudFormation template (Section 2) and the SQS-Based S3 Input (Section 7) must both be in the same AWS Region as the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account.


    Rotate the Access Key¶

    The access key from step 4 does not expire on its own; replace it as your security policy requires. An IAM User can hold two access keys at a time, so you can switch without a gap (AWS: Managing access keys for IAM users):

    1. In the IAM console of your Secondary account, open the IAM User and create a second access key, as in step 4. Save the new key ID and secret.
    2. On each instance that runs the input, open the Splunk Add-on for AWS, then Configuration → Account, edit the account from step 5, enter the new access key ID in Key ID and the new secret in Secret Key, and save.
    3. Check that events still arrive (step 8) and that the _internal search in step 8.d shows no new authentication errors.
    4. In IAM, make the old key Inactive. Once nothing has failed for a day, delete it.


    Next Steps¶

    1. Verify Your Data.
    2. Load the history you need with AWS S3 Direct.
    3. Install the LogServ App and seed its dashboards.

    AWS Remote S3 Filter Setup Guide¶

    Introduction¶

    This guide adds a Lambda function in your AWS account that filters SAP LogServ’s notifications before Splunk sees them, so the forwarder never downloads the objects you do not want. Use it when the forwarders’ load, or the backlog waiting in SAP’s queue at the first start, needs cutting; otherwise the AWS Remote S3 Connect Setup is the default (Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario).

    The deployment diagram below shows two different AWS accounts. For brevity and clarity, the AWS account at the top of the diagram will be referred to as the SAP ECS account and the second AWS account on the bottom left of the diagram will be referred to as the Secondary account from this point onward.

    Your SAP ECS LogServ subscription for AWS (e.g. in your SAP ECS account) should have one S3 Bucket in that account where LogServ will store your LogServ logs. It should also have one SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account that receives notifications when new logs are added to the S3 Bucket in that account.

    You will need to obtain the AWS ARN for the SQS Queue and the S3 Bucket that resides in your SAP ECS account prior to performing the steps in this setup guide.

    Take note of the AWS Region in your SAP ECS account where the S3 Bucket and SQS Queue are located as you will need to deploy the CloudFormation template provided in that same region in your Secondary account.

    The Lambda reads SAP’s SQS Queue, downloads each new object from SAP’s S3 Bucket, and checks the _time, clz_dir and clz_subdir fields of its records. When at least one record passes, it sends the original notification on to an SQS Queue in your Secondary account; the Splunk input reads that queue and downloads the whole object from SAP’s S3 Bucket. The Lambda reads every object once, so S3 GET requests rise rather than fall; the saving is on the forwarder. No AWS scenario loads history on its own: to load older days, use AWS S3 Direct once this setup works.


    High Level Steps¶

    Below are the high level steps for this setup process listed in the order they should be followed.

    Please ensure the user you log in with in your AWS Secondary account has the appropriate permissions to perform all the steps outlined below.

    • Before you begin: check where each step runs, and install the Splunk Add-on for AWS on each instance that will run the input (see Before You Begin)
    1. Obtain the ARNs for the SQS Queue and the S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account
    2. Create a new S3 Bucket, with a name of your own, in the correct AWS Region in your Secondary account and upload the splunk-logserv-filter-lambda.zip file to the root of the bucket (do not rename the file — the CloudFormation template looks for the object key splunk-logserv-filter-lambda.zip at the bucket root)
    3. Deploy the AWS CloudFormation Template provided for this remote S3 filter deployment approach in your Secondary account
    4. Contact SAP LogServ support and request an update to the access policies for the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket residing in your SAP ECS account, and wait for SAP to confirm that both are applied
    5. Create an Access Key for the new IAM User that was created with the CloudFormation template in your Secondary account
    6. Configure your AWS Secondary account in the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS)
    7. Configure the new cross-account IAM Role from your AWS Secondary account in the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS).
    8. Configure a new SQS-Based S3 Input in the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS), and give it the _meta = cloud_provider::aws line.
    9. Once SAP has confirmed both policies, create the SQS Queue Trigger on the Lambda function the CloudFormation template created (the template does not create the trigger)
    10. Confirm that LogServ logs are being ingested into Splunk


    Before You Begin¶

    Where These Steps Run¶

    Steps Where
    1 to 5, and 9 The AWS console of your Secondary account, and a request to SAP LogServ Support
    Install the Splunk Add-on for AWS (below), 6 to 8 Splunk Web on each instance that will run the input: each heavy forwarder (recommended), the single instance, or, with no heavy forwarder, your Splunk Cloud search head. Configure each heavy forwarder directly, not through a Deployment Server
    10 A search head that can search the LogServ data index

    Several heavy forwarders can read the same local SQS Queue: the queue hands each message to one of them, so they share the work. Give each one the same account, IAM role and input; see Adding Capacity in Capacity Planning and First Start.

    Check These First¶

    Steps 1 to 4 need nothing in Splunk, so do them on day one (step 1 of the Deployment Roadmap). Check the items below before you go on with step 5.

    • The prerequisites are met and the Data TA is on each of those instances (Plan and Prerequisites, Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA). On heavy forwarders, check its build with Version Check. Routing to the LogServ sourcetypes happens at index time, so events indexed before the Data TA arrives keep the sourcetype sap_logserv_logs for good.
    • You have decided cloud attribution and filtering. Both apply at index time, to what is indexed after you save them. The Lambda filter in this guide is separate from the Data TA’s filters and behaves differently (AWS Lambda-Based Filtering).
    • You have planned the first start. Once its trigger is active, the Lambda works through every notification already waiting in SAP’s queue. Read First Start: The Queue Backlog before step 9, including whether to ask SAP to purge the older messages.

    Install the Splunk Add-on for AWS¶

    Install the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS) (Splunkbase app 1876) on each instance from the table above. It runs the SQS-Based S3 input and holds the AWS account and IAM role you configure in steps 6 to 8; the LogServ dashboards do not need it on the search head. See the add-on’s installation documentation.

    • Version: 8.2.2 or later is recommended. Splunk advisory SVD-2026-1005 (fixes in third-party packages) says to upgrade to 8.2.2 or higher. The solution enforces no minimum version; these guides were checked on 8.3.1, and the AWS S3 Direct screen shows a warning below 8.1.0.
    • Install it directly on each heavy forwarder. Do not add it to the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class, and do not distribute it with a Deployment Server: a push replaces an app’s local/ folder on the forwarder, which is where Splunk Web saves the account, the IAM role and the input you create in steps 6 to 8.
    • Just install it now; steps 6 to 8 configure it.


    1. Obtain ARNs from SAP ECS Account¶

    Before you can create the local S3 Bucket and deploy the CloudFormation template in your Secondary account, you need to obtain the AWS ARN for two resources that reside in your SAP ECS account:

    • The S3 Bucket that stores your LogServ logs
    • The SQS Queue that receives notifications when new logs are added to the S3 Bucket

    You will also need to note the AWS Region where these resources are located, because the S3 Bucket and CloudFormation template in the next two sections must be created and deployed into that same region in your Secondary account.

    What does an ARN look like?

    AWS Amazon Resource Names (ARNs) follow a predictable format. Examples:

    • S3 Bucket ARN: arn:aws:s3:::sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd
    • SQS Queue ARN: arn:aws:sqs:ap-south-1:121212121212:sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd-logserv

    How to obtain the ARNs:

    1.a If you do not have console access to your SAP ECS account, contact SAP LogServ Support to obtain the ARN for the S3 Bucket, the ARN for the SQS Queue, and the AWS Region where these resources reside.

    1.b If you do have console access to your SAP ECS account, obtain the ARNs yourself:

    • For the S3 Bucket: navigate to the S3 console, find the bucket used for LogServ logs, click on the bucket name, and copy the ARN from the Properties tab.
    • For the SQS Queue: navigate to the SQS console, find the queue that receives S3 notifications, click on the queue name, and copy the ARN from the Details section.

    1.c Save both ARNs and the AWS Region in a secure location – you will reference them when creating the S3 Bucket (next section), deploying the CloudFormation Template, and configuring the SQS-Based S3 Input later in this guide.


    2. Create S3 Bucket with Lambda Function ZIP File¶

    This bucket holds the Lambda function’s code. The CloudFormation template does not create it.

    2.a Take note of the AWS Region in your SAP ECS account where the S3 Bucket and SQS Queue are located.

    2.b Log into your AWS Secondary account and change to the region that matches the region in your SAP ECS account. Create the bucket in that Region, the one you will deploy the stack in: Lambda requires its code bucket in the function’s Region.

    2.c Choose a name of your own for the new S3 bucket. S3 bucket names are global: each name can be used by only one AWS account, so pick one no other account is likely to hold, for example splunk-logserv-lambda-code-<your-account-id>-<region>. Write it down; you enter it in step 3.j.

    2.d Navigate to the S3 console and create a general purpose S3 bucket using all the default settings

    2.e Upload the splunk-logserv-filter-lambda.zip file to the root of the S3 bucket

    Example


    3. Deploy CloudFormation Template¶

    Before you deploy the CloudFormation template, take note of the AWS Region in your SAP ECS account where the S3 Bucket and SQS Queue are located as you will need to deploy the CloudFormation template provided in that same region in your Secondary account.

    What does the CloudFormation template do?

    Creates the following resources:

    • An IAM User - Default name is splunk_logserv_user
    • An IAM Policy named splunk-logserv-ta-policy
    • An IAM Role named splunk-logserv-ta-role
    • An Inline IAM Policy on the IAM User to assume the IAM Role created above
    • An SQS Queue - Default name is splunk-logserv-local-target-queue
    • A Dead Letter SQS Queue - Default name is splunk-logserv-local-target-queue-dlq. It takes the messages of the local SQS Queue that are received three times without being deleted; it does not protect the SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account
    • A Lambda Function (Python 3.12 runtime) - Default name is splunk-logserv-lambda-filter
    • A LogGroup used by the Lambda Function

    It does not create the bucket for the Lambda code (step 2), the access key (step 5) or the Lambda’s SQS trigger (step 9).

    3.a Navigate to the CloudFormation console (ensure the region you are in matches the region in your SAP ECS account)

    3.b Click on the Create stack button and select With new resources (standard)

    Example

    3.c Upload the AWS CloudFormation Template file provided for this remote S3 filter deployment approach, then click the Next button

    Example

    3.d Enter a name for the CloudFormation Stack - splunk-logserv-remote-s3-filter

    Example

    3.e Enter just the name (not the ARN) of the S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account in the CrossAccountS3Bucket parameter - If your ARN looks like this arn:aws:s3:::sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd then just use the name like this sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd

    Example

    3.f Enter the complete ARN of the SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account in the CrossAccountSQSQueueArn parameter

    Example

    3.g Enter the number of days in the past to filter messages on, in the DaysInThePast parameter: from 1 to 365, default 7. The Lambda passes an object on only when at least one of its records has a _time newer than this many days before the moment it processes the notification. This is not the Data TA’s Days in the Past, which counts from midnight UTC.

    Example

    3.h Enter comma-separated patterns for paths to exclude (e.g., ‘linux/cron,*/messages’). Format: <clz_dir>/<clz_subdir>. Leave empty to exclude nothing. The Lambda matches with Python’s fnmatch, so * also matches across the / (linux* matches linux/cron), and a bare * here excludes everything.

    Example

    3.i Enter comma-separated patterns for paths to include (e.g., ‘hana/hanaaudit,linux/*,webdispatcher/accesslog’). Format: <clz_dir>/<clz_subdir>. Use ‘*/*’ to include all paths. Do not leave it empty: an empty value discards every notification.

    Example

    3.j Enter the exact name of the S3 Bucket you created in step 2 in the LambdaCodeBucket parameter. The parameter has no default; the example image shows an older default name, which you must not use.

    Example

    3.k Choose and enter a name for the Lambda Function to be created in your Secondary account in the LambdaFunctionName parameter

    Example

    3.l Choose and enter a name for the SQS Queue to be created in your Secondary account in the LocalSQSQueueName parameter

    Example

    3.m Choose and enter a name for the IAM User to be created in your Secondary account in the NewIAMUserName parameter, then click on the Next button

    Example

    3.n Scroll down to the bottom of the page and check the I acknowledge that AWS CloudFormation might create IAM resources with custom names checkbox, then click on the Next button

    Example

    3.o Scroll down to the bottom of the page and click on the Submit button

    Example

    3.p Ensure the deployment of the CloudFormation template completes successfully

    Example


    4. Contact SAP LogServ Support¶

    Once the deployment of the CloudFormation templates completes successfully, you will need to provide SAP LogServ Support with the ARN of the IAM Role named splunk-logserv-ta-role that was created by the template.

    The ARN for the IAM Role should look like the one below but with your 12-digit AWS account Id of your Secondary account.

    arn:aws:iam::secondary-account-id:role/splunk-logserv-ta-role

    Example access policies for the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket residing in your SAP ECS account are provided as a reference to provide clarity on the specific permissions that need to be applied by the SAP LogServ Support team.

    • Example SQS Queue Access Policy
    • Example S3 Bucket Access Policy

    Ask SAP to keep s3:ListBucket on the bucket itself (arn:aws:s3:::<bucket-name>) in the S3 Bucket policy, as the example does. The Lambda and the SQS-Based S3 input do not need it, but AWS S3 Direct, which loads history and recovers outages, does: for a bucket in SAP’s account, AWS requires both your IAM Role’s policy and SAP’s bucket policy to allow it. The template already grants it on your side.

    Wait until SAP LogServ Support confirms that both policies are applied before you create the SQS Queue Trigger in step 9. With only the queue policy in place, the Lambda takes SAP’s notifications but cannot read the objects, and those notifications are lost to this path. Steps 5 to 8 can be done in the meantime.

    6. Configure Secondary Account (AWS Add-on)¶

    Please ensure the user you log in with in your Splunk instance has the appropriate permissions to perform all the steps outlined below. Do steps 6 to 8 on each instance that will run the input (Where These Steps Run).

    6.a Login to your Splunk console then find and open the Splunk Add-on for AWS App

    Example

    6.b Click on the Configuration tab, then click on the Account tab, then click on the Add button

    6.c Choose and enter a descriptive name for the account in the Name field. Enter the access key ID you created for the IAM User in the Key ID field and its secret in the Secret Key field. Leave the Region Category set to Global. Click on the Add button.

    7. Configure IAM Role (AWS Add-on)¶

    7.a Click on the IAM Role tab to the right of the Account tab, then click on the Add button

    7.b Choose and enter a descriptive name for the role in the Name field. Enter the IAM Role ARN in the IAM Role ARN field, then click the Add button. The ARN for the IAM Role should look like the one below but with your 12-digit AWS account Id of your Secondary account.

    8. Configure SQS-Based S3 Input (AWS Add-on)¶

    Create the input only after the Data TA is on this instance (Check These First). It reads the local SQS Queue, which stays empty until the trigger in step 9 is active.

    8.a Click on the Inputs tab. Click on the Create New Input button. Select the Custom Data Type option at the bottom of the drop-down, then select the SQS-Based S3 (Recommended) option.

    Example

    8.b Fill out the first three fields in the SQS-Based S3 Input (Name, AWS Account, Assume Role)

    • Choose and enter a descriptive name for the input
    • Select the AWS Account you configured previously
    • Select the IAM Role you configured previously
    Example

    8.c Fill out the next three fields in the SQS-Based S3 Input (Force using DLQ, AWS Region, Use Private Endpoints)

    • Leave the Force using DLQ (Recommended) checkbox checked
    • Select the AWS Region where you deployed the CloudFormation template previously
    • Leave the Use Private Endpoints checkbox unchecked
    Example

    8.d Fill out the next three fields in the SQS-Based S3 Input (SQS Queue Name, SQS Batch Size, S3 File Decoder)

    • Select the SQS Queue Name you entered in step 3.l (LocalSQSQueueName) when previously deploying the CloudFormation template
    • Leave the SQS Batch Size set to 10
    • Leave the S3 File Decoder set to Custom Logs
    Example

    8.e Fill out the next three fields in the SQS-Based S3 Input (Signature Validate All Events, Source Type, Index)

    • Uncheck the Signature Validate All Events checkbox (sqs_sns_validation = 0 in inputs.conf). The notifications reach the queue directly, not through SNS, so they carry no SNS signature; with the box checked, the add-on logs that a message has no valid SNS signature and does not process it.
    • Enter the value of sap_logserv_logs in the Source Type field
    • Enter sap_logserv_logs in the Index field: the LogServ data index, or the name you gave it if you renamed it (Renaming an Index)
    • Click on the Add button
    Example

    8.f Add the cloud attribution to the input. Leave the Data TA’s Cloud Provider dropdown at Not set, and give this input its own stamp instead (Choose Cloud Attribution). The form has no field for it. The local SQS Queue stays empty until the trigger in step 9 is active, so add the line now, before the input has anything to read:

    • Add this line to the input’s stanza, [aws_sqs_based_s3://<input name>], in $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/Splunk_TA_aws/local/inputs.conf:
    _meta = cloud_provider::aws
    • Restart Splunk.
    • After any later edit of this input in the form, check that the line is still there.

    This follows Add the _meta Line to an AWS Input; the disable and enable steps there are not needed while the local SQS Queue is empty. The sequence has not yet been run end to end on Splunk Add-on for AWS 8.3.1, and whether a later edit of the input in the form keeps the line is not known. Once events arrive (step 10), check the result with the search in Check the Result.

    Events the input reads without the line carry no cloud_provider field: the LogServ App’s dashboards count them as AWS, but searches of the raw events do not see it. On Splunk Cloud, where you cannot edit the file, see Splunk Cloud Without a Heavy Forwarder.


    9. Create the SQS Queue Trigger¶

    Create the trigger only after SAP LogServ Support has confirmed that both policies from step 4 are applied, and at least 5 minutes after the stack was created. The Lambda does not retry: when it cannot read an object from the SAP ECS S3 Bucket, or cannot send the notification to your local SQS Queue, it logs the error and reports the message as processed, so SAP’s notification is deleted and that object is not ingested through this path (see the warning in step 10.e).

    Once the trigger is active, the Lambda works through every notification already waiting in the SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account (up to 14 days of them) and passes on those its DaysInThePast, IncludeFilters and ExcludeFilters settings keep, for the forwarder to parse on top of the live feed. Before you activate it, see First Start: The Queue Backlog, which includes asking SAP to purge the older messages.

    9.a Navigate to the Lambda console in your Secondary account and ensure the region you are in matches the region in your SAP ECS account. Find the Lambda function that was created by the CloudFormation template and click on its name to view details.

    Example

    9.b The CloudFormation template does not create this trigger: the Lambda can read SAP’s SQS Queue only after SAP has applied the policies, so the trigger is a manual step. On a new stack, follow the Create SQS Queue Trigger steps below. Use Configure SQS Queue Trigger only if the Function overview diagram already shows an SQS trigger, as in the example image below: for example one you created earlier, or one left from a stack you deleted and created again with the same Lambda function name (AWS does not delete a function’s triggers when it deletes the function).

    10. Confirm LogServ Logs are Being Ingested¶

    After completing all the previous steps, verify that LogServ logs are successfully being ingested into Splunk.

    The first events typically appear within 5-10 minutes of activating the SQS Queue Trigger in step 9. The filter Lambda function receives SQS notifications from the SAP ECS account, drops any that fail your include/exclude/days filters, and re-emits the rest to the local SQS Queue in your Secondary account. The Splunk SQS-Based S3 Input then polls the local SQS Queue at the configured interval (default 300 seconds, under the input’s Advanced Settings), so allow a short lag before the first events arrive.

    10.a Log in to Splunk Web on a search head that can search the LogServ data index and open the Search & Reporting app.

    10.b Search with the index name itself (sap_logserv_logs, or the name you gave it). The sap_logserv_idx_macro macro is defined only where the LogServ App or the Data TA is installed, which a search head may not have yet.

    index=sap_logserv_logs earliest=-1h | stats count by sourcetype, host

    10.c You should see the LogServ sourcetypes of the log types that match your include patterns and are not blocked by your exclude or days filters, from several hosts; Supported Log Types lists them. Log types without a route of their own keep the sourcetype sap_logserv_logs. Verify Your Data has the full set of checks, including the routing and attribution searches.

    10.d Check that the trigger is active: in the Lambda console, open the function’s Monitor tab and choose View CloudWatch logs (AWS: Viewing CloudWatch logs for Lambda functions). The Lambda logs one Processing message line for each notification it takes from SAP’s SQS Queue.

    10.e If no events appear after 15-20 minutes, troubleshoot as follows:

    • Filter dropped everything – Review the DaysInThePast, IncludeFilters, and ExcludeFilters parameters you entered in Section 3. An empty IncludeFilters, a bare * in ExcludeFilters, a narrow include pattern, a short DaysInThePast window, or an over-broad exclude pattern can drop every message before it reaches your local SQS Queue. Check the Lambda function’s CloudWatch Logs for filter-decision messages and adjust the CloudFormation stack parameters if needed.
    • Lambda function errors – In the AWS Console, open CloudWatch Logs for the filter Lambda created by the CloudFormation template (Section 3). Look for cross-account access errors reading from the SAP ECS S3 Bucket or pushing to the local SQS Queue. Common causes are missing access policies on the SAP ECS resources (Section 4) or an IAM Role propagation delay (wait 5 minutes after initial setup).
    • Local SQS Queue has no messages – Verify the SAP LogServ Support team has applied the updated access policies (from Section 4) to the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account. Without those policies, the filter Lambda cannot receive SQS notifications from the SAP ECS account or read from the SAP ECS S3 Bucket. Also verify the SQS Queue Trigger on the Lambda function is active (Section 9).
    • Authentication or permission errors – In the Splunk Add-on for AWS, check the logs for errors: run index=_internal source=*aws* level IN (ERROR,WARNING) earliest=-1h | head 50. Common causes are a mis-copied Access Key/Secret Key (Section 5), an incorrect IAM Role ARN (Section 7), or the IAM Role not yet propagated through AWS (wait 5 minutes after initial setup).
    • SQS URL format – Double-check the SQS Queue Name field in the SQS-Based S3 Input (Section 8) points to the local SQS Queue that was created by the CloudFormation template in your Secondary account (not the SAP ECS SQS Queue).
    • Wrong AWS Region – The CloudFormation template (Section 3) and the SQS-Based S3 Input (Section 8) must both be in the same AWS Region as the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account.

    Notifications the Lambda cannot process are lost from this path

    The filter Lambda does not retry. When it cannot read an object from the SAP ECS S3 Bucket, or cannot send the notification to your local SQS Queue, it logs the error and reports the message as processed, so SAP’s notification is deleted and that object is not ingested through this path. An unexpected error while processing a message is handled the same way. Only an invalid configuration of the Lambda itself returns messages to SAP’s queue.

    The objects stay in SAP’s S3 Bucket. After you fix the cause, load the days the errors cover with AWS S3 Direct. In the Lambda’s CloudWatch Logs, search for these lines:

    • Could not retrieve S3 object, discarding message
    • Failed to forward message to target SQS, discarding
    • Unexpected error processing message


    Rotate the Access Key¶

    The access key from step 5 does not expire on its own; replace it as your security policy requires. An IAM User can hold two access keys at a time, so you can switch without a gap (AWS: Managing access keys for IAM users). The Lambda does not use the key: it runs as the IAM Role.

    1. In the IAM console of your Secondary account, open the IAM User and create a second access key, as in step 5. Save the new key ID and secret.
    2. On each instance that runs the input, open the Splunk Add-on for AWS, then Configuration → Account, edit the account from step 6, enter the new access key ID in Key ID and the new secret in Secret Key, and save.
    3. Check that events still arrive (step 10) and that the _internal search in step 10.e shows no new authentication errors.
    4. In IAM, make the old key Inactive. Once nothing has failed for a day, delete it.


    Next Steps¶

    1. Verify Your Data.
    2. Load the history you need with AWS S3 Direct.
    3. Install the LogServ App and seed its dashboards.

    AWS Remote S3 Copy Setup Guide¶

    Introduction¶

    This guide adds a Lambda function in your AWS account that copies each new LogServ object into a bucket of your own, which Splunk then reads. Use it only if you want your own copy of new log files; otherwise the AWS Remote S3 Connect Setup is the default (Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario).

    The deployment diagram below shows two different AWS accounts. For brevity and clarity, the AWS account at the top of the diagram will be referred to as the SAP ECS account and the second AWS account on the bottom left of the diagram will be referred to as the Secondary account from this point onward.

    Your SAP ECS LogServ subscription for AWS (e.g. in your SAP ECS account) should have one S3 Bucket in that account where LogServ will store your LogServ logs. It should also have one SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account that receives notifications when new logs are added to the S3 Bucket in that account.

    You will need to obtain the AWS ARN for the SQS Queue and the S3 Bucket that resides in your SAP ECS account prior to performing the steps in this setup guide.

    Take note of the AWS Region in your SAP ECS account where the S3 Bucket and SQS Queue are located as you will need to deploy the CloudFormation template provided in that same region in your Secondary account.

    What the copy holds, and what it does not

    The Lambda copies the object named in each notification it receives from SAP’s SQS Queue: the notifications still waiting there when you activate its trigger (step 9), then every new object. It never lists SAP’s bucket, so it does not copy history: objects whose notifications are already gone stay only in SAP’s bucket. To load those days, use AWS S3 Direct against SAP’s bucket once this setup works.

    The copy is not byte-identical. A gzipped object is stored decompressed, under the same key without .gz (...json.gz becomes ...json), with a content type guessed from its name; only an object that fails to decompress is stored as the original gzip under its original key. The copy therefore takes several times the storage of SAP’s bucket, and each copy’s LastModified time is the time it was copied.


    High Level Steps¶

    Below are the high level steps for this setup process listed in the order they should be followed.

    Please ensure the user you log in with in your AWS Secondary account has the appropriate permissions to perform all the steps outlined below.

    • Before you begin: check where each step runs, and install the Splunk Add-on for AWS on each instance that will run the input (see Before You Begin)
    1. Obtain the ARNs for the SQS Queue and the S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account
    2. Create a new S3 Bucket, with a name of your own, in the correct AWS Region in your Secondary account and upload the splunk-logserv-lambda-binary.zip file to the root of the bucket (do not rename the file — the CloudFormation template looks for the object key splunk-logserv-lambda-binary.zip at the bucket root)
    3. Deploy the AWS CloudFormation Template provided for this remote S3 copy deployment approach in your Secondary account
    4. Contact SAP LogServ support and request an update to the access policies for the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket residing in your SAP ECS account, and wait for SAP to confirm that both are applied
    5. Create an Access Key for the new IAM User that was created with the CloudFormation template in your Secondary account
    6. Configure your AWS Secondary account in the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS)
    7. Configure the new cross-account IAM Role from your AWS Secondary account in the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS).
    8. Configure a new SQS-Based S3 Input in the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS), and give it the _meta = cloud_provider::aws line.
    9. Once SAP has confirmed both policies, create the SQS Queue Trigger on the Lambda function the CloudFormation template created (the template does not create the trigger)
    10. Confirm that LogServ logs are being ingested into Splunk


    Before You Begin¶

    Where These Steps Run¶

    Steps Where
    1 to 5, and 9 The AWS console of your Secondary account, and a request to SAP LogServ Support
    Install the Splunk Add-on for AWS (below), 6 to 8 Splunk Web on each instance that will run the input: each heavy forwarder (recommended), the single instance, or, with no heavy forwarder, your Splunk Cloud search head. Configure each heavy forwarder directly, not through a Deployment Server
    10 A search head that can search the LogServ data index

    Several heavy forwarders can read the same local SQS Queue: the queue hands each message to one of them, so they share the work. Give each one the same account, IAM role and input; see Adding Capacity in Capacity Planning and First Start.

    Check These First¶

    Steps 1 to 4 need nothing in Splunk, so do them on day one (step 1 of the Deployment Roadmap). Check the items below before you go on with step 5.

    • The prerequisites are met and the Data TA is on each of those instances (Plan and Prerequisites, Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA). On heavy forwarders, check its build with Version Check. Routing to the LogServ sourcetypes happens at index time, so events indexed before the Data TA arrives keep the sourcetype sap_logserv_logs for good.
    • You have decided cloud attribution and filtering. Both apply at index time, to what is indexed after you save them.
    • You have planned the first start. Once its trigger is active, the Lambda copies the object of every notification already waiting in SAP’s queue. Read First Start: The Queue Backlog before step 9, including whether to ask SAP to purge the older messages.

    Install the Splunk Add-on for AWS¶

    Install the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS) (Splunkbase app 1876) on each instance from the table above. It runs the SQS-Based S3 input and holds the AWS account and IAM role you configure in steps 6 to 8; the LogServ dashboards do not need it on the search head. See the add-on’s installation documentation.

    • Version: 8.2.2 or later is recommended. Splunk advisory SVD-2026-1005 (fixes in third-party packages) says to upgrade to 8.2.2 or higher. The solution enforces no minimum version; these guides were checked on 8.3.1, and the AWS S3 Direct screen shows a warning below 8.1.0.
    • Install it directly on each heavy forwarder. Do not add it to the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class, and do not distribute it with a Deployment Server: a push replaces an app’s local/ folder on the forwarder, which is where Splunk Web saves the account, the IAM role and the input you create in steps 6 to 8.
    • Just install it now; steps 6 to 8 configure it.


    1. Obtain ARNs from SAP ECS Account¶

    Before you can create the local S3 Bucket and deploy the CloudFormation template in your Secondary account, you need to obtain the AWS ARN for two resources that reside in your SAP ECS account:

    • The S3 Bucket that stores your LogServ logs
    • The SQS Queue that receives notifications when new logs are added to the S3 Bucket

    You will also need to note the AWS Region where these resources are located, because the S3 Bucket and CloudFormation template in the next two sections must be created and deployed into that same region in your Secondary account.

    What does an ARN look like?

    AWS Amazon Resource Names (ARNs) follow a predictable format. Examples:

    • S3 Bucket ARN: arn:aws:s3:::sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd
    • SQS Queue ARN: arn:aws:sqs:ap-south-1:121212121212:sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd-logserv

    How to obtain the ARNs:

    1.a If you do not have console access to your SAP ECS account, contact SAP LogServ Support to obtain the ARN for the S3 Bucket, the ARN for the SQS Queue, and the AWS Region where these resources reside.

    1.b If you do have console access to your SAP ECS account, obtain the ARNs yourself:

    • For the S3 Bucket: navigate to the S3 console, find the bucket used for LogServ logs, click on the bucket name, and copy the ARN from the Properties tab.
    • For the SQS Queue: navigate to the SQS console, find the queue that receives S3 notifications, click on the queue name, and copy the ARN from the Details section.

    1.c Save both ARNs and the AWS Region in a secure location – you will reference them when creating the S3 Bucket (next section), deploying the CloudFormation Template, and configuring the SQS-Based S3 Input later in this guide.


    2. Create S3 Bucket with Lambda Function ZIP File¶

    This bucket holds the Lambda function’s code. The CloudFormation template does not create it; it creates only the bucket for the copies (step 3.i).

    2.a Take note of the AWS Region in your SAP ECS account where the S3 Bucket and SQS Queue are located.

    2.b Log into your AWS Secondary account and change to the region that matches the region in your SAP ECS account. Create the bucket in that Region, the one you will deploy the stack in: Lambda requires its code bucket in the function’s Region.

    2.c Choose a name of your own for the new S3 bucket. S3 bucket names are global: each name can be used by only one AWS account, so pick one no other account is likely to hold, for example splunk-logserv-lambda-code-<your-account-id>-<region>. Write it down; you enter it in step 3.g.

    2.d Navigate to the S3 console and create a general purpose S3 bucket using all the default settings

    2.e Upload the splunk-logserv-lambda-binary.zip file to the root of the S3 bucket

    Example


    3. Deploy CloudFormation Template¶

    Before you deploy the CloudFormation template, take note of the AWS Region in your SAP ECS account where the S3 Bucket and SQS Queue are located as you will need to deploy the CloudFormation template provided in that same region in your Secondary account.

    What does the CloudFormation template do?

    Creates the following resources:

    • An IAM User - Default name is splunk_logserv_user
    • An IAM Policy named splunk-logserv-ta-policy
    • An IAM Role named splunk-logserv-ta-role
    • An Inline IAM Policy on the IAM User to assume the IAM Role created above
    • An S3 Bucket with an Event Notification to the SQS Queue below- Default name is splunk-logserv-local-target-bucket
    • An SQS Queue - Default name is splunk-logserv-local-target-queue
    • A Dead Letter SQS Queue - Default name is splunk-logserv-local-target-queue-dlq. It takes the messages of the local SQS Queue that are received three times without being deleted; it does not protect the SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account
    • A Lambda Function (Python 3.12 runtime) - Default name is splunk-logserv-lambda-logforwarder
    • A LogGroup used by the Lambda Function

    It does not create the bucket for the Lambda code (step 2), the access key (step 5) or the Lambda’s SQS trigger (step 9).

    A stack created from an earlier copy of this template runs the Lambda on python3.9, which AWS deprecated on 15 December 2025 (AWS: Lambda runtimes). To move it to Python 3.12, update the stack with the current template and keep the existing parameter values. The runtime is the only resource setting the two templates differ in; the function’s code is the same.

    3.a Navigate to the CloudFormation console (ensure the region you are in matches the region in your SAP ECS account)

    3.b Click on the Create stack button and select With new resources (standard)

    Example

    4. Contact SAP LogServ Support¶

    Once the deployment of the CloudFormation templates completes successfully, you will need to provide SAP LogServ Support with the ARN of the IAM Role named splunk-logserv-ta-role that was created by the template.

    The ARN for the IAM Role should look like the one below but with your 12-digit AWS account Id of your Secondary account.

    arn:aws:iam::secondary-account-id:role/splunk-logserv-ta-role

    Example access policies for the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket residing in your SAP ECS account are provided as a reference to provide clarity on the specific permissions that need to be applied by the SAP LogServ Support team.

    • Example SQS Queue Access Policy
    • Example S3 Bucket Access Policy

    Ask SAP to keep s3:ListBucket on the bucket itself (arn:aws:s3:::<bucket-name>) in the S3 Bucket policy, as the example does. The copy Lambda does not need it, but AWS S3 Direct does when it loads history from SAP’s bucket: for a bucket in SAP’s account, AWS requires both your IAM Role’s policy and SAP’s bucket policy to allow it. The template already grants it on your side.

    Wait until SAP LogServ Support confirms that both policies are applied before you create the SQS Queue Trigger in step 9. Steps 5 to 8 can be done in the meantime.

    • Select the IAM Role you configured previously
    Example

    8.c Fill out the next three fields in the SQS-Based S3 Input (Force using DLQ, AWS Region, Use Private Endpoints)

    • Leave the Force using DLQ (Recommended) checkbox checked
    • Select the AWS Region where you deployed the CloudFormation template previously
    • Leave the Use Private Endpoints checkbox unchecked
    Example

    8.d Fill out the next three fields in the SQS-Based S3 Input (SQS Queue Name, SQS Batch Size, S3 File Decoder)

    • Select the SQS Queue Name you entered in step 3.j (LocalSQSQueueName) when previously deploying the CloudFormation template
    • Leave the SQS Batch Size set to 10
    • Leave the S3 File Decoder set to Custom Logs
    Example

    8.e Fill out the next three fields in the SQS-Based S3 Input (Signature Validate All Events, Source Type, Index)

    • Uncheck the Signature Validate All Events checkbox (sqs_sns_validation = 0 in inputs.conf). The notifications reach the queue directly from S3, not through SNS, so they carry no SNS signature; with the box checked, the add-on logs that a message has no valid SNS signature and does not process it.
    • Enter the value of sap_logserv_logs in the Source Type field
    • Enter sap_logserv_logs in the Index field: the LogServ data index, or the name you gave it if you renamed it (Renaming an Index)
    • Click on the Add button
    Example

    8.f Add the cloud attribution to the input. Leave the Data TA’s Cloud Provider dropdown at Not set, and give this input its own stamp instead (Choose Cloud Attribution). The form has no field for it. The local SQS Queue stays empty until the trigger in step 9 is active, so add the line now, before the input has anything to read:

    • Add this line to the input’s stanza, [aws_sqs_based_s3://<input name>], in $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/Splunk_TA_aws/local/inputs.conf:
    _meta = cloud_provider::aws
    • Restart Splunk.
    • After any later edit of this input in the form, check that the line is still there.

    This follows Add the _meta Line to an AWS Input; the disable and enable steps there are not needed while the local SQS Queue is empty. The sequence has not yet been run end to end on Splunk Add-on for AWS 8.3.1, and whether a later edit of the input in the form keeps the line is not known. Once events arrive (step 10), check the result with the search in Check the Result.

    Events the input reads without the line carry no cloud_provider field: the LogServ App’s dashboards count them as AWS, but searches of the raw events do not see it. On Splunk Cloud, where you cannot edit the file, see Splunk Cloud Without a Heavy Forwarder.


    9. Create the SQS Queue Trigger¶

    Create the trigger only after SAP LogServ Support has confirmed that both policies from step 4 are applied, and at least 5 minutes after the stack was created.

    Once the trigger is active, the Lambda copies the object of every notification already waiting in the SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account (up to 14 days of them) into the S3 Bucket in your Secondary account, and the forwarder parses them all on top of the live feed. It copies nothing older: objects whose notifications are already gone stay only in SAP’s bucket, and AWS S3 Direct loads them. Before you activate it, see First Start: The Queue Backlog, which includes asking SAP to purge the older messages.

    9.a Navigate to the Lambda console in your Secondary account and ensure the region you are in matches the region in your SAP ECS account. Find the Lambda function that was created by the CloudFormation template and click on its name to view details.

    Example

    9.b The CloudFormation template does not create this trigger: the Lambda can read SAP’s SQS Queue only after SAP has applied the policies, so the trigger is a manual step. On a new stack, follow the Create SQS Queue Trigger steps below. Use Configure SQS Queue Trigger only if the Function overview diagram already shows an SQS trigger, as in the example image below: for example one you created earlier, or one left from a stack you deleted and created again with the same Lambda function name (AWS does not delete a function’s triggers when it deletes the function).

    10. Confirm LogServ Logs are Being Ingested¶

    After completing all the previous steps, verify that LogServ logs are successfully being ingested into Splunk.

    The first events typically appear within 5-10 minutes of activating the SQS Queue Trigger in step 9. The Lambda function copies objects from the SAP ECS S3 Bucket to the local target S3 Bucket in your Secondary account when an SQS notification arrives, then the SQS-Based S3 Input polls the local SQS Queue at the configured interval (default 300 seconds, under the input’s Advanced Settings), so allow a short lag before the first events arrive.

    10.a Log in to Splunk Web on a search head that can search the LogServ data index and open the Search & Reporting app.

    10.b Search with the index name itself (sap_logserv_logs, or the name you gave it). The sap_logserv_idx_macro macro is defined only where the LogServ App or the Data TA is installed, which a search head may not have yet.

    index=sap_logserv_logs earliest=-1h | stats count by sourcetype, host

    10.c You should see the LogServ sourcetypes your SAP LogServ subscription delivers, from several hosts; Supported Log Types lists them. Log types without a route of their own keep the sourcetype sap_logserv_logs. Verify Your Data has the full set of checks, including the routing and attribution searches.

    10.d Check that copies arrive: the S3 Bucket in your Secondary account gains new objects under logserv/, without the .gz ending.

    10.e If no events appear after 15-20 minutes, troubleshoot as follows:

    • Lambda function errors – In the AWS Console, open CloudWatch Logs for the Lambda function created by the CloudFormation template (Section 3). Check for errors copying objects from the SAP ECS S3 Bucket to your local S3 Bucket. Common causes are missing access policies on the SAP ECS resources (Section 4) or an IAM Role propagation delay (wait 5 minutes after initial setup).
    • Local SQS Queue has no messages – Verify the SAP LogServ Support team has applied the updated access policies (from Section 4) to the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account. Without those policies, the Lambda function cannot receive SQS notifications from the SAP ECS account or read from the SAP ECS S3 Bucket. Also verify the SQS Queue Trigger on the Lambda function is active (Section 9).
    • Authentication or permission errors – In the Splunk Add-on for AWS, check the logs for errors: run index=_internal source=*aws* level IN (ERROR,WARNING) earliest=-1h | head 50. Common causes are a mis-copied Access Key/Secret Key (Section 5), an incorrect IAM Role ARN (Section 7), or the IAM Role not yet propagated through AWS (wait 5 minutes after initial setup).
    • SQS URL format – Double-check the SQS Queue Name field in the SQS-Based S3 Input (Section 8) points to the local SQS Queue that was created by the CloudFormation template in your Secondary account (not the SAP ECS SQS Queue).
    • Wrong AWS Region – The CloudFormation template (Section 3) and the SQS-Based S3 Input (Section 8) must both be in the same AWS Region as the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account.


    Rotate the Access Key¶

    The access key from step 5 does not expire on its own; replace it as your security policy requires. An IAM User can hold two access keys at a time, so you can switch without a gap (AWS: Managing access keys for IAM users). The Lambda does not use the key: it runs as the IAM Role.

    1. In the IAM console of your Secondary account, open the IAM User and create a second access key, as in step 5. Save the new key ID and secret.
    2. On each instance that runs the input, open the Splunk Add-on for AWS, then Configuration → Account, edit the account from step 6, enter the new access key ID in Key ID and the new secret in Secret Key, and save.
    3. Check that events still arrive (step 10) and that the _internal search in step 10.e shows no new authentication errors.
    4. In IAM, make the old key Inactive. Once nothing has failed for a day, delete it.


    Next Steps¶

    1. Verify Your Data.
    2. Load the history you need with AWS S3 Direct.
    3. Install the LogServ App and seed its dashboards.

    SAP LogServ on Azure — Setup Guide¶

    This page covers ingesting LogServ data from Microsoft Azure Blob Storage using the standalone LogServ Azure add-on (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure, shown in Splunk Web as Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on Azure) and its sap_logserv_azure_queue modular input — the Azure twin of Splunk_TA_aws’s SQS-Based S3 input. An Azure Event Grid subscription drops a BlobCreated notification onto a Storage Queue; this input consumes the queue, fetches each named blob over a SAS, and emits its NDJSON. This is the model SAP’s LogServ-on-Azure collector uses (Storage Queue notifications). You install this small, first-party add-on on the heavy forwarder that runs the input — the same deployment model as the Splunk Add-on for AWS — and the LogServ Data TA on the same instance provides the downstream sourcetype routing, filtering, and stamping. The downstream pipeline (sourcetype routing, filtering, dashboards, ES integration) is identical to the AWS S3 path.

    The Azure infrastructure is provided by SAP — you only install the add-on and configure the input

    In a RISE / SAP ECS deployment the storage account, blob container, Storage Queue, Event Grid subscription, and SAS are all provisioned and managed by SAP in the SAP ECS Azure account. You do not create or configure anything in Azure. Your only tasks are to install the splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure add-on on the heavy forwarder that will run the input and create one Splunk input per Azure queue on it — one per Azure landscape (most deployments have a single landscape, hence one input; you can define several on the same HF if you ingest from more than one — see Multiple landscapes / fleets), using a small set of parameter values that you obtain from your SAP support contact — see Parameters to obtain from SAP.

    High Level Steps¶

    Follow these steps in order. Each step links to its section below.

    1. Get the parameters from SAP: the storage account name, the queue name and the SAS. Ask also when the SAS expires (its se= value) and how SAP will give you a new one. See Parameters to obtain from SAP.
    2. Decide about the queue backlog with SAP before the input exists. A purged day cannot be loaded later. See First Start: The Queue Backlog and Historical backfill.
    3. Check the Data TA and the indexes. The Data TA must be on the instance that will run the input, and the indexes must exist, before the input reads anything: events indexed without the Data TA keep the base sourcetype for good. See Prerequisites.
    4. Download and install the add-on on that instance, directly (never through the Deployment Server). See Install the Azure add-on.
    5. Before the input starts, check the Data TA’s two index-time settings. Leave Cloud Provider at Not set: the input stamps cloud_provider=azure itself (see cloud_provider attribution and Choose Cloud Attribution). Decide filtering, including whether to drop the Unix command output that arrives under undefined/undefined (see Decide Filtering). Whatever the queue holds when the input starts is indexed with the settings in place at that moment.
    6. Create one input for the queue, with a role that holds admin_all_objects. See Configure the input.
    7. Check that data arrives. See Validation.
    8. Put the SAS expiry in your calendar, and replace the SAS before it. See Rotate credentials.

    Architecture overview¶

    SAP LogServ RISE-ECS
  |
  +-> writes NDJSON.gz blobs to Azure Blob Storage under the logserv/ prefix
        |
        +-> Azure Event Grid subscription (Microsoft.Storage.BlobCreated)
              |
              +-> Azure Storage Queue (one message per new blob)
                    |
                    +-> [Azure add-on: sap_logserv_azure_queue]  (runs on the Heavy Forwarder)
                          |   reads the queue, fetches each blob over a SAS, gunzips, splits NDJSON
                          |
                          +-> emits via EventWriter, sourcetype=sap_logserv_logs, cloud_provider=azure
                                |
                                +-> [LogServ Data TA pipeline]  (same Heavy Forwarder):
                                      sourcetype routing by clz_dir/clz_subdir or source path,
                                      Configuration -> Filters nullQueue, _time drop,
                                      splunk_solution stamping
                                      |
                                      +-> forwarded to the Indexer
                                            |
                                            +-> dashboards + ES integration

    Everything from the LogServ blob writer down through the Storage Queue lives in the SAP ECS Azure account and is managed by SAP. The Azure add-on’s sap_logserv_azure_queue input — the only component you install and configure — runs on your heavy forwarder, consumes the queue SAP exposes to you, and hands its events to the LogServ Data TA (also on that HF) for routing/filtering/stamping. This is exactly how Splunk_TA_aws and the Data TA cooperate for the AWS S3 path.

    Why EventWriter, not HEC: the input runs on the heavy forwarder and emits through the HF’s native index-time pipeline, so every existing LogServ Data TA feature — sourcetype routing (by the clz_dir / clz_subdir folder fields or by the source path, depending on the log type; see Supported Log Types), the Configuration → Filters nullQueue filtering, the days_in_past / _time drop, and the splunk_solution stamping — applies to Azure events unchanged, exactly as it does to AWS S3 events. The cloud_provider value comes from the add-on itself (see cloud_provider attribution). The input is stdlib-only (Azure Storage REST over urllib — no Azure SDK), so it adds no AArch64 / native-binary burden and is Splunk Cloud-clean.

    Prerequisites¶

    Provided by SAP (in the SAP ECS Azure account — you obtain the values, you do not build the resources):

    • An Azure Storage Account holding the LogServ container (blobs under the logserv/ prefix — same path convention as AWS S3: <container>/logserv/<clz_dir>/<clz_subdir>/<YYYY>/<MM>/<DD>/<file>.json.gz).
    • A Storage Queue in that account, fed by an Event Grid subscription that routes Microsoft.Storage.BlobCreated events to it.
    • A SAS that is both blob-readable and queue-processable (see What the SAP-provided SAS must cover).

    Obtain the storage account name, the queue name, and the SAS from your SAP support contact — see Parameters to obtain from SAP.

    On your side (the instance that runs the input — a heavy forwarder is strongly recommended):

    • LogServ Data TA 0.1.1+ installed on that instance (it provides the index-time routing/filtering/stamping; see Installing the Data TA). On heavy forwarders the Data TA is normally distributed by the Deployment Server (see Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders). Its build decides the parsing cost on the forwarder: use build 1792189743 or later, and see Version Check to read the build on a forwarder.
    • The indexes (sap_logserv_logs, and the AI Assistant audit index) on your indexer tier, before any data arrives. See Create the indexes.
    • LogServ Azure add-on (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure) 0.1.1+ installed on the same instance (see Install the Azure add-on). It registers the sap_logserv_azure_queue input kind. The input is inert until you create an input instance.
    • A Splunk role that holds the admin_all_objects capability on that instance, to create, edit or delete the input (see Configure the input).
    • Network egress from that instance to <account>.blob.core.windows.net and <account>.queue.core.windows.net (port 443 / HTTPS). The add-on has no proxy setting of its own; if the instance reaches the internet through a proxy, see Outbound proxy under Heavy Forwarders.

    Compact JSON format required

    Each blob is gzipped NDJSON (one event per line). The index-time routing transforms assume compact JSON (no whitespace after :). The SAP LogServ collector emits compact JSON natively, so no action is required on your side. (For reference: pretty-printed JSON would bypass the transforms and land as sourcetype=sap_logserv_logs, breaking dashboards.)

    Parameters to obtain from SAP¶

    You do not create any Azure resources. SAP has already provisioned the storage account, container, queue, and Event Grid subscription in the SAP ECS Azure account. Contact your SAP support contact to obtain the following values for your environment, then plug them into the Splunk input (Configure the input):

    Parameter Input field Description
    Storage account name account_name The Azure Storage account holding the LogServ container (^[a-z0-9]{3,24}$).
    Storage Queue name queue_name The queue receiving the Event Grid BlobCreated notifications.
    SAS token sas_token An account SAS covering both services (ss=bq, srt=o) with blob read (r) and queue process (p, which covers Get Messages and Delete Message); add a only if you configure a dead_letter_queue. List (l) is not needed, because the input never lists the container. See below. Treat it as a secret.

    The blob container name and logserv/ prefix are already covered by the SAS and the queue — they are not separate input fields. The account name also determines the two endpoints your heavy forwarder must reach (<account>.blob.core.windows.net and <account>.queue.core.windows.net).

    Ask SAP also when the SAS expires (its se= value) and how they will give you a new one before then. When the SAS expires the input stops (see Rotate credentials).

    What the SAP-provided SAS must cover¶

    The input fetches blobs and reads/deletes queue messages with the single SAS SAP gives you, so that SAS must cover both services. Confirm with your SAP support contact that the SAS includes:

    SAS field Must include For
    ss (services) b (blob) and q (queue) blob fetch + queue ops
    srt (resource types) o (object) is what the add-on actually needs; sco is fine if that is what SAP issues account-SAS resource scope
    sp (permissions) r (blob read) and p (queue process — covers Get + Delete Messages); add a (add) only if you configure a dead_letter_queue (poison messages are written to it) fetch blobs + consume queue
    se (expiry) a date far enough ahead, and a renewal agreed with SAP the input stops when it passes

    l (list) and d (delete) are not needed: the input never lists the container, and in an account SAS p already covers deleting queue messages.

    You can decode a SAS string to check its scope and expiry before configuring the input:

    echo "$SAS" | tr '&' '\n' | grep -E '^(ss|srt|sp|se)='

    If the SAS is queue-only

    If ss lacks b, blob fetches fail with HTTP 401/403 and the input logs it explicitly: “blob read forbidden … the SAS likely lacks Blob-read permission or has expired.” The decisive question for your SAP support contact is “is the LogServ SAS Blob-readable, or queue-only?” If it is queue-only, you will need a second, blob-read credential from SAP.

    Install the Azure add-on¶

    Download splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure-0.1.2.tar.gz from the release_binaries folder of the Splunk for SAP LogServ GitHub repository. Its AppInspect report sits beside it, and the folder’s README.md lists each tarball’s md5. The build and md5 of each package are also listed under Download the Packages.

    Install it directly on the instance that runs the input. A heavy forwarder is strongly recommended — it is the tier where Splunk_TA_aws runs for the AWS path. A search head is not blocked (see Running the TAs on a search head). You can install the add-on on every heavy forwarder that may run an input, for example to keep a standby ready; the input for a given queue still runs on one of them (see Configure the input).

    • Splunk Web → Manage Apps → Install app from file → upload the tarball, or
    • /opt/splunk/bin/splunk install app /path/splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure-0.1.2.tar.gz, or
    • configuration management (Ansible / Puppet / Chef) drops the app into etc/apps/, then chown -R splunk:splunk and restart.

    Do NOT distribute the Azure add-on via the Deployment Server

    Install it directly on each instance that runs an input — never as a deployment-app. The input’s SAS is stored, encrypted, in the add-on’s own local/passwords.conf; a Deployment Server push replaces the app’s local/ directory, which would wipe the per-HF SAS. (This is the same reason Splunk_TA_aws is configured per-HF rather than DS-distributed.) The Data TA stays DS-managed as before — only the Azure add-on is per-HF.

    After installing + restarting, the sap_logserv_azure_queue input kind is registered and the add-on’s Inputs page is available under Apps → Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on Azure.

    Upgrading from an earlier build? See Upgrading to This Release.

    Single instance¶

    On a single Splunk Enterprise instance (no separate forwarder or indexer), install the Data TA and the Azure add-on on that instance and create the input there, as described below. The Data TA’s bundled indexes.conf creates both indexes on that instance; set the retention of sap_logserv_logs if you want one other than the default (see Create the indexes). There is no Deployment Server step: the Data TA’s settings are saved on the instance itself. The LogServ App goes on the same instance.

    Splunk Cloud¶

    With Splunk Cloud, run the input on a heavy forwarder you manage:

    1. Create both indexes in your Splunk Cloud stack first (Settings → Indexes, or the Admin Config Service), with the retention you want, before any data arrives. See Create the indexes.
    2. Set the heavy forwarder up to forward to your stack, with your stack’s universal forwarder credentials app installed on it.
    3. Put the Data TA on the heavy forwarder (through your Deployment Server, or directly if you have none), and install the Azure add-on on it directly, as above.
    4. Create the input on the heavy forwarder (Configure the input).

    The LogServ App goes on the Splunk Cloud search head. The Data TA is not needed on the Cloud stack in this layout.

    Without a heavy forwarder. The add-on’s app.manifest declares the search-head workload, so a search head is an allowed target for it; installing it on a Splunk Cloud search head has not been tested. In this layout, install the Data TA and the Azure add-on on the search head as private apps, and create the input there. The Data TA must sit beside the add-on, because it parses the events where the input runs. We strongly recommend against this layout, because the input puts ingest load on the tier your users search on. Creating the input needs a role that holds admin_all_objects there too. See Running the TAs on a search head and Splunk Cloud Considerations.

    Configure the input¶

    Create one input for each Azure queue, on one instance (normally one heavy forwarder). You can install the add-on on every HF, for example to keep a standby ready, but run the input for a given queue on one HF only. Every other input on the same queue, on the same HF or another one, keeps its own dedup record, so a redelivered message can be indexed twice (see Scaling one queue by cloning below). The SAS is encrypted into the add-on’s own local/passwords.conf and is not Deployment-Server-managed — it survives restarts and Data-TA pushes.

    Creating or editing an input needs admin_all_objects

    On Splunk Enterprise and Splunk Cloud alike, creating, editing (including replacing the SAS) and deleting an input runs as the signed-in user and needs a role that holds the admin_all_objects capability. Without it, Save fails with HTTP 403, “This operation is forbidden”. The REST call below has the same requirement.

    A new input starts with what is already in the queue

    The queue may already hold notifications from before your input exists: up to 7 days of them by default, and with no limit if SAP’s Event Grid subscription sets them never to expire. A new input works through all of them on top of the live feed. Before you create it, see First Start: The Queue Backlog, which includes asking SAP to purge the older messages. The add-on cannot load purged days later (see Historical backfill).

    Decide on the Unix command output before the input starts

    SAP files some Azure data under a storage folder named undefined/undefined, without folder fields. Most of it is Unix command output (ps, top, netstat and others, about 0.7 million events a day on the reference system), which stays under the base sourcetype unparsed. Filtering is index time, so decide before the input starts whether to drop it with the Data TA’s Exclude Sources. See Decide Filtering and Data Delivered Without Folder Fields.

    Via Splunk Web (per Heavy Forwarder)¶

    Splunk Web → Apps → Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on Azure → Inputs → Create New Input → Azure Storage Queue, and fill in the fields below with the values you obtained from SAP. (For a second landscape on the same HF, use the Inputs table’s Clone action and give it a new name — the SAS is not carried on clone, so re-enter it.)

    Via REST (scriptable, per Heavy Forwarder)¶

    # Write the SAS to a single-line temp file (no trailing newline), then create the input:
curl -sk -u admin:<pwd> -X POST \
  https://localhost:8089/servicesNS/nobody/splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure/splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure_sap_logserv_azure_queue \
  --data-urlencode name=logserv_azure \
  --data-urlencode account_name=<storage-account> \
  --data-urlencode queue_name=logservqueue \
  --data-urlencode index=sap_logserv_logs \
  --data-urlencode event_sourcetype=sap_logserv_logs \
  --data-urlencode interval=60 \
  --data-urlencode sas_token@/tmp/azure_sas.txt
rm -f /tmp/azure_sas.txt

    The resulting stanza in the add-on’s local/inputs.conf looks like:

    [sap_logserv_azure_queue://logserv_azure]
account_name = <storage-account>
queue_name = logservqueue
sas_token = ******
index = sap_logserv_logs
event_sourcetype = sap_logserv_logs
interval = 60
disabled = 0

    (Only the masked placeholder sas_token = ****** is written to inputs.conf — the real SAS is stored encrypted in the add-on’s own local/passwords.conf.)

    Field Default Notes
    account_name — Storage account name from SAP (^[a-z0-9]{3,24}$).
    queue_name — The Storage Queue name from SAP (receives Event Grid notifications).
    sas_token — The SAS from SAP (blob + queue scoped). Encrypted credential: the value lives in the add-on’s local/passwords.conf; inputs.conf carries only the masked ****** placeholder.
    index sap_logserv_logs Target index. Does not affect parsing — the Data TA’s index-time pipeline keys on the sourcetype, not the index. You may point it at a custom index, but the dashboards query through the sap_logserv_idx_macro macro, so update that macro to match (see caveat below).
    event_sourcetype (UI label Sourcetype) sap_logserv_logs Fixed at sap_logserv_logs. The add-on hard-codes this sourcetype (it is not read from the stanza), and the field is shown read-only when editing the input. Leave it at the default.
    interval 60 Seconds between firings (10–3600). Each firing drains the queue within a per-firing time budget (currently min(240 s, interval × 0.9)).
    batch_size 32 Queue messages dequeued per request (1–32, the Azure max).
    visibility_timeout 300 Seconds a dequeued message is hidden while processing (30–604800).
    max_blobs_per_fire 500 Cap on blobs ingested per firing (1–100000; backlog safety valve).
    poison_threshold 5 A message redelivered more than this many times (1–100) is dead-lettered / dropped.
    dead_letter_queue (empty) Optional queue name for poison messages (Storage Queue has no native DLQ).
    include_filters / exclude_filters (empty) Optional comma-separated, case-insensitive substrings matched against the blob path (the Event Grid subject), applied on top of the built-in logserv requirement. Subjects containing azure-webjobs-hosts are always skipped.
    verify_ssl 1 TLS verification for Azure REST calls.

    Sourcetype is fixed; the Index is yours to change

    The Sourcetype is effectively fixed at sap_logserv_logs — the add-on always emits it (the value is hard-coded in the input, not read from the stanza), and the field is shown read-only (disabled) when editing an existing input. When you create an input the field can still be typed into, but whatever you enter is ignored and the add-on still emits sap_logserv_logs.
