    A read-only view of the same rollup health, freshness and 30-day-history completeness, is available to every user on the Data Doctor’s Diagnostics page (Platform → Diagnostics), which points back here for the backfill and clear controls.

    Legal Acknowledgement Modals¶

    Two legal acknowledgements gate the General sub-tab’s Save Defaults. Both follow Splunk’s splunk_instrumentation optInVersion pattern: each has a version (optInVersion in the App’s default/ai_assistant_acks.conf), the deployment records the version it last answered and the answer (in the logserv_ai_assistant_acks KV Store collection), and raising the version asks again. Both answers, Yes and No, are recorded, and each answer also writes an audit event with the admin’s user name, the network address Splunk records for the request (host), the time, and the SHA-256 of the acknowledgement text.

    On a fresh install, the first Save Defaults that turns the AI Assistant on shows both, the liability terms first (Set Up the AI Assistant). If an answer cannot be recorded, or the save after a Yes fails, the dialog closes and the error shows on the page.

    “AI Assistant — Liability terms” Dialog (orange-bordered)¶

    The AI Assistant — Liability terms dialog opens:

    • on every save that turns Enable AI Assistant on, whatever was answered before; and
    • on a save while the AI Assistant is on, when its terms are at a newer version than the one last answered on this deployment (the current version is 3).

    The text has seven clauses: data egress acknowledgement, customer responsibility, AS-IS warranty disclaimer, indemnification, limitation of liability, authority warrant, and record of acknowledgement. Its Active LLM provider line names the provider in effect and, when the same save also changes the provider, the one a Yes saves.

    • I accept (record Yes and enable): the save goes ahead (with the second acknowledgement first, when it is due) and the version is recorded as answered. An ai_assistant_enable_acceptance audit event records the answer.
    • I do not accept: the save stops. An AI Assistant being turned on stays off. One that is already on (asked again after a version change) is turned off: only Enable AI Assistant changes, nothing else in that save, and it is written before the No is recorded, so if turning it off fails, nothing is recorded and the question comes back at the next save. Turning it on again asks every time.

    “Audit log integrity” Dialog (red-bordered)¶

    The Audit log integrity dialog opens:

    • on every save that turns Audit log forwarder off; and
    • on a save with the forwarder off, when its terms are at a newer version than the one last answered on this deployment (the current version is 2).

    The text covers the integrity responsibility: with the forwarder off, the audit events exist only in the local index, which a host-root admin can edit.

    • I accept (record Yes and save): the save goes ahead with forwarding off.
    • I do not accept (record No): the save stops and the forwarder setting stays as it was, but the answer is recorded, so the next save does not ask again unless forwarding is turned from on to off.

    Its forwarder_disabled_acceptance audit event is posted as soon as the answer is recorded, for either answer, so a Yes is logged even when the save after it fails. The event goes where the audit settings in place at that moment send it: when the same save turns forwarding off, it is also sent to the forwarder being turned off, and if that send fails, its audit_forwarder_failure record goes to the event’s audit index.

    Why the hybrid trigger logic¶

    Version-only gating (answer once, never asked again until the version changes) is what Splunk’s own telemetry uses. The App also asks on every deliberate turn-on of the AI Assistant and every deliberate turn-off of the forwarder, because each is a change of the legal and security posture that may be made by a different admin, with different context, than the last one.

    Live UI Refresh on Save¶

    When a save changes what users see (Enable AI Assistant, MCP Required, Power Mode roles, Templates-only mode and the like), the App applies the new settings to the running page without a reload: turning the AI Assistant off removes the AI Assistant button, and turning it on shows it. Other users’ open pages pick the change up at their next page load. For the callback wiring, see LogServ App and AI Assistant Internals.

    Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness¶

    Most LogServ App dashboard panels read hourly summaries (rollups) kept in KV Store. This page covers the admin tasks on Settings → Dashboard Data: filling the rollups with history after an install, rebuilding days whose data arrived late, and clearing a rollup. It then explains how fresh each panel is, and ends with the reference for the scheduled searches behind the rollups.

    The Dashboard Data settings tab¶

    The Dashboard Data tab on the Application Settings page (Settings → Dashboard Data) is the single control surface for the KV-Store rollup layer, for every dashboard and the Environment Topology view. It holds the hourly-aggregation master switch, the retention window, the backfill, the late-arriving data check, a per-rollup status and action table, and a global clear.

    Who can use it. The Settings page opens only for users who hold a role named exactly admin, sc_admin or sc_subadmin, and the rollup collections accept writes only from those roles. A user who holds none of them does not see Settings in the navigation rail and gets “Admin access required” on the page’s URL, so Backfill and Clear need one of those three roles.

    The Environment Topology graph and its detail tabs are rows in the same table: their aggregation, backfill, retention and clear work exactly as for every dashboard rollup. The backfill runs each of their searches as its own top-level job, so it does not truncate at high event volume.

    Non-admins can SEE this health without Settings access

    The Data Doctor’s Diagnostics page (Platform → Diagnostics) shows every rollup collection’s freshness and its 30-day-history completeness — the same completeness convention this tab uses — read-only, to every user. It names this tab as the remedy when a backfill is needed, but the controls themselves stay here.

    Backfilling on first install¶

    A freshly installed rollup collection is empty until its scheduled aggregation has run, and those runs read only the most recent hours. Any install whose index already holds events (data loaded with AWS S3 Direct, ingest that ran before the App was installed, or a few days of normal arrival) needs a backfill to show that history.

    1. Open Settings → Dashboard Data.
    2. Review the per-rollup status. Rollups with no history show a “Dashboard history backfill needed” banner and a warning row. Rollups whose history could not be measured just now get a banner of their own with Re-check; they are not counted as needing a backfill.
    3. In Backfill window, pick the window (see below).
    4. Click Run backfill (the button targets only the incomplete rollups; once all are complete it becomes Re-run backfill (all)).

    By default the backfill seeds 30 days of history into every rollup collection. The Backfill window control above the button also offers 60, 90, 180 and 365 days, or a custom range of whole UTC days, reaching back as far as the 365-day retention (an earlier start is refused rather than silently clamped). A window longer than a month is dispatched in monthly chunks per search, and choosing one longer than 90 days shows a cost warning. The two flat Environment Topology collections (inventory, IP enrichment) always refresh over the last 30 days: they describe current state rather than history — the inventory maps each IP address or host to its most recent SAP system. When backfilling after a historical S3 ingest, match the dates in the S3 keys you ingested — on the Data TA’s AWS S3 Direct screen, its Scan from and Scan until — not a hand-made input’s write-time scan window; see AWS S3 Direct: Backfill and Recovery.

    The backfill dispatches each rollup’s component aggregation searches as top-level Splunk jobs — this matters at scale: the bundled *_backfill saved searches use a single \| union that Splunk auto-finalizes at a subsearch wall-clock limit, which silently truncates results at high event volume. The Dashboard Data button avoids that by running each component as its own unrestricted job. It shows a progress bar, is idempotent (re-running upserts the same rows), and is resumable (it detects collections that are already complete and skips them).

    After the initial backfill, the hourly aggregation keeps each collection current and the 365-day retention grows the cached history toward a full year (seed-and-grow). You only need to run the backfill again if you reinstall, deliberately clear a collection, an upgrade note asks for one, or you roll the App back to an earlier build across one that changed a rollup key: the restored build writes rows under its old keys beside the newer build’s rows, and those hours are counted twice until you Clear and Backfill the rows that build changed (see Upgrading).

    How long it waits. Each search is waited on for as long as Splunk reports it running — there is no fixed time limit, because one month of a large estate can take hours. A rollup is marked failed — re-run only on Splunk’s own verdict: the job failed, its search process died, or the job disappeared. If you cancel, or the panel stops waiting (after 24 hours, or after 15 minutes without being able to reach Splunk), a search that is still running is marked still running on server instead: it finishes on its own and writes its rows. Hover the row for the search IDs to follow them under Activity → Jobs; re-running that rollup before they finish repeats their work.

    Environment Topology node counts and inventory. Two of the Environment Topology (graph) collections combine the results of several searches: a node’s event count is the sum over every log source that reports it, and an IP address or host is mapped to its most recent SAP system with its events counted over every source (of the systems seen in its most recent hour, the one with the most events; an exact tie keeps the previous mapping). For those two, each search writes its results into a scratch KV Store collection, logserv_backfill_stage, and once every search of a month (for the inventory, of its 30 days) has finished, one more search adds them up and writes the rows — but only after the page has counted every collected result back from the scratch collection, before and after. Keep the page open until the Environment Topology (graph) row has finished: a month whose searches did not all finish, or whose results did not all read back (KV Store still starting after a restart, for example), is discarded rather than written in part — the row reads failed — re-run, also when the panel stopped waiting for one of those searches — and the next backfill rebuilds it. The scratch rows are deleted once a month is written; rows a closed page or a failed month left behind are deleted by a later backfill after seven days.

    Keep long backfills clear of the nightly retention run

    Each rollup’s *_retention search rewrites its whole collection once a night (00:34–00:58, 01:30–01:58 and 02:34–02:36 in the search head’s time zone). Rows a backfill writes into a collection while that collection’s retention is running can be lost. Start a long backfill so that it does not overlap that window — or re-run it afterwards, which restores anything lost (the backfill is idempotent).

    If you skip the backfill

    You don’t have to run it. Without a backfill, rolled-up panels simply start populating from the next hourly aggregation onward, filling in one hour at a time. The backfill is purely to make that history available immediately.

    Late-arriving data¶

    SAP LogServ data reaches Splunk through S3, Azure Blob and GCS notification queues, and some of it arrives after its hour has been aggregated: a log file delivered a few minutes after the hour, a weekly log rotation that delivers a week of lines at once, a queue backlog drained after an outage. Each hourly aggregation re-reads the hour before as well, so an event up to about an hour late is still counted, and an hour whose aggregation was skipped is rebuilt by the next run. Anything later is missing from the rolled-up panels until its hours are rebuilt.

    The Late-arriving data row at the top of the Backfill section finds those hours. It compares the index with the Multi-Cloud Overview rollup — which counts every event, per cloud provider, sourcetype and hour — per hour and sourcetype over the last 30 days (UTC), and lists the days on which the index holds events the rollups do not, most recent first:

    2026-09-26: 28,193 events in 42 hours (linux_secure, sap_logserv_logs)

    It leaves out the last three hours, which the hourly schedule may still rebuild, and anything older than the Multi-Cloud Overview rollup’s oldest hour. It also finds hours whose aggregation was switched off or skipped. Fewer events in the index than in a rollup — deleted or frozen data — is never reported. Backfill N days rebuilds every rollup for exactly those days, one window per run of consecutive days, with the same per-search dispatch as the backfill above, and the check runs again when it finishes; check again re-runs it at any time. A banner at the top of the tab repeats the count while any day is listed.

    The check needs the Multi-Cloud Overview aggregation switched on and that rollup’s history measured; otherwise the row says why it did not run.

    The same check also runs every day at 05:40 (search-head time) as the saved search logserv_late_arrival_check, over the last 30 days up to three hours ago, and records a triggered alert (Activity → Triggered Alerts, kept 2 days) when it finds a day — so a delivery that arrived days late is reported even if nobody opens this tab. Add an alert action, an email for example, to be told. The daily run never judges an hour older than the Multi-Cloud Overview rollup’s oldest, so a new install that has not run its first backfill raises no alert; it does raise one while hourly aggregation is switched off, because the rollups then fall behind the index. To run it at another time, change its schedule in Settings → Searches, reports, and alerts; keep the window ending at least three hours back, and keep it out of the nightly retention window (00:34–02:36), which rewrites the rollup it compares against.

    Why the schedule does not re-read days

    Each rollup’s search is one | union of several searches, and Splunk stops a union’s inner searches after about 30 seconds. An hourly run that re-read days would hit that limit on a large estate and overwrite good rows with lower counts. The backfill avoids it by running each inner search on its own — which is why late days are rebuilt from this tab rather than by the schedule.

    Per-rollup table¶

    One row per logical rollup (each dashboard, plus Environment Topology (graph), Environment Topology (detail tabs), and Beaconing detection). Some rows serve more than one dashboard, and their labels name each one: ABAP Operations is rebuilt with Work Process Performance / ABAP Operations, Web Dispatcher reads Web & API Performance / Web Dispatcher as well as its own Web Dispatcher Slowest Traces, and Network Perimeter reads its Firewall Drops in Transit count from Linux System & Security / Network Perimeter. Rebuild every row a dashboard reads. Columns:

    Column Meaning
    Dashboard The dashboard / view this rollup powers.
    Schedule The aggregate search’s cron (e.g. 5 * * * *); hover for the next scheduled run.
    Aggregation Per-rollup enable toggle (acts on that rollup’s aggregate search(es); a multi-collection rollup like the topology graph toggles all of its searches).
    History How far back the rollup reaches, measured from its oldest bucket — e.g. 106.7d of history (about 30 days or more counts as complete), empty, or live backfilling N/M while a backfill runs, then refreshing… for the moment it takes to re-measure the depth once that row’s searches have finished. After a run it can also read failed — re-run, truncated — re-run, or still running on server (hover for the search IDs). When the panel could not measure the history — Splunk had no free search slot, as is common just after a backfill, or the check search itself failed — the cell reads check failed — re-check: hover for the reason, and re-check measures that row again (checking… meanwhile). The checks run three at a time, and one that Splunk turns away is tried again after 2, 4 and 8 seconds.
    Actions Backfill (this rollup only, per-arm top-level dispatch) · Clear (delete this rollup’s collection(s), confirm-gated).

    Aggregation & retention (global controls)¶

    • Hourly aggregation — master switch. Enables/disables the scheduled saved searches that populate every rollup collection. Reads the live state of all aggregate searches and shows Enabled (all), Disabled (all), or Mixed (N/M on). Toggling flips them all (Mixed → enable all). Use the per-rollup toggles in the table to control one at a time.
    • Retention window — 365 days (read-only). Bucket rows older than this are trimmed daily by each rollup’s *_retention saved search. The trim never empties a collection on an empty read (override_if_empty=false), so a collection whose rows are all older than 365 days keeps them until new rows arrive. Uniform across all rollups; change default/savedsearches.conf to alter, and keep override_if_empty=false on every outputlookup of a retention search you change.

    Danger zone¶

    Clear all rollups — a confirm-gated button that deletes every row from all rollup collections at once. Use sparingly (e.g. to wipe a contaminated dataset before re-running a backfill against a corrected schema). Every dashboard is empty until the hourly aggregation or a backfill repopulates it.

    What “data freshness” means per panel¶

    • tstats and raw panels are real-time — they reflect events the instant they are indexed.
    • Rolled-up panels are accurate to the most-recently-completed hour, for time ranges of 90 minutes or wider. The hourly aggregation runs in the first half of each hour (:03–:28, one rollup per minute), so within the current partial hour a rolled-up panel shows data through the last completed hour, not the live partial hour. An event that reaches Splunk more than about an hour after its hour is counted once its days are rebuilt — see Late-arriving data.
    • Sub-hour time ranges are real-time — every rolled-up panel switches to raw events automatically (see below).

    Sub-hour time ranges (automatic)¶

    The rollups are keyed on whole-hour buckets, so a sub-hour time range — anything narrower than 90 minutes, such as Splunk’s Last 15 minutes or Last 60 minutes — cannot be answered correctly from the hourly cache alone: a window that falls inside a single hour matches no completed bucket (the panel would read empty), and a window that straddles an hour boundary would pull the whole hour (over-counting). To keep short ranges correct, every rolled-up panel automatically routes a sub-hour window to its underlying raw-event query instead of the cache — so a Last 15 minutes range shows accurate, real-time data at minute granularity with no action needed. For a window of 90 minutes or wider, the panel reads the fast hourly cache as usual.

    The switch is based purely on the selected range’s span (a 90-minute threshold), is transparent to the user, and applies across every rolled-up dashboard — including the two Sourcetype Mapping link graphs and the Host Details Role Activity tab. At 90 minutes and wider, a rolled-up chart never draws buckets finer than one hour, because the summaries are hourly; at Last 24 hours it draws hourly bars where a chart counted from the index draws 15-minute ones. Every time chart prints its bucket in its subtitle (see Chart Time Buckets). Because the sub-hour path runs the panel’s actual raw query, it is exact — not an approximation of the cache. (The trade-off is only speed, not correctness: a sub-hour raw query is inexpensive because it scans a small window, while a multi-day raw scan is what the hourly cache exists to avoid.)

    Investigating live activity

    Sub-hour ranges are already real-time (above), so you can simply narrow the time-range picker to see live activity on any rolled-up dashboard. For deeper ad-hoc investigation at any range, a panel’s Open in Search toolbar action jumps into Splunk’s Search app with the panel’s actual query and your selected time range pre-applied — the rollup read for a cached panel at a wide range, the raw query at sub-hour ranges.

    How the dashboards source their data¶

    Every panel reads from the cheapest correct data source for what it shows. There are two fast tiers plus a small set of panels that stay on raw events.

    Tier Used for Freshness Cost
    tstats on indexed fields Pure counts and averages over indexed dimensions (event volumes, host / sourcetype / cloud-provider breakdowns) Real-time Very low — reads the index’s tsidx, no raw-event scan
    KV-Store precompute rollups Most charts, tables, and KPIs across the dashboard suite Hourly for wide ranges; real-time for sub-hour ranges (automatic — see above) Near-zero at read time — a scheduled search precomputes the data once per hour
    Raw events Per-event listings, streamstats periodicity (beaconing), and a few timing traces that cannot be rolled up Real-time Bounded with \| head N where the panel is a time-ordered listing

    No CIM data-model acceleration is required

    The dashboards do not depend on accelerating the Common Information Model (CIM) Web / Authentication / Network data models. The fast path is the app’s own KV-Store rollups, which work regardless of whether you have accelerated any CIM model. (The app’s CIM tagging for Splunk Enterprise Security correlation is a separate, independent feature — see Enterprise Security → CIM Compliance.)

    The KV-Store rollup layer¶

    Behind the rolled-up panels is a set of KV-Store rollup collections (logserv_*_rollup, plus the Environment Topology graph collections). For each, a scheduled saved search (one per rollup) aggregates the last two completed hours of raw events into hour-bucketed rows — the previous hour, and the one before it again, so an event that arrives a little late is still counted (see Late-arriving data); the aggregates are staggered one per minute across :03–:28 of every hour. (Three rollups aggregate daily rather than hourly and are day-bucketed: the two beaconing detections and the topology IP-enrichment names.) The dashboard reads the collection back, filtered to the global time-range picker’s window via a bucket_ts range. Because the heavy aggregation happens once per hour in the background, opening a dashboard re-reads precomputed rows in roughly 0.1–0.6 seconds instead of dispatching a full raw scan.

    A daily retention search trims each collection to a rolling 365-day window. It never empties a collection on an empty read (override_if_empty=false), so a KV Store that is still starting up after a Splunkd restart cannot wipe a rollup.

    Reference¶

    Scheduled-search schedule¶

    The app’s scheduled searches are organized into three non-overlapping bands, plus one daily check, so that no two enabled scheduled searches ever fire in the same minute and the hourly aggregation never contends with the daily retention. This keeps the scheduler from bursting at high event volume.

    Band When What runs
    Hourly aggregates :03–:28 every hour, one per minute The always-on rollup-aggregate searches (logserv_*_aggregate / logserv_topology_aggregate_*), plus the Data Doctor’s platform snapshot at :02
    Daily retention + daily aggregates 00:30–00:58, 01:30–01:58 and 02:32–02:36, two minutes apart Every rollup’s retention trim, the two daily beaconing aggregates, the topology IP-enrichment aggregate, and the Data Doctor report/snapshot trims
    Enterprise Security :00–:01, :29, odd :31–:59, plus :30 in hours 02–05 (the daily anomaly scans) The splunk_sap_logserv_es_* searches (enabled by default) — see note below
    Late-arriving data check 05:40 daily logserv_late_arrival_check — a read-only tstats comparison of the index with the Multi-Cloud Overview rollup (about 5 s on the reference box); see Late-arriving data

    The per-search tables below give each search’s run time as typical / busy — the average and worst single-run duration observed on the validation fleet (~10.7M events/day). Aggregate run times scale with the per-hour event volume; retention run times scale with the collection size. Run times are indicative, measured on a ~10.7M events/day validation instance. Every hourly aggregate completes well within its one-minute slot; the heaviest daily retention trims take about a minute and sit in the two-minutes-apart daily band.

    Hourly aggregate band (:03–:28)¶

    Each rollup aggregate dispatches the last two completed hours (-2h@h..@h) and rewrites both. The newest bucket is still the just-completed hour, so the firing minute is freshness-neutral — spreading them one-per-minute simply avoids a burst at :05. Peak concurrency is ~1–2 instead of 26. The run times below were measured when each run read one hour; reading two roughly doubles them. Two keep a one-hour window: logserv_topology_aggregate_inventory (keyed by value, not by hour) and the Data Doctor’s platform snapshot at :02.

    Daily band (00:30–02:36)¶

    Retention trims and the daily aggregates run off-peak — 15 searches at 00:30–00:58, 15 more at 01:30–01:58, and 3 at 02:32–02:36, all two minutes apart. Keeping them at minute :30 or later guarantees they never collide with the hourly aggregate band (which fires at :03–:28 of every hour); the two Data Doctor trims take the last two slots of hour 01, 01:56 and 01:58. Each retention search trims its collection to the rolling 365-day window and never empties it on an empty read (override_if_empty=false); the two beaconing aggregates (00:30, 00:32) precompute the per-day DNS/perimeter beaconing statistics. (Retention run times scale with collection size, so the larger rollups — Environment Topology detail, Host Role Activity, DNS, Web & API, Network Perimeter — take longest; all are off-peak and collision-free.)

    01:48 logserv_beaconing_detail_retention Trim beaconing gap-stats 1 / 1 s
    01:50 logserv_topology_detail_retention Trim Environment Topology (detail tabs) 63 / 69 s
    01:52 logserv_stmap_retention Trim Sourcetype Mapping 24 / 24 s
    01:54 logserv_hostrole_retention Trim Host Role Activity 38 / 38 s
    01:56 logserv_diag_reports_retention Trim the Data Doctor’s saved diagnostic reports (365 d + row cap) < 1 s
    01:58 logserv_diag_platform_retention Trim the Data Doctor’s platform snapshot (30 d) < 1 s
    02:32 logserv_topology_enrichment_aggregate Recompute the topology IP-node hostname/user names (daily, last 30 d) 5 / 8 s
    02:34 logserv_topology_enrichment_retention Trim the topology IP-enrichment names (365 d on last-seen) < 1 s
    02:36 logserv_topology_edges_retention Trim Environment Topology (graph — edges) about 8 s

    The two Environment Topology (graph) trim times are single-night estimates, not typical / busy measurements like the other rows.

    Enterprise Security band (enabled by default)¶

    The 22 splunk_sap_logserv_es_* searches ship enabled (see Enterprise Security → The ES schedule) on crons that sit entirely in the minutes the always-on bands leave free — :00–:01, :29, and the odd minutes :31–:59 — so they are collision-free with both the aggregate band (:02–:28, including the Data Doctor’s :02 platform snapshot) and the daily band (00:30–00:58, 01:30–01:58 and 02:32–02:36). 16 correlation searches run hourly, the 2 Asset/Identity feeds every 4 hours, and the 4 behavioral-anomaly searches once a day each, at :30 (hours 02–05). Two of them (splunk_sap_logserv_es_anomaly_user_auth_volume and splunk_sap_logserv_es_anomaly_after_hours_admin) scan 30 days of raw events, and the other two read the KV Store rollups.

    Measured behavior¶

    On the validation fleet (335M events), the hourly aggregates each complete in seconds and the slowest daily retention trim is ~1 minute (see the per-search tables above); the scheduler logs 0 skipped / 0 deferred. The two heaviest ES searches — the 30-day anomaly scans (~150–340 s and ~50–120 s) — run once a day, so they add no hourly load.

    The Data Doctor adds two scheduled searches: logserv_diag_platform_aggregate (hourly at :02, a seconds-fast scan of the last hour of index=_internal) and logserv_diag_platform_retention (daily at 01:58, trims the platform snapshot to 30 days). The shipped schedule is verified by a permanent build gate: every enabled scheduled search has a unique (hour, minute) — zero cron collisions.

    Behavior with multiple search heads¶

    How these scheduled searches behave depends on the search-head topology:

    Search Head Cluster (SHC) — the supported multi-SH topology. Works cleanly, with no extra configuration:

    • The SHC captain delegates each scheduled search to a single member per fire, so every aggregate and retention search runs once cluster-wide per interval — not once per member. There is no multiplication of load by the number of search heads.
    • KV Store is automatically replicated across the cluster. Whichever member runs an aggregate writes the rollup to its local KV Store, and Splunk replicates the collection to every member — so all search heads serve the dashboards from the same rolled-up data, regardless of which member computed it. (The rollup design depends on KV Store, which is cluster-replicated by default.)
    • The app’s saved searches and collection definitions deploy to all members via the SHC deployer (splunk apply shcluster-bundle), Splunk’s standard process. The one-click Settings → Dashboard Data → Run backfill also works cluster-wide — an admin runs it from any member and the results replicate.
    • The one-search-per-minute staggering helps here too: it keeps the per-minute scheduled load at ~1, which the captain can place on any member without bunching.

    Independent (non-clustered) search heads. If the app is installed on two or more standalone search heads that are not in a SHC, each one runs its own copy of the schedule against its own KV Store (there is no replication between independent search heads). The aggregates therefore run N times — once per search head — which is redundant indexer load, and each search head maintains its rollups independently (they can drift slightly in timing). It is not broken — each search head’s dashboards work off its own rollups — but it is wasteful. Recommendation: use a SHC for multi-SH deployments. If independent search heads are unavoidable, keep the schedule enabled, and run the backfill, on every one of them: each search head’s dashboards read only the rollups in its own KV Store, so a search head whose aggregates are switched off shows empty rolled-up panels at ranges of 90 minutes or wider.

    Single search head (the default — one SH, with or without separate indexers): the search head runs the whole schedule itself, dispatching the raw scans to its indexer peers and writing the rollups to its own KV Store. Nothing special is required.

    KV Store must be enabled and healthy

    The rollups live in Splunk’s KV Store, so KV Store must be enabled on the search head(s) — it is by default, and is already required for the Environment Topology view and the AI Assistant settings. On a SHC, KV Store replication must be healthy for rollups computed on one member to appear on the others.

    What to know at a glance¶

    • Most panels are hourly-fresh; counts and per-event listings are real-time. If a rolled-up trend looks an hour behind at a multi-day range, that’s expected.
    • Sub-hour time ranges (under 90 minutes) are real-time automatically — a rolled-up panel routes a Last 15 minutes-style window to its raw query, so short ranges stay minute-accurate with no manual step.
    • Scheduled searches are staggered into collision-free bands — hourly aggregates at :03–:28 (plus the platform snapshot at :02), daily retention + maintenance at 00:30–00:58, 01:30–01:58 and 02:32–02:36, the late-arriving data check at 05:40, and the ES content (enabled by default) in the minutes those bands leave free — :00/:01 for the feeds, :29 and odd :31–:59 for the hourly correlations, and :30 at hours 02–05 for the daily anomaly searches — so no two enabled scheduled searches collide.
    • After installing on an index that already holds history, run Settings → Dashboard Data → Run backfill once — 30 days by default, or a longer window up to 365 days, or a custom range. It needs a role named admin, sc_admin or sc_subadmin.
    • Late-arriving data is listed and rebuilt in Settings → Dashboard Data. The hourly aggregation re-reads the hour before, which catches events up to about an hour late; the days holding anything later are listed under Late-arriving data, with a one-click backfill of exactly those days.
    • No CIM acceleration is needed for dashboard performance.
    • Use a panel’s Open in Search action for ad-hoc raw-event investigation at any range (sub-hour ranges are already real-time on the dashboard itself). The panel toolbar is described in the Dashboards Overview.

    AWS S3 Direct: Backfill and Recovery¶

    Use this page to load LogServ days straight from an S3 bucket: history older than the notifications SAP’s queue still holds, and windows whose notifications expired, were purged or were discarded. It works with every AWS scenario (Connect, Filter and Copy), and none of them loads history on its own.

    The three AWS setup guides all use the SQS-Based S3 input: a bucket sends a notification for every new object (SAP’s bucket under Connect and Filter, where the Filter Lambda passes on the notifications it keeps; your copy bucket under Copy), a queue holds it, and the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services fetches exactly that object. That is the steady-state ingest path, and nothing on this page replaces it.

    This page covers the Generic S3 input (aws_s3://) that the same add-on also ships. It polls a bucket prefix directly and needs no queue at all. It exists for the cases the notification path cannot serve:

    • Backfilling a date range that predates your input — logs that were already in the bucket before you configured LogServ ingest.
    • Recovering from an outage — if the heavy forwarder is down long enough for queue messages to age out, those notifications are gone permanently, but the objects are still in the bucket. The same holds for notifications SAP purged, and for those the AWS Remote S3 Filter Lambda discarded because it could not read or forward them.
    • A bucket with no notification wiring — for example, a copy of the logs you hold yourself.

    The quickest way to run one is the AWS S3 Direct screen in the Data TA (section 2a): you choose dashboards and a range of days, and it builds the inputs. Appendix A explains the input itself, for anyone configuring one by hand.

    Note

    Direct S3 polling is a secondary channel, intended to be switched on for a specific job and switched off again. Splunk’s own guidance is to use SQS-Based S3 for ongoing ingest; see Scale limits below.


    1. Before You Start¶

    Check these before the first backfill. Each one, missed, makes a backfill find nothing, lose its events again soon after, or label them wrongly.

    • Where it runs. Run the screen on the heavy forwarder that will hold the inputs (strongly recommended): a Generic S3 input collects from the instance it is defined on. With no heavy forwarder, the single instance or your Splunk Cloud search head works too. The Splunk Add-on for AWS must be installed there directly, not distributed by a Deployment Server, with the AWS account and IAM role from your setup guide. If a Deployment Server manages the add-on, the screen only shows the configuration to apply there, because the next push would delete inputs created on the forwarder.
    • Your Splunk role holds admin_all_objects. The screen creates inputs only for such an account; without it, it shows the configuration for an administrator to apply (see the note under Creating and managing backfills).
    • The IAM role can list the bucket. It needs s3:ListBucket on the bucket, and for a bucket in SAP’s account SAP’s bucket policy must allow it as well (IAM Permissions).
    • The index keeps old data long enough. Splunk removes data from an index a bucket at a time, once the newest event in the bucket is older than the index’s retention period: the events’ own time counts, not when they were indexed. Check that the retention of sap_logserv_logs (or the name you gave it) reaches back past the oldest day you will load. On Splunk Cloud it is the index’s Searchable retention (days) (Settings → Indexes, then the index’s name). On Splunk Enterprise it is frozenTimePeriodInSecs for the index on the indexers; the Data TA’s index definition sets none, so Splunk’s default of 188697600 seconds (about six years) applies unless you or whoever created the index set another. With a shorter retention, the backfilled events are removed soon after they are indexed, and the dashboard rebuild in section 3 cannot find them. A longer retention uses more storage. The index’s size limit (Max raw data size on Splunk Cloud, maxTotalDataSizeMB on Splunk Enterprise) removes the oldest data the same way once it is reached, so check that the backfill fits too.
    • Days in the Past. With Enable Filtering on, the Data TA drops at index time every event older than its Days in the Past cutoff, backfilled events included; the screen leaves those days out and says so. To load older history, raise Days in the Past on Configuration → Filters first (Decide Filtering, Days in the Past). Where a Deployment Server manages this forwarder’s Data TA, make the change there: Save it, click Deploy to Forwarders, and wait for the forwarders to restart (allow 5 minutes or more) before you create the backfill (Changing Settings Later). The screen on the forwarder still judges by the settings stored there, which the Deployment Server does not keep up to date (What it checks); if it still leaves the older days out, create the inputs for those days by hand (Appendix A).
    • The Cloud Provider dropdown at Not set. The screen stamps each input with _meta = cloud_provider::aws, as the recommended setup does for the SQS-Based S3 inputs (Choose Cloud Attribution). The Data TA’s Cloud Provider dropdown adds its value next to the input’s, so with the dropdown on AWS the backfilled events can carry aws twice. This follows from how Splunk writes _meta and has not been reproduced in the lab (the dropdown set to AWS).


    2. Create the Backfill¶

    Create the inputs with the AWS S3 Direct screen (section 2a). You can also create them by hand over REST or inputs.conf (Appendix A), but not with the Splunk Add-on for AWS’s own Generic S3 form, which needs an AWS permission that cannot be scoped to one bucket (A2).

    2a. The AWS S3 Direct screen¶

    The Data TA ships a screen for this job: Splunk Web → Splunk TA for SAP LogServ → AWS S3 Direct. It is the main way to create these inputs. It creates and manages LogServ-scoped Generic S3 inputs inside the AWS add-on from your browser, as the signed-in user, and adds no capability of its own. Its one server-side part is a small Data TA endpoint, POST /services/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/s3_direct_meta, which writes the _meta = cloud_provider::aws stamp into an input this screen created and restarts that input. It also runs as the signed-in user, so Splunk checks that user’s own permissions.

    Run it on the heavy forwarder that will hold the inputs — strongly recommended. A Generic S3 input collects from the instance it is defined on, so creating one on a search head or indexer means that instance starts polling S3, which puts ingest load on the tier your users search on. The screen does not prevent it: on Splunk Cloud, and on an instance with no enabled AWS inputs, it shows a warning that recommends a heavy forwarder, and works as usual. It accepts the Splunk Add-on for AWS 8.1.0, the version it was validated against, and any later version without a warning; an older version gets an advisory banner. It reads the add-on’s accounts from its combined account list and, when that cannot be read, from the account endpoint the add-on’s API reference documents. When it cannot read the add-on’s accounts, IAM roles or Generic S3 inputs, it names each request that failed and shows the configuration to apply instead of creating inputs; the account or the IAM role is typed in where its list could not be read. An SQS-Based S3 input list it cannot read is reported too and does not stop a create, but the warning about days those inputs may still be delivering cannot name them, and unless it read an enabled Generic S3 input, the screen cannot tell whether this instance already runs AWS inputs. When it cannot read Splunk’s list of apps, it reads the add-on’s own lists instead: if they answer, it works as usual without the version check; if not, it says it cannot tell whether the add-on is installed. When it cannot read the list of indexes, or the list is empty, it says so, and the Index field takes a typed name, filled in as sap_logserv_logs; a typed name must follow Splunk’s index naming rule (lower-case letters, digits, underscores and hyphens, not starting with an underscore or a hyphen and not containing kvstore).

    Example — three rows chosen, and the plan the screen builds from them

    You choose dashboards and days; the screen builds the keys¶

    • Dashboards — the same rows as the LogServ App’s Settings → Dashboard Data list. Tick one or several. The screen reads every S3 folder (<clz_dir>/<clz_subdir>) those rows are built from, and a folder two rows share is read once.
    • Scan from and Scan until — two UTC dates, both included, with no time of day. They select the date in the key, logserv/<clz_dir>/<clz_subdir>/YYYY/MM/DD/, which is the date of the events inside. Scan until can be today at the latest, and a range covers at most 366 days.

    From those the screen creates one input per S3 folder and calendar year:

    • its key prefix is the tightest one that holds the chosen days — the day itself, else its month, else its year;
    • a whitelist names the exact days, so an input for 14 to 18 September reads those five day folders and nothing else under …/2026/09/;
    • it is named logserv_backfill_<job>_<folder>_<year>, where <job> is the name you give the backfill (lower-case letters, digits and hyphens, up to 24 characters).
    Which S3 folders each dashboard row reads

    Derived from the searches that build each rollup, and checked against the LogServ App on every build. The four rows whose searches read the whole index take all 32 folders. Squid appears under both of its real layouts, proxy/squid (the AWS bucket) and linux/proxy (Azure), and the Pacemaker cluster log under linux/pacemaker (GCP); a folder your bucket does not have gives an input that finds nothing.

    A row is not always a whole dashboard. Environment Health, DNS Analytics and Network Perimeter also read the Beaconing detection row, the Firewall Drops in Transit count on Network Perimeter reads the Linux System & Security / Network Perimeter row, ABAP Operations is built from the Work Process Performance / ABAP Operations row, and Web Dispatcher reads both Web & API Performance / Web Dispatcher and Web Dispatcher Slowest Traces — tick all the rows a dashboard uses. The Windows event logs are one sourcetype fed by four channel folders, so a row that reads Windows events reads all four.

    The write-time window is set for you¶

    Every input the screen creates selects objects whatever their write time (initial_scan_datetime = 2000-01-01T00:00:00Z) and stops by itself a day after it is created (terminal_scan_datetime = the moment of creation plus 24 hours). The margin is deliberate: the add-on records a scan as finished once a pass that started after the terminal time completes, and a finished input no longer fetches. With no margin, a forwarder restart part-way through the first pass would strand the objects it had found but not yet read. A day out, the next run carries on from the add-on’s own checkpoint. Until then each input re-lists its prefix every 30 minutes, which finds nothing new in a closed day.

    What it checks before it creates anything¶

    • Days already covered. A folder-day that an earlier backfill from this screen already covers — enabled or disabled — is skipped, and the plan says which backfill covers it. Inputs made another way select by write time, so the screen cannot tell which days they read: where they overlap, it warns but does not skip.
    • The SQS window. A range that reaches today or either of the two days before it (UTC) warns that the SQS-Based S3 input is probably still delivering those days, and objects it has already delivered would be ingested a second time.
    • This forwarder’s own filters. A folder the Configuration → Filters include or exclude patterns drop is left out, and days older than the days_in_past cutoff are left out of the whitelist — their events would be sent to nullQueue on arrival — each with a warning that names the setting to change. If nothing is left, the screen refuses. These checks apply only while Enable Filtering is on.
      • Source rules are notes, not verdicts. Include Sources and Exclude Sources match each event’s source (its file), which the screen cannot see from a folder, so they never change whether a folder is planned. A folder the include filter leaves out is noted some files may be kept by Include Sources and stays left out — add it to Include Filters to backfill it; a planned folder is noted some files may be dropped by Exclude Sources. See Configuring Filters.
      • A refused stored value is reported first. If a stored filter setting holds a value the Data TA refuses (after a hand edit of its settings file, for example), the forwarder keeps the filter it generated before, which the screen cannot see, so the screen says its filter notes may not match that filter until the value is corrected on the Filters tab.
      • On a forwarder a Deployment Server manages, the filter it runs comes from the Deployment Server, which pushes the generated rules but not the settings; the settings stored on the forwarder, which the screen reads, can be older than those rules. Whenever it shows a filter note, the screen says so: check the Filters tab on the Deployment Server before relying on the notes.
    • The basics. A job name not already in use, an AWS account, an IAM role, a region, a valid bucket name and an index.
    • When the Generic S3 input list cannot be read, the screen cannot see which days earlier backfills cover or which job names are taken, so it skips those two checks and says so, in the form and as a comment at the top of the generated stanzas and REST calls.

    Creating and managing backfills¶

    A plan below the form lists every input to be created with its key prefix and days, and updates as you type. Create backfill (N inputs) re-lists the existing inputs first, and creates nothing if that list cannot be read; then it creates the plan’s inputs one at a time. It stops at the first failure and reports what was and was not created, and it never retries a create. To finish a partial run, create the same selection again under a new job name: the days the created inputs cover are skipped.

    Each input is stamped _meta = cloud_provider::aws, the value the recommended setup puts on each SQS-Based S3 input (Choose Cloud Attribution), so the Multi-Cloud dashboard attributes the backfilled events the same way. Leave the Data TA’s Cloud Provider dropdown at Not set: it adds its value next to the input’s, so with it on AWS the backfilled events can carry the value twice (how Splunk writes _meta; not yet reproduced in the lab). The add-on’s create cannot carry that field, so the screen writes it into the new input’s stanza through the Data TA endpoint described above, straight after the create, and restarts the input, before its first scan. If a stamp does not complete, the confirmation names the input and the reason.

    After a create, the screen names the next step — rebuild the dashboard rollups in the LogServ App for the same rows and the same dates (section 3).

    The list at the top groups backfills by job, with Enable all, Disable all and Delete all. Under each backfill are two searches to copy into Search: whether its inputs finished their scan, and how many events reached the index over its own days. Inputs made another way are listed individually. A backfill cannot be edited: to change one, delete it and create another.

    Prefer Disable to Delete once a backfill has finished. The screen knows which days are covered only while the inputs that covered them exist. Deleting a finished backfill makes its days eligible again, and a later backfill of the same rows would read them a second time.

    Note

    If your Splunk account lacks admin_all_objects the screen cannot write the inputs for you. It does not fail silently: under the heading Apply this as an administrator it renders the exact inputs.conf stanzas and curl commands to hand to an administrator, one per input. The inputs stop by themselves a day after the configuration was generated, so apply it the same day or generate it again. On Splunk Cloud, see Capability-gated REST endpoints.

    Everything in the sections below and in Appendix A applies to an input created this way — the screen is a front end to the same aws_s3:// input.


    3. Rebuild the Dashboards for the Backfilled Dates¶

    Until you do, the data is searchable but the dashboards will not show it, because every dashboard panel reads an hourly KV Store rollup rather than the index directly, and the hourly aggregation searches only ever process the hour just past. They will never reach back over events that arrived today carrying last year’s timestamps.

    In the LogServ App, go to Settings -> Dashboard Data (The Dashboard Data settings tab), choose a Custom range covering the dates you just ingested, and backfill the rows for the dashboards you backfilled.

    Match the dates in the key, not a write-time window

    The dates to enter are the dates in the keys you read — the YYYY/MM/DD part of logserv/<clz_dir>/<clz_subdir>/YYYY/MM/DD/. If you used the AWS S3 Direct screen, those are its Scan from and Scan until dates: enter the same two, for the same rows. If you created an input by hand, they are not its initial_scan_datetime / terminal_scan_datetime: those bound the S3 object’s upload time, which for a re-staged archive can differ from the event dates by months — see A1. Entering the scan window here rebuilds the wrong months and reports success.

    The backfill is idempotent, so re-running it over a range you have already built is safe. Long windows are dispatched a month at a time. Keep the page open until every row has finished, the Environment Topology (graph) row in particular: its rows are written only while the page is open (Backfilling on first install).

    Two topology collections always use the last 30 days

    The Environment Topology inventory and IP enrichment collections describe current state rather than history — they have no time dimension — so they always refresh over the last 30 days whatever window you choose. The inventory records each IP address or host under its most recent SID (of the SIDs seen in its newest hour of activity, the one with the most events; an exact tie keeps the previous row), so an IP reassigned during the window maps to its new SID once its newest hour names only that one.


    IAM Permissions¶

    Generic S3 needs one permission more than the SQS-based path:

    Action Scopable to one bucket? Needed for Already in the shipped CloudFormation?
    s3:GetObject ✅ Yes Fetching each object ✅ Yes
    s3:ListBucket ✅ Yes Discovering keys under the prefix ✅ Yes, on the role. A bucket in SAP’s account also needs it in SAP’s bucket policy
    s3:ListAllMyBuckets ❌ No — Resource: "*" only The UI dropdown only, never the runtime ❌ No, and not required

    s3:ListBucket is the one that catches people out. The SQS-based input never needs it — the queue message supplies the exact object key, so GetObject alone is enough. An environment that was provisioned narrowly for SQS-based ingest will therefore fail at the discovery step with an AccessDenied that mentions the bucket rather than the missing action. The CloudFormation templates shipped with this solution grant it to the role (splunk-logserv-ta-role). For a bucket in your own account, such as the copy bucket of AWS Remote S3 Copy, that is enough (for history under Copy you read SAP’s bucket, so SAP’s bucket policy applies there too). SAP’s bucket belongs to the SAP ECS account, and for such a cross-account request AWS also requires SAP’s bucket policy to allow s3:ListBucket for that role on the bucket ARN (arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>, not /*). The example bucket policy shipped with the setup guides includes it, but SQS-based ingest never needed it, so confirm with SAP LogServ Support that it was applied before you run a backfill.


    Idempotency¶

    The input keeps a checkpoint keyed on the highest LastModified it has processed, so a prefix that has already been drained is not re-ingested on the next poll. Re-running the same input is safe.

    If you deliberately want to ingest a prefix a second time, create an input under a new name rather than editing the old one — a fresh input starts with a fresh checkpoint. Two inputs over the same keys do not share a checkpoint, so both ingest; that is why the AWS S3 Direct screen skips days an earlier backfill from it already covers.


    Scale limits¶

    The add-on displays this advisory on the Generic S3 setup page:

    Amazon S3 buckets with an excessive number of files or abundant size will result in significant performance degradation and ingestion delays. Configure an SQS-Based S3 input to achieve efficiency.

    Take it seriously, and note two things about it:

    • It is unconditional. The equivalent message appears in the input’s own log on every discovery run — it was emitted while scanning a prefix containing five objects. Seeing it in a log is not evidence of a problem with your bucket.
    • The reason behind it is real. Generic S3 has to list the prefix on every polling interval, and listing cost scales with the number of keys underneath it, not with the amount of new data — a whitelist narrows what is fetched, not what is listed.

    The practical consequence for LogServ buckets is that prefix scope matters enormously, because LogServ keys are dense:

    Prefix Objects
    logserv/hana/hanaaudit/2025/06/11/ (one type, one day) 39
    logserv/proxy/squid/ (one type, all dates) 182,565

    Nothing in the input caps the work for you. The input declares max_items = 100000, but the Splunk Add-on for AWS never reads it (checked in 8.1.0 and 8.3.1), so it bounds nothing.

    Scope every backfill input to a log type and a date range. The AWS S3 Direct screen already does — one input per folder and year, with the prefix narrowed to the month or the day when the range allows. A range that spans several months lists that folder’s whole year on each pass, so for a very dense folder prefer one backfill per month.


    Troubleshooting¶

    Symptom Cause Fix
    AccessDenied on the bucket dropdown in the UI The dropdown calls ListBuckets, which needs the unscopable s3:ListAllMyBuckets Use the AWS S3 Direct screen, or create the input over REST or inputs.conf — section 2a and A4
    AccessDenied that looks like a bucket or prefix problem aws_iam_role was left empty, so the input authenticated as the bare IAM user Set aws_iam_role on the input (A3)
    AccessDenied during key discovery while GetObject works s3:ListBucket missing — the SQS-based path never needed it Add s3:ListBucket on the bucket ARN to the role’s policy. For SAP’s bucket, also ask SAP LogServ Support to allow it for your role in the bucket policy (IAM Permissions)
    The AWS S3 Direct screen shows Apply this as an administrator instead of creating inputs Your account lacks admin_all_objects, a configuration read failed, or a Deployment Server manages the AWS add-on; the reason is shown on the screen Sign in with an account that holds admin_all_objects, or hand the generated configuration to an administrator the same day. On Splunk Cloud, see Capability-gated REST endpoints
    A hand-made input runs but finds nothing The scan window is bounding LastModified, not event time — and a blank initial_scan_datetime is not “no lower bound”, it is now minus seven days Express the date range in key_name (and a whitelist), and set initial_scan_datetime to an explicit floor such as 2000-01-01T00:00:00Z (not a 1970 date - Splunk’s time parser rejects those, and the input then polls forever without fetching anything). Never leave it blank — A1
    The AWS S3 Direct screen offers no Create button Something blocks the plan; the reason is shown above it Fix what the red banners say — often a job name already in use, or every day skipped as covered or filtered
    The screen skips days you expected it to read An earlier backfill from this screen covers them, or this forwarder’s filters drop them — the plan names which To read covered days again, delete the backfill that covers them first. That ingests its events a second time, so do it only if they never arrived
    Backfilled events can be searched at first, then disappear The index’s retention is shorter than the age of the days you loaded, or the backfill took the index past its size limit, so Splunk removes them Raise the retention or the size limit before you load (section 1), then load those days again
    400 Wrong datetime with format The offset form from the add-on’s spec was used Use the literal Z form, 2026-09-01T00:00:00Z
    Two inputs ingesting the same prefix name was sent on an update, which forks rather than renames Delete the duplicate; send name only on create
    Events land under sourcetype sap_logserv_logs rather than a real type The Data TA is not installed on this forwarder, or the object is not a LogServ envelope See installing the Data TA
    Backfilled events do not appear in the dashboards Dashboard panels read hourly rollups, which summarise only the hour just past Section 3 — rebuild the rollups from Settings → Dashboard Data in the LogServ App, with a Custom range matching the dates in the key (the screen’s Scan from and Scan until)


    A note on Azure and GCP¶

    There is no equivalent to this on the other two clouds. The Azure and GCP add-ons are notification-driven only: if a Storage Queue message or a Pub/Sub notification is purged or expires before it is consumed, the object stays in the bucket but nothing in the shipped add-ons will fetch it. If you need to recover such a window, contact your Splunk team.


    Appendix A. Generic S3 Inputs by Hand¶

    The AWS S3 Direct screen handles everything below for you. Read this appendix to create a Generic S3 input yourself, or to understand what the screen’s inputs do.

    A1. The prefix selects the events — the scan window does not¶

    This is the single most important thing to understand before configuring the input by hand, and it is easy to get backwards.

    A LogServ object key looks like this:

    logserv/<clz_dir>/<clz_subdir>/<YYYY>/<MM>/<DD>/<filename>.json.gz

    The date in that path is the event date — the day the logs inside the object were produced.

    The input also has two datetime fields, initial_scan_datetime and terminal_scan_datetime. Both bound the object’s S3 LastModified timestamp — the moment the object was written to the bucket. Neither has any relationship to the timestamps of the events inside it. The add-on names the field last_modified internally, and it is last_modified that its resume checkpoint is keyed on.

    Those two clocks routinely diverge by a wide margin, because SAP writes objects into event-dated paths some time after the events occur. Objects sampled from a LogServ bucket carried 2025 event dates while every one of them had a LastModified in 2026.

    So: to ingest a particular range of log dates, express it in the key — the key_name prefix, and for several days a whitelist (A4). Use the scan-window fields only when you genuinely want to bound by upload time — for example, “only objects written since the outage began”. The AWS S3 Direct screen works this way: its Scan from and Scan until are dates in the key.

    A blank scan field does not mean “no bound”

    Leaving initial_scan_datetime empty does not mean “from the beginning of the prefix”. The add-on substitutes now minus seven days — aws_s3_conf.py::_get_last_modified_time treats both an empty value and the literal string default that way. A backfill of a historical prefix left blank therefore selects nothing, logs an ordinary keys are scanned line and reports success. Set it to an explicit floor instead - but not a 1970 date. Splunk’s own search/timeparser rejects those (HTTP 400 Invalid time.), and the add-on resolves this field through that parser on every poll while validating only locally on create: the input saves cleanly, reports success and then fetches nothing, permanently. 2000-01-01T00:00:00Z is below anything S3 can hold (S3 launched in 2006) and parses correctly.

    Leaving terminal_scan_datetime empty is the opposite problem: the add-on returns an open-ended sentinel and the input keeps polling indefinitely. Set it so a backfill run terminates on its own.

    The AWS S3 Direct screen (section 2a) sets both itself and never sends a blank.

    How this was established

    Objects were copied into a bucket so that their LastModified (2026-09-09) and their envelope event time (2025-06-11) were about fifteen months apart. Three inputs were then created over the identical prefix, differing only in their scan bounds:

    test initial_scan_datetime terminal_scan_datetime keys selected events
    T1 2020-01-01 2026-09-01 (after the events, before the write) 0 0
    T2 2020-01-01 2026-12-31 5 5
    T3 2026-09-05 (after the events, before the write) — 5 5

    Bounding on LastModified predicts 0 and 5; bounding on event time predicts 5 and 0. The measured results match LastModified in both directions.

    A2. Why the add-on’s own form cannot create this input¶

    The add-on’s S3 Bucket field on the Generic S3 setup page is a dropdown with no free-text entry, and the endpoint that populates it calls the AWS ListBuckets API. That requires the s3:ListAllMyBuckets permission, which cannot be scoped to a single bucket — AWS accepts only Resource: "*" for it.

    The consequence is worth stating plainly, because the symptom is confusing:

    • The input works perfectly at runtime on a bucket-scoped policy. Only the form that creates it is blocked.
    • If you try to use the UI you will see AccessDenied on the bucket dropdown, and the form cannot be saved, because there is no way to type the bucket name instead.

    Whether granting s3:ListAllMyBuckets is even an option depends on which topology you deployed:

    Topology Whose bucket is it? s3:ListAllMyBuckets
    AWS Remote S3 Connect SAP ECS account Expect SAP to refuse — it would expose their entire bucket inventory
    AWS Remote S3 Filter SAP ECS account Same
    AWS Remote S3 Copy Your Secondary account for the copies; the SAP ECS account for history (your copy holds only the files copied since the Lambda’s trigger was activated) Your call for your own bucket, the same as above for SAP’s — and not required either way, since the steps below avoid the form

    There are two ways round it, and neither needs s3:ListAllMyBuckets:

    • The AWS S3 Direct screen shipped with the Splunk TA for SAP LogServ (Splunk Web → Splunk TA for SAP LogServ → AWS S3 Direct). It types the bucket name rather than listing buckets, so the blocked endpoint is never called. See section 2a.
    • REST or inputs.conf directly, as in A4, which likewise never touches that endpoint.

    A3. Set aws_iam_role explicitly¶

    All three AWS topologies authenticate through a cross-account IAM role, and the Generic S3 input does not infer it. If you set only aws_account and leave aws_iam_role empty, the input authenticates as the bare IAM user — which holds essentially no S3 permissions — and returns an AccessDenied that reads exactly like a bucket or prefix problem. Always set both.

    A4. Run-once backfill procedure by hand¶

    The pattern is: create the input scoped to the keys you want, let it drain, confirm, then disable it. The AWS S3 Direct screen does steps a and b for you, one input per folder and year; this is the same job by hand. Check section 1 first.

    A4.a Work out the prefix. Narrow it as far as you can — ideally to a single log type and a single day, for example logserv/hana/hanaaudit/2025/06/11/. Prefix scope is your main control over how much work the input does; see Scale limits. To read several days in one input, give it the month or year as its prefix and name the days in a whitelist (below).

    A4.b Create the input on the heavy forwarder, either by writing a stanza into $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/Splunk_TA_aws/local/inputs.conf or over REST. Set both scan bounds explicitly (A1): the floor, and a terminal time a day or so from now so the input stops by itself. The stanza form:

    [aws_s3://logserv_backfill_hana_20250611]
aws_account = <your configured AWS account name>
aws_iam_role = <your cross-account IAM role name>
bucket_name = <the LogServ bucket>
key_name = logserv/hana/hanaaudit/2025/06/11/
initial_scan_datetime = 2000-01-01T00:00:00Z
terminal_scan_datetime = <tomorrow, e.g. 2026-09-26T00:00:00Z>
index = sap_logserv_logs
sourcetype = sap_logserv_logs
parse_csv_with_delimiter =
polling_interval = 1800
_meta = cloud_provider::aws

    The equivalent REST call (curl prompts for the password). It cannot carry _meta — the add-on’s endpoint refuses it with 400 Argument "_meta" is not supported by this handler — so add that line to the stanza afterwards, then disable and enable the input so it starts from the stanza as written:

    curl -sk -u '<your-splunk-username>' \
  https://<heavy-forwarder>:8089/servicesNS/nobody/Splunk_TA_aws/data/inputs/aws_s3 \
  -d name=logserv_backfill_hana_20250611 \
  -d aws_account=<account> \
  -d aws_iam_role=<role> \
  -d bucket_name=<bucket> \
  -d index=sap_logserv_logs \
  -d sourcetype=sap_logserv_logs \
  -d parse_csv_with_delimiter= \
  --data-urlencode initial_scan_datetime=2000-01-01T00:00:00Z \
  --data-urlencode terminal_scan_datetime=<tomorrow, e.g. 2026-09-26T00:00:00Z> \
  --data-urlencode key_name=logserv/hana/hanaaudit/2025/06/11/
    Several days in one input: the whitelist

    Give the input the month (or year) as its key_name and a whitelist naming the days — this is what the AWS S3 Direct screen writes:

    key_name = logserv/hana/hanaaudit/2025/06/
whitelist = ^logserv/hana/hanaaudit/2025/(?:06/(?:10|11|12))/.+$

    The add-on matches the whitelist against the whole key with Python’s re.search, and appends $ when the pattern does not end with one — so write the pattern to run to the end of the key, as above. A whitelist overrides any blacklist. It filters what the listing returns; the listing itself still covers everything under key_name, so keep the prefix as tight as the days allow.

    Note

    Creating the input starts it immediately. The add-on rejects disabled on create (400 Argument "disabled" is not supported by this handler); it is accepted only on a later update. If you need to stage a configuration without running it, create it and then disable it as two calls.

    A4.c Watch it work. The input logs to $SPLUNK_HOME/var/log/splunk/splunk_ta_aws_aws_s3_<input name>.log. A healthy run logs Start processing last_modified=..., then one line per key, then updates its checkpoint.

    A4.d Confirm the data. Search the target index over the event dates you backfilled — not today — and check that the sourcetype resolved to the real LogServ type rather than the fallback:

    index=sap_logserv_logs earliest=-1y | stats count by sourcetype

    A4.e Disable the input once the prefix is drained. An input past its terminal time stops fetching, but disabling it says so plainly — and until the terminal time it re-lists the prefix on every polling interval.

    curl -sk -u '<your-splunk-username>' -X POST \
  https://<heavy-forwarder>:8089/servicesNS/nobody/Splunk_TA_aws/data/inputs/aws_s3/logserv_backfill_hana_20250611/disable
    Field names and formats that differ from the add-on’s documentation
    • The prefix field is key_name, not key_prefix.
    • An update must echo the full required set — aws_account, bucket_name, index, parse_csv_with_delimiter, sourcetype — or the endpoint returns 400 The following required arguments are missing. Optional fields you omit are preserved.
    • Never send name on an update. It does not rename the input; it creates a second input pointed at the same prefix, and both will ingest. Send name only on create.
    • The datetime fields require a literal trailing Z (2026-09-01T00:00:00Z). The offset example in the add-on’s own inputs.conf.spec (2011-07-06T21:54:23-0700) is rejected by the setup handler.
    • When posting datetimes or a whitelist in a form-encoded body, use --data-urlencode; a plain + in a form body decodes to a space.

    A4.f Rebuild the dashboard rollups for the dates you backfilled — section 3.

    A5. What to expect¶

    Direct polling produces the same events as the SQS-based path — the same envelope handling, the same sourcetype routing, the same index-time filtering. Measured against a LogServ bucket:

    Check Result
    Gzipped .json.gz objects Decompressed natively — no decoder configuration
    NDJSON splitting 39 objects produced 1,238 events
    Sourcetype routing sap:hana:audit — the real type, not the sap_logserv_logs fallback
    _time The embedded envelope epoch (2025-06-11), not the ingest time
    host / source Taken from the envelope, overriding the S3 key
    clz_dir / clz_subdir Indexed, as usual
    _raw Envelope stripped to the inner log line
    Repeat polls 1,238 → 1,238 across two polling cycles — no duplication

    • After a backfill, rebuild the dashboards for its dates (section 3), then check them with Verify Your Data.
    • New install: Install the LogServ App and seed its dashboards.

    Troubleshooting¶

    This page lists common symptoms and the section that explains each one. If you are not sure the data arrives at all, start with Verify Your Data; if a dashboard panel is empty, start with the LogServ App’s Data Doctor.

    Data Arrival and Parsing¶

    Symptom Likely cause Where to look

    Events keep the sourcetype sap_logserv_logs, have no folder fields and no splunk_solution The Data TA was not on the instance that parsed them, or the input started before the Data TA reached it. Those events stay as they were indexed Verify Your Data, check 1; Version Check; Distribute the Data TA
    Events arrive under another sourcetype, with no folder fields and no splunk_solution The AWS SQS-Based S3 input’s Source Type is not sap_logserv_logs, so the Data TA’s rules do not run on its events. Events already indexed stay as they are Your AWS guide’s SQS-Based S3 input step: Connect, Filter, Copy; Verify Your Data, check 1
    A folder the Data TA routes by folder alone (for example hana/hanaaudit) stays under sap_logserv_logs The routes did not run as shipped on the forwarder that parsed it: check its Data TA build, and look for a local/ override of the routes Verify Your Data, check 4; Version Check
    Most Azure data stays under sap_logserv_logs The Unix command output SAP delivers without folder fields stays there by design Data Delivered Without Folder Fields; Configuring Filters → Events Without Folder Fields

    A search that uses sap_logserv_idx_macro fails on the search head (the macro cannot be found) Neither the Data TA nor the LogServ App is on that search head yet Verify Your Data has the same checks with the index name

    Upgrade

    Upgrading to This Release¶

    Use this page to bring an existing Splunk for SAP LogServ installation up to the current release: LogServ App build 394, Data TA build 1792598960, LogServ Azure add-on build 1792558069 and LogServ GCP add-on build 1792558072, all at version 0.1.2. It applies whether you come from 0.0.5, 0.0.6, 0.1.1 or an earlier 0.1.2 build: find your builds, note the rows of the work list that apply to them, then follow the upgrade sequence.

    What an upgrade does not touch

    No data is re-ingested. Events already indexed keep the sourcetype, host, source and folder fields they were indexed with: the Data TA’s routing changes apply only to events parsed after you update it. The local/ configuration of every package and the App’s KV Store data (settings, acknowledgements, saved layouts, dashboard data) survive the upgrade. Two things do change for data you already have: some search-time fields, which every search computes anew, and the values some dashboard rollups store, which is why some rows in Settings → Dashboard Data need a one-time rebuild.


    1. Find Your Builds¶

    LogServ App. Click About at the bottom of the App’s left navigation rail. The dialog shows the version, the build and the build date. (App builds 302 to 338 have About in the top navigation bar; earlier builds have none.) On any build, the same from a search on the search head:

    | rest /services/apps/local splunk_server=local
| search title=splunk_app_sap_logserv
| table title version build

    Data TA. Check each instance that parses LogServ data, every heavy forwarder or the single instance, not only the Deployment Server: see Version Check. Every 0.1.2 Data TA build has the version 0.1.2; the builds are told apart only by their build number, which is the time the package was built, in epoch seconds.

    LogServ Azure and GCP add-ons. Run the search above on each heavy forwarder, or search head, that runs them, with title=splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure or title=splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp.

    Then read your App build in the work list’s terms:

    Your LogServ App Use in the work list
    Version 0.1.2 Its build number
    Version 0.1.1, build 282 to 335, or version 0.0.6, build 258 or later (266 is its last build, and carries the 0.1.1 changes up to build 299) Build 335
    Version 0.1.1, build 245 to 281, or version 0.0.6 before build 258 Build 281: a full rebuild of the dashboard data
    Version 0.0.5, or version 0.1.1, build 244 or earlier Build 244: a pre-rollup build


    2. The Work List¶

    Each row of the tables below starts at the last build that lacks a change. Apply every row whose build is at or above yours, all of them, in one pass after the upgrade. Rows about Settings → Dashboard Data say which rows there to rebuild; How to Rebuild a Row gives the steps.

    Rows to Rebuild, by Starting Build¶

    The Dashboard Data steps of the App work list, combined for the builds an upgrade usually starts from. A row that one change clears and another only backfills needs its Clear and Backfill once. The rows are named as in Settings → Dashboard Data; Beaconing detection there reads Beaconing detection (Environment Health / DNS / Network Perimeter).

    Your App build Clear, then Backfill Backfill only, without Clear
    383 or later None None
    379 Work Process Performance / ABAP Operations None
    378 Work Process Performance / ABAP Operations Host Role Activity (Host Details); Environment Topology (graph)
    364 to 377 12 rows: Work Process Performance / ABAP Operations; HANA Audit; HANA Trace; Environment Health; ABAP Network & Security; Host Role Activity (Host Details); Environment Topology (graph); Environment Topology (detail tabs); Multi-Cloud Overview; Data Pipeline Overview; Host Details; Sourcetype Mapping (Host Details / Data Pipeline) Change & Configuration Activity; Cross-Stack Authentication
    358 to 363 (the released builds 360, 362 and 363) 14 rows: the 12 above, Proxy Analytics and Cross-Stack Authentication Change & Configuration Activity; Network Perimeter; Beaconing detection
    355 or earlier: 336 (the first 0.1.2 build), or 335 (from the table above) 17 rows: the 14 above, Beaconing detection, Change & Configuration Activity and Linux System & Security / Network Perimeter Network Perimeter
    281 (from the table above) Every row, with Clear all data None
    244 (from the table above) Every row, with Clear all data: the rollups start empty, but the Environment Topology (graph) row already holds the earlier build’s rows None

    The other steps of the work list still apply to you, whichever line of this table you are on.

    LogServ App¶

    Coming from App build 388 or later, there is nothing to rebuild, and no acknowledgement is asked again.

    Coming from App build Changed in After upgrading
    386 or earlier 388 With the AI Assistant enabled, the next admin who clicks Save Defaults in Settings → AI Assistant → General is asked once to accept the enablement acknowledgement, now at version 3; answering No turns the AI Assistant off. While it is disabled nothing is asked, until it is turned on, which always asks. A local/ai_assistant_acks.conf that sets optInVersion under [logserv-ai-assistant-enable-tc] keeps the old version: remove that line. See Legal Acknowledgement Modals.
    385 or earlier 386 With audit forwarding off, the next Save Defaults asks once to acknowledge the audit-log integrity text, now at version 2. With forwarding on nothing is asked. An optInVersion line under [logserv-ai-assistant-tc] in local/ai_assistant_acks.conf keeps the old version: remove it.
    383 or earlier 385 The App’s collections that hold dashboard data (the rollups, the five Environment Topology data collections and the Data Doctor’s platform snapshot) can be written by the admin, sc_admin and sc_subadmin roles only; every role still reads them. The topology layout collections (saved layouts, their defaults and each user’s layout mode), the dashboard refresh intervals and the Data Doctor’s saved reports and ingest facts stay writable by every role. The App’s scheduled searches and the Settings backfill keep working. Its searches that write these collections run as the user who starts them. A [collections/<name>] stanza with an access line in the App’s metadata/local.meta keeps its own permissions: remove it to take the new ones. A scheduled search of your own that writes into one of these collections and is owned by a non-admin user stops writing. Start the App’s writing searches (a retention, a backfill, an ES feed) through the REST API only with an admin-tier account.
    379 or earlier 383, the first released build after 379 Clear, then Backfill Work Process Performance / ABAP Operations, or use the narrower repair. wp_category_name takes SAP’s names for the work process trace components: ten values are renamed and nine more letters get names (field changes). The AI Assistant’s settings, acknowledgements and model cache can be written by admin-tier roles only.
