Users whose roles hold neither edit_tcp nor edit_log_alert_event now see a warning in the AI Assistant panel: their AI Assistant activity is not written to the audit index (Who Can Write Audit Events).
    378 or earlier 379 Backfill, without Clear, Host Role Activity (Host Details) and Environment Topology (graph). Where the next row applies too, its Clear and Backfill cover both.
    377 or earlier 378 Clear, then Backfill eleven rows and Backfill two more: see Coming From App Build 377 or Earlier. HANA audit, HANA trace and ICM fields change (field changes).
    376 or earlier 377 Nothing to rebuild. A search override in local/savedsearches.conf for logserv_topology_aggregate_nodes, logserv_topology_aggregate_edges, logserv_topology_detail_aggregate, logserv_topology_enrichment_aggregate or one of their backfill twins keeps the old loopback filter, which leaves out only 127.0.0.1: remove it to take the shipped search, which leaves out every loopback address (127.0.0.0/8). Claude 5.x turns now count toward the AI Assistant’s daily spend cap (daily_spend_cap_usd, Settings → AI Assistant → General): raise it if your users run those models heavily.
    375 or earlier 376 Before upgrading, export the threat-intel lists you keep by hand (step 1 of the upgrade sequence). After upgrading, if ES reads the asset and identity feed CSVs and your upgrade method does not keep the App’s lookups/ directory, dispatch both feeds once (Customer Wire-up). A search override of logserv_topology_retention in local/savedsearches.conf keeps the old search, which trims the edges inside a subsearch of the nodes trim: remove it. The nightly retention window now ends at 02:36.
    374 or earlier 375 Earlier builds could empty a rollup when Splunkd restarted just before the nightly retention. In Settings → Dashboard Data, a row whose aggregation is on but whose History reads empty, or much shorter than you expect, can be rebuilt with Backfill over the history you want, as far back as its raw events are still in the index (at most 365 days). A search override for a logserv_*_retention stanza in local/savedsearches.conf keeps the old behaviour: remove it, or add override_if_empty=false to each outputlookup it runs.
    366 or earlier 367 Nothing to rebuild. vendor_product and app on linux:slapd change for Pacemaker lines (field changes).
    363 or earlier 364 to 365 Clear, then Backfill Proxy Analytics, HANA Audit and Cross-Stack Authentication; then Backfill, without Clear, Network Perimeter, Environment Health, Beaconing detection and the two Environment Topology rows, which recount what they hold. Rows written before keep the old values, some under the old key (none). Proxy request totals fall where Squid’s store.log and cache.log are collected: those lines are not requests and are no longer counted. Several fields change (field changes).
    357 or earlier 356 to 358 Clear, then Backfill Linux System & Security / Network Perimeter: it recorded fragments of ordinary words as Kernel Event Types. Coming from 356 or earlier, also Change & Configuration Activity: it stored the after-hours flag in the time zone of the search that wrote the row, so where a Settings backfill ran in another time zone than the search head’s, hours were stored twice. Coming from 355 or earlier, also Beaconing detection: it keyed each day on midnight in the writing search’s time zone, so a day could be stored twice. Each rebuild is safe whether or not your data was affected.
    281 or earlier 282 The dashboard rollups (all but the Environment Topology’s) added cloud_provider to the keys of their rows. Clear all data (Settings → Dashboard Data, Danger zone), then Run backfill over the history you want. This replaces every other Clear and Backfill of this list.
    244 or earlier 245 The dashboards move to the rollup collections, which the upgrade creates empty; the Environment Topology collections already hold the earlier build’s rows: see Coming From a Pre-rollup Build. Clear all data (Settings → Dashboard Data, Danger zone), then one Run backfill over the history you want. This replaces every other Clear and Backfill of this list.

    Coming From App Build 377 or Earlier¶

    App build 378 changes values that several rollups store, most of them in the keys the rows are stored under:

    • the search-time host of HANA audit events is the HANA host that wrote the record (the client’s host name is src_host), and HANA audit records with no client fields now parse;
    • HANA trace lines take severity, component and duration from their exact format (backup.log levels; hdbcons timings in microseconds and seconds converted to milliseconds; hdbcons, SQL-trace, load and availability files carry no severity);
    • RFC edges in the Environment Topology count connections, in the direction they were made;
    • the three digits after a session ID in the ICM trace (dev_icm) are read as the SAP client (sap_client), no longer as an HTTP status, so the ICM error counts change and the ICM status panels are replaced.

    Rows written earlier keep the old values, most under the old keys. The first hourly run after the upgrade rewrites the last hour or two under the new keys, so those hours count twice until rebuilt, and so does any later Backfill over earlier days, Backfill N days for late-arriving data included. Until you rebuild: HANA Audit’s Failed Operations by HANA Host lists client hosts beside the HANA hosts for the days before the upgrade; HANA Trace keeps record files under UNKNOWN and backup.log lines under fragment components, and misses microsecond-timed commands; ABAP Network & Security counts ICM sessions in SAP clients 400 to 599 as ICM errors; the Environment Topology draws a second, reversed edge for the old RFC rows, and an edge with a node of its own for each client host name of the old HANA audit rows. After the upgrade, the average on HANA Trace’s hdbcons Command Duration (Avg / Max) panel usually falls, because microsecond-timed commands now count.

    After the upgrade (a Clear before it is undone by the old build’s last runs), Clear, then Backfill each of these rows with a window that covers its whole history, using each row’s own Backfill:

    • HANA Audit
    • HANA Trace
    • Environment Health
    • ABAP Network & Security
    • Host Role Activity (Host Details)
    • Environment Topology (graph)
    • Environment Topology (detail tabs)
    • Multi-Cloud Overview
    • Data Pipeline Overview
    • Host Details
    • Sourcetype Mapping (Host Details / Data Pipeline)

    Then Backfill, without Clear, Change & Configuration Activity and Cross-Stack Authentication: they gain the HANA audit records that have no client fields, under keys that do not change.

    • A Backfill without the Clear counts the upgraded hours twice, on Environment Health too, which sums its error counts across hosts. On ABAP Network & Security alone it keeps the old ICM error counts instead. Where the search below returns 0, your ICM error counts were never affected, and a Backfill alone is enough on that row:

      | inputlookup logserv_abapnet_rollup where metric="icmerr" | stats count

    • Keep the Settings page open until the Environment Topology (graph) row has finished: that row writes each month only once every search of the month has finished. SAP Router edges have no history until the Environment Topology rows are backfilled.

    • The Clear removes everything a row holds, including history older than the raw events still in your index, which no Backfill can bring back. To keep that history, use the narrower repair instead.
    • This rebuild also re-keys the RFC rows by application server, the change of 0.1.1 builds 324 to 325. No separate RFC migration is needed: do not run the RFC-only steps in the 0.1.1 release notes on this release. The shipped edges backfill now has two gateway searches, one per direction, and those steps keep only one of them.
    • A search override in local/savedsearches.conf for a rollup aggregation or backfill search keeps the old search after the upgrade: compare it with the shipped one, or remove it.
    • sap:abap:icm leaves the CIM Web data model (its sap_abap_icm_request eventtype is removed). If that data model is accelerated, ICM events summarized before the upgrade stay in its summaries until they age out of the summary range or you rebuild the acceleration.
    • With a Data TA build before 1792189743, the AWS S3 Direct screen does not list the sap/saprouter folder under the two Environment Topology rows: when you load SAP Router history from S3 for the topology, also select its SAP Router row.

    Coming From a Pre-rollup Build¶

    Current dashboards read most panels from KV Store rollup collections. On the first upgrade from a pre-rollup build (0.0.5, or a 0.1.1 build 244 or earlier) the rollup collections are created empty, and the rolled-up panels show no data until they fill. The Environment Topology collections are not empty: the earlier build already kept and filled them, with RFC edges keyed before the per-application-server breakdown and drawn in the opposite direction, and HANA audit edges to client hosts. A Backfill does not remove those rows, and the topology keeps them for up to 365 days beside the new ones, so the Environment Topology would draw doubled or reversed RFC edges and nodes for client hosts.

    1. Clear all data first: in Settings → Dashboard Data, Danger zone, after the upgrade and clear of the nightly retention window. It empties every rollup and the Environment Topology collections; the rollups are empty anyway.
    2. Run the backfill once (recommended on any install with real data): choose a Backfill window that covers the raw history your index holds, usually the 365-day preset, then click Run backfill. The window is 30 days by default; it also offers 60, 90, 180 or 365 days, or a custom range of whole UTC days back to the 365-day retention. The backfill is idempotent and can be run again. See Backfilling on First Install. Without it, the hourly aggregation searches fill the collections one hour at a time from the upgrade on.

    The tstats panels (Data Pipeline Overview, the Host Details counts, Multi-Cloud Overview and the count KPIs) read the index directly and work at once, and so does every panel at a time range under 90 minutes, which reads raw events.

    Coming from a 0.0.5 build before 192 or a 0.1.1 build before 240, open the App once as an admin after the upgrade: on that first page load it copies the AI Assistant settings and acknowledgements that those builds kept in local/ conf files into the KV Store.

    New Scheduled Searches, New Collections, and a Restart¶

    Relative to a pre-rollup build, the upgrade adds the rollup aggregation, retention and detection searches and the rollup collections. A Splunkd restart is required for the collections to be created and the new searches to register; Splunk Web’s Install app from file upgrade asks for it. The scheduled searches are staggered so the scheduler never bursts; see Scheduled-Search Schedule.

    Visible UI / Panel Changes When Coming From v0.0.5-era Builds¶

    • Every chart and table panel header has a toolbar (Open in Search, Download CSV, Inspect, Refresh), a loading spinner and the Data Doctor’s Diagnose action; empty panels explain themselves (Data Doctor).
    • Percentile charts (p50 / p95 / p99) become Avg + Max by hour; HANA Trace’s slowest-operations panel is a top-by-max table; Web Dispatcher’s Top URIs has no Unique Clients column.
    • Rolled-up panels are hourly-fresh at wide time ranges; ranges under 90 minutes use the panels’ raw searches, so short-range investigation stays real-time.
    • The App uses the Cisco Magnetic theme (dark by default, with a light mode), a left navigation rail, and the current Environment Topology layout and node designs.
    • Your browser may briefly serve a cached bundle; a hard refresh loads the new build.

    Search-Time Field Changes¶

    The App computes these fields when a search runs, so the change applies to events old and new as soon as the App is upgraded. The App’s dashboards use the new fields. Saved searches, alerts and reports of your own that read them need the new names or values.

    Coming from App build Sourcetype Change
    379 or earlier sap:abap:workprocess wp_category_name takes SAP’s names for the trace components: C, D, M, N, O, Q, R, S, T and X are renamed (for example C = Database (DBSL), D = Diag Processor, Q = Other), and E, G, H, I, J, L, P, V and W, which read <letter> = Other, get names.
    377 or earlier sap:hana:audit host is the HANA host that wrote the record; the client’s host name is the new src_host. Searches that group by host now group by HANA host. Records with no client fields parse fully.
    377 or earlier sap:hana:tracelogs Record files (hdbcons, SQL trace, loads, system availability) carry no hana_trace_severity; backup.log lines carry their own level and component. New fields: hana_trace_file_type, hana_backup_level, hana_op, hana_op_duration, hana_op_duration_unit; hana_op_duration_ms is always in milliseconds.
    377 or earlier sap:abap:icm icm_status_code, status and action are gone. The SAP client of a session is sap_client, its user icm_user, its terminal icm_terminal. icm_is_error is true only on lines the ICM logged as errors. On connection lines src and dest follow the connection’s direction (icm_conn_role). The sap_abap_icm_request eventtype and its tag are removed.
    377 or earlier sap:webdispatcher:access New sap_sid and sap_instance, read from the log’s path.
    377 or earlier sap:saprouter, sap:abap:gateway New fields for the SAP Router targets (saprouter_target_*, saprouter_fail_target_ip) and the gateway’s connection records (gw_remgw_*, gw_client_*, rfc_peer_port, rfc_local_port).
    366 or earlier linux:slapd vendor_product and app read Pacemaker and pacemaker on pacemaker.log lines; slapd.log lines keep OpenLDAP and slapd.
    364 or earlier linux:slapd os_user is removed. Pacemaker lines carry resource_agent and cluster_resource, or pacemaker_daemon and pacemaker_function.
    364 or earlier sap:hana:audit sql_statement and command are shown without JSON escapes.
    364 or earlier sap:sapstartsrv source_location reads file names that contain a dot and skips the [Thr N] thread marker.
    364 or earlier squid:cache, squid:store New sourcetype stanzas for the Data TA’s new Squid routes, with no automatic key=value fields.
    363 or earlier linux:sudolog command holds the whole command, with continuation lines joined and escapes removed.
    363 or earlier lastlog USERNAME accepts user names with -, the header line is skipped, and the new PORT field holds lastlog’s Port column (for example <console>).
    363 or earlier sap:hana:audit status and target_user are read for every action, not only connect-type actions; user and privilege statements match in any letter case and when quoted; audit_datetime is set on records whose time ends in Z.
    363 or earlier squid:access Proxy fields are also extracted from Squid’s logformat=splunk_recommended_squid form.
    363 or earlier sap:abap:gateway, sap:scc:http_access, sap:sapstartsrv, sap:saphostexec gw_error_detail, the Cloud Connector’s http_version and the error_message of the Start Service and the Host Agent end where the line ends.

    Data TA¶

    The Data TA does its work where LogServ data is parsed, on the heavy forwarders or a single instance, so its changes reach events parsed after it is updated there; events indexed earlier keep their sourcetype and fields. Apply every row whose build is later than yours. Coming from 0.0.5, 0.0.6 or 0.1.1, every 0.1.2 row applies: their routing is that of the first 0.1.2 build.

    Coming from Data TA Changed in What changes, and what to do
    A build before 1792598960 1792598960 (2026-10-21) Parsing, routing and filtering are unchanged, and nothing has to be saved again. The AWS S3 Direct screen accepts the Splunk Add-on for AWS 8.1.0 and any later version (earlier builds warned about any version but 8.1.0) and no longer blocks a search head or Splunk Cloud.
    A build before 1792189743 1792189743 (2026-10-16) Before you update, remove routes of your own from the Data TA’s local/transforms.conf, such as the six (?s)^ routes of build 1791935359 if you added them there as a test (Version Check): local/ wins over default/ key by key, so the old REGEX would stay in effect with the new 100,000-character window, a combination that exceeds Splunk’s regex match limit. Every metadata rule and sourcetype route now reads up to 100,000 characters of a line; earlier builds read 4,096. An AWS event longer than about 4 KB used to keep the input’s own host and source, get no folder fields and stay sap_logserv_logs, while the filters (from 1791565776) already judged it by its folder fields; it now gets its real host, source, folder fields and sourcetype. Searches of your own that find such events under sap_logserv_logs need their final sourcetype. The ICM route takes only the ABAP ICM folder (abap/icm): a webdispatcher/icm folder keeps sap_logserv_logs. The BIND, Windows and sssd routes match only within the source value.
    A build before 1791935359 1791935359 (2026-10-13) Data TA builds from 0.0.4.1 up to, but not including, this one carry five or six routes whose cost grows with the square of the line length: 2.4 ms of CPU per event on the lab heavy forwarder, about 400 events a second for one pipeline set. Update every instance that parses LogServ data before you size or add hardware (Capacity Planning and First Start).
    A build before 1791565776 1791565776 (2026-10-09) Configuration → Filters gains Include Sources and Exclude Sources (empty by default), and the filter rules read the whole line. Behaviour change: an Include Filters list that mixes */* or a standalone * with other entries now keeps every event. Before, */*, linux/cron dropped every event without folder fields, and *, linux/cron kept only linux/cron. To keep an allow-list, remove */* and * from it. HANA .trc files and backup.log delivered without folder fields get sap:hana:tracelogs from their path (Data Delivered Without Folder Fields). With Filtering on, open Configuration → Filters after the update, click Save, and on a Deployment Server click Deploy to Forwarders, so the forwarders get the regenerated rules. On a Deployment Server with Filtering on and Days in the Past above 0, the daily filter refresh now finds and reloads the server class (before, whether it found it depended on the default app of the user the refresh runs as, and when it did not, the forwarders kept the previous cutoff), so each forwarder in the server class restarts about once a day to apply the new cutoff (Days in the Past). Use App build 377 or later with it: the Data Doctor of App build 376 and earlier ignores source rules and reports folder patterns with * or ? as only partly read (Reading the Active Filter Configuration).
    A build before 1790374045 1790374045 (2026-09-25) The Data TA declares the folder paths linux/proxy and linux/pacemaker: with Filtering on and an explicit Include Filters list, add them where those logs should be kept, because events under them are dropped at the forwarder (Upgrade Notifications).
    A build before 1790368041 1790368041 (2026-09-25) Squid’s cache.log goes to squid:cache and store.log to squid:store; access.log stays squid:access, and all three keep the proxy/squid filter path. Events indexed earlier keep squid:access. The App’s dashboards count access.log lines only; searches of your own that read the other two files under squid:access need the new names.
    A build before 1790292318 1790292318 (2026-09-24) Long NDJSON lines are unwrapped and kept whole: lines with many escaped characters, from about 1.5 KB, no longer keep their envelope, and lines up to 100,000 bytes are no longer cut at 10,000. Events indexed earlier keep their envelope.
    A 0.0.5 build whose version reads 0.0.5.0 (four parts), or 0.0.5.1 0.0.5 (version 0.0.5) The audit index is logserv_ai_assistant_audit; those builds define _ai_assistant_audit instead. Where the Data TA holds your index definitions, the update defines the new index; where they are defined elsewhere (the indexer tier, Splunk Cloud), create logserv_ai_assistant_audit there (Create the Indexes), and update a copy of the Data TA that an indexer holds. Then check that Audit index name under Settings → AI Assistant → General → Audit & Telemetry reads logserv_ai_assistant_audit. Audit events written earlier stay in _ai_assistant_audit and are not searchable under the new name.
    0.0.4.2 or earlier 0.0.5 The cron, warn, sudo and slapd logs move from Splunk’s syslog sourcetype to linux:cron, linux:warn, linux:sudolog and linux:slapd. Events indexed as syslog keep it until retention removes them; the App’s Linux and Change & Configuration searches read both.

    Splunk Add-on for AWS. Nothing in the solution enforces a version. Splunk’s advisory SVD-2026-1005 (third-party package fixes) says to upgrade the add-on to 8.2.2 or later, so run 8.2.2 or later on the forwarders; these docs were checked with 8.3.1. The AWS S3 Direct screen was validated with 8.1.0 and shows an advisory for an older version.

    AWS Copy stacks. A stack created from an earlier splunk-logserv-remote-s3-copy.yaml runs its Lambda on python3.9, which AWS has deprecated. The current template uses python3.12; the function’s code is unchanged. Update the stack with the current template, keeping your parameter values (AWS Remote S3 Copy guide). Filter stacks already run python3.12 and need no change.

    Cloud Provider dropdown. If the Data TA’s Configuration → Cloud Provider tab is set to a cloud on your forwarders, read Choose Cloud Attribution before you change anything. The inputs of the LogServ Azure and GCP add-ons always stamp cloud_provider, the AWS S3 Direct screen stamps every input it creates, and the dropdown adds its value beside such a stamp, not in its place, so those events carry the field twice. The recommended setting is Not set, with _meta = cloud_provider::aws on each SQS-Based S3 input; to move a fleet from the dropdown set to AWS to that setting, see Alternative for AWS-Only Fleets. A change applies to events parsed after it.

    LogServ Azure and GCP Add-ons¶

    • Update them on each heavy forwarder, or search head, that runs them, never through the Deployment Server: each input’s credential (the Azure SAS, the GCP service-account key) is stored, encrypted, in the add-on’s own local/passwords.conf on that instance. An app upgrade keeps that file, and nothing has to be moved to system/local; a Deployment Server push would replace it. See Install the Azure Add-on and the GCP Setup Guide.
    • Any 0.1.2 build runs the same code. Builds 1792558069 (Azure) and 1792558072 (GCP) change only the workloads the add-ons declare (so that a search head is an allowed target, Splunk Cloud included) and their README and Inputs-page text, and builds 1792213309 and 1792213464 only their third-party notices, package pins and README text; every Python file is that of the first 0.1.2 builds.
    • Azure, coming from 0.0.5. 0.0.5 read Azure data with the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Cloud Services (Splunkbase 3110), which its setup guide placed in the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class. Set up the LogServ Azure add-on on the forwarder that will read SAP’s queue (Configure the Input), then disable the Microsoft Cloud Services input that read the LogServ storage, so no blob is indexed twice.
    • GCP, onboarded with an SAP-issued key. The add-on signs in with the service-account key its input holds, wherever that account lives, so a deployment that uses a key SAP issued for a service account in the SAP-managed LogServ project needs no change. New onboarding uses the customer-homed sequence in The Onboarding Sequence.
    • GCP, coming from the Splunk Add-on for Google Cloud Platform (Splunkbase 3088). As of its version 5.0.3 (checked 2026-07-05), its Cloud Pub/Sub Based Bucket input does not decompress gzipped objects, so it fails on LogServ’s *.json.gz objects, and it needs roles/pubsub.viewer beyond the roles SAP documents. Use the LogServ GCP add-on, and disable any 3088 input on the LogServ subscription.


    3. Upgrade Sequence¶

    The packages can be updated in either order. This order checks the forwarders before the App and leaves the Dashboard Data rebuild, which reads the indexed events, for the end.

    1. Prepare.
      • Find your builds and note the work-list rows that apply.
      • Export the threat-intel lists you keep by hand. logserv_ti_malicious_domains.csv, logserv_ti_malicious_ips.csv and logserv_ti_compromised_credentials.csv ship in the App’s lookups/ directory as header-only files, so an upgrade may replace rows you added. For example | inputlookup logserv_ti_malicious_domains | outputcsv logserv_ti_malicious_domains_backup writes to $SPLUNK_HOME/var/run/splunk/csv/ on the search head; re-upload the list afterwards under Settings → Lookups → Lookup table files. A list that a recurring saved search writes (Threat Intelligence Integration) is refilled on that search’s next run.
      • Note the local/ overrides the rows name: search overrides in local/savedsearches.conf, [collections/...] stanzas in the App’s metadata/local.meta, optInVersion lines in local/ai_assistant_acks.conf, and routes of your own in the Data TA’s local/transforms.conf. Remove those routes before you update the Data TA.
      • Plan the Dashboard Data rebuild for a time clear of the nightly retention window: 00:34–00:58, 01:30–01:58 and 02:34–02:36 in the search head’s local time.
    2. Update the Data TA where it parses data, as described in Updating the Data TA below.
    3. Update the LogServ Azure and GCP add-ons on each heavy forwarder, or search head, that runs them: Apps → Manage Apps → Install app from file with Upgrade app selected, or $SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk install app <tarball> -update 1, then restart Splunk. On a Splunk Cloud search head, update them as private apps (On Splunk Cloud).
    4. Check each forwarder’s build (Version Check).
    5. Update the LogServ App on the search head. On Splunk Enterprise: Apps → Manage Apps → Install app from file, select the tarball and Upgrade app, then restart Splunk when asked. On a search head cluster, never update the members one by one: on the deployer, replace $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/shcluster/apps/splunk_app_sap_logserv with the new build, keeping any local/ you keep there, then run splunk apply shcluster-bundle (Splunk Enterprise: search head cluster). On Splunk Cloud, see On Splunk Cloud.
    6. Hard-refresh the browser, then open About and check that it shows build 394.
    7. Work through the App rows of the work list, the Dashboard Data rebuild included (How to Rebuild a Row). If you also load history from S3 with the AWS S3 Direct screen, let that backfill finish first, so that one rebuild includes it.
    8. Enterprise Security content. The App ships its splunk_sap_logserv_es_* searches enabled: correlation searches hourly, behavioral anomalies daily, feeds every 4 hours. They run on their schedules whether or not Enterprise Security is installed, and their notable and risk actions need it. On a search head without Enterprise Security, disable them (Disabling or Tuning the ES Content). Thirteen of them also run the AI Assistant’s Security-pack prompts: if you use those prompts, read that section before you disable anything.
    9. Check the result. In Settings → Dashboard Data, every row shows its history and none reads failed — re-run or truncated — re-run; the dashboards show data for the ranges you rebuilt.

    Updating the Data TA¶

    Install the new tarball over the existing one where the Data TA runs: Apps → Manage Apps → Install app from file with Upgrade app selected, or $SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk install app <tarball> -update 1, then restart Splunk when asked. An app upgrade keeps local/.

    • Single instance, or heavy forwarders without a Deployment Server: on each instance. Coming from a build before 1791565776 with Filtering on, click Save on Configuration → Filters on each one.
    • Heavy forwarders with a Deployment Server: on the Deployment Server only, then into deployment-apps/ and out to the forwarders, as below. Do not install it directly on a forwarder that the Deployment Server manages: the next push replaces that copy, its local/ included.
    • A Splunk Cloud search head that runs LogServ inputs: as a private app (On Splunk Cloud).
    • An indexer: only if you installed the Data TA there. On an indexer only its indexes.conf takes effect. The 0.0.5 builds with the version 0.0.5, and 0.0.6, 0.1.1 and 0.1.2, define the same two indexes, sap_logserv_logs and logserv_ai_assistant_audit, so such a copy can stay as it is; updating it there as well does no harm. Early 0.0.5 builds (version 0.0.5.0) and 0.0.5.1 define _ai_assistant_audit instead: update that copy, or create logserv_ai_assistant_audit on the indexer tier (Data TA).

    With a Deployment Server:

    1. Install the new build over etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/ on the Deployment Server.

    2. Replace the copy in etc/deployment-apps/, keeping its local/ folder. A Save on the Configuration page copies the Data TA into deployment-apps/ only when that copy is missing or its version differs, and every 0.1.2 build has the version 0.1.2, so a later 0.1.2 build never gets there by itself (Later Builds With the Same Version). As the user Splunk runs as:

      cd $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/deployment-apps
mv splunk_ta_sap_logserv ~/splunk_ta_sap_logserv.before-upgrade
tar -xzf /path/to/splunk_ta_sap_logserv-0.1.2.tar.gz -C .
cp -a ~/splunk_ta_sap_logserv.before-upgrade/local splunk_ta_sap_logserv/
grep -E "^(version|build)" splunk_ta_sap_logserv/default/app.conf

      The last command shows the new build. If the old copy has a metadata/local.meta, copy it into splunk_ta_sap_logserv/metadata/ as well. Keep the moved copy until every forwarder runs the new build. The same steps work coming from 0.0.5, 0.0.6 or 0.1.1. (There a Save would also replace the deployment-apps/ copy, because the version changes, with a copy of etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/, local/ included, which drops anything you added by hand under deployment-apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/local/.)

    3. Coming from a build before 1791565776 with Filtering on: open Configuration → Filters on the Deployment Server and click Save, so the rules are generated in the new form and copied into deployment-apps/.

    4. Click Deploy to Forwarders on the Filters tab. Each forwarder picks the change up at its next phone-home (60 seconds by default) and restarts; allow 5 minutes or more. The button reloads every server class on the Deployment Server (Deploy to Forwarders).
    5. Check the build on each forwarder (Version Check).

    On Splunk Cloud¶

    Update each package on the Splunk Cloud stack the way you installed it, as a private app: in Splunk Web, open the gear icon next to Apps, then Install app from file and Upload App, sign in with your splunk.com account and upload the tarball. When the Uploaded Apps table shows it as Approved (Splunk Cloud vets the package first), click Install. The Data TA is needed on the stack only where LogServ inputs run on the search head (Splunk Cloud Considerations).

    Every 0.1.2 build keeps the version 0.1.2. On a Splunk Cloud 10.5 stack, later 0.1.2 builds of the App and the Data TA installed over earlier ones in this way, without a restart prompt (tested 2026-10-21); other Splunk Cloud versions have not been tested. If your stack does not offer Install because version 0.1.2 is already installed, stop there: do not uninstall the installed app to make room for the new one, because uninstalling removes its local/ configuration. Open a Splunk Cloud support case instead.

    Forwarders you run yourself are updated as described above. The narrower repairs below need the search head’s management port, which on Splunk Cloud must first be opened for you. If you cannot reach it, use the Clear and Backfill instead.


    4. How to Rebuild a Row¶

    1. Rebuild after the upgrade, on the new build: a Clear done before the upgrade is undone by the old build’s last hourly runs.
    2. Pick a time clear of the nightly retention window, 00:34–00:58, 01:30–01:58 and 02:34–02:36 search-head time. A retention search rewrites its whole collection and erases rows that a backfill running at the same time has just added.
    3. Open Settings → Dashboard Data (The Dashboard Data Settings Tab). Under Backfill window, choose a window that covers the history you want: the 365-day preset reaches as far back as a rollup keeps rows, and a custom range takes whole UTC days. The default is 30 days. A window longer than 90 days shows a cost warning first; for scale, a 365-day backfill of every row took 195 minutes on the reference system. The two flat Environment Topology collections (the host-to-SID inventory and the IP enrichment) always read the last 30 days.
    4. For each Clear, then Backfill row: note its History, click Clear and confirm, then click the same row’s Backfill. Wait until it has finished before you start the next row.
    5. For each Backfill only row: click its own Backfill, without Clear.
    6. Use each row’s own Backfill, not the button under the window (Run backfill, or Re-run backfill (all)): it backfills only the rows it considers incomplete, or every row when it considers all of them complete. Use it only where this page says so: after Clear all data, coming from build 281 or earlier.
    7. Keep the page open until the Environment Topology (graph) row has finished.
    8. A row that shows failed — re-run or truncated — re-run needs its Backfill again; repeating a backfill is safe.

    The Clear removes everything a row holds, including history older than the raw events your index still holds, which no Backfill can bring back. For the two biggest rebuilds a narrower repair keeps that history.

    Narrower Repair After App Build 378¶

    Use this instead of the Clear and Backfill of Coming From App Build 377 or Earlier to keep history older than your raw events. It deletes only the rows inside the window you will backfill and leaves older rows as they are. It needs the search head’s management port; if you cannot reach it (on Splunk Cloud it must first be opened for you), use the Clear and Backfill instead.

    1. Pick the window. Its first day, W, is the first UTC day whose raw events your index still holds in full, and no earlier than 365 days ago, the furthest a Backfill reaches. This search finds the oldest event over all time (earliest=0; the time picker does not limit it) and returns W as the epoch seconds of that UTC midnight:

      | tstats min(_time) as first where `sap_logserv_idx_macro` earliest=0
| eval W = max((floor(first/86400)+1)*86400, floor(relative_time(now(), "-365d")/86400)*86400)

      The day of the oldest event may be held only in part, so W is the UTC midnight after it. Rows older than W keep their old values, and no raw event is left that a later Backfill could count beside them. The custom range of step 3 starts on W’s date in UTC.

    2. Delete the rows from W onward, after the upgrade and clear of the nightly retention window: one REST call per collection in the table, on the search head’s management port, with an admin-tier account. For example:

      curl -k -u admin -G -X DELETE \
  "https://<search-head>:8089/servicesNS/nobody/splunk_app_sap_logserv/storage/collections/data/logserv_hana_category_rollup" \
  --data-urlencode 'query={"bucket_ts":{"$gte":<W>}}'

      The same call with -X GET in place of -X DELETE returns rows the query matches (at most 50,000 by default, so it shows what the query matches, not how many): check it first. A DELETE without its query empties the whole collection.

      Row Collections
      HANA Audit logserv_hana_category_rollup
      HANA Trace logserv_hana_trace_rollup
      Environment Health logserv_severity_rollup
      ABAP Network & Security logserv_abapnet_rollup
      Host Role Activity (Host Details) logserv_hostrole_rollup
      Environment Topology (graph) logserv_topology_nodes and logserv_topology_edges; and all of logserv_topology_inventory (the call without query), which has no time field and holds only the current mapping of addresses and hosts to systems: the Backfill rebuilds it from the last 30 days
      Environment Topology (detail tabs) logserv_topology_detail_rollup
      Multi-Cloud Overview logserv_mc_rollup
      Data Pipeline Overview logserv_pipeline_rollup
      Host Details logserv_hostdetails_rollup
      Sourcetype Mapping (Host Details / Data Pipeline) logserv_stmap_rollup

    3. Then backfill. Do every delete before any Backfill. Then Backfill each of the eleven rows with its own Backfill over a custom range from W to today, and Backfill Change & Configuration Activity and Cross-Stack Authentication without Clear. Keep the Settings page open until the Environment Topology (graph) row has finished.

    Narrower Repair After App Build 383¶

    The Clear of Work Process Performance / ABAP Operations also removes the dispatcher, ICM and ABAP Operations panels’ history, although their stored values did not change. To keep the older history, delete only the trace-component rows (metric wp) from W onward, with W chosen as in the build-378 repair above:

    curl -k -u admin -G -X DELETE \
  "https://<search-head>:8089/servicesNS/nobody/splunk_app_sap_logserv/storage/collections/data/logserv_wp_perf_rollup" \
  --data-urlencode 'query={"metric":"wp","bucket_ts":{"$gte":<W>}}'

    Check the query with -X GET first, as above. Then Backfill the row with its own Backfill over a custom range from W to today. The Backfill rewrites the row’s other rows in that range under the keys they already have, so nothing is counted twice; trace-component rows older than W keep their old names. If you cannot reach the management port, use the Clear and Backfill instead.


    What Is Preserved¶

    • local/ configuration survives an app upgrade: the App’s ai_assistant_settings.conf, any acknowledgement files written by 0.0.5 builds before 192 or 0.1.1 builds before 240 (later builds keep the acknowledgements in the KV Store) and the credentials in its passwords.conf; the Data TA’s filter and Cloud Provider settings; the Azure and GCP inputs and their credentials. On forwarders that a Deployment Server manages, the Data TA’s local/ is the one in the Deployment Server’s deployment-apps/ copy.
    • KV Store data persists: settings, acknowledgements, saved topology layouts, dashboard preferences and the rollup collections. Collections and their data survive an app upgrade; the work list names the rows whose stored values must be rebuilt.
    • Indexed events keep their index, sourcetype and index-time fields. Search-time fields follow the installed App (Search-Time Field Changes).
    • Dashboard URLs are unchanged across recent releases. The Settings page moved from #/settings/ai-assistant to #/settings (the old URL redirects) and is titled Application Settings, with two top-level tabs, AI Assistant and Dashboard Data: update any runbook that names the old page title.


    Restricted Deployments: Templates-only and v0.0.6¶

    • The published App is the full-LLM build. No templates-only package is published for 0.1.2. After you upgrade a deployment that ran the templates-only build, or the v0.0.6 line, its stored templates_only_mode setting governs, and a deployment with no stored value takes the shipped default, off. Free-form questions are then allowed whenever the AI Assistant is enabled. Nothing goes to an LLM vendor until an admin selects a provider and saves its credential (the shipped provider is a built-in mock), but a provider credential stored before the upgrade is used again. An upgrade creates no credential.
    • To keep the deployment restricted, turn Templates-only mode on under Settings → AI Assistant → General after the upgrade and click Save Defaults, or build the templates-only variant from this release’s source and install that instead (Restricting the LLM Path, Building the Packages from Source).
    • v0.0.6 remains the option where a policy requires the LLM vendor code to be absent from the package. It is frozen at App build 266 and receives no fixes: it lacks every change of 0.1.1 after build 299 and of every 0.1.2 build (Release Notes: 0.1.1, Release Notes: 0.1.2). An upgrade from v0.0.6 to 0.1.2 brings the vendor code back, restricted only by the setting above.


    Rollback¶

    Reinstalling an earlier App tarball restores its default/ content, and your local/ configuration stays. It does not roll back the KV Store data:

    • Collections that only the newer build created stay in place, unused by the older App.
    • If the build you leave changed what a rollup stores (the Clear rows of the work list: builds 282, 356 to 358, 364 to 365, 378 and 383), the restored build’s hourly aggregation rewrites the last hour or two (Beaconing detection: the last two days) under its old keys, beside the rows the newer build wrote, and any Backfill it runs over earlier days does the same. Those hours are then counted twice. After rolling back across such a build, wait until the restored build is running, then Clear and Backfill the rows its work-list entry names (How to Rebuild a Row). A Clear done before the rollback is undone by the newer build’s last runs, and upgrading again later needs the same rebuild again.
    • Rolling back to App build 374 or earlier brings back retention searches that can empty a rollup after a restart.

    The Data TA rolls back the same way, and its local/ filter configuration stays. Rolling it back also removes the parsing, routing and filtering changes made since that build (Data TA); events parsed in the meantime keep the sourcetype they got. With a Deployment Server, an earlier build that has the same version goes into deployment-apps/ by hand, as for an upgrade.


    Removing the Solution¶

    To take Splunk for SAP LogServ out of a deployment, stop the data first, then remove each package from the tier it is on. The indexed data and the App’s KV Store data are handled in their own steps.

    1. Stop the data.
      • AWS: on each heavy forwarder, disable or delete the SQS-Based S3 inputs of the Splunk Add-on for AWS that read SAP’s queue. The backfill inputs that the AWS S3 Direct screen created also live in the Splunk Add-on for AWS: delete them with Delete all on that screen while the Data TA is still installed. In AWS, delete the CloudFormation stack you created from the Connect, Filter or Copy template. With Copy, empty its bucket first: CloudFormation does not delete a bucket that still holds objects. The Lambda code bucket you created for Filter or Copy is not part of the stack.
      • Azure and GCP: delete the inputs on each heavy forwarder or search head that runs them, or remove the add-ons in step 4.
      • Tell SAP that the access it granted for the connection is no longer needed.
    2. Decide what happens to the indexed data, before you remove the Data TA. Removing a package does not delete indexed data: the buckets of sap_logserv_logs and logserv_ai_assistant_audit stay on disk. Where the Data TA’s own indexes.conf defines the two indexes (a single instance, or an indexer you installed it on), removing the Data TA removes their definitions, and the data can no longer be searched. To keep it searchable, define both indexes elsewhere now, for example by copying the two stanzas of the Data TA’s default/indexes.conf into system/local/indexes.conf on that instance. Deleting the data is step 5.

    3. Search head: the LogServ App.

      • If Enterprise Security reads the App’s asset and identity lookups (splunk_for_sap_logserv_assets, splunk_for_sap_logserv_identities), remove them from ES’s Asset and Identity Management first (Add to ES Identity Management): they are removed with the App.

      • Its settings, acknowledgement records, saved layouts and dashboard data are in its KV Store collections, all named logserv_*, not in its directory. Export what you want to keep. If none of it may remain, delete the collections’ contents right before you remove the App, while it is still installed: one REST call per collection, with an admin-tier account, on the management port (on Splunk Cloud it must first be opened for you). The collections are the stanzas of the App’s default/collections.conf, 40 in build 394. This lists their names from the tarball you installed:

        tar -xzOf splunk_app_sap_logserv-0.1.2.tar.gz splunk_app_sap_logserv/default/collections.conf \
  | sed -n 's/^\[\(.*\)\]$/\1/p'

        Then, for each name:

        curl -k -u admin -X DELETE \
  "https://<search-head>:8089/servicesNS/nobody/splunk_app_sap_logserv/storage/collections/data/<collection>"

      • Remove the App: on Splunk Enterprise, $SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk remove app splunk_app_sap_logserv as the user Splunk runs as, then restart Splunk (or stop Splunk, delete $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/splunk_app_sap_logserv and start Splunk); on a search head cluster, delete splunk_app_sap_logserv from the deployer’s $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/shcluster/apps/ and push the bundle with splunk apply shcluster-bundle, which removes it from the members; on Splunk Cloud, uninstall it as you would any private app. Its own credentials (local/passwords.conf), lookups and configuration go with its directory. Notable and risk events its searches already wrote stay in Enterprise Security’s indexes.

      • The add-ons the App needs on the search head (CIM, the Windows and Unix and Linux add-ons, the Splunk MCP Server) are separate apps: remove them only if nothing else uses them.

    4. Heavy forwarders and the Deployment Server.

      • With a Deployment Server: the Data TA reached the forwarders through the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class. In Settings → Forwarder Management (Agent Management in Splunk Enterprise 10.0 and later), take the Data TA out of that class, or delete the class if it holds nothing else (the 0.0.5 Azure setup put the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Cloud Services in it too). In the files, the class is the [serverClass:SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders] stanza and the Data TA’s place in it the [serverClass:SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders:app:splunk_ta_sap_logserv] stanza, in the serverclass.conf that $SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk btool serverclass list --debug | grep SAP_LogServ shows. Remove only those stanzas, never the whole file, which holds your other server classes too, then run $SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk reload deploy-server. Then check each forwarder, and where $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv is still there, remove it. Last, remove the Data TA from the Deployment Server itself, etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv and etc/deployment-apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv together: while it is installed in etc/apps/, its daily filter refresh can copy it back into deployment-apps/.
      • Without a Deployment Server: remove the Data TA from each forwarder ($SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk remove app splunk_ta_sap_logserv, then restart).
      • LogServ Azure and GCP add-ons: remove them from each forwarder or search head that runs them. Each input’s credential is in the add-on’s own local/passwords.conf and goes with it.
      • Single instance, an indexer you installed it on, or a Splunk Cloud search head that ran the inputs: remove the Data TA there too, after step 2.

    5. Delete the indexes, if the data is not to be kept. To delete the data, remove the indexes where you created them (Create the Indexes): under Settings → Indexes on a standalone indexer or on Splunk Cloud; on an indexer cluster, with Splunk’s procedure for removing an index from the cluster. Where the Data TA’s own indexes.conf defined them and you removed it in step 4, their buckets are still on disk, in the directories that file gave them: stop Splunk, delete $SPLUNK_DB/sap_logserv_logs and $SPLUNK_DB/logserv_ai_assistant_audit, and start Splunk again.


    At a Glance¶

    • Find your builds (About in the App; Version Check for the Data TA), then apply every work-list row at or above your build.
    • No data re-ingest; local/ and KV Store data are kept. Indexed events keep their sourcetype; some search-time fields change.
    • Rebuild the Dashboard Data rows the work list names, after the upgrade, clear of the nightly retention window, with each row’s own Backfill.
    • With a Deployment Server, a later 0.1.2 Data TA build goes into deployment-apps/ by hand.
    • The published App is the full-LLM build: turn Templates-only mode on to keep a deployment restricted.
    • On a search head without Enterprise Security, disable the App’s ES searches.


    Next Steps¶

    1. Verify Your Data: check that events arrive with their sourcetypes after the update.
    2. Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness: what each Dashboard Data row holds and how fresh it is.
    3. Release Notes: 0.1.2: what each build changed.

    Dashboards

    Dashboards Overview¶

    The LogServ App’s dashboards are organized as in the App itself: one landing page, the Environment Topology view, and four groups (Applications, Integration, Security, Platform). This page lists them and describes the controls every dashboard shares. The App is built on @splunk/react-ui + @splunk/visualizations + @xyflow/react, ships as a single React bundle, and requires Splunk 9.4.3 or later.

    Navigation rail and header¶

    The navigation rail on the left holds, in this order:

    Environment Health (default landing) · Topology · Applications › · Integration › · Security › · Platform › · Settings (admin-tier roles only) · About

    Each of the four groups opens a flyout beside the rail that lists its dashboards, with a ✓ on the one you are viewing. The button at the top of the rail collapses it to a 56 px strip of icons; the choice is remembered per user in the browser.

    The header’s first row carries the product name, the App version and build pills (on windows wider than 900 px) and the light/dark theme toggle. Its second row carries the global time range (the Last 24h / 7d / 30d / 90d pills and Splunk’s own time-range picker) and, on the right, Actions ▾ · Refresh · AI Assistant (when enabled).

    Dashboards¶

    Dashboard or group What it covers
    Environment Health Cross-cutting operations view of errors, security failures and performance across the whole SAP landscape. The default landing page. Reads all sourcetypes.
    Environment Topology Interactive graph of SAP systems, integration partners and endpoints, built from sap:abap:gateway, sap:abap:icm, sap:saprouter, sap:hana:audit, sap:hana:tracelogs and sap:webdispatcher:access, with IP-node names also from XmlWinEventLog, sap:sapstartsrv, linux_secure and linux_messages_syslog. Refreshed hourly from KV Store (the IP-node names once a day); named layouts saved per user.
    Applications The SAP application runtime: ABAP Network & Security, ABAP Operations, Work Process Performance, HANA Audit, HANA Trace.
    Integration How SAP connects to other systems: SAP Services, SAP Router, Cloud Connector, Web Dispatcher, Web and API Performance.
    Security Cross-source security and compliance views: Network Perimeter, Cross-Stack Authentication, Change & Configuration Activity.
    Platform The infrastructure and ingest underneath SAP: Data Pipeline Overview, DNS Analytics, Linux, Windows, Proxy, Host Details, Multi-Cloud Overview, and the Data Doctor’s Diagnostics page.

    Each group page lists its dashboards with their purpose and key data sources.

    Common dashboard controls¶

    Time range¶

    The selected time range is held app-wide: it follows you when you move between dashboards. Drill-downs carry it to their destination (see Click-Through Drilldowns).

    Cloud filter¶

    Every dashboard except Multi-Cloud Overview, Environment Topology, Diagnostics and Settings carries a Cloud filter (the button reads Cloud: All; options All / aws / azure / gcp) in its title row, to the left of the auto-refresh picker. Choosing a provider filters every panel on the dashboard to that cloud. The choice is global and remembered per user in this browser, so it carries across dashboard navigation and page reloads. Leave it on All to see the whole estate. Events with no cloud attribution are counted as aws, matching the Multi-Cloud Overview convention.

    Per-dashboard auto-refresh¶

    Each dashboard’s title row carries a Refresh picker (Never / 30s / 1m / 5m / 15m / 30m / 1hr), to the right of the Cloud filter. The selection is per user and per dashboard: your choice on Environment Health doesn’t carry over to HANA Audit. It persists across browser sessions in Splunk KV Store. The Diagnostics page has no auto-refresh picker; it re-runs its checks on demand.

    Refresh the current view on demand¶

    The header’s second row carries a Refresh button, between the Actions menu and the AI Assistant button. Clicking it re-runs every panel on the dashboard you’re currently viewing for the selected time range. It is distinct from the per-dashboard auto-refresh picker above (which re-runs on a timer) and from each panel’s own Refresh toolbar action (which re-runs a single panel). Because it lives in the app-wide header, it’s available on every dashboard and on the Environment Topology view. On the Environment Topology view it re-runs the detail searches; the graph itself re-reads only from the view’s own toolbar Refresh button.

    In-dashboard help: the ? icon¶

    Every dashboard’s title row ends with a blue rotating ? help icon. Clicking it opens this online documentation in a new browser tab, at the page for the dashboard you’re looking at. For multi-tab dashboards (Data Pipeline Overview and Host Details) the icon is present on every tab and always links to the same dashboard’s page.

    Per-panel toolbar¶

    Every chart and table panel header carries a small action toolbar plus a “<1m ago” stamp showing when the panel’s search last ran:

    Action What it does
    Diagnose Runs the Data Doctor’s checks on this panel and opens the diagnosis drawer — explains why the panel is empty or partially blank (Data Doctor).
    Open in Search Opens Splunk’s Search app in a new tab with the panel’s dispatched query and the current time range pre-applied (the rollup read for a cached panel; the raw query at sub-hour ranges).
    Download (CSV) Exports the panel’s current result set as CSV.
    Inspect Opens Splunk’s Job Inspector for the panel’s last search — useful for diagnosing performance or verifying what ran.
    Refresh Re-runs the panel’s search immediately.

    KPI single-value cards show the loading spinner and a corner Diagnose button (revealed on hover or keyboard focus) but no full toolbar — they have no tabular result to export or inspect. While any panel’s search is in flight it renders a dot-ring loading spinner with “Loading data…”.

    Dashboard Export (Actions Menu)¶

    The header’s Actions menu includes Download PNG and Download PDF. Both captures use html2canvas to render the full dashboard DOM (including off-screen content), so the saved output always covers the entire dashboard length — not just what’s visible in the viewport. Useful for sharing in slide decks, embedding in incident reports, or capturing a dashboard’s state at a specific moment for compliance evidence. The same menu carries the two Data Doctor reports — Diagnose dashboard (PDF) and Environment report (PDF).

    Which build am I running? The About dialog¶

    The About item at the bottom of the navigation rail opens a dialog showing the app icon, the product name, and the version, build number and build date (UTC) of the app you are running. Use it to confirm an upgrade landed, or to quote the exact build when reporting an issue. The values are read from the app’s own app.conf at build time (the date is stamped as the bundle is compiled), so they always match the installed bundle. The header’s App and build pills show the same version and build number at a glance.

    Searching LogServ data¶

    All dashboards use the sap_logserv_idx_macro macro to query the LogServ index. You can use this same macro in your own searches: `sap_logserv_idx_macro` | stats count by sourcetype. Some App builds change search-time fields that your own searches may read; when you upgrade, check Upgrading to This Release.

    Performance and data freshness¶

    The dashboards are tuned to stay fast at high event volume: most panels read from an hourly KV-Store rollup layer rather than scanning raw events on every open. After installing on an index that already holds history, an admin runs a one-time backfill. See Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness for how each panel sources its data, what “hourly fresh” means, and the backfill step.

    Visual Style¶

    All dashboards share a consistent framed-card visual language, built on Cisco’s Magnetic design tokens, so that patterns are easy to recognize as you move between views. The app ships light and dark modes — toggled via the sun/moon button at the right end of the header, persisted per user — and every color is a mode-resolved design token rather than a fixed hex:

    • Page background with slightly lighter panel cards outlined by a muted border token — each visualization sits inside its own framed card with consistent spacing
    • KPI typography — large numeric headline with a small muted label; number color carries semantic meaning (white for neutral counts, red for errors/failures/denials, orange for warnings, teal for healthy/positive signals)
    • Standard colors — a single semantic red token is used across all error/failure signals so that “red means something went wrong” is unambiguous in both modes
    • Tables use a fixed header row with alternating row striping; clickable cells are highlighted in the accent color to indicate a drilldown affordance
    • Charts strip non-essential ink (no axis titles, no data labels, no progress bars) so the data shape is what your eye lands on

    The implementation uses styled-components on top of @splunk/react-ui primitives.

    KPI Sparklines¶

    Most KPI panels display a small inline sparkline directly below the headline number. The sparkline visualizes the daily trend across the dashboard’s current time range, so you get both the cumulative total and the shape of how that total accumulated in a single glance. There is no separate “up/down by N” trend value — the sparkline alone carries the trend signal.

    Sparklines come in a few flavors depending on what the KPI measures:

    • Count-based KPIs (e.g., Total Events, Auth Failures) — sparkline shows daily event count
    • Distinct-count KPIs (e.g., Active Hosts, Unique Components) — sparkline shows daily distinct count
    • Rate KPIs (e.g., HTTP Error Rate, Web Error Rate %) — sparkline shows daily error percentage
    • Volume KPIs (e.g., Total Volume, Total Bandwidth) — sparkline shows daily MB; headline shows formatted KB/MB/GB
    • No-data rendering — while a KPI’s search runs, the card shows a small spinner; a search that returns no rows renders an em-dash (—) plus a short inline explanation of why (see Data Doctor). KPIs with an empty-safe SPL wrap render 0 instead, with a flat-zero sparkline

    Hovering a sparkline shows the value of the nearest day and its date. A sparkline’s days follow your Splunk time-zone preference, and the hover shows the date in that zone. The Beaconing Domains sparklines are the exception: beaconing is detected per UTC day, so each of their points is one UTC day and the hover shows its date labelled (UTC day). A day’s beaconing count is written once that UTC day has ended, so on DNS Analytics and Network Perimeter, whose lines run to the end of the selected range, a UTC day that has not ended yet is drawn at 0 and its hover reads (UTC day, not yet computed). That is today’s UTC day, and west of UTC also the next one, which begins before your local day ends.

    Chart Time Buckets¶

    Time charts follow the time-range picker: the wider the range, the wider each bar or line point (its bucket), so a chart stays readable from Last 24 hours to Last 90 days. Every time chart prints the bucket it is drawing in its subtitle – for example Proxy request count — span 6h.

    Selected range Charts counted from the index Summary-backed charts
    Under 90 minutes 1 minute 1 minute (they read raw events at this range)
    90 minutes to 6 hours 1 minute 1 hour
    Up to 24 hours (Last 24 hours) 15 minutes 1 hour
    Up to 7 days (Last 7 days) 1 hour 1 hour
    Up to 30 days (Last 30 days) 6 hours 6 hours
    Longer (Last 90 days) 1 day 1 day

    Summary-backed charts never draw buckets finer than an hour, because the summaries they read are hourly (see Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness). Day-sized buckets, and the days of the KPI sparklines, follow your Splunk time-zone preference; shorter buckets are aligned to UTC, so a 6-hour bucket starts at 00:00, 06:00, 12:00 or 18:00 UTC.

    Click-Through Drilldowns¶

    Table rows are the main drill-down surface; Environment Health additionally makes its KPI cards and chart panels clickable, and other dashboards wire panel-level drill-downs selectively. A pointer cursor and a hover highlight mark what you can click:

    • Clicking a KPI opens a contextual destination — typically the related drill-down dashboard with the current time range preserved, or Splunk’s Search app with a pre-built SPL query for cross-cutting KPIs (e.g., the Environment Health “Total Errors” KPI runs a cross-cutting OR search spanning every error-bearing sourcetype across the estate).
    • Clicking a table row opens a filtered view — Host Details for host columns, the relevant specialist dashboard for sourcetype columns, or Splunk’s Search app with the row’s context spliced into a SPL filter.
    • Clicking a chart panel — on dashboards that wire a panel-level drill-down, clicking anywhere in the panel (outside its toolbar) opens the related dashboard or search. Individual chart points are not separately clickable.
    • Every drill-down opens in a new browser tab with noopener,noreferrer security flags. Time-range query params (?earliest=...&latest=...) are preserved across the navigation, and the destination sets its time-range picker from them, so it loads at the source dashboard’s window.

    The AI Assistant’s result tiles carry their own drill-down chips back into these dashboards; see Drill-down Chips.

    Environment Health¶

    Why This Dashboard Matters¶

    The Environment Health dashboard is a single-pane-of-glass operations view that aggregates the most critical signals from across the entire SAP landscape. Instead of switching between individual dashboards to piece together overall health, administrators can use this dashboard to immediately identify active errors, security failures, and performance degradation. Every panel links to the relevant detailed dashboard for investigation, making this the recommended starting point for daily operations monitoring and incident triage.

    Environment Health is the default landing page when you open the LogServ App. It is the first entry in the navigation rail, above Topology and the four dashboard groups. Its panels are listed below in screen order: the KPI row, then the charts, then the two tables.

    Panels¶

    • Total Errors – Aggregate count of errors across all monitored sourcetypes. Click to open a detailed search showing errors by category, sourcetype, affected hosts, and last-seen time.
    • HANA Failed Ops – Count of non-successful HANA audit operations (login failures, permission denials, DDL errors). Click to drill down to HANA Audit dashboard.
    • Auth Failures – Combined count of sapstartsrv authentication failures and HANA audit connection failures. Click to drill down to SAP Services dashboard.
    • Firewall Drops at Host – Count of Linux kernel firewall drops of packets addressed to the host itself (IN_DROP, the INPUT chain) across all monitored hosts. Drops of traffic a host was routing on to another system (FWD_DROP, in transit) are not counted as errors here; the Linux and Network Perimeter dashboards show both. Click to drill down to Linux dashboard.
    • Web Error Rate – Percentage of Web Dispatcher requests returning 4xx/5xx status codes. Click to drill down to Web Dispatcher dashboard.
    • Beaconing Domains – Count of DNS domains exhibiting periodic query patterns that may indicate malware or C2 communication. Its sparkline has one point per UTC day (beaconing is detected per UTC day), and hovering a point shows that UTC date. Click to drill down to DNS Analytics dashboard.
    • Data Pipeline – Events/Day (Avg) – Average daily event volume over the selected range (days follow your Splunk time-zone preference, and the current partial day counts as a day), with a daily sparkline, for monitoring pipeline health and detecting ingestion gaps. Click to drill down to the Data Pipeline Overview dashboard.
    • Event Volume Trend – Full-width chart of total events over time across all sourcetypes. Click to drill down to the Data Pipeline Overview dashboard.
    • ABAP Error Trend – Stacked column chart of ABAP errors over time by sub-source (Dispatcher, ICM, Gateway; the ICM series counts dev_icm messages logged as ERROR). Click to drill down to the ABAP Network & Security dashboard.
    • HANA Error Trend – Stacked column chart of HANA errors over time (Audit Failures, Trace Errors). Click to drill down to HANA Audit dashboard.
    • Security Error Trend – Stacked column chart of security errors over time (Auth Failures, Firewall Drops at Host). Click to drill down to SAP Services dashboard.
    • Web/Network Error Trend – Stacked column chart of web/network errors over time (WebDisp 4xx/5xx, Router Errors, Proxy Denied). Click to drill down to Web Dispatcher dashboard.
    • OS/Infra Error Trend – Stacked column chart of Windows events over time by severity (High, Medium). Click to drill down to Windows dashboard.
    • Cloud Connector Error Trend – Stacked column chart of Cloud Connector HTTP errors over time (4xx Client, 5xx Server). Click to drill down to Cloud Connector dashboard.
    • Web Dispatcher Response Time – Column chart of average response time (ms) over time for web dispatcher requests. Click to drill down to Web Dispatcher dashboard.
    • ICM Warnings & Errors – Stacked column chart of ABAP ICM trace messages over time by class (ERROR, WARNING). Click to drill down to the ABAP Network & Security dashboard.
    • Recent Critical Events – Table of the most recent critical signals (up to 200): HANA audit non-successful operations, ABAP dispatcher ERROR/FATAL, HANA trace fatal, sapstartsrv auth failures, and Windows critical-severity events, most-recent first. Click any row to drill down to Host Details for that host.
    • Affected Hosts – Table of hosts ranked by total error count with breakdowns by category (ABAP, HANA, Services, Firewall (at host), Other). Click any host to drill down to Host Details.

    Drill-Down Behavior¶

    Every KPI card, chart panel, and table row on this dashboard is clickable and opens its drill-down destination in a new browser tab with the source dashboard’s currently-selected time range pre-applied (?earliest=...&latest=...). The destination’s TimeRangeProvider parses the URL and hydrates its initial time-range from those params on mount, so a click from “Last 7 days” lands you in the destination at the same window. Two destination patterns:

    • Cross-dashboard drill-downs — most KPIs and charts navigate to the relevant React dashboard (/applications/hana-audit, /integration/cloud-connector, etc.).
    • Splunk Search drill-downs — the Total Errors KPI runs a cross-cutting OR query spanning every error-bearing sourcetype it counts — a query no single dashboard owns; it opens Splunk’s universal Search app with the SPL pre-filled. Same time-range carry-through.

    The dashboard’s title-row toolbar carries a Refresh picker so you can have the page tick continuously (Never / 30s / 1m / 5m / 15m / 30m / 1hr) for use as an operations wallboard.

    Where the Data Comes From¶

    The dashboard reads three kinds of source, chosen per panel for the cheapest path that stays exact:

    • Summary-backed panels — the error/severity KPIs, all six error-trend charts, the web error-rate and response-time panels, the ICM warnings and errors panel, the Auth Failures KPI and the Affected Hosts matrix read the logserv_severity_rollup KV Store collection (metrics toterr, trend, tophost, web, icmsev, authfail — each pre-computes one panel group’s exact classification per hour). Populated at minute :10 of every hour by logserv_severity_aggregate, which classifies events from thirteen sourcetypes across the estate (HANA audit + tracelogs, the ABAP family, Web Dispatcher, SAP Cloud Connector, SAProuter, sapstartsrv, Windows event logs, Linux secure and Squid proxy).
    • The Beaconing Domains KPI reads the daily logserv_beaconing_rollup (populated at 00:30 by a per-UTC-day gap-variance detection over DNS query events — daily cadence because the detection needs at least a day of inter-arrival history).
    • Pure-count pipeline panels run tstats directly against indexed fields — no summary needed, fast at any volume.
    • Recent Critical Events is a live event listing: it dispatches its SPL against the raw events at view time, capped at the 200 most recent matches.

    Summary-backed panels switch automatically to their exact raw-equivalent search when the selected window is shorter than 90 minutes, so sub-hour investigation stays real-time. The collection keeps 365 days of hourly history (trimmed by a daily retention search). After install, Settings → Dashboard Data → Run backfill fills it with the history your index holds: the last 30 days by default, or up to 365 days, or a custom range (see Backfilling on first install). The Cloud filter in the title row filters the summaries through the cloud_provider dimension stored in every rollup row. Full schedule and freshness reference: Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness.

    What to Look For¶

    • Rising error trend – An upward slope in any error category chart indicates a worsening condition. Correlate the timing with recent changes, deployments, or infrastructure events. Each chart drills directly to the relevant dashboard for investigation.
    • Auth failure spikes – Sudden increases in the Auth Failures KPI or Security Error Trend may indicate brute-force login attempts, expired credentials, or misconfigured service accounts. Cross-reference with the HANA Audit and SAP Services dashboards.
    • HANA audit failures – Non-zero HANA Failed Ops always warrant investigation. Failed operations may indicate unauthorized access attempts, privilege escalation, or application misconfigurations.
    • Cloud Connector errors – A spike in the Cloud Connector Error Trend (especially 5xx Server errors) may indicate backend system unavailability, network issues between the SCC and SAP BTP, or certificate expiration.
    • Pipeline volume drops – A sudden drop in the Event Volume Trend may indicate an SQS queue backup, S3 input failure, HF outage, or filter misconfiguration. Check the Data Pipeline Overview for per-host visibility.
    • Response time degradation – An increasing trend in Web Dispatcher response time often precedes user-facing performance complaints. Check the ICM Warnings & Errors panel and the Web Dispatcher’s 5xx responses for the same window.
    • Host concentration – If the Affected Hosts table shows errors concentrated on one or two hosts, those systems may have a localized issue (disk full, service crash, misconfiguration) rather than an environment-wide problem.

    Environment Topology¶

    Why This View Matters¶

    The Environment Topology view answers a question every SAP administrator has: “what’s actually talking to what?” Traditional dashboards show events, errors, and aggregates per source — but the shape of how SAP systems integrate with each other (RFC partners, HANA tenant relationships, web traffic boundaries, cross-zone connections) is hidden in those tabular surfaces. This view materializes that shape as an interactive graph drawn from your existing log data — no new ingest, no CMDB integration, no tagging effort required.

    Use it to:

    • Validate that your topology matches the as-designed architecture (every system shows up; no rogue partners are talking inbound).
    • Investigate a single SID’s call surface — who calls it, what does it call, where are the errors concentrated?
    • Drill from an edge (a single integration relationship) into the raw events with one click — every edge carries a denormalized SPL filter expression so you can pivot to Splunk’s universal search instantly.
    • Onboard a new analyst by giving them a one-page picture of the SAP landscape before they start digging into individual dashboards.
    • Spot orphaned IPs / hosts that don’t belong to any known SID — these are typically misconfigured load balancers, scanners, or unauthorized integration partners.

    This view replaces the manual hand-drawn architecture diagrams that SAP admin teams typically maintain in slides or wikis. Because it’s data-driven, it stays current as systems are added or retired.

    What’s on Screen¶

    The view is laid out in four regions:

    Top toolbar — the layout-mode dropdown (Force / Layered / Tree), Refresh button (re-runs the KV Store fetch while preserving saved positions), Save Layout, Load Layout dropdown with the ⚙ Manage Layouts entry, Snap mode toggle, the saved-layout name chip showing what’s currently loaded, a Saved/Unsaved-changes indicator next to it, and a legend row of colour swatches — one per integration type, matching the edge colours on the canvas.

    Left sidebar — two stacked panels. The Systems · Integration panel rolls up the inventory (systems, total calls, partner count) and lists each SAP system with a per-system call-volume bar; High Traffic systems (see below) render highlighted. The Integration types panel is a checkbox list of the nine integration types (RFC sync, iDoc async, qRFC, tRFC, bgRFC, Web service / SOAP, OData / Gateway, BTP iFlow / CPI, SAP Router) — un-ticking a type dims its edges in the canvas without removing them. Three of them carry edges today: RFC (sync) draws RFC connections and HANA tenant traffic, Web service / SOAP draws HTTP and HANA audit edges, and SAP Router draws the connections an SAP Router routed; the other six stay listed so that saved layouts keep their filter state. The Edge Details pane names each edge by what it records (HTTP, RFC, HANA Audit, HANA Tenant, SAP Router).

    Center canvas — the interactive graph itself, rendered with @xyflow/react. Nodes:

    • High Traffic SIDs — the five SAP systems with the most total calls touching them (inbound + outbound + bidirectional) in the visible window, ranked at render time. There is no configured focus list — the ranking is purely data-derived, and only SAP systems compete for the five slots (a high-volume client IP cannot occupy one). On an estate with five or fewer systems, every SID is High Traffic.
    • Regular Traffic SIDs — every other internal SAP system. Same large circle and outline as High Traffic; the kinds differ only in the panel’s Kind row and the Systems-panel highlight.
    • Every SAP system circle carries an interior icon: an app-server rack for application systems, a database cylinder for database systems.
    • HANA tenant databases — full-size circles with a combined app-servers + database icon, tagged “APP SERVERS - HANA TENANT” (chip: “HANA TENANT”). A tenant is a logical database inside a HANA system, named after the application SID it backs — its circle deliberately shares that name.
    • DB-tagged partners — circular discs with a cylinder icon when the partner is a database vendor (HANA, Oracle, MSSQL, Postgres, DB2). HANA systems specifically are tagged when their SID appears as a sap_sid clause on a hana_tenant-type edge — distinct from HANA tenants (which are logical databases inside a HANA system, named after the application SID they back).
    • SAP Router hosts — rounded squares with a ⇄ routing glyph, tagged “SAP ROUTER”: the host whose SAP Router log recorded the routed connections. A router is never folded into an SAP system, even when the inventory attributes the same host name to one — a VM that runs both an SAP instance and the router keeps both, the system’s circle and the router’s square.
    • Other partners — rounded squares for non-DB external endpoints (web partners, gateways, generic IPs).

    IP-labeled squares can carry name lines. When the logs themselves identify the machine or the people behind an IP endpoint, the square renders up to two extra lines directly under the IP: the hostname, and a user line (the user name when exactly one distinct user was seen; a count like “7 users” otherwise — hover the line for the full list). The evidence comes from four same-event sources, refreshed daily into the logserv_topology_ip_enrichment KV Store collection: HANA audit client registrations (client_ip + client host name + executing_user), Windows successful-logon events (4624 — IpAddress + WorkstationName + TargetUserName), SAP start service authentication lines (auth_user + remote address) and Linux sshd session lines. Two honesty rules govern what renders: a hostname shows only when it is unambiguous — the IP must map to exactly one machine name (a short name and its FQDN count as one), and that name must not be claimed by a crowd of IPs — and nothing is ever guessed (gateway logs, for example, record partner hostnames and peer IPs on different lines, so they are deliberately not correlated). The names are “latest known” rather than time-range-scoped: they do not blink out when you narrow the picker, and the Details panel’s “Names as of” row tells you how fresh the mapping is.

    Each SID and DB partner carries a 3-segment health ring painted around its perimeter, showing the proportion of normal (green) / warning (orange) / error (red) calls in the visible time window. Non-DB partners (the rounded squares) carry an equivalent rounded-square perimeter outline. Nodes with no calls or with all calls in a single bucket render as a solid full ring in the dominant color (a healthy node with all-normal calls shows a solid green ring; an idle node still shows green so you can tell the canvas painting succeeded). The classification: edges with errorRate < 10% route their errors to the warning bucket; edges with errorRate ≥ 10% route to the error bucket; everything else is normal. HANA-tagged nodes additionally route WARNING-severity trace events and slow hdbcons commands (hana_op_duration_ms > 1000 — the HANA console commands timed in the tenant’s trace files, each converted to milliseconds from the unit its line records) into the warning bucket as a vendor-specific health signal — these counts are first-class fields on the edge bucket rows, computed at hourly aggregation time from sap:hana:tracelogs.

    Edges render as gently bowed curves drawn center-to-center between nodes and clipped at each node’s visible boundary — arrowheads land on the health ring / outline outer edge rather than inside the node. When two systems call each other in both directions, the two edges bow apart so each direction stays separately visible and clickable. Edge labels sit at the curve’s apex.
