    Right sidebar (selection-driven) — what shows here depends on whether you’ve selected a node or an edge.

    When a node is selected, four tabs surface that node’s per-selection context:

    • Overview — a facts table, an hourly chart (Count / hr: the node’s log events per hour), and the partner breakdown. The facts table splits the node’s calls and connections three ways — inbound, outbound and bidirectional — alongside the total, using exact figures so they reconcile against everything below them. On SAP system and tenant nodes it also shows “Hosts (in range)” — the distinct hosts that logged the node’s events in the window, the same figure the Hosts tab’s caption reports (both read the same hourly rollup; on a tenant node the count is scoped by the shared name and the panel says so inline). The same number appears as a Hosts row in the hover tooltip on SAP system circles. On IP-labeled partner squares with name evidence (see IP-labeled squares can carry name lines above), the facts table adds Hostname (with its evidence source), Users (every user seen from that address, grouped by source) and Names as of rows directly under the Tag row. The hourly chart is hardcoded to the last 24 hours regardless of the global time-range picker (its purpose is “what’s happening RIGHT NOW on this node,” not “what happened over the picker’s window”). For HANA-tagged nodes, an additional roll-up section shows tenants list, tenant trace events, p95/max hdbcons command duration, and auth success/fail counts — derived from incident edges in JS, no extra SPL.

      Beneath those sit two partner donuts: partners that call this system, and partners this system calls. Each lists every partner — there is no “other” bucket and the legend is not capped, so a system with a wide fan-out makes the panel taller rather than the list shorter. Edges the data records as bidirectional (HANA Tenant traffic) are counted on their own line instead of being assigned a direction the stored row denies. Each donut’s caption names what it counts - calls, connections (RFC and SAP Router edges count connections), or calls + connections when that side has both, with “total” under the donut’s centre. Legend rows show the endpoint and its count. (Inventory ownership badges render where ownership can actually vary — the Hosts tab rows and the Edge Details “By app server” table; see Self-Derived IP→SID Inventory.)

      Hover any slice (or its legend row) for that endpoint, its exact count, and its share of the chart’s total. Reach for it whenever a slice is small: a slice too small to survive its own outline is drawn slightly larger so it stays visible, so the angle of the smallest slices is approximate while the number in the tooltip is exact. The panel says so inline whenever that widening has actually been applied.

    • Top Programs — the top ABAP programs seen on this node, from sap:abap:icm’s icm_program field (top 8). RFC remote gateway services and client programs, HANA action types and web URIs are not in this tab — they surface per-edge on the Edge Details Operations tab.

    • Errors — categorized error breakdown for the node (HTTP 4xx/5xx, severity ERROR / CRITICAL / FATAL, gateway gw_error_detail and error_function). Aggregated by sourcetype + error_kind.

    • Hosts — two tables. The first lists the hosts that logged events for this system, with first-seen / last-seen / dc(sourcetype) per host — and, where the events carry them, the SAP instance numbers seen on that host (inst 00, 01) — and — on a SAP system node — an ownership verdict per row. The read returns the 100 busiest hosts; if a system has more, the panel says so rather than presenting the cap as the count.

      The second, Calls by host and edge type, breaks the node’s traffic down per receiving host. A row names a host only where the data supports one: a hostname is only ever the receiving end of a call, so per-host rows are always inbound, and everything else — calls this node makes, and traffic recorded against a system as a whole — appears as an edge-type row. Because every incident edge lands in exactly one row, the column sums to the Total calls + connections figure on the Overview tab, which makes it checkable. Note that its Calls column counts edge calls and connections (RFC and SAP Router edges count connections) while the Events column in the table above counts log events, from a different rollup — the two are not the same measure.

    When an edge is selected, five tabs surface that edge’s per-call context:

    • Overview — endpoint cards (source / direction / target), pre-computed aggregates (call count, error count, error rate, sourcetype), and an inline activity trend chart. The pane names the counts after what the edge records: an RFC edge counts connections — a remote-gateway connection or a client session that closed, plus each distinct broken connection; the gateway trace records connections, not individual RFC calls — and its errors are the broken connections; an SAP Router edge counts routed connections (the router’s CONNECT TO lines) and failed connections (server-side receive failures that name the same target address, counted from their own trace lines, so the failure rate is capped at 100 %). RFC edges add a “By app server” table splitting the edge’s connections and broken connections by the address of the gateway that recorded them — the SAP system’s side of the connection, whichever direction it was made — with inventory owner badges: the app servers as the gateway log names them, not a full instance inventory. Connection records (a remote-gateway connection or a client session that closed) name no local address and are grouped as “(not recorded)”. The rows partition the edge’s connections, so they sum to the count above them.
    • Activity — full-width stacked-area chart of successful calls + errors over the visible time window (for RFC and SAP Router edges: connections + broken or failed connections). Computed in the browser from the same hourly rows that produce the Overview totals, so the two always agree.
    • Operations — donut chart of the top 10 entities for this edge type (HTTP URIs; RFC remote gateway services and client programs; HANA actions; HANA trace components; SAP Router target services such as sapmsXCI, 3300 or sapgw00). Its centre total and hover text count in the edge’s own unit — connections for RFC and SAP Router edges, calls for the others.
    • Performance — for HTTP edges, latency percentiles (P50 / P95 / Max) and bytes-out plus a per-status-class call-count histogram. For HANA Audit, cached auth success / auth fail headline counts plus a dispatched action-status mix. For HANA Tenant, a cached p95 + max hdbcons command duration headline (the HANA console commands timed in the tenant’s trace files, each duration converted to milliseconds from the microsecond, millisecond or second unit its line records; the p95 is a call-weighted blend of the per-hour p95s stored on the edge rows — an approximation), and below it a dispatched avg + max chart: true percentiles cannot be merged across hourly buckets, so the chart reads mean and maximum and says so inline. For RFC, a dispatched connection record mix (remote gateway connection closed / client session closed / broken connection); for SAP Router, a target role mix (message server, gateway, dispatcher, …). Neither has headline cells.
    • Errors — the top 15 failure modes with error_kind, error_detail, count, and last-seen timestamp. For HANA Audit this covers all unsuccessful operations, which is broader than the Overview row (labelled “Auth failures (CONNECT)”) directly above it. For RFC the rows come from the broken-connection lines; for SAP Router they are the failed connections by return code (rc=<code> · server-side connection failed).

    Tabs that are legitimately empty

    Not every tab has content for every edge type — an empty tab is not necessarily a fault. An RFC edge whose connections were all broken ones has no Operations rows (a broken connection names no remote service or client program), an SAP Router edge with only failed connections in the window has neither Operations nor Performance rows (a failure line names the target address only), and any edge type can have an empty Errors tab simply because nothing failed. The pane distinguishes the two cases: when a tab was queried and came back empty it says so, and when nothing could be queried at all it says that instead.

    Selection is mutex — clicking a node clears any selected edge and vice versa, so the right pane never shows mixed context. Clicking empty canvas (the pane) clears both. Each side preserves its own preferred tab independently when you swap between selections. (This inspection selection — the cyan glow plus the Details panel — is separate from group membership below, which uses a dashed outline: a node can be inspected, in a group, both, or neither.)

    Group select and move¶

    Hold Shift and drag on empty canvas to draw a selection box: every node the box touches joins the group and gains a dashed outline, and a status chip at the canvas top-right shows the count. Then drag any highlighted node to move the whole group rigidly — relative positions are preserved, and the edges follow their nodes (an edge has no position of its own, so moving the nodes is moving the edges; edges are not independently selectable). The gesture set:

    • Shift + drag on empty canvas — draw the selection box (plain drag still pans).
    • Shift / Ctrl / Cmd + click a node — add it to or remove it from the group (these clicks never open the Details panel).
    • Plain click any node — inspect it in the Details panel and release the group.
    • Escape or a click on empty canvas — clear the group.
    • Drag a highlighted node — move the whole group. Dragging a node outside the group releases the group and moves only that node.
    • Arrow keys (with a focused, selected node) — nudge the whole group.

    With Snap mode on, releasing a group drag applies one shared grid offset to every member, so the group’s shape is preserved — members are not rounded to the grid independently. Group moves mark the layout Unsaved and are captured by Save Layout exactly like single-node drags. The group survives data refreshes and time-range changes; it clears when the node set itself changes (a layout-mode switch or loading a saved layout).

    Bottom panel — Live Activity table showing the eight busiest integration edges (any type) by count (calls, or connections for RFC and SAP Router edges) for the current time range. The panel fills its allotted height exactly — the partners table scrolls internally under a sticky header when it outgrows the panel, so the panel frame always closes cleanly. Drag the divider above the panel to resize it (120–640 px, persisted with saved layouts); expanding the collapsed panel restores at least the 300 px default height. Collapsing or expanding the panel automatically re-fits the graph so it claims (or yields) the freed vertical space.

    MiniMap (bottom-right of the canvas) — drag the cursor inside the minimap to pan the main canvas. Direction follows the cursor: dragging right → main canvas shows more right-side content; dragging down → shows more bottom content. Magnitude is proportional to your cursor delta scaled by the minimap’s viewBox-to-pixel ratio. Single-click does nothing — drag-to-pan is the only minimap interaction.

    Where the Data Comes From¶

    The view reads a time-bucketed KV Store that hourly scheduled searches fill, so opening it does not run a search over raw events. The searches, their minutes and their run times are listed in the schedule reference.

    The aggregation searches read from these SPL sources:

    Source What it contributes
    sap:abap:gateway RFC connections in the direction they were made: remote-gateway connections that closed (GwDiscRemGw lines — outbound, to the last /H/ hop of the target as a lower-cased short host name, or its address), client sessions that closed (GwDisconnectClient lines — inbound, from the client address), and distinct broken connections from the network-trace lines (P=<peer> / L=<local>; a local port 33NN or 48NN, the gateway’s own listener, means the peer called in). The local IP is canonical for IP→SID inventory because it always belongs to this host’s SID.
    sap:saprouter SAP Router edges: each CONNECT TO line’s target address (saprouter_target_ip), from the router host that logged it, and server-side receive failures that name a target address (NiBufReceive S… '<IPv4>' failed) as failed connections — client-side failures (NiBufReceive C…) and failures that name a host are not counted. A target named sapms<SID> (that SID’s message server) attributes the target address to the SID in the inventory, so the edge ends on the SID’s circle. Loopback targets (127.0.0.0/8, such as the niping self-test) are excluded.
    sap:abap:icm ICM local addresses (icm_local_ip): a node for each, and IP→SID inventory entries (except from a Web Dispatcher’s own ICM trace, see below); and the programs on the Top Programs tab (icm_program).
    sap:hana:tracelogs HANA host + tenant SID extracted from the source path (/usr/sap/<HANA_SID>/HDB<inst>/<host>/trace/DB_<TENANT_SID>/). Yields the rich HANA-side topology including multi-tenant relationships.
    sap:webdispatcher:access HTTP client IP → web-server host edges (clientip / host / uri / status). The source of every HTTP edge and its status-class distribution. Its events also carry sap_sid / sap_instance from the log’s path, so they count toward the host’s node and the Hosts and Errors tabs of the system the path names, but they never attribute a host to a system in the inventory (see below).
    sap:hana:audit HANA authentication edges (client_ip → HANA host) with auth success/fail counts; also feeds the IP-node name enrichment (client hostname + executing user).
    XmlWinEventLog / sap:sapstartsrv / sshd session lines IP-node name enrichment only — the daily pass that puts a hostname / user line under unresolved IP squares.
    Default Splunk host field (cross-source fallback) Picks up hosts that aren’t surfaced in the above, and attributes a host to the one SAP system its SAP events name (sap_sid) — a Web Dispatcher’s access log and ICM trace excepted (see below).

    The node, edge and detail collections are trimmed nightly to 365 days of hourly history, and the IP-name enrichment to the names seen in the last 365 days; none of the trims empties a collection on an empty read (override_if_empty=false). To fill the view with history after an install, use Settings → Dashboard Data and backfill the Environment Topology (graph) and Environment Topology (detail tabs) rows: they take the window you choose (30 days by default, up to 365 days, or a custom range), while the inventory and the IP-name enrichment always refresh over the last 30 days. See Backfilling on first install.

    The KV Store collections behind the view, and how the view reads them
    KV Store collection Schema Populated by
    logserv_topology_nodes one row per (canonical entity, hourly bucket); 9 fields including event_count, last_seen logserv_topology_aggregate_nodes (hourly)
    logserv_topology_detail_rollup one row per (metric, scope, hourly bucket); powers the right pane’s per-node and per-edge tabs. Edge metrics (edge_op / edge_perf / edge_err) are keyed by the same stored edge id as logserv_topology_edges.id logserv_topology_detail_aggregate (hourly)
    logserv_topology_edges one row per (edge, hourly bucket) — RFC edges one row per (edge, app-server local_ip, hourly bucket), so multi-app-server counts stay exact; SAP Router edges one row per (router host, target address, hourly bucket); 20 fields including pre-computed response_time_p50 / _p95 / _max, hana_op_p95_ms / hana_op_max_ms, auth_success_count / auth_fail_count, error_count, warning_count, plus canonical spl_sourcetype + spl_filter_clauses for right-pane drilldowns logserv_topology_aggregate_edges (hourly)
    logserv_topology_inventory flat (no bucket dimension), keyed by canonical_value; IP / host → SID mapping for retargeting raw IPs to their owning SID node logserv_topology_aggregate_inventory (hourly)
    logserv_topology_ip_enrichment flat (no bucket dimension), keyed by <ip>:<evidence_source>; hostname + user names behind IP endpoints logserv_topology_enrichment_aggregate (daily)

    When you open the view, the React app fetches a time-window slice of these collections via the Splunk Web REST proxy (/en-US/splunkd/__raw/servicesNS/nobody/<APP>/storage/collections/data/<NAME>?query={"bucket_ts":{"$gte":...,"$lte":...}}). The fetch returns in well under a second on production-scale data. Clicking an edge dispatches three small searches against the hourly logserv_topology_detail_rollup — Operations, Performance and Errors — scoped by the stored edge id(s) behind the edge you clicked. Overview and Activity need no search at all: both are derived from the rows already in the browser. Because inventory retargeting can collapse several stored edges into one you see on the canvas, those three reads cover the whole set, and say so if an edge ever spans more than one.

    Self-Derived IP→SID Inventory¶

    The “which IP belongs to which SID” mapping isn’t read from a CMDB or an admin-maintained lookup — it’s self-derived from the same logs you’re already ingesting. A multi-source union SPL counts, for each IP address and host, how many events each SAP SID logged for it and when it logged the newest one, and the inventory records the endpoint under its most recent SID: of the SIDs whose newest event falls in the endpoint’s most recent hour, the one with the most events (counted over the search window: the last hour for the hourly update, 30 days for a backfill). An address that moves to another system follows it once its most recent hour names only the new SID, and a host that logs a few stray lines under another SID keeps the SID it logs most. A host that really runs two systems at once is shown under the one that logged more. An exact tie writes nothing: the endpoint keeps the row it had, or has no inventory row if it had none.

    Coverage depends on what your data exposes — unique hostname/IP appearances across multiple SAP sourcetypes attribute cleanly, while shared NAT IPs and external partners typically have no row at all (their SAP affiliation isn’t observable from logs alone, or they legitimately don’t belong to any single SID).

    Reading the ownership badges — and why an address on a system’s panel is never one of its own

    An address the inventory has attributed to a system is drawn inside that system’s node: the view folds it in before the graph is laid out. So an address you can still see as a separate endpoint is one no system has claimed — which makes owner not established the expected verdict on the partner donuts, not a data-quality alarm. On the Hosts tab, where hosts are listed by name rather than folded away, both verdicts occur.

    “Owner not established” means the inventory has no entry for that host or address. There are several reasons it might not have one: it may emit no system identifier the inventory reads, every update that saw it may have ended in an exact tie between two systems, or it may simply not have been observed since the collection was populated. The panel deliberately does not guess between them.

    One scope caveat the panel states inline: ownership is not limited to the selected time range. The inventory accumulates across all observed history, so a badge on a 24-hour view can reflect an attribution learned earlier.

    In addition to the inventory, the node-aggregation SPL captures every distinct edge endpoint as a node row in its own right — webdispatcher clientip, ABAP gateway peer_ip, HANA Audit client_ip, SAP Router hosts and their CONNECT TO target addresses (excluding loopback addresses, 127.0.0.0/8). This means external partners that appear only on the receiving side of integration edges still carry real event counts, not zero, even when they don’t have a SID resolution in the inventory.

    A Web Dispatcher’s own logs are not an attribution source: neither its access log nor its ICM trace (dev_icm), which LogServ files under webdispatcher/icm and which Data TA builds of 2026-10-13 and earlier typed sap:abap:icm, like an ABAP system’s ICM trace (later builds leave it sap_logserv_logs). Both carry the SID of their log path, but a Web Dispatcher often has its own SID (for example WDP) on a host that also runs another system, and it logs far more often than that system’s own components: counting it would hand the host, or the address its ICM listens on, to the Web Dispatcher’s SID in most hours. The inventory leaves out sap:webdispatcher:access events and, by the LogServ folder the Data TA records with every event (clz_dir = webdispatcher), the ICM trace. So a Web Dispatcher host is attributed only by its other SAP events, and a host that runs nothing but a Web Dispatcher stays a host square until another source names its system.

    One attribution source is the SAP Router itself: a CONNECT TO line whose target service is sapms<SID> names the SID whose message server listens at that address, so each such line counts toward that SID, and the address joins the inventory under its most recent SID, as described above. (Targets reached by port or sapgw<NN> name no SID and stay addresses until another source attributes them.)

    The inventory itself is extensible per-customer without new ingest: appending another union arm to the inventory aggregation SPL adds a new attribution source. Future arms could include ICM icm_peer_ip, additional CMDB-style lookup tables, or any other field that uniquely associates an IP / host with a SAP SID.

    Layout Modes¶

    The LAYOUT dropdown switches between three layout algorithms:

    • Force — a d3-force star-system arrangement: every high-traffic hub (focused SIDs, plus any secondary SID with enough leaf partners of its own) gets a proportional horizontal slot, its partners ring around it at a radius scaled to partner count, and smaller secondary systems anchor as satellites fanned around their nearest hub. The layout is deterministic — the same data renders the same picture on every load — and the graph world sizes itself to the canvas aspect ratio. Best for hub-and-spoke SAP landscapes; the default for first-time viewers.
    • Layered — ELK Sugiyama-layered top-to-bottom flow with orthogonal edges and near-zero edge crossings. Best for traffic-flow analysis where you want to see “what flows into what” structurally.
    • Tree — ELK mrtree classic top-down tree with hubs at top and spokes radiating downward. Best when the topology is approximately hub-and-spoke shaped.

    Both ELK-based modes (Layered + Tree) share the same lazy-loaded elkjs chunk, fetched only when you first pick a Layered or Tree layout. Force mode remains synchronous (no bundle hit on initial load).

    Each layout mode has its own saved-layout slot — saving a layout in Force doesn’t bleed into Layered or Tree. Switching layouts via the LAYOUT dropdown drops the current saved-positions cache so each mode renders fresh from its own algorithm. The Manage Layouts modal (⚙ entry at the top of the Load Layout dropdown) lets you set a per-mode default layout that auto-loads on mount.

    Saved Layouts¶

    User-arranged graph layouts are persisted in Splunk KV Store collection logserv_topology_layouts. Each saved layout carries:

    • Layout mode — Force / Layered / Tree (so a Force-saved arrangement loads back in Force mode, not Layered)
    • Node positions — where you’ve manually placed each node on the canvas
    • Panel state — sidebar tab + width
    • Viewport — zoom level + pan offset (x, y)
    • Enabled integration types — which checkboxes are ticked on the leftbar. A type added to the view after the layout was saved (SAP Router, for layouts saved before it existed) starts enabled when the layout loads; a type you had switched off stays off
    • Selected node / edge — what was selected when you saved
    • Active right-sidebar tab — Overview / Top Programs / Errors / Hosts (node mode) or Overview / Activity / Operations / Performance / Errors (edge mode)
    • Snap mode — whether new nodes snap to a grid

    Layouts are saved per-user-named — you can save your own variants (“focus on XCQ”, “all DBs”, “external partners only”) and switch between them from the Load Layout dropdown.

    The Manage Layouts modal (⚙ entry at the top of the Load Layout dropdown) is where two cross-browser preferences live:

    • Per-mode default layout — pick one saved layout per mode (Force / Layered / Tree) to auto-load on mount when you’re using that mode. Each mode section in the modal has its own radio list of mode-matching layouts plus a “(no default)” option.
    • Default layout mode — tick the Open in this mode by default checkbox on one of the three sections to declare which mode the dashboard should open in on next login. The checkbox is mutex across the three sections (or none — “no explicit default” leaves the dashboard opening in Force mode). Ticking the checkbox also switches the active mode immediately so you can see what the default-on-next-login experience will look like.

    Both preferences are persisted to Splunk KV Store keyed by Splunk username (collections logserv_topology_layout_defaults and logserv_topology_active_mode). Browser localStorage is used as a fast-mount cache mirror, so on a fresh browser the choices hydrate from KV Store on first paint. If you pick defaults in Chrome and open the topology in Firefox, you’ll see the same defaults the next time you log in to the same Splunk instance. When no defaults are stored, the dashboard opens in Force mode with no auto-loaded layout.

    Data Refresh Cadence¶

    The topology collections get a new hourly bucket in the first minutes of each hour: four hourly searches run at :05–:08, and the IP-node name enrichment runs once a day at 02:32, recomputing the names over the last 30 days (see the schedule reference). The view re-reads the KV Store:

    • On initial page load
    • On global TimeRange picker change
    • When the user clicks the toolbar’s Refresh button (useful right after a backfill from Settings → Dashboard Data)
    • When the user selects a different node (dispatches on-demand reads against the hourly logserv_topology_detail_rollup KV Store collection — same data layer, dispatched per selection rather than at page load)

    The graph itself does not poll. The title row’s Refresh picker and the header’s Refresh button re-run only the searches behind the selected node’s or edge’s detail tabs and the Hosts (in range) count; to re-read the graph, use the toolbar’s Refresh button. The hourly aggregation governs data freshness, and the newest bucket is the last completed hour. Running the aggregates more often would add no newer data, because each run reads whole completed hours.

    What to Look For¶

    • Health rings with prominent orange or red segments — a SID showing >25% red (error bucket) is a system whose external integrations are systematically failing. Click into the node and the Errors tab to see which specific edges are degraded.
    • Unattributed endpoints with high edge weight — an IP or hostname square carrying hundreds of calls but no inventory owner. Open it and check the Hostname / Users rows: a machine with no SAP identifier and heavy inbound traffic is either a shared NAT / load-balancer address or an integration partner nobody documented. Both warrant investigation.
    • Asymmetric edge counts — RFC edges are drawn in the direction the connection was made, from the calling side to the called side, so two systems joined by edges both ways connect to each other in both directions; a single edge names the caller. The Operations tab shows the remote services and client programs involved.
    • SAP Router failures — an SAP Router edge with failed connections points at a target that refuses or drops routed connections; the SAP Router dashboard’s error tables show the functions and return codes. A router edge that ends on a bare address rather than a system circle is a target the inventory has not attributed — the router’s route table says what it is.
    • Orphan SIDs — a node with no edges is a system that’s running but not integrated with anything else. May be a quiet test system, or a system whose integration partners aren’t monitored.
    • HANA tenants drifting from their HANA system — multi-tenant HANA produces edges from the parent system to each tenant. Missing tenant edges indicate either tenant outage or audit-log gap. The HANA-tagged DB partners specifically use slow hdbcons commands (>1000 ms) in the tenant traces as a warning signal; a tenant lighting up with orange in its ring after a deploy points at slower console commands or new trace warnings — the HANA Trace dashboard shows which.
    • Unexpected external partners — IP-labeled squares with no inventory owner and inbound edges into a production SID are the strongest signal of an undocumented external integration. Use the name lines under the square (hostname / user, where the logs carry them) and the Details panel’s endpoint facts to identify the caller.
    • Edge errors clustered on one sourcetype — clicking an edge and reading the Errors tab can reveal that 90% of failures are 4xx (client-side, not your problem) vs 5xx (server-side, your problem). The status-class breakdown is pre-aggregated hourly into the detail rollup, so clicking through to the Performance tab is a small keyed lookup rather than a scan of raw web-server events.
    • Host counts on the Hosts tab — a SID showing 3 hosts when you expected 2 may indicate a stale forwarder / VM that should have been decommissioned. A row badged with a different system’s name is worth a look on its own: it usually means a shared forwarder, or a management host running commands against this system from elsewhere.
    • A lopsided pair of partner donuts — a system that receives heavily but calls almost nothing (or the reverse) is a useful shape to notice: it separates the integration hubs from the leaf consumers, and a system that has quietly stopped calling out shows up here before it shows up in an error count.

    Notes¶

    • The view’s route is #/topology/integration-topology — the slug stayed integration-topology when the user-visible label changed from “Integration Topology” to “Environment Topology”, so existing bookmarks and saved-layout records remain valid.
    • Layout persistence works across browser tabs and across Splunk Web sessions — your KV Store records survive Splunkd restarts.
    • Layouts are saved per Splunk user — every KV Store record is keyed by <username>::<slug>, so different users have completely separate records and can’t overwrite each other’s layouts. If the same user edits the topology in two browser tabs concurrently, the tabs race each other and last-tab-save wins (multi-tab edit-collision protection is planned for a future release).
    • The minimap supports drag-only panning. Single-click and scroll-zoom inside the minimap rectangle are intentionally inert — drag is the one interaction.
    • Upgrading from an earlier build? See Upgrading: it lists the Environment Topology rows an upgrade must rebuild.

    Applications

    Applications¶

    The Applications category covers dashboards that monitor the SAP application runtime layer itself — the ABAP application server and the HANA database engine. These are the workloads SAP customers run every day, and dashboards here answer questions about work processes, dispatcher health, database audit trails, and diagnostic trace output.

    Dashboard Purpose Key Data Sources
    ABAP Network & Security ICM traffic analysis, gateway monitoring, and ABAP audit events sap:abap:icm, sap:abap:gateway, sap:abap:audit
    ABAP Operations ABAP runtime health, dispatcher status, work process activity, and system uptime sap:abap:dispatcher †, sap:abap:enqueueserver, sap:abap:event †, sap:abap:messageserver, sap:abap:sapstartsrv, sap:abap:workprocess †
    Work Process Performance SAP ABAP work process utilization, dispatcher health, function-level activity, and Async RFC queue depth sap:abap:workprocess †, sap:abap:dispatcher †, sap:abap:icm (Async RFC panels)
    HANA Audit SAP HANA database audit events, security monitoring, user activity, risk-tiered events, and after-hours admin activity sap:hana:audit
    HANA Trace SAP HANA database trace logs, component health, and error analysis sap:hana:tracelogs

    † SAP stopped delivering sap:abap:workprocess, sap:abap:dispatcher and sap:abap:event through LogServ in April 2026, so the panels built on them show historical data only, unless you have arranged continued collection with SAP. See Supported Log Types.

    The controls these dashboards share (time range, Cloud filter, auto-refresh, panel toolbar, drill-downs, export) are described once in the Dashboards Overview.

    ABAP Network & Security¶

    Why This Dashboard Matters¶

    The ABAP Network & Security dashboard monitors the network-facing components of SAP ABAP systems. The Internet Communication Manager (ICM) handles all HTTP/HTTPS traffic into and out of ABAP, while the Gateway controls RFC connections between SAP systems. Together they carry the traffic that reaches ABAP systems over the network, so connection problems and unexpected peers show up in their logs.

    Requires¶

    • Sourcetypes: sap:abap:icm (LogServ folder abap/icm), sap:abap:gateway (abap/gateway) and sap:abap:audit (abap/audit; it adds to the event counts only). The Data TA assigns them at index time where the data is parsed; see Supported Log Types.
    • Search-head add-ons: none beyond the LogServ App prerequisites.
    • Dashboard Data row: ABAP Network & Security. Backfill it once after installing the App so the panels show history: 30 days by default, up to 365 days or a custom range. See Backfilling on first install.

    Upgrading from an earlier build? See Upgrading.

    Panels¶

    Every panel reads the hourly summary, which adds each hour at minute :14 of the next hour, so on wide time ranges the panels can leave out up to about the last 75 minutes; ranges shorter than 90 minutes are answered from the raw events automatically. See Dashboard Data.

    • Total Events – Aggregate event count across the ICM, Gateway and Audit sourcetypes
    • ICM Errors – Count of dev_icm trace messages the ICM logged as *** ERROR =>
    • Gateway Errors – Count of Gateway events that carry an error detail
    • Event Volume by Sourcetype – Trend over time of each sourcetype
    • ICM Warnings & Errors Over Time – Column chart of the dev_icm trace messages logged as WARNING or ERROR, one bar per level in each time bucket
    • ICM Peer Connections – Table of the addresses at the other end of ICM connections — connections the ICM opened and connections clients opened to it — ranked by connection count, with the protocols seen; click a row for that peer’s ICM events in Search
    • ICM Request Types – Donut chart of the ICM session-list entries by request type (asynchronous RFC, HTTP, internal)
    • ICM Session Entries by SAP System and Client – Donut chart of the ICM session-list entries by SAP system and client (sap_sid / sap_client; 000 is the system client). A client number belongs to its system, so the same client in two systems is two slices
    • Gateway Remote Hosts – Table of gateway peers by remote host and function, with event count, the services seen, and the most recent error detail for that host/function pair; click a row for that host’s gateway events in Search
    • Gateway Errors Over Time – Timeline of gateway error events
    • Activity by SID / Instance – Column chart showing event distribution across SAP systems; click it to open ABAP Operations

    What the ICM trace records

    The ICM trace (dev_icm) records sessions, connections and the ICM’s own warning and error messages; it records no HTTP status code for individual requests. In a session-list line such as ASYNC_RFC T229_U23835_M0, 200, BATCH_ALM, , time=10:35:59, ... the three digits after the session ID are the SAP client, extracted as sap_client, followed by the user (icm_user) and the terminal (icm_terminal).

    What to Look For¶

    • ICM errors and warnings – A burst of ICM ERROR messages (for example failed TLS handshakes or connections) or of warnings such as connections a client closed prematurely can point to front-end, network or certificate problems. Open the raw dev_icm lines for the message text.
    • Unexpected SAP clients – Sessions in a client you do not expect for that system — one that is not in use, or business-user activity in the system client 000 — warrant a closer look. System users such as SAPSYS in client 000 are normal.
    • Unfamiliar peer IPs – New IP addresses appearing in the ICM Peer Connections table warrant investigation, especially if they account for many connections or use unusual protocols.
    • Gateway connections from unknown hosts – The Gateway Remote Hosts table should show expected RFC partners. Unknown remote hosts or unusual service names may indicate unauthorized access attempts.
    • Error rate trends – A gradually increasing error rate across days can signal infrastructure degradation (disk space, memory pressure, certificate expiry) before it becomes an outage.

    Related Dashboards¶

    • ABAP Operations – the runtime side of the same ABAP systems; opens from the Activity by SID / Instance chart.
    • Work Process Performance – its Async RFC Queue Depth panels read the same ICM log.
    • Environment Health – its ICM Warnings & Errors and ABAP Error Trend panels open this dashboard.
    • Host Details – its Data Freshness table opens this dashboard from an sap:abap:icm, sap:abap:gateway or sap:abap:audit row.
    Where the data comes from

    Every panel is summary-backed — there are no live raw scans. Panels read the logserv_abapnet_rollup KV Store collection (metrics vol, icmsev, icmclient, icmreq, icmpeer, icmerr, gwhost, gwlatest), populated at minute :14 of every hour by logserv_abapnet_aggregate from three sourcetypes:

    Source What it contributes
    sap:abap:gateway RFC-side facts — remote hosts, functions, services, and the latest gateway error detail per host/function
    sap:abap:icm ICM facts from the dev_icm trace — event volume, the ICM’s warning and error messages, session-list entries by request type and by SAP system and client, and connection peers and protocols
    sap:abap:audit Event volume only (Total Events, Event Volume by Sourcetype, Activity by SID / Instance)

    Summary-backed panels switch automatically to their exact raw-equivalent search when the selected window is shorter than 90 minutes, so sub-hour investigation stays real-time. The collection keeps 365 days of hourly history (trimmed by a daily retention search). The Cloud picker in the title row filters every panel by cloud_provider; events with no cloud_provider value count as aws. Full schedule and freshness reference: Dashboard Data.

    ABAP Operations¶

    SAP stopped delivering three of the six ABAP logs this dashboard reads through LogServ in April 2026: the work process, dispatcher and event logs. Their panels (Dispatcher Errors, Dispatcher Severity Over Time, System Uptime (Latest), Work Process Categories and Work Process Functions) show only data indexed before then, unless you have arranged continued collection with SAP. The enqueue server, message server and sapstartsrv logs keep arriving.

    Why This Dashboard Matters¶

    The ABAP Operations dashboard provides runtime health monitoring for the SAP ABAP application layer. It covers the dispatcher (request routing), work processes (transaction execution), enqueue server (lock management), and system uptime. These components are the engine of every SAP ABAP system, and their health directly impacts user experience and business process execution.

    Requires¶

    • Sourcetypes: sap:abap:enqueueserver, sap:abap:messageserver, sap:abap:sapstartsrv, and the three discontinued ones sap:abap:workprocess, sap:abap:dispatcher and sap:abap:event (LogServ folders abap/<log>). The Data TA assigns them at index time where the data is parsed; see Supported Log Types, which marks the discontinued log types.
    • Search-head add-ons: none beyond the LogServ App prerequisites.
    • Dashboard Data row: Work Process Performance / ABAP Operations (one row serves both dashboards). Backfill it once after installing the App so the panels show history: 30 days by default, up to 365 days or a custom range. See Backfilling on first install.

    Upgrading from an earlier build? See Upgrading.

    Panels¶

    Every panel reads the hourly summary, which adds each hour at minute :09 of the next hour, so on wide time ranges the panels can leave out up to about the last 70 minutes; ranges shorter than 90 minutes are answered from the raw events automatically. See Dashboard Data.

    • Total Events – Aggregate event count across all six ABAP runtime sourcetypes
    • Active SIDs – Count of distinct SAP System IDs reporting data
    • Dispatcher Errors – Count of ERROR/FATAL severity dispatcher events
    • Event Volume by Sourcetype – Trend over time across all six sourcetypes
    • Dispatcher Severity Over Time – Column chart of dispatcher log severity levels, one bar per level in each time bucket; click it to open Work Process Performance
    • Enqueue Lock Activity – Timeline of lock management operations (enqueue server events)
    • System Uptime (Latest) – Table showing the most recent uptime in days and hours per SID/instance, from the event log; click a row to open Work Process Performance
    • Work Process Categories – Donut chart showing activity distribution across the SAP trace components of the work process trace: the letter that starts each dev_w* line (e.g., B = Database Interface, C = Database (DBSL), M = Task Handler, N = Security (SNC/SSF), X = Extended Memory). The donut uses the wp_category_name field populated by the app’s props.conf EVAL, whose names follow SAP’s list of trace components, so every mapped letter gets a name; unmapped letters render as <letter> = Other.
    • Work Process Functions – Table of wp_function + sub-function combinations ranked by event volume (events with no sub-function are not listed)
    • Activity by SID / Sourcetype – Table of SID × sourcetype combinations ranked by event volume; click a row to open the raw events in Search

    What to Look For¶

    • Uptime resets – A system showing low uptime (hours instead of days) indicates a recent restart. Unexpected restarts may signal crashes, memory issues, or unplanned maintenance.
    • Dispatcher ERROR/FATAL increases – Rising error severity in the dispatcher can point at work process, connection or configuration problems before users report them. The Recent Dispatcher Errors table on Work Process Performance lists the reasons.
    • Trace component shifts – A sudden change in the mix of work process trace components (for example many more B = Database Interface or L = Background (Batch) lines) shows which subsystem is writing more trace lines.
    • Enqueue lock spikes – A sharp increase in lock operations can indicate application deadlocks, long-running transactions holding locks, or database performance issues causing lock wait times to increase.
    • SID/instance imbalance – If one system or instance is generating significantly more events than its peers, investigate whether it’s handling disproportionate load or experiencing issues.

    Related Dashboards¶

    • Work Process Performance – the work process and dispatcher detail, from the same summary; opens from the Dispatcher Severity chart and the System Uptime table.
    • ABAP Network & Security – the ICM and Gateway side of the same systems; its Activity by SID / Instance chart opens this dashboard.
    • Host Details – its Data Freshness table opens this dashboard from an sap:abap:dispatcher, sap:abap:enqueueserver, sap:abap:event, sap:abap:messageserver or sap:abap:sapstartsrv row.
    Where the data comes from

    Every panel is summary-backed. Panels read the logserv_wp_perf_rollup KV Store collection (metrics wp, dp, abap, abap_wpfn, uptime), which this dashboard shares with Work Process Performance — one hourly aggregation serves both. It is populated at minute :09 of every hour by logserv_wp_perf_aggregate from the six ABAP runtime sourcetypes (sap:abap:dispatcher, sap:abap:enqueueserver, sap:abap:event, sap:abap:messageserver, sap:abap:sapstartsrv, sap:abap:workprocess). The uptime metric stores a per-hour latest value, so the uptime panels show the most recent reading inside your selected window.

    Summary-backed panels switch automatically to their exact raw-equivalent search when the selected window is shorter than 90 minutes, so sub-hour investigation stays real-time. The collection keeps 365 days of hourly history (trimmed by a daily retention search). The Cloud picker in the title row filters every panel by cloud_provider; events with no cloud_provider value count as aws. Full schedule and freshness reference: Dashboard Data.

    Work Process Performance¶

    SAP stopped delivering the ABAP work process and dispatcher logs through LogServ in April 2026. Every panel here except Async RFC Queue Depth and Top Programs by Queue Depth therefore shows only data indexed before then, unless you have arranged continued collection with SAP. Those two panels read the ICM log, which keeps arriving.

    Why This Dashboard Matters¶

    Work Process Performance focuses specifically on the ABAP work process layer: the finite pool of processes that execute every dialog request, background job, and RFC call. When all work processes of a type are busy, new requests have to wait for one to become free. Each work process writes its trace lines under SAP’s trace components — the letter at the start of each dev_w* line, such as B = Database Interface, X = Extended Memory or R = Rolling — so a shift in the mix shows which subsystem is writing more: more B and C lines point at the database layers, more X and R lines at extended memory and rolling. This dashboard breaks activity down by those trace components so you can look at the right subsystem first.

    Requires¶

    • Sourcetypes: sap:abap:workprocess and sap:abap:dispatcher (both discontinued), and sap:abap:icm for the two Async RFC queue panels (LogServ folders abap/workprocess, abap/dispatcher, abap/icm). The Data TA assigns them at index time where the data is parsed; see Supported Log Types, which marks the discontinued log types.
    • Search-head add-ons: none beyond the LogServ App prerequisites.
    • Dashboard Data row: Work Process Performance / ABAP Operations (one row serves both dashboards). Backfill it once after installing the App so the panels show history: 30 days by default, up to 365 days or a custom range. See Backfilling on first install.

    Upgrading from an earlier build? See Upgrading.

    Panels¶

    All panels except Recent Dispatcher Errors read the hourly summary, which adds each hour at minute :09 of the next hour, so on wide time ranges they can leave out up to about the last 70 minutes; ranges shorter than 90 minutes are answered from the raw events automatically. See Dashboard Data.

    • Total WP Events – Aggregate sap:abap:workprocess event count
    • Active SIDs – Count of distinct SAP System IDs reporting work process data
    • Dispatcher Errors – Count of dispatcher events with severity ERROR
    • Active WP Functions – Count of distinct work process function codes observed
    • Work Process Category Trend – Column chart showing activity over time by trace component, with the named codes of the shared wp_category_name field (for example C = Database (DBSL))
    • Category Distribution – Donut chart showing the overall trace-component mix across the time range (same names)
    • Work Process Functions – Table of work process functions (wp_function, the first word after the trace-component letter of each trace line) ranked by event volume
    • Dispatcher Severity Over Time – Column chart of dispatcher severity levels over time, one bar per level in each time bucket
    • Activity by SID / Instance – Table ranking each SAP system/instance by event count, with its number of distinct functions and trace components; click a row for that SID’s work process events in Search
    • Recent Dispatcher Errors – Table of the most recent dispatcher ERROR events (up to 200) with SID, function, reason, and host; click a row to open Host Details for that host. This panel always reads raw events.
    • Async RFC Queue Depth – Average and peak ICM ASYNC_RFC tasks-in-queue per dispatch over time (from sap:abap:icm)
    • Top Programs by Queue Depth – Table of the 20 ABAP programs with the highest ICM queue depth at dispatch (Max Tasks), with call count, average tasks and peak memory (KB)

    What to Look For¶

    • Trace component dominance – If a single trace component (e.g., B = Database Interface or C = Database (DBSL), the two database layers, or X = Extended Memory) dominates the Category Distribution donut when it historically didn’t, that subsystem may be a bottleneck. For the database layers, check HANA Trace; for memory, the OOM Kills panels of Linux show the operating-system side.
    • Trend shifts between trace components – A gradual increase in C = Database (DBSL) lines, the database client layer, can point at trouble between the ABAP server and its database. N = Security (SNC/SSF) lines come from secure network communication and digital signatures, and E = Enqueue (Lock Mgmt) lines from lock handling, so a rise in either points at that area.
    • Dispatcher error bursts – Spikes of ERROR in the Dispatcher Severity Over Time chart can go with work process problems. Compare them with the Work Process Category Trend to see which trace components rose at the same time, and read the reasons in Recent Dispatcher Errors.
    • Instance imbalance – If one instance’s WP activity is an order of magnitude higher than its peers in the Activity by SID/Instance table, investigate whether that instance is handling disproportionate load or experiencing a local issue.
    • Function hotspots – The Work Process Functions table ranks the first word after the trace-component letter of each trace line, often the name of the kernel routine that wrote it (for example ThrtSetEgUsageSizes or dbsync), by the number of lines. A routine that suddenly leads the table shows which code path is writing more trace lines.
    • Async RFC backlog – A rising Max Queue Depth line in Async RFC Queue Depth, or one program far ahead in Top Programs by Queue Depth, can mean asynchronous RFC work is queuing up at the ICM.

    Related Dashboards¶

    • ABAP Operations – dispatcher, enqueue and uptime health from the same summary; its Dispatcher Severity chart and System Uptime table open this dashboard.
    • ABAP Network & Security – the ICM and Gateway activity of the same systems.
    • Host Details – opens from a row of Recent Dispatcher Errors; its Data Freshness table opens this dashboard from an sap:abap:workprocess row.
    Where the data comes from
    • Summary-backed panels — the work-process, dispatcher and ICM panels read the logserv_wp_perf_rollup KV Store collection (metrics wp, dp, icm), which this dashboard shares with ABAP Operations. Populated at minute :09 of every hour by logserv_wp_perf_aggregate from sap:abap:workprocess (work-process function/category mix), sap:abap:dispatcher (severity counts) and sap:abap:icm (per-program call/task/memory aggregates — sums and maxima are stored so averages reconstruct exactly).
    • Recent Dispatcher Errors is a live event listing: it dispatches directly against the raw sap:abap:dispatcher events at view time, capped at the 200 most recent ERROR events.

    Summary-backed panels switch automatically to their exact raw-equivalent search when the selected window is shorter than 90 minutes, so sub-hour investigation stays real-time. The collection keeps 365 days of hourly history (trimmed by a daily retention search). The Cloud picker in the title row filters every panel by cloud_provider; events with no cloud_provider value count as aws. Full schedule and freshness reference: Dashboard Data.

    HANA Audit¶

    Why This Dashboard Matters¶

    The HANA Audit dashboard supports database security compliance and threat detection. SAP HANA stores the most sensitive business data in the SAP landscape, and it writes an audit record for each action its audit policies cover, such as logons, user and privilege changes, and administrative actions. This dashboard summarizes the audit trail for both real-time threat detection and compliance reporting.

    Requires¶

    • Sourcetypes: sap:hana:audit (LogServ folder hana/hanaaudit). The Data TA assigns it at index time where the data is parsed; see Supported Log Types.
    • Search-head add-ons: none beyond the LogServ App prerequisites.
    • Dashboard Data row: HANA Audit. Backfill it once after installing the App so the panels show history: 30 days by default, up to 365 days or a custom range. See Backfilling on first install.

    Upgrading from an earlier build? See Upgrading.

    Panels¶

    Most panels read the hourly summary, which adds each hour at minute :11 of the next hour, so on wide time ranges they can leave out up to about the last 75 minutes; the High-Risk Events and After-Hours tables always read raw events, and any range shorter than 90 minutes is answered from raw events automatically. See Dashboard Data.

    • Total Audit Events – Aggregate count of HANA audit log entries
    • Failed Operations – Count of audit events with non-successful status
    • Active Users – Count of distinct users generating audit activity
    • User Administration Activity Timeline – Tracks user administration actions (password resets, activations, deactivations) over time
    • Daily Security Health Score – Full-width table with one row per day: total events, active users, failures, and success rate (%), newest day first
    • Audit Category Breakdown – Table of audit event categories (action_category) with event counts
    • Security Events Timeline – Shows failed operations, object modifications (CREATE / DROP), permission grants and permission revokes
    • Password Management Activities – Table of password-related audit events with user and IP details, classified as Password Change, Disable Lifetime, Reset Attempts or Other in any letter case; click a row to open Cross-Stack Authentication
    • Failed Operations by HANA Host – Table showing which HANA hosts recorded the most failed operations: the host that wrote the audit record, not the client that connected; click a row to open Host Details for that host
    • Users by Activity – Table ranking executing users by event count, with the number of distinct action types and failure count; click a row to open Cross-Stack Authentication
    • Activity by Hour of Day – Column chart showing successes vs. failures by hour for after-hours detection
    • Client IP Analysis – Table of connecting IPs with user counts, failures, and last-seen time; click a row for that IP’s audit events in Search
    • Risk-Tiered Event Timeline – Column chart of events over time by risk_level (HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW), one bar per tier, so severe events never get hidden inside overall volume
    • After-Hours / Weekend Admin Activity – Table of admin activity (is_admin_user=true) falling outside business hours (weekday 08:00-18:59) or on a weekend, surfacing privileged activity outside normal windows; the Period column labels each row Weekend, After Hours, or Weekend / After Hours. The HANA Host and Client Host columns show the HANA host that wrote the record and the host name of the client that ran the action. Click a row to drill down by user and HANA host
    • High-Risk Events – Full-width table filtered to is_critical=true, showing up to the 500 most recent critical audit events with time, user, action, category, risk, status, HANA host, client host, client IP, and SQL statement; click a row to drill down by user

    Which host is which

    Every audit record names two machines: the HANA host that wrote it and the client that ran the action. In this App, host on sap:hana:audit events is the HANA host — the LogServ host that delivered the record, as the index stores it for the event. The client’s host name (the record’s Client Name field) is src_host, beside src_ip (the client IP, also client_ip) and dest_host (the database host the record names). The HANA Host columns read host and the Client Host columns read src_host; a record that names no client leaves its Client Host and Client IP cells empty.

    What to Look For¶

    • Failed operations from unusual IPs – Authentication failures from IP addresses not in your expected range may indicate brute-force attacks or credential stuffing attempts.
    • Privileged actions from an unexpected client host – The High-Risk Events and After-Hours / Weekend Admin Activity tables name both the HANA host and the client host. An administrative action run from a machine that does not normally administer that database is worth a check against your change records.
    • Critical events in the High-Risk Events table – The table lists the audit events written at the CRITICAL audit level, and each row warrants a look. The Action and Status columns show what was done and whether it failed; the SQL Statement column shows the statement when it is a user or privilege change (ALTER, CREATE or DROP USER, GRANT, REVOKE).
    • After-hours privileged activity – The After-Hours / Weekend Admin Activity table surfaces admin operations outside business hours; correlate with change management records to separate planned maintenance from suspicious activity.
    • Risk-tier shifts over time – HIGH counts every failed operation, plus user and privilege changes that target the SYSTEM user, so a rising HIGH series in the Risk-Tiered Event Timeline usually means more failures: check Failed Operations by HANA Host and Client IP Analysis. MEDIUM counts successful logons audited at the CRITICAL level and the other User Administration events, so a sudden spike there points at a burst of such logons or user changes, for example from a script.
    • Privilege escalation patterns – Watch for sequences where a user’s privileges are modified followed by unusual data access patterns. The Security Events Timeline surfaces GRANT and REVOKE operations.
    • Declining security health score – A downward trend in the daily success rate or an increase in failures can signal growing security issues that need investigation.
    • Password management anomalies – Bulk password resets or resets for service accounts should be correlated with change management records.

    Related Dashboards¶

    • Cross-Stack Authentication – HANA authentication beside SAP and Windows; opens from a row of Users by Activity or Password Management Activities.
    • Change & Configuration Activity – HANA user, role, privilege and DDL changes beside the Windows and Linux change trails.
    • Host Details – opens from a row of Failed Operations by HANA Host.
    • Environment Health – its HANA Failed Ops card and HANA Error Trend chart open this dashboard.
    • HANA Trace – the database engine’s own trace output.
    Where the data comes from

    The single source is sap:hana:audit. The action status and target principal are read from their fixed positions in the audit record, so every action has them. The SQL Statement column shows user and privilege management statements, in any letter case and also when the record quotes them; quoted identifiers read as in the database — grant "ROLE" to USER — without the JSON escapes real ingest keeps.

    • Summary-backed panels — the KPIs, category/action/user/client breakdowns and the compliance timelines read the logserv_hana_category_rollup KV Store collection: metric main carries an hourly grain over (executing user, client IP, status, HANA host, action type), and metrics useradmin, security and password pre-compute the three classified activity timelines. Populated at minute :11 of every hour by logserv_hana_aggregate.
    • Live panels — the High-Risk Events and After-Hours / Weekend Admin Activity tables are per-event listings dispatched against the raw audit events at view time (capped at the 500 most recent matches each) — deliberately raw, so a compliance reviewer sees the actual event rows.

    Summary-backed panels switch automatically to their exact raw-equivalent search when the selected window is shorter than 90 minutes, so sub-hour investigation stays real-time. The collection keeps 365 days of hourly history (trimmed by a daily retention search). The Cloud picker in the title row filters every panel by cloud_provider; events with no cloud_provider value count as aws. Full schedule and freshness reference: Dashboard Data.

    HANA Trace¶

    Why This Dashboard Matters¶

    The HANA Trace dashboard provides visibility into SAP HANA’s internal diagnostic trace system. Unlike audit logs that capture user actions, trace logs capture what the database engine itself is doing: memory management, query compilation, I/O operations, and internal errors. Use it to diagnose HANA performance issues, stability problems and the root cause of database outages.

    Requires¶

    • Sourcetypes: sap:hana:tracelogs (LogServ folder hana/tracelogs, or the HANA trace directory’s source path when the data arrives without folder fields). The Data TA assigns it at index time where the data is parsed; see SAP HANA Trace Logs.
    • Search-head add-ons: none beyond the LogServ App prerequisites.
    • Dashboard Data row: HANA Trace. Backfill it once after installing the App so the panels show history: 30 days by default, up to 365 days or a custom range. See Backfilling on first install.

    Upgrading from an earlier build? See Upgrading.

    Panels¶

    Every panel except Recent Errors / Fatal Events reads the hourly summary, which adds each hour at minute :19 of the next hour, so on wide time ranges the panels can leave out up to about the last 80 minutes; ranges shorter than 90 minutes are answered from raw events automatically. See Dashboard Data.

    • Total Trace Events – Aggregate count of trace log entries
    • Errors / Fatal – Count of error and fatal events: trace lines at level e or f, and backup.log entries at ERROR or FATAL
    • Unique Components – Number of distinct HANA components generating traces, with the same noise filter as the Components table, so the count matches its rows
    • Trace Volume Over Time – Trend of total trace events over time
    • Trace Events by Severity – Column chart showing the severity mix of trace lines and backup.log entries, one bar per severity in each time bucket: INFO, WARNING, ERROR and FATAL, plus DEBUG where present and UNKNOWN for lines that carry no level, such as the continuation lines of a multi-line entry. Record files – the hdbcons command timings, SQL trace (*_statements.N.trc), load traces and system availability – carry no severity: they are left out of this chart and of Component by Severity, and still count in Total Trace Events, Trace Volume Over Time and Activity by SID / Instance (the hdbcons timings also feed the two duration panels). The chart’s subtitle says it leaves them out
    • Components – Table of HANA components ranked by event volume, with distinct source-file count and the severities seen; click a row for that component’s raw trace events (parsing artefacts – very short names and values such as INFO, of, service: – are filtered out). backup.log entries appear under their own component, for example LOGBCKUP
    • Component by Severity – Column chart showing the severity mix per component, one bar per severity (same noise filter applied)
    • Source File Hotspots – Table identifying specific source files generating the most trace entries (same noise filter applied); click a row for that file’s raw trace events
    • Activity by SID / Instance – Event distribution across HANA systems
    • Slowest hdbcons Commands – Table of the top 20 HANA console (hdbcons) commands ranked by maximum duration (ms), with average duration and run count per command and SID. These are the commands the hdbcons trace times (for example profiler stop, statreg print or replication info), not SQL statements. The trace times each command in microseconds, milliseconds or seconds; all three are converted to ms. (Reads the hourly rollup layer; the per-event time/host columns are not retained at the aggregate grain – use the Recent Errors / Fatal Events table or the Search app for individual events.)
    • hdbcons Command Duration (Avg / Max) – Average and peak hdbcons command duration (ms) over time, across every timed hdbcons command whatever unit the trace used
    • Recent Errors / Fatal Events – Table of the latest error and fatal events (up to 500) with component and source location; backup.log entries have a component but no source file or line. Click a row for that SID’s and component’s error events in Search

    What to Look For¶

    • Error/fatal severity spikes – A sudden increase in error-level traces can come before a HANA outage or performance degradation. Investigate the component and source file generating the errors.
    • Single component dominance – If one component suddenly generates significantly more traces than usual, it may indicate a runaway process, memory leak, or infinite loop within that subsystem.
    • New source files appearing – Trace entries from source files not seen before may indicate recently applied patches or code changes that are generating unexpected behavior.
    • SID/instance imbalance – Uneven trace volumes across instances of the same HANA system may indicate hardware issues, unbalanced workload distribution, or replication problems.
    • Persistent warning trends – Warnings that gradually increase over days can signal resource exhaustion (disk space, memory pools) that will eventually escalate to errors.

    Related Dashboards¶

    • HANA Audit – who did what in the same databases.
    • Environment Topology – draws HANA Tenant edges from these traces; an edge’s Performance tab shows its hdbcons command durations and its Operations tab its trace components.
    • Host Details – its Data Freshness table opens this dashboard from an sap:hana:tracelogs row.
    Where the data comes from

    The single source is sap:hana:tracelogs. Each line is read by its own format:

    • Trace lines – [pid]{connection}[transaction/update] date time level component file(line) : text – give the level, component, source file and line. Only a line that starts this way is read as one, so text further along a line is never taken for a level or a component.
    • backup.log lines – time P<pid> <thread> LEVEL COMPONENT text – give their level (INFO, WARNING, ERROR, FATAL) and component, for example LOGBCKUP.
    • hdbcons lines give the command and its duration, converted to ms (hana_op, hana_op_duration_ms).
    • Record files (hdbcons, SQL trace, load traces, system availability) carry no severity.

    The hana_trace_file_type field names the kind of file each event comes from – trace, alert, backup, hdbcons, sql_trace, load_trace, availability or other – for your own searches; no panel groups by it.

    • Summary-backed panels — volume, severity and component panels read metric main of the logserv_hana_trace_rollup KV Store collection; the hdbcons duration panels read metrics dur (per-hour duration sums/counts/maxima in ms — the Avg + Max charts reconstruct exact averages from these) and durop (the same, per command and SID — the Slowest hdbcons Commands table ranks by stored Max/Avg). Populated at minute :19 of every hour by logserv_hana_trace_aggregate.
    • Recent Errors / Fatal Events is a live event listing dispatched against the raw trace events at view time, capped at the 500 most recent error/fatal entries.

    Summary-backed panels switch automatically to their exact raw-equivalent search when the selected window is shorter than 90 minutes, so sub-hour investigation stays real-time. The collection keeps 365 days of hourly history (trimmed by a daily retention search). The Cloud picker in the title row filters every panel by cloud_provider; events with no cloud_provider value count as aws. Full schedule and freshness reference: Dashboard Data.

    Integration

    Integration¶

    The Integration category covers dashboards that monitor how SAP connects to other systems — host-level services (sapstartsrv, saphostexec), the SAP Router, the Cloud Connector (SAP BTP tunnel), and HTTP traffic through the Web Dispatcher. Use these dashboards to diagnose connectivity issues, auth failures at the integration boundary, and performance problems in the request path.

    Dashboard Purpose Key Data Sources
    SAP Services sapstartsrv authentication, SSL/TLS failure analysis, and host agent health sap:sapstartsrv, sap:saphostexec
    SAP Router SAP Router connection activity, error analysis, and network boundary monitoring sap:saprouter
    Cloud Connector SAP Cloud Connector HTTP traffic, audit events, and access denied events sap:scc:audit, sap:scc:http_access
    Web Dispatcher HTTP traffic analysis, response times, status codes, and client patterns sap:webdispatcher:access
    Web and API Performance Four-stage request timing, response-time Avg/Max trends, TLS posture, cross-source error correlation sap:webdispatcher:access, sap:scc:http_access

    The controls these dashboards share (time range, Cloud filter, auto-refresh, panel toolbar, drill-downs, export) are described once in the Dashboards Overview.

    SAP Services¶

    Why This Dashboard Matters¶

    The SAP Services dashboard monitors two host-level services that are critical to SAP system availability: sapstartsrv (system startup and management) and the SAP Host Agent (host monitoring and management). These services operate at the infrastructure layer, below the application, and their failures can prevent SAP systems from starting or being managed remotely. sapstartsrv accepts logons over the network (its SOAP web service interface), so failed logons matter; the dashboard’s main investigation panel is SSL Authentication Failure Sources. (SAP Router activity lives on its own SAP Router dashboard.)

    Requires¶

    • Sourcetypes: sap:sapstartsrv (LogServ folder sap/sapstartsrv) and sap:saphostexec (sap/saphostexec). The Data TA assigns them at index time where the data is parsed; see Supported Log Types.
    • Search-head add-ons: none beyond the LogServ App prerequisites.
    • Dashboard Data row: SAP Services. Backfill it once after installing the App so the panels show history: 30 days by default, up to 365 days or a custom range. See Backfilling on first install.

    Panels¶

    All panels except Sapstartsrv Authentication Events read the hourly summary, which adds each hour at minute :21 of the next hour, so on wide time ranges they can leave out up to about the last 85 minutes; ranges shorter than 90 minutes are answered from the raw events automatically. See Dashboard Data.

    • Total Events – Aggregate event count across sapstartsrv and saphostexec
    • Auth Failures – Count of sapstartsrv authentication failures
    • SSL/TLS Events – Count of events involving SSL/TLS negotiation
    • Event Volume by Service (Normal vs Errors) – Full-width column chart with four series side by side: sapstartsrv (normal), sapstartsrv (errors), saphostexec (normal), saphostexec (errors). Errors are defined per service: sapstartsrv = failed authentication events; saphostexec = severity ERROR/WARNING.
    • Sapstartsrv Authentication Events – Table of the most recent authentication attempts (up to 200) showing user, IP, method, and result; click a row for that remote IP’s events in Search
    • Host Agent Severity – Pie chart of SAP Host Agent log severity distribution; click it for a severity-by-host breakdown in Search
    • SSL Authentication Failure Sources – Full-width table aggregating SSL/TLS auth failures by source IP, with failure count, distinct user count, user list, first/last seen, and activity span (hours); the table paginates, and a row click opens the full event set for that IP.

    What to Look For¶

    • Auth failure sources – The SSL Authentication Failure Sources table is the primary investigation surface. A single source IP with many distinct usernames suggests credential stuffing; many sources with a few usernames each suggest a distributed brute-force attempt; a long activity span suggests a persistent rather than an opportunistic attacker.
    • Authentication failures from new IPs – Any new source IP appearing in the SSL Authentication Failure Sources table should be cross-referenced with your expected SAP admin network. Production sapstartsrv should rarely see failed authentications from unfamiliar ranges.
    • Error bars rising in the volume chart – If an error series in the Event Volume chart grows relative to its normal series, look at that service first. For sapstartsrv the errors are failed logons (see Sapstartsrv Authentication Events); for saphostexec they are ERROR and WARNING lines (the Host Agent Severity pie shows which grew).
    • Host Agent ERROR severity – If the Host Agent severity distribution shifts toward ERROR, the host monitoring infrastructure may be degrading, which impacts central management capabilities.

    Related Dashboards¶

    • Cross-Stack Authentication – sapstartsrv authentication failures beside HANA and Windows failures.
    • Environment Health – its Auth Failures card and Security Error Trend chart open this dashboard.
    • SAP Router – the third SAP service log (sap/saprouter), with its own dashboard.
    • Host Details – its Data Freshness table opens this dashboard from an sap:sapstartsrv or sap:saphostexec row.
    Where the data comes from
    • Summary-backed panels read the logserv_sapservices_rollup KV Store collection — metric main (service/auth activity over sap:sapstartsrv + sap:saphostexec) and metric ssl (SSL/TLS negotiation facts from sapstartsrv). Populated at minute :21 of every hour by logserv_sapservices_aggregate.
    • Sapstartsrv Authentication Events is a live listing dispatched against the raw events at view time, capped at the 200 most recent matches.

    Summary-backed panels switch automatically to their exact raw-equivalent search when the selected window is shorter than 90 minutes, so sub-hour investigation stays real-time. The collection keeps 365 days of hourly history (trimmed by a daily retention search). The Cloud picker in the title row filters every panel by cloud_provider; events with no cloud_provider value count as aws. Full schedule and freshness reference: Dashboard Data.

    SAP Router¶

    Why This Dashboard Matters¶

    SAP Router is the network gateway that sits between SAP systems and external networks, forwarding RFC and HTTP traffic across trust boundaries. Because it is exposed to the network, its logs are an audit trail for cross-boundary SAP traffic: they record the connections it opens and closes, protocol errors, and invalid data it receives. This dashboard separates the SAP Router signal from other services so that spikes in router errors (connectivity breakage, misconfigured routetab, or attempted protocol abuse) are visible on their own.

    Requires¶

    • Sourcetypes: sap:saprouter (LogServ folder sap/saprouter; it covers both the .log connection events and the .trc error traces). The Data TA assigns it at index time where the data is parsed; see Supported Log Types.
    • Search-head add-ons: none beyond the LogServ App prerequisites.
    • Dashboard Data row: SAP Router. Backfill it once after installing the App so the panels show history: 30 days by default, up to 365 days or a custom range. See Backfilling on first install. The router edges of the Environment Topology come from the Environment Topology rows, not from this one.

    Panels¶

    All panels except Recent Connection Log read the hourly summary, which adds each hour at minute :13 of the next hour, so on wide time ranges they can leave out up to about the last 75 minutes; ranges shorter than 90 minutes are answered from the raw events automatically. See Dashboard Data.

    • Total Router Events – Aggregate SAP Router event count
    • Router Errors – Count of router error events
    • Invalid Data Events – Count of events where the router received malformed or unexpected protocol data – can indicate a misconfigured client or probing
    • Unique Peer IPs – Distinct count of peer IPs seen in the time window
    • Connection Actions Over Time – Column chart of CONNECT, DISCONNECT, and error actions over time, one bar per action in each time bucket
    • Router Errors Over Time – Trend of router error events over time (column chart)
    • Peer IPs by Connection Volume – Table of peer IPs ranked by connection count; a row click opens that peer’s full router event log
    • Return Code Distribution – Donut chart of router return codes over the time range, decoded to readable labels (“0 = OK (Success)”, “-93 = Connection Refused”, “-92 = Host Unknown (DNS)”, …)
    • Error Detail by Function – Table of router error functions (for example NiIRead or NiBufIIn) with count, unique peer count, the return codes seen, and the most recent error detail text (paginated 5 rows at a time); a row click opens that function’s error events
    • Recent Connection Log – Table of the most recent connection events (CONNECT / DISCONNECT / INVAL DATA, up to 500) with time, action, connection ID, peer IP, source IP/port, and an error flag; a row click opens that peer/source pair’s events. On CONNECT TO rows the Source IP column shows the connection’s target (see Where the data comes from below)

    What to Look For¶

    • Invalid Data spikes – A sudden increase in the Invalid Data KPI suggests either a misconfigured client speaking a wrong protocol or a port scan / probe. Check the Peer IPs by Connection Volume table for new entries.
    • Unfamiliar peers near the top of the table – Known SAP-to-SAP traffic should come from a predictable IP set; new IPs near the top of the Peer IPs by Connection Volume table warrant investigation, especially if they generate high connection volume or show up only in the Error Detail by Function table.
    • Return code imbalance – The Return Code Distribution pie should be dominated by normal-case codes. A sudden growth of the “-93 = Connection Refused” or “-92 = Host Unknown (DNS)” slices can mean that a target system is down or not accepting connections, that a host name does not resolve, or that a routetab entry is wrong.
    • Rising error trend – An upward slope in Router Errors Over Time can precede an outage. Cross-reference with ABAP Operations (dispatcher errors) and Cloud Connector (for hybrid flows) to see whether the root cause is local to the router or broader.
    • Concentrated errors by function – If one row of the Error Detail by Function table accumulates most errors, read its error detail text: the function is the routine of SAP’s network layer that reported the failure (for example NiIRead for a failed or invalid read), which narrows the investigation to one kind of failure.

    Related Dashboards¶

    • Environment Topology – draws the router’s routed connections as SAP Router edges (below).
