    • Dashboard Data row: Windows on Settings → Dashboard Data. On a new install, Run backfill there seeds the last 30 days by default (60, 90, 180 or 365 days, or a custom range, are also offered); without a backfill the panels fill one hour at a time. See Backfilling on first install.

    Requires the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows on the Search Head

    Several panels here depend on the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742) being installed on the Search Head tier. The LogServ App ships no XmlWinEventLog field extraction of its own — EventCode and severity are search-time fields provided by add-on 742 (its xmlwindows_severities.csv lookup maps the event <Level> to severity: 1→critical, 2→high, 3→medium, 0/4/5→informational).

    Without add-on 742 on the search tier, Windows events still index fine and the Total Events, Event Volume by Log, Active Hosts, and PowerShell Activity panels populate (they read envelope fields), but the Event Codes table collapses to a single row labelled (none) and the Severity Distribution, Critical / Error, and Service Events panels stay empty.

    Tier matters: EventCode/severity are search-time extractions, so add-on 742 must be on the Search Head — installing it on a heavy forwarder or indexer does nothing for these panels. On Splunk Cloud, install it on the Cloud SH via self-service app management (it is replicated to the indexer search peers through the knowledge bundle). See Where Each Package Goes.

    If the App ran before you installed the add-on, rebuild the summaries on Settings → Dashboard Data:

    1. On the Windows row, note its History, click Clear, then Backfill it with a window that covers that history (the 365-day preset or a custom range). The Clear is needed because the rows written without the add-on are keyed on empty event codes and severities; a Backfill alone would add the new rows beside them and the totals would count those hours twice. The Clear removes all of the row’s history; the Backfill restores only the hours whose raw events your index still holds.
    2. Backfill, with the same window, the other rows that read Windows fields: Environment Health, Cross-Stack Authentication, Change & Configuration Activity, Host Role Activity (Host Details), Host Details and Environment Topology (detail tabs). None of them needs a Clear. The first four stored no Windows rows that depend on the add-on. Host Details keys its rows by host and hour, so the Backfill replaces their counts with ones that include the Windows failed logons (EventCode 4625) and critical events; Environment Topology (detail tabs) gains new rows for the Windows events whose add-on severity is critical, which it did not count before. The names that Environment Topology shows for IP addresses take in the Windows logons on their own at the next daily refresh (02:32 search-head time), which reads the last 30 days.

    Run the rebuild outside the nightly retention window (00:34–00:58, 01:30–01:58 and 02:34–02:36 search-head time), when the retention searches rewrite the rollups and can erase rows a backfill is writing; see Backfilling on first install.

    Panels¶

    • Total Events – Aggregate Windows event count
    • Critical / Error – Count of Windows Critical (Level 1) and Error (Level 2) events. In CIM severity vocabulary these are severity="critical" and severity="high" — there is no error severity value
    • Active Hosts – Count of distinct Windows hosts reporting data
    • Event Volume by Log – Trend over time by Windows log source (Application, Security, System, PowerShell)
    • Severity Distribution Over Time – Column chart of events over time, one bar per severity in each time bucket
    • Event Codes – Featured full-width table of the most frequent EventCodes with 7 enriched columns: Event Code, Description (signature), Source log, Severity, Events, Hosts (distinct count), Last Seen. Row drilldown opens the search app filtered by that event code.
    • Service Events – Table of Windows service start/stop activity with latest state
    • PowerShell Activity – Column chart of PowerShell operational event volume over time

    What to Look For¶

    • High-frequency Event Codes – The Event Codes table is the primary starting point. EventCode 7031 / 7034 (service terminated unexpectedly), 1000 (application crash), and 41 (unexpected shutdown) are high-priority. Click through to see every occurrence of a specific code.
    • Service crashes – EventCode 7031 (service terminated unexpectedly) in either the Event Codes table or the Service Events panel indicates a critical service failure. For SAP services (sapstartsrv, SAPService), this requires immediate attention.
    • PowerShell activity spikes – Sudden increases in PowerShell execution may indicate lateral movement by an attacker using PowerShell-based attack tools. Correlate with the Cross-Stack Authentication dashboard to see whether any Windows logons were concurrent.
    • Critical/error severity trends – A rising trend in critical and error events over multiple days indicates accumulating system health issues that need proactive investigation.
    • Event Code hosts expanding – The Hosts column on the Event Codes table makes it obvious when a normally-host-isolated error starts appearing on multiple hosts – a sign the underlying cause is environmental (failed update, domain policy change) rather than local.

    Related Dashboards¶

    • Cross-Stack Authentication – Windows logon failures beside the SAP and HANA layers.
    • Change & Configuration Activity – Windows account and group changes.
    • Host Details – one host’s event codes beside its other activity.
    Where the data comes from

    The single source is XmlWinEventLog. Every panel is summary-backed: panels read the logserv_windows_rollup KV Store collection — metric main carries an hourly grain over (event code, severity, source/channel, host) plus per-bucket latest values for the descriptive columns, and metric svc carries the service-event facts. Populated at minute :20 of every hour by logserv_windows_aggregate.

    Summary-backed panels switch automatically to their exact raw-equivalent search when the selected window is shorter than 90 minutes, so sub-hour investigation stays real-time. The collection keeps 365 days of hourly history (trimmed by a daily retention search). The global Cloud dropdown filters the summaries through the cloud_provider dimension stored in every rollup row. Full schedule and freshness reference: Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness.

    Proxy Analytics¶

    Why This Dashboard Matters¶

    The Proxy Analytics dashboard monitors outbound internet access through the Squid proxy server. In SAP environments, proxy logs reveal which systems and users are accessing external resources, enabling detection of data exfiltration attempts, policy violations (unauthorized internet access), and compromised systems communicating with malicious infrastructure. Proxy logs complement DNS analytics by showing the actual HTTP connections that follow DNS resolution.

    Requires¶

    • Sourcetypes: squid:access, its access.log lines only.
    • Search-head add-ons: none beyond the LogServ App, which has the Squid parsing built in. Do not install the standalone Squid add-on alongside it; see the note below.
    • Dashboard Data row: Proxy Analytics on Settings → Dashboard Data. On a new install, Run backfill there seeds the last 30 days by default (60, 90, 180 or 365 days, or a custom range, are also offered); without a backfill the summary-backed panels fill one hour at a time. See Backfilling on first install.

    Squid parsing is built into the LogServ App

    The App absorbed the native-format parsing from the archived Splunk Add-on for Squid Proxy, and parses the splunk_recommended_squid format with its own transforms. Do not install the standalone Squid TA alongside it — you would get double parsing, and its CIM-standard action="blocked" vocabulary differs from the App’s customized action="denied", which the Denied Requests KPI and the Cache Action panel depend on. The App shows a detection banner on the home view when a conflicting add-on is enabled.

    Panels¶

    • Total Requests – Aggregate proxy request count
    • Total Bandwidth – Sum of bytes transferred through the proxy (formatted KB/MB/GB)
    • Denied Requests – Count of requests blocked by proxy policy: those whose action is denied, which the App’s Squid action lookup assigns to TCP_DENIED, UDP_DENIED, TCP_SWAPFAIL and UDP_INVALID. Network Perimeter counts denied requests as status=403 or TCP_DENIED instead, so the two counts can differ
    • Request Volume Over Time – Request trend over time
    • Status Code Distribution – Column chart of requests over time, one bar per response category in each time bucket: 2xx, 3xx, 4xx, 5xx, and Other for a status below 200 or none at all
    • Domains – Table of the most accessed domains with request counts, bandwidth, and unique client counts
    • Clients – Table of the most active client IPs with request counts, bandwidth, and domain diversity. Click a row to open Host Details for that client
    • Clients by Domain Diversity – Table ranking client IPs by the count of distinct URL domains they accessed. Click a row to open Host Details for that client
    • Cache Action Distribution – Table of Squid cache/result actions (vendor_action, e.g. TCP_TUNNEL, TCP_HIT, TCP_MISS, TCP_DENIED, TCP_TUNNEL_ABORTED) ranked by event count; it shows how well the proxy cache is working
    • Bandwidth Over Time – Column chart of total bytes out over time
    • URL Domains by Bytes Out – Table of URL domains ranked by MB delivered (the data-exfiltration detection surface); paginated, not capped. Click a row for that domain’s full proxy log
    • Bandwidth Over Time by Domain (Top 5) – Column chart of the five highest-bandwidth domains over time, one bar per domain in each time bucket – pairs with URL Domains by Bytes Out to show whether exfiltration is ongoing or historical
    • Slowest Destinations – Top destinations by peak response time, with request count and average/max latency (ms), from the Squid duration field
    • Response Time (Avg / Max) – Average and peak proxy response time over time

    What to Look For¶

    • Denied request spikes – A sudden increase in denied requests may indicate a compromised system attempting to reach blocked destinations, or a policy change affecting legitimate traffic.
    • High-bandwidth domains – The URL Domains by Bytes Out panel is tuned specifically for exfiltration detection. A new domain appearing near the top, or a known-OK domain spiking, warrants investigation.
    • Sustained-bandwidth domains – The Bandwidth Over Time by Domain chart shows whether a top domain’s traffic is steady (expected service) or a sudden burst (exfiltration attempt, large file transfer).
    • Client domain diversity – A client IP with extremely high domain diversity in the Clients by Domain Diversity panel is unusual for a well-behaved SAP server – most production systems talk to a predictable small set of external domains.
    • Cache miss dominance – If Cache Action Distribution is dominated by TCP_MISS, the proxy cache may not be earning its keep (or a new workload is defeating it). For security-relevant investigations, TCP_TUNNEL dominance signals mostly CONNECT-tunnelled HTTPS traffic that the proxy can’t inspect.
    • New high-volume clients – A system that suddenly appears as a top proxy client may be compromised and performing outbound scanning, beaconing, or data exfiltration.

    Related Dashboards¶

    • Network Perimeter – proxy traffic beside firewall drops and DNS, with the cross-source Suspicious Activity Indicator.
    • DNS Analytics – the lookups that come before the connections.
    • Host Details – where the client rows lead.
    Where the data comes from

    The single source is squid:access, and only its access-log lines count as requests. The Data TA routes Squid’s cache.log and store.log to squid:cache and squid:store; data indexed by older Data TA builds still carries them as squid:access, where they record cache housekeeping, not requests, so every panel scopes to source="*access.log*". Both access-log formats are parsed: Squid’s native format, and the logformat=splunk_recommended_squid key=value format that SAP LogServ proxy logs use.

    • Summary-backed panels read the logserv_proxy_rollup KV Store collection — metrics core (per-hour request/denied/bandwidth sums), status (HTTP status classes), dur + destdur (response-time sums/counts/maxima overall and per destination — the Avg/Max panels reconstruct exact averages from these), domain (per-domain traffic and bandwidth) and cacheaction (Squid cache verdicts). Populated at minute :24 of every hour by logserv_proxy_aggregate.
    • Pure-count panels (Total Requests and Request Volume Over Time) run tstats directly against indexed fields.

    Summary-backed panels switch automatically to their exact raw-equivalent search when the selected window is shorter than 90 minutes, so sub-hour investigation stays real-time. The collection keeps 365 days of hourly history (trimmed by a daily retention search). The global Cloud dropdown filters the summaries through the cloud_provider dimension stored in every rollup row. Full schedule and freshness reference: Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness.

    Host Details¶

    Why This Dashboard Matters¶

    The Host Details dashboard is the forensic drill-down tool for investigating one or more hosts. Accessed by clicking a host row in any dashboard’s host-keyed table (Data Pipeline Overview, Cross-Stack Authentication, Environment Health, etc.) or by selecting hosts from the title-row Multiselect, it surfaces event volume, data freshness, authentication activity, inventory, errors, and role-specific signals (HANA audit, ABAP work process, web dispatcher traffic, etc.) for the selected scope. This view is essential for root cause analysis, incident response, capacity investigations, and validating that all expected data sources are present.

    Requires¶

    • Sourcetypes: any; the Overview and Sourcetype Mapping tabs read every event of the selected hosts. Each Role Activity panel needs its own sourcetype (listed with the panel below), and Host Inventory needs osquery facts in linux_messages_syslog.
    • Search-head add-ons: the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (742), for the Windows hosts’ Windows Event Codes panel, their failed logons (EventCode 4625) in the Auth Failures KPI and their critical events (severity=critical) in the Errors / Criticals KPI. Without it those two KPIs undercount on Windows hosts; see Windows Events.
    • Dashboard Data rows on Settings → Dashboard Data: Host Details (the Data Volume, Errors / Criticals and Auth Failures KPIs), Host Role Activity (Host Details) (the Role Activity tab) and Sourcetype Mapping (Host Details / Data Pipeline) (the Sourcetype Mapping tab). On a new install, Run backfill there seeds the last 30 days by default (60, 90, 180 or 365 days, or a custom range, are also offered); without a backfill the summary-backed panels fill one hour at a time. See Backfilling on first install.

    Panels¶

    The title-row host picker is a Multiselect (with filter input + Select All Matches) supporting three scopes:

    • All Hosts (no hosts selected) — no host filter is applied and panels aggregate across every host. The adjacent Top-N picker (default All hosts; options Top 5 / 10 / 20 / 50) narrows this to the busiest N hosts in the selected time range, and is disabled whenever specific hosts are selected.
    • Single host — splices host="X" into all SPL; URL becomes ?host=X (back-compatible deep-link form).
    • Multiple hosts — splices host IN ("X","Y","Z") into all SPL; URL becomes ?hosts=h1,h2,h3 (CSV form). The last host selection is remembered in the browser (localStorage, shared across tabs of the same browser profile) and restored the next time you open the dashboard; a ?host=/?hosts= URL parameter takes priority over it.

    The dashboard is organized into three tabs:

    • Overview – universal panels that populate for any host with any event: KPIs, the per-sourcetype event timeline, inventory, top sources, and data-freshness checks.
    • Role Activity – panels scoped to a specific role (HANA, ABAP, Web Dispatcher, SAP Router, Windows, Linux sudo, DNS). Each panel auto-hides when the selected host(s) have no data for that role, so the tab only shows what’s relevant for the host(s) in front of you.
    • Sourcetype Mapping – Link graph showing the distribution of events across sourcetypes and sources for the selected host(s).

    This dashboard accepts host and global time-range query params from the URL, so the time range and host selection carry over from the Data Pipeline Overview and other dashboards.

    Overview Tab¶

    The screenshot at the top of this page shows this tab.

    • KPI row (5 values) – Total Events, Data Volume (auto-scaled B/KB/MB/GB), Active Sourcetypes, Errors / Criticals, and Auth Failures. The last two turn amber above zero and red above 100
    • Event Count by Sourcetype – Multi-line chart of event volume per sourcetype for the selected scope; the time bucket adapts to the selected range (shown in the panel subtitle)
    • Host Inventory – Table of hardware specs (CPU, cores, RAM), EC2 instance type, OS, region, and availability zone. Sourced from osquery data in linux_messages_syslog.
    • Sources – Paginated table of the log sources contributing events for the selected scope, ranked by event count with percentage share. Click a row to open that source’s events in the search app
    • Data Freshness – Per-sourcetype event count and last-seen timestamp, sorted newest-first; a sourcetype whose Last Seen has fallen behind the others is the collection gap. Click a row to open the specialist dashboard for that sourcetype.

    Role Activity Tab¶

    Role-specific panels. Each panel only appears when the host has data for that role; irrelevant panels auto-hide.

    • HANA Audit - Top Actions – Table of audit action types from sap:hana:audit, with count and share
    • ABAP Work Process Trace Components – Table of the trace components of sap:abap:workprocess (dev_w*) lines: the letter that starts each line, with its name (for example B = Database Interface; a letter without a name shows as <letter> = Other), with count and share. Lines without a component letter are not counted. SAP stopped delivering the ABAP work process log through LogServ in April 2026, so this panel shows only data indexed before then, unless you have arranged continued collection with SAP (see Supported Log Types)
    • Web Dispatcher Traffic – Table of HTTP status codes from sap:webdispatcher:access (individual codes, not 2xx/3xx buckets)
    • SAP Router Peers – Connection counts by peer IP from sap:saprouter
    • Windows Event Codes – Table of EventCode values from XmlWinEventLog* (paginated, not capped); EventCode comes from the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (742) on the search head
    • Sudo Commands – Table of the users invoking sudo, with event count and share. It reads only linux_messages_syslog lines that contain sudo:; the separate sudo log (linux:sudolog) is not counted here — the Change & Configuration Activity dashboard covers it
    • DNS Top Queries – Top query strings from isc:bind:query

    Why some panels may show for certain hosts but not others

    Panels on the Role Activity tab — and Host Inventory on the Overview tab — render only when their search returns rows, so the layout adapts to what the host actually is. A panel whose search fails still renders, showing the error, so a broken query is never mistaken for an absent role.

    This means the dashboard adapts its layout to what the host actually is:

    • A HANA host sees the HANA Audit - Top Actions panel on Role Activity and hides ABAP, Web Dispatcher, Router, Windows, Sudo, and DNS.
    • An ABAP application server with work process data in the selected range sees the ABAP Work Process Trace Components panel and hides the HANA / Windows / DNS panels. Because SAP stopped delivering that log in April 2026, a range after that usually shows no ABAP panel.
    • A Windows host sees Windows Event Codes and hides the SAP-specific panels.
    • A full-stack Linux host (with osquery + sudo + SAP ABAP) sees all of Host Inventory, Sudo Commands, and, for ranges with ABAP work process data, ABAP Work Process Trace Components.
    • A sparse host with only one or two sourcetypes will see just the universal Overview panels plus whichever Role Activity panels match.
    • Selecting All Hosts aggregates across every host — most panels populate because at least one host in the environment contributes data to each.

    Empty panels aren’t a bug; they’re the dashboard telling you the selected host doesn’t have that role or doesn’t forward that log type. If you expect a panel to populate for a specific host (for example, a HANA host that should have sap:hana:audit data but doesn’t), that’s a genuine collection issue worth investigating — check the forwarder configuration and the host’s logging policy. An empty ABAP Work Process Trace Components panel for a range after April 2026 is expected (see above).

    Sourcetype Mapping Tab¶

    Full-width link graph showing how the host’s events flow from source files to sourcetypes. Source paths are normalized — embedded UUIDs, dates, and long numeric runs are collapsed to placeholders — so rotated per-day files appear as a single logical source rather than one node per day. Useful for spotting a noisy logical source that’s producing an outsized share of the host’s volume, or for validating that a host’s expected sources are all represented.

    What to Look For¶

    • Sourcetype gaps – If a host is missing a sourcetype that similar hosts have (e.g., a HANA host without sap:hana:audit), it may indicate a misconfigured audit policy or broken log forwarding.
    • Stale sourcetypes – A row in the Data Freshness table whose Last Seen has fallen well behind the others signals that a specific log pipeline has stopped delivering. The three ABAP log types SAP discontinued in April 2026 (sap:abap:workprocess, sap:abap:dispatcher, sap:abap:event) stop there by design.
    • Volume anomalies – Compare the selected host’s event volume to its peers. Significantly higher or lower volume may indicate a workload issue, logging configuration problem, or security event.
    • Sudden volume changes – A host that normally generates a steady volume but suddenly spikes or drops warrants investigation. Spikes may indicate security events; drops may indicate system or agent failures.
    • Auth failure spikes – A non-zero Auth Failures KPI on a host that usually has zero is worth immediate attention. Use Cross-Stack Authentication for the cross-source failure detail.
    • Sudo command patterns – On the Role Activity tab, unexpected users invoking sudo on a host may reflect lateral-movement attempts or misconfigured automation.
    • Single-sourcetype dominance – If the Sourcetype Mapping link graph shows one sourcetype accounting for the vast majority of the host’s events, the balance may indicate a noisy process (check ICM, workprocess, or web dispatcher logs for runaway activity).

    Related Dashboards¶

    • Data Pipeline Overview – the whole estate’s hosts and sourcetypes.
    • Cross-Stack Authentication – the failure detail behind the Auth Failures KPI.
    • Environment Health – errors and failures across the landscape.
    • Data Doctor (Diagnostics) – when a panel you expect is empty.
    Where the data comes from

    As the estate-wide drill-down target, this dashboard mixes all three source kinds:

    • Summary-backed KPIs — Data Volume, Errors/Criticals and Auth Failures (plus their sparklines) read the logserv_hostdetails_rollup KV Store collection (metrics vol, err, auth, one row per host per hour; populated at minute :27 of every hour by logserv_hostdetails_aggregate over the entire index).
    • The Role Activity tab reads the logserv_hostrole_rollup collection (minute :04) — seven per-role metrics (hana_action, abap_wp, webdisp_status, saprouter_peer, win_eventcode, sudo_user, dns_query), each an hourly (host, value) count grain that reproduces the original top-N tables exactly.
    • The Sourcetype Mapping tab reads the logserv_stmap_rollup collection (minute :03), with source values normalised at aggregation time (UUIDs / dates / digit runs collapsed).
    • tstats panels — Total Events, Active Sourcetypes, the events-by-sourcetype chart, Top Sources, Data Freshness and the host picker run tstats against indexed fields, honouring the host filter at any volume.
    • Host Inventory is live: it reads the osquery facts embedded in linux_messages_syslog events at view time (hosts without an osquery agent simply don’t appear).

    Summary-backed panels switch automatically to their exact raw-equivalent search when the selected window is shorter than 90 minutes, so sub-hour investigation stays real-time. Each collection keeps 365 days of hourly history (trimmed by a daily retention search). The global Cloud dropdown filters the summaries through the cloud_provider dimension stored in every rollup row. Full schedule and freshness reference: Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness.

    Multi-Cloud Overview¶

    Why This Dashboard Matters¶

    The Multi-Cloud Overview dashboard answers the question: “Where is our LogServ data coming from, and is it balanced between cloud providers?” It splits ingest by the indexed cloud_provider field so admins running any mix of AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, and Google Cloud Storage ingest can confirm each pipeline is healthy and see relative volume at a glance.

    Customers running a single cloud see the dashboard collapse cleanly to one provider (the unused providers’ KPIs show 0, the active provider’s series carries the trend chart). Customers running two or three clouds see comparative KPIs + side-by-side trend so they can spot a stalled ingest channel before it becomes a visible gap in their other operational dashboards.

    How cloud_provider is attributed

    cloud_provider is an indexed field, written when each event is indexed:

    • The LogServ Azure and LogServ GCP add-ons stamp azure and gcp on every event their inputs read (_meta = cloud_provider::azure / ::gcp, set automatically).
    • Inputs the Data TA’s AWS S3 Direct screen creates stamp aws automatically, and the screen names any input whose stamp did not complete. Inputs made from the curl commands it generates under Apply this as an administrator carry no stamp: add the _meta line to their stanzas by hand (the inputs.conf stanzas it generates there already carry it).
    • For the Splunk Add-on for AWS SQS-Based S3 inputs, you add _meta = cloud_provider::aws to each input’s stanza, and leave the Data TA’s Configuration → Cloud Provider dropdown at Not set.

    Events with no stamp are counted as aws by the LogServ App’s dashboards, this one included, but not by searches outside the App (see Requires below). The recommended setup, and the one case where the dropdown is an alternative, are on Choose Cloud Attribution.

    Requires¶

    • Sourcetypes: any. The dashboard reads every event in the LogServ data index and splits it by cloud_provider.
    • Search-head add-ons: none beyond the LogServ App.
    • Dashboard Data row: Multi-Cloud Overview on Settings → Dashboard Data. On a new install, Run backfill there seeds the last 30 days by default (60, 90, 180 or 365 days, or a custom range, are also offered); without a backfill the panels fill one hour at a time. See Backfilling on first install.

    • Attribution at ingest. The dashboard works on any LogServ App install (it shows 0 for unused providers), but how well it splits your data depends on the ingest configuration:

      1. For Azure ingest: nothing to do. The LogServ Azure add-on sets _meta = cloud_provider::azure on its input kind ([sap_logserv_azure_queue] in the add-on’s default/inputs.conf), so every input inherits it. See the Azure Setup Guide.
      2. For GCP ingest: nothing to do. The LogServ GCP add-on sets _meta = cloud_provider::gcp on its input kind ([sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub]), so every input inherits it. See the GCP Setup Guide.
      3. For AWS ingest: add _meta = cloud_provider::aws to each [aws_sqs_based_s3://<your input name>] stanza in Splunk_TA_aws’s local/inputs.conf on each heavy forwarder (on Splunk Cloud with no heavy forwarder, see Choose Cloud Attribution), before the input first runs: events indexed before the line is added keep no stamp. For inputs it creates, the AWS S3 Direct screen adds the line itself, and says so when it could not. Leave the Data TA’s Configuration → Cloud Provider dropdown at Not set (its default). The dropdown writes its value in addition to any _meta an input already sets, so an event whose input stamps a different provider carries both values. Choose Cloud Attribution explains this, including the case where both name the same provider.
      4. Unstamped events: the LogServ App’s dashboards count events with no cloud_provider as aws (their summaries apply coalesce(cloud_provider, "aws"), and the global Cloud filter set to aws also matches events with no value). This is not a field default: ad-hoc searches, tstats, cloud_provider=aws term filters and Enterprise Security see no value on those events. To apply the same default in your own searches, call the sap_logserv_cloud_provider_default_macro macro.
      5. Macro must be present: the LogServ App’s default/macros.conf defines [sap_logserv_cloud_provider_default_macro] with definition = eval cloud_provider=coalesce(cloud_provider, "aws"). If you’ve overridden macros.conf in your local app directory, ensure this macro is still defined.

    Panels¶

    Unlike the other dashboards, this one has no Cloud Provider picker in its title row: the provider split is the dashboard, so every panel reports all providers side by side. The time-range picker and the per-dashboard Refresh picker work as on any other LogServ App dashboard. The tables are inventory views and have no row drill-downs.

    • Total Events – Aggregate event count across ALL ingest channels with a daily-volume sparkline. Useful as the baseline for comparing the per-provider KPIs that follow.
    • AWS Events – Event count where cloud_provider = "aws": events stamped aws at ingest, plus events with no stamp, which this dashboard counts as aws. Sparkline shows daily AWS-only volume.
    • Azure Events – Event count where cloud_provider = "azure". Sparkline shows daily Azure-only volume. On an install without Azure ingest, this KPI shows 0 and its sparkline is empty.
    • GCP Events – Event count where cloud_provider = "gcp". Sparkline shows daily GCP-only volume. On an install without GCP ingest, this KPI shows 0 and its sparkline is empty.
    • Event Volume by Cloud Provider – Column chart of event counts over time, one bar per provider in each time bucket. Useful for spotting shifts over time: when one provider’s bars drop suddenly while the others stay level, that provider’s ingest has likely stalled.
    • Event Count by Provider – One-row-per-provider table with the raw cumulative event counts. The same data as the per-provider KPIs but in tabular form so the ratios are easy to read.
    • Distinct Hosts by Provider – One-row-per-provider table showing how many unique host values reported under each cloud_provider. Confirms forwarder coverage across the cloud boundary.
    • Distinct Sourcetypes by Provider – One-row-per-provider table showing how many distinct sourcetypes have at least one event per provider. Useful for confirming every cloud is producing the full sourcetype mix (e.g., not just linux_messages_syslog from Azure while AWS has the SAP stack).
    • About the cloud_provider field – Inline reference panel (not a search result) explaining how the field is set and linking to the Azure and GCP Setup Guides. Where its short text and Choose Cloud Attribution differ on the Cloud Provider dropdown, follow Choose Cloud Attribution.
    • Top Sourcetypes by Cloud Provider – Wide table of the 30 most-active sourcetypes with per-provider columns (AWS Events / Azure Events / GCP Events / Total). The Total column is sorted descending so the high-volume sourcetypes lead. Useful for spotting per-sourcetype anomalies (e.g., sap:hana:audit is only appearing under one cloud when several should be producing it).

    What to Look For¶

    • Stalled ingest channel – If one provider’s KPI sparkline goes flat-zero for the most recent 1–3 days while the others continue to climb, the affected channel’s input has likely stalled. Check the LogServ Azure add-on’s sap_logserv_azure_queue input on the heavy forwarder (per-firing summary in splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure_queue.log: Input '<name>' done: messages=N blobs=N events=N ...), the LogServ GCP add-on’s sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub input (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub.log: Input '<name>' done: messages=N objects=N events=N ...), or, for AWS, the Splunk Add-on for AWS SQS-Based S3 input’s own log (index=_internal sourcetype=aws:sqsbaseds3:log).
    • Asymmetric sourcetype coverage – If both clouds report comparable total event counts but the Top Sourcetypes table shows one cloud with a narrow sourcetype mix (e.g., AWS only producing sap:hana:audit while Azure produces 25+ sourcetypes), the AWS-side filter rules may be set to include-only rather than include-all. Check Configuring Filters.
    • Unexpected appearance of aws from an Azure- or GCP-only customer – If your environment has no AWS ingest but the AWS Events KPI shows non-zero values, some events carry no cloud_provider stamp and this dashboard counts them as aws: for example, events from an input that sets no _meta. An indexed event cannot be stamped afterwards; those events keep counting as aws until they age out of the index. To find them, run | tstats fillnull_value="(unstamped)" count WHERE `sap_logserv_idx_macro` BY cloud_provider, sourcetype and look at the (unstamped) rows.
    • Distinct Hosts count substantially lower than expected – If a single cloud’s “Distinct Hosts” count is much lower than the actual count of SAP hosts in that cloud, your add-on input config may be too narrow (wrong container prefix on the Azure side, wrong subscription on the GCP side, wrong bucket prefix on the AWS side). Compare against your topology source-of-truth.
    • Total Events ≠ sum of the per-provider KPIs – The per-provider KPIs match aws / azure / gcp exactly, while Total Events adds up every value. If Total exceeds their sum, some events carry another cloud_provider value — run | tstats fillnull_value="(unstamped)" count WHERE `sap_logserv_idx_macro` BY cloud_provider to see every value (unstamped events show as (unstamped); this dashboard counts them as aws). An event that carries two different values, for example when the Cloud Provider dropdown is set on a forwarder whose inputs stamp a different provider, is counted once under each value; find such events with search `sap_logserv_idx_macro` earliest=-24h | where mvcount(cloud_provider) > 1 | stats count by host, sourcetype and see Choose Cloud Attribution → Check the Result. If instead the AWS KPI under-reports, check that the sap_logserv_cloud_provider_default_macro macro is defined on your search head — the LogServ App ships it in default/macros.conf; confirm with | rest /services/configs/conf-macros | search title=sap_logserv_cloud_provider_default_macro.

    Related Dashboards¶

    • Data Pipeline Overview – the same ingest by host and sourcetype, across all clouds.
    • Data Doctor (Diagnostics) – rollup freshness and sourcetype presence.
    • Azure Setup Guide and GCP Setup Guide – the cloud-side configuration of each channel.
    Where the data comes from

    Panels read the logserv_mc_rollup KV Store collection — metric count carries per-hour event counts by (cloud provider, sourcetype) and metric hosts the per-provider host sets (kept separate so distinct-host counts stay correct when an event carries a multivalue host). Populated at minute :22 of every hour by logserv_mc_aggregate over the entire index, keyed on the cloud_provider indexed field stamped at ingest (see Requires); the aggregate applies the sap_logserv_cloud_provider_default_macro macro, so events with no provider attribution are counted as aws.

    Summary-backed panels switch automatically to their exact raw-equivalent search when the selected window is shorter than 90 minutes, so sub-hour investigation stays real-time. The collection keeps 365 days of hourly history (trimmed by a daily retention search). Unlike the other dashboards, this one is exempt from the global Cloud dropdown — its panels pin their own provider values (AWS / Azure / GCP side by side), so a global filter would be circular. Full schedule and freshness reference: Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness.

    Data Doctor (Diagnostics)¶

    The LogServ Data Doctor is the app’s built-in missing-data diagnostic. When a panel is empty and you don’t know why, it answers the question a support ticket would otherwise ask — “is something broken, or is there genuinely no data?” — in plain language, with the evidence, and without needing a Splunk administrator to run it. Every check it performs is readable by a normal, non-admin user.

    It has four surfaces, from smallest to widest scope:

     empty panel hint  ->  panel diagnosis drawer  ->  dashboard sweep  ->  Diagnostics page
 (automatic, free)     ("Run full diagnosis")     (Actions menu)       (#/diagnostics)

    First health check after install¶

    Run this check once the LogServ App is installed, and again after the first Dashboard Data backfill. It needs no admin role.

    1. Open Platform → Diagnostics. The checks start on their own and finish within about two minutes.
    2. In Summary, check that the index the app macro resolves to is your SAP data index, that events and sourcetypes are present in the selected window, and that the search-tier add-ons are installed: Splunk_SA_CIM, Splunk_TA_windows and Splunk_TA_nix. On a dedicated search head splunk_ta_sap_logserv is expected to be absent, and Splunk_MCP_Server matters only for the AI Assistant.
    3. In Summarised data, the History column reads NEVER BUILT on a fresh install, or INCOMPLETE once the first hourly run has written an hour or two. That is expected until an admin runs the one-time backfill (Settings → Dashboard Data → Run backfill, see Backfilling on first install); until then the dashboards show only the last hour or two of data. After the backfill, click Re-run checks. A row reads COMPLETE once its rollup holds data reaching back at least 29 days, so it needs events of that rollup’s log types at least that old in the index. A row whose log types you do not collect stays NEVER BUILT, and a row with less history in the index reads INCOMPLETE; neither means the backfill failed. A backfill that finishes with issues says so on Settings → Dashboard Data and marks the affected rollups there; running it again retries them.
    4. Click Download report (PDF) and keep the report. It records the install’s starting state, and it is the one file to attach to a support case.

    Empty-panel hints (automatic)¶

    Every chart, table and KPI card that comes back empty explains itself. Without running any extra search, the app checks the facts it already has — did the search actually run, did it error, is a global filter narrowing it (the Cloud picker, a host selection), is the selected range shorter than the panel’s data granularity, does the query contain a clause that can never match — and corrects the panel’s own empty message when one of those is the reason. On KPI cards, which sit in a height-equalised row, the hint renders in a compact 2–5-word form with the full sentence in the tooltip.

    These free checks are deliberately forbidden from claiming a system fault: without dispatched evidence, the most they assert is what the panel itself proves. When they can’t explain the emptiness, a chart or table panel offers “Why is this empty?” instead. (A KPI card has no room for that link — its entry point is the small corner diagnose affordance, revealed on hover or keyboard focus.)

    The panel diagnosis drawer¶

    Clicking Why is this empty? / Run full diagnosis opens a side drawer that dispatches a short, budgeted series of probes (90-second wall-clock budget, at most two concurrent, every probe carries server-side max_time/auto_cancel bounds) and walks a gated cascade of verdicts — the panel’s own error first, then index visibility and presence, the ingest-cutoff boundary, sourcetype presence/staleness, and finally the summarised-data (rollup) layer. The result is one plain-language headline (“Most likely: …”) with a confidence level, who can act on it (you / a Splunk administrator / whoever sends the logs), and a “What was checked” ledger showing every probe’s outcome — including the ones that were skipped, and why.

    Three properties matter more than the checks themselves:

    • It can say “nothing is broken.” If the data genuinely does not exist for the selected range, that is the verdict — stated as working-as-intended, not as a fault.
    • It never concludes from unknown. A probe that failed or ran out of budget renders NOT CHECKED, never OK and never a fault.
    • Panels that read summarised data are traced back to their source events. A rollup-backed panel names no sourcetype, so the diagnostic reads the aggregation search that populates its collection, extracts what that search consumes, and probes those sourcetypes — distinguishing “the events exist but were never summarised (run the backfill)” from “there genuinely are no such events”.

    The drawer’s footer offers Copy technical summary and Download PDF.

    For a rollup-backed panel, the drawer’s Show technical detail section (and the technical summary, and both the panel and dashboard PDFs) also prints the full SPL of the saved search(es) currently configured to populate the panel’s summary collection — each labelled with its parsed outputlookup target, its cron schedule verbatim, and its last-modified timestamp. The section states explicitly that this SPL is configuration read at diagnosis time (including any local/ override), was not run by the diagnosis, and that rows already stored in the summary may predate it. Each aggregate is accompanied by a note naming its install-backfill stanza, which as shipped carries the identical search text (a build-time check derives that identity from the shipped configuration on every release). The dashboard PDF carries one de-duplicated section covering every rollup the dashboard’s panels read — healthy panels included.

    In the drawer, each printed definition carries two corner actions: copy to clipboard (copies the definition verbatim) and open in the Search app in a new browser tab, scoped to the diagnosed time window. The opened search has the terminal | outputlookup write removed first, so running it cannot modify the summary collection — the drawer never offers a control that can change data.

    Deep evidence (drawer-only)¶

    Several further checks run only in the drawer — they are the only probes permitted to scan raw events, so a dashboard-wide sweep never fires them:

    • Summarised-vs-raw reconciliation. An empty summarised panel is re-run as its exact raw-query equivalent over the already-summarised period. Raw rows the summary lacks produce the confirmed “the summary appears to be missing data it should have” (a Splunk administrator re-runs the backfill from Settings → Dashboard Data); agreement produces the health-certifying “the raw equivalent returns nothing for this range either — there is genuinely nothing to show.” Panels whose raw equivalent is a scalar count carry no row-count signal and are skipped with an honest ledger note.
    • Field presence probe. A raw panel filtering on a field is checked against a sample of its sourcetype’s own events (up to 2,000, without the panel’s host/provider/breakdown filters): a field present on zero sampled events reads as a search-time-extraction gap — graded likely when the whole available sample was examined, possible when the 2,000-event sample cap was reached; a populated field whose expected value never appears reads as possible vocabulary or casing drift. The ledger row is “Field presence probe (sampled)”.
    • Clause relaxation. For an empty raw panel, a control probe first confirms the emptiness comes from the base search; each filter clause is then removed in turn, and the verdict names which clause excludes every event and how many events removing it would match. The ledger row is “Clause relaxation”.
    • Lookup registration. A panel that uses a non-summarised lookup verifies the lookup is registered on this search head (a CSV placed under default/lookups/ does not register — Splunk auto-registers only the app-root lookups/ directory).

    Two smaller additions ride along: a summarised verdict under a Cloud Provider filter states whether any summarised rows carry that provider in the range, and the environment report’s rollup table gains a “Recent buckets” continuity column (context only — the live Diagnostics page deliberately omits it, since it re-gathers on every picker change).

    Diagnosing a panel that HAS data (partial-data diagnosis)¶

    Missing data is not always an empty panel: a table can have rows with one column blank, and a KPI can display a zero you believe should not be zero. The Data Doctor covers both, with two entry points that work on populated panels:

    • The Diagnose toolbar icon. Every chart and table panel’s toolbar carries a Diagnose this panel icon — first, ahead of Open-in-Search / Download CSV / Inspect / Refresh. On a populated panel it opens the drawer under the header “Panel diagnosis” (rather than “Why is this empty?”) and runs the partial-data checks below.
    • The KPI corner affordance. Each KPI card carries a small diagnose control in its corner, revealed on hover or keyboard focus. On a card showing a zero (including formatted zeros like “0 ms” or “0%”) it routes the diagnosis into the zero-value resolution.

    What a partial-data diagnosis does:

    • Column coverage. The table itself reports which displayed columns are blank — as counts only, never values (nothing from your rows leaves the panel). Each fully-blank column is traced to the raw-event field it displays (through any renames in the query) and corroborated against a sample of the source events, yielding one of three findings: the field is not populated on the source events at all (a search-time-extraction gap), the source events carry it but the summarised rows do not (a summarisation gap — the backfill settles it), or the aggregation provably does not store that column — in which case the diagnosis says plainly that a backfill cannot add it. Columns computed inside the query, or drawn by a custom renderer, are honestly set aside rather than probed.
    • Zero-value resolution. A zero KPI is reconciled against the summarised layer and — when the panel’s raw-equivalent query emits a single comparable value — against a live raw computation. Summarised rows that genuinely sum to zero, or a raw equivalent that also computes zero, certify “the value genuinely is zero” (never a backfill prescription); a raw equivalent that disagrees is reported as a possible summarisation gap, never a confirmed fault (the two computations are independent implementations).
    • The honest floor. When every displayed column is populated and accounted for, the diagnosis says so: “This panel has data, and the columns it displays are populated — no defect found.” The floor is unreachable while any column could not be checked — those are named instead.

    A populated panel’s rows are living proof the index, sourcetype and summary read path work, so the emptiness battery is skipped (each check listed in the ledger as “Not applicable — this panel returned data”), and a panel that has not finished loading is refused with a plain explanation rather than diagnosed on unknown facts.

    Data Doctor reports (PDF + JSON)¶

    Reports exist at all three scopes, each downloading a branded LogServ Data Doctor Report PDF plus a machine-readable .json twin (schema logserv.diag/1 — greppable, and diffable against a report from a week earlier):

    Scope Where What it contains
    Panel the diagnosis drawer → Download PDF the verdicts, the exact dispatched SPL + window, the evidence ledger
    Dashboard Actions menu → Diagnose dashboard (PDF) every panel on the open dashboard classified, with the full cascade run on the empty ones
    Environment Actions menu → Environment report (PDF), or the Diagnostics page index, sourcetype and rollup health for the whole install

    Every report carries a data-exposure banner: it contains search strings, index/host names, sourcetypes and SAP system identifiers, scheduled-search names and scheduler messages from apps on this instance, the full text of the saved searches that populate this app’s summary collections, and any ingest-filter configuration supplied to the diagnostic by your administrator — but no raw log events — and it is generated entirely in your browser; nothing is sent outside your Splunk instance. Note that every report you download (except one carrying raw samples) is also saved to the app’s KV Store, where all app users can read it — see Saved reports below. It is designed to be attached to a Splunk support ticket.

    The Diagnostics page (#/diagnostics)¶

    Platform → Diagnostics is the environment-wide surface, visible to every user (it is deliberately not admin-gated). On open — and on every time-range change, or the nav-bar Refresh button — it runs the environment checks (120-second budget) and renders them live:

    • Summary — events in the selected window, sourcetypes present, the index the app macro resolves to, a search-head canary round-trip, Splunk version + search-head clock, and whether the companion apps (Splunk_SA_CIM, Splunk_TA_windows, Splunk_TA_nix, splunk_ta_sap_logserv — whose absence is expected on a dedicated search head, as the row itself notes — Splunk_MCP_Server) are installed.
    • Summarised data (rollup collections) — one row per rollup collection, grouped by the dashboard it powers, with TWO independent verdicts: Freshness (how recently the hourly or daily aggregation last wrote — a healthy hourly collection lags 1–2.5 h and is flagged STALE only above 3 h; daily collections are flagged above 50 h) and History (whether ~30 days of backfilled history exists — the same completeness convention Settings → Dashboard Data uses, computed from the same threshold). When rollups lack history the page says so and names the fix — a Splunk administrator can run the backfill in Settings → Dashboard Data — as text, not a button: the page intentionally carries no destructive or admin controls.
    • Sourcetypes — per-sourcetype events in the window plus all-time last-seen.
    • What was checked — the same honest ledger as the drawer, including anything skipped.
    • What cannot be checked from here — the explicit list of things a browser session on the search head can never see for itself (the Data TA’s ingest filters on the heavy forwarders — unless an operator supplies them, see below — the upstream LogServ feed, index=_internal for a restricted role), each with who to ask.
    • Saved Data Doctor reports — see below.

    The page’s evidence is always labeled with the window it was gathered under (“Evidence as of …”), the checks can be cancelled mid-run (partial results stay visible and say they are partial), and Download report (PDF) produces the environment report from exactly the evidence on screen.

    Why the page has no auto-refresh picker

    The per-dashboard auto-refresh interval picker is suppressed here: the page dispatches roughly one probe per rollup collection plus a set of environment checks — dozens per run — which should happen when you ask (open, time-range change, Re-run, or the nav-bar Refresh), not on a 30-second timer.

    Platform health (snapshot)¶

    An hourly scheduled search (logserv_diag_platform_aggregate, two minutes past each hour) copies platform signals from index=_internal — scheduler outcomes and skip/deferral reasons, search-concurrency warnings, per-index throughput, pipeline-queue depth and PCRE-limit events — into a world-readable collection, so this page (and the environment report) can show platform health to any role, not just admins.

    • When the snapshot is stale, empty or unreadable, the panel says NOT AVAILABLE with the verified reason (the producing search is disabled / has not run yet / has run but written nothing) — it never renders stale numbers as current facts.
    • All snapshot figures are context, never a cause: the scheduler tables include this app’s own hourly summarisation jobs, and the queue-depth gauge does not measure ingest-filter drops (the operator-supplied ingest-filter configuration below is the drop evidence).
    • A stale dashboard summary’s diagnosis can cite matching scheduler skips from the snapshot as an evidence line — always badged as recorded by the hourly platform snapshot, a collection only Splunk administrators can write, and never able to raise a verdict’s confidence (rows written by an earlier App build, when every role could write the collection, may be forged).

    The snapshot keeps 30 days (daily retention at 01:58). It needs no backfill — it warms within the hour of install.

    Raw event samples (opt-in)¶

    The panel diagnosis drawer’s Download PDF offers an Include raw event samples checkbox (default off, reset every time the drawer opens). When ticked, the report appends up to 5 recent events of the sourcetype(s) the panel reads — credential-scrubbed, email- and username-redacted, each included in full (a 20,000-character safety ceiling applies, disclosed on the event if ever reached — twice Splunk’s default per-event truncation, so real events are never cut), and clearly labelled as not filtered by the panel’s own host/provider selections (they show what the raw data looks like, not what the panel would have matched). The PDF renders events in a Latin-1 font, so characters outside that range may not display correctly there — the .json twin that downloads alongside every report carries the exact text. The report’s cover banner states the samples’ presence, and a sample-bearing report is download-only: it is never saved to the Saved-reports list, because storing raw events in a world-readable collection would bypass index access controls.

    Supplying the ingest-filter configuration¶

    The one thing the Data Doctor cannot see for itself is the Data TA’s ingest-tier filtering — the include/exclude rules and the days-in-past cutoff run on the heavy forwarder / indexer tier and silently discard events before they are indexed. Historically this is the single most common cause of “I see zero events”.

    The Diagnostics page closes that gap with the Ingest-tier filters (operator-supplied) panel: it prints the exact command to run, an operator pastes the output, and the diagnosis gains two more checks that can turn that class of emptiness into a named, plain-language verdict:

    • “Events this old are discarded at ingest by design — your selected range ends before the configured cutoff” (the days-in-past reconciliation), and
    • “<log type> events are excluded by the configured filter rule <rule> — they are dropped before they reach the index” — or, when an include list is the cause, “not covered by the configured include list <list>“ (the include/exclude reconciliation), with the reminder that an intentional exclusion means nothing is broken.

    Run one of these commands where your Data TA configuration lives, and paste the output into the panel.

    Deployment Server (distributed install), or this host on a single instance:

    curl -k -u <splunk-admin> "https://<deployment-server>:8089/servicesNS/nobody/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/splunk_ta_sap_logserv_settings/filter_settings?output_mode=json"

    Omit ?output_mode=json for the XML form. The response carries filter_enabled, include_filters, exclude_filters, include_sources, exclude_sources and days_in_past.

    Heavy forwarder managed by a Deployment Server: the generated filter file.

    sudo cat /opt/splunk/etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/local/transforms.conf

    Heavy forwarder that no Deployment Server manages: it holds its own configuration, because its Filters saves are made on it. Run the REST command against that forwarder (https://<heavy-forwarder>:8089/...), or paste its local/transforms.conf.

    Four paste formats are accepted: the REST response as JSON or XML, the generated local/transforms.conf, and the settings conf (local/splunk_ta_sap_logserv_settings.conf). Practical notes:

    • Where to run the command matters. On a distributed install the Deployment Server’s REST endpoint is authoritative; on a single instance, this host’s; on a heavy forwarder that no Deployment Server manages, that forwarder’s. On a deployment-server-managed heavy forwarder, do not use the REST endpoint: it returns the shipped defaults with the HF’s copy of the settings file on top, and the Deployment Server sends that file only when it copies the whole Data TA (on the first Filters or Cloud Provider save, and on the first save after a Data TA version change; later saves send only local/transforms.conf and local/props.conf). So the endpoint can show an earlier save’s settings, or the shipped defaults, and neither tells you what the HF filters now. Paste the HF’s generated local/transforms.conf instead. If a paste exactly matches the shipped defaults, the diagnosis says so and keeps asking rather than treating filtering as ruled out; a paste taken from an HF’s REST endpoint can be out of date even when it does not match the defaults.
    • The paste is credential-scrubbed before it is stored (curl -u credentials, Authorization headers, passwords, tokens, session cookies), and for a fully parsed paste the raw text is not retained at all — only the parsed settings.
    • Everything derived from a paste is labelled — “Recorded as supplied by \<user>, \<date>“ — in the drawer’s evidence, on this page, and in every report; it is never presented as something the app observed. After seven days the page asks for a re-supply, and verdicts built on older facts are hedged accordingly. If newer events contradict a supplied configuration (for example, events of a supposedly excluded type keep arriving), the diagnosis says the configuration appears out of date instead of trusting it.
    • Saving re-runs the checks, so the page, the boundary text and any report you download move together. Re-pasting overwrites the previous supply; there is no delete.

    The supplied configuration is used as evidence as follows:

    • Replayed or backdated arrivals are caught by the out-of-date check. The diagnosis compares the supply time against both the newest event timestamp and the newest index time (from bucket metadata) of a supposedly excluded type. Events recorded as indexed after the supply — even when their event timestamps are old — soften the exclusion verdict and add a note asking for a re-supply, with a five-minute grace so ordinary clock skew cannot manufacture a contradiction.
    • The days-in-past verdict corroborates against the index’s own oldest event where that was probed: either “events older than the cutoff do exist” (indexed while they were still within the then-current cutoff) or an explicitly non-committal “an always-active ingest filter, a young index, and ordinary retention all look identical here”. Context only — it never changes the verdict’s confidence.
    • A window that ends before the cutoff gets a context line even when the index is not empty — when one log type has nothing in such a window, the “events of this age arriving now would be dropped at ingest; the cutoff slides forward daily” aside is attached to the verdict, so the sliding cutoff is considered without over-claiming it as the cause.
    • The Data TA’s Cloud Provider stamp rides the paste. A local/transforms.conf paste (or a settings-conf paste, which can also carry the explicit Not set) records the configured cloud_provider stamp; on provider-filtered panels the diagnosis explains how the stamp interacts with the panel’s filter — including that an aws filter also matches events with no provider at all, so a stamp mismatch never by itself explains an empty AWS panel. Absence of the stamp block in a paste is never read as “Not set” (the paste may be truncated).
    • HANA trace files that arrive without folder fields are judged apart from their folder. SAP delivers some HANA trace files with no clz_dir / clz_subdir, and the Data TA can route them to sap:hana:tracelogs by their file path, where folder filters do not reach them. The diagnosis therefore does not read trace events that keep arriving despite an Exclude Filters rule on hana/tracelogs as an out-of-date configuration, and does not call that rule a full exclusion. On a HANA Trace panel it also names an Include Filters allow-list that keeps the hana/tracelogs folder but drops these files: as an additional finding, listed after the panel’s main verdict in Show technical detail and in the report’s All findings, never in its place, because the paste does not show whether SAP delivers such files to you. Panels that also read other log types do not report it. Any verdict these files change reads Partly excluded? at no more than possible, because the paste does not show whether your forwarders route these files this way either. See Events Without Folder Fields.
    • The drawer points back here. When a panel diagnosis lands on an ingest-ambiguous verdict and no usable configuration has been supplied, the “Why is this empty?” drawer (and its Copy technical summary text) adds: “If a Splunk administrator supplies the Data TA’s ingest-filter configuration on the Diagnostics page, this diagnosis can take those filters into account.” The pointer is suppressed when the stored supply merely could not be read.

    The stored configuration is writable by every authenticated user and is validated on read, like the saved reports and the per-user preferences (the dashboard rollups, the topology collections, the platform snapshot and the AI Assistant’s settings, acknowledgements and model cache can be written by the admin tier only); the supplier’s name is shown as (name not verified). Treat it as a shared, unauthenticated-integrity artifact. The supplied values steer wording and attribution, but the strong verdicts still require the diagnostic’s own first-hand observations (an actually-empty window, an actually-absent sourcetype) to fire.

    Saved reports¶

    Every downloaded Data Doctor report — panel, dashboard or environment, from any surface — is also saved automatically into the app’s KV Store (logserv_diag_reports), and the Diagnostics page lists them: when it was generated, its scope, a one-line verdict summary, who generated it, and the app build it came from. Any listed report can be re-downloaded as the same PDF or its JSON twin, both marking the author as (name not verified) — useful for comparing a report from before and after a fix, or for retrieving a report a colleague generated.

    Housekeeping and integrity:

    • Reports are kept for 365 days, capped at the newest 100 (a nightly retention search at 01:56 search-head local time enforces both).
    • Very large reports (over ~200 KB of model data) are listed but not stored for re-download — the row says so; the copy downloaded at generation time is the complete one.
    • Saved reports are visible to all users of the app and writable by them (one of the six App KV collections every user can write; a re-downloaded report marks its author as (name not verified) wherever it prints the name, its JSON copy included). Treat them as shared, unauthenticated-integrity artifacts — the authoritative copy of any report is the one downloaded when it was generated. Stored rows are validated before re-rendering; anything malformed is skipped.

    What to Look For¶

    • “NEVER BUILT” or “INCOMPLETE” in the History column on a fresh install — expected until the one-time backfill is run (Settings → Dashboard Data → Run backfill). Dashboards show only the last hour or two of data until then. After the backfill, a row whose log types you do not collect stays NEVER BUILT, and one with under 29 days of history in the index stays INCOMPLETE.
    • “STALE” Freshness on one collection while its neighbours are OK — that rollup’s hourly aggregation has stopped writing. An administrator should check its saved search (Settings → Dashboard Data shows the per-rollup schedule and enable state).
    • A sourcetype with recent “Last seen” but zero events in your window — the feed is alive; your window simply predates or postdates its activity. The panel-level diagnosis states this explicitly (“the most recent one is from <date>, after this range … Nothing is stopped”).
    • A sourcetype whose “Last seen” is days old — the upstream feed for that log type may have stopped. That is an ingest-side question (heavy forwarder inputs, the LogServ feed itself) — the “What cannot be checked from here” section names the exact owner to ask — and once an operator supplies the ingest-filter configuration, the days-in-past / include-exclude class of emptiness gets a named verdict instead of a boundary note.
    • NOT CHECKED rows after a run — the budget ran out or the run was cancelled/superseded. Re-run checks; the page never guesses about what it did not probe.

    Enterprise Security Integration

    Enterprise Security Integration — Overview¶

    The LogServ App ships content for Splunk Enterprise Security (ES), so SOC analysts can investigate SAP-side threats through ES’s Incident Review queue, Risk-Based Alerting (RBA) and CIM-aligned correlation searches. Use this page to check the prerequisites, set the content up in order, and turn it off on search heads that do not run ES.

    The ES content ships enabled, with or without ES

    All 22 splunk_sap_logserv_es_* saved searches ship with disabled = 0 and a schedule, so they run on every search head that runs the App. Without ES they do no useful work, and they are not silent: the notable and risk alert actions do not exist there, so Splunk logs errors in _internal (from sendmodalert and SearchScheduler) saying that these alert actions were not found, and, because there is no Risk data model, the scheduler skips the Risk Notable with the reason “Data model ‘Risk’ was not found”. On a search head without ES, we recommend turning the ES content off: see Disabling or tuning the ES content. No dashboard, rollup or AI Assistant prompt reads the results of the scheduled runs.

    With ES installed, the 19 detection searches raise notable events in Incident Review and risk events for RBA; one tier-2 Risk Notable fires when accumulated risk on a single object crosses a threshold; and two feeds supply SAP systems and user identities to ES asset and identity management.

    Prerequisites¶

    • Splunk Enterprise Security on the search head that runs the App. Notables, risk events and ES asset and identity management exist only where ES runs, so the App must be installed on the ES search head.
    • If ES runs on a search head of its own. ES can run on a different search head from the one your users open for other apps. On Splunk Cloud Platform in particular, check which search head of your stack runs ES. Install the LogServ App on the ES search head as well, the same way as on the main one (Install the App and Seed the Dashboards); the App’s dashboards and rollup searches then run there too. On a search head that runs the App without ES, turn the ES content off (Disabling or tuning the ES content).
    • The Splunk Common Information Model add-on (Splunk_SA_CIM) 5.0.0 or later. It is the only dependency the App declares in its app.manifest. Check that it is installed on the ES search head; if it is not, install it (where to get it: LogServ App Prerequisites). The App does not declare a dependency on ES (SplunkEnterpriseSecuritySuite), so it installs and works without ES. If you add ES later, turn back on any ES searches you turned off; nothing else in the App changes.
    • The CIM data models must search the LogServ index. On the CIM add-on’s setup page, add sap_logserv_logs (or the index your sap_logserv_idx_macro points at) to the index lists of Authentication, Change, Network_Sessions, Network_Resolution and Web. Add it even where a list is empty: the App does not make sap_logserv_logs an index that any role searches by default, so do not rely on an empty list to include it. The App’s cross-stack authentication-failure search reads the Authentication data model, and ES’s own correlation searches read these data models. Verifying the integration is live shows whether SAP events reach the models.

    Where the ES content runs¶

    The ES content is search-time and scheduled content inside the LogServ App: nothing is installed or changed on the forwarders or indexers for it. Where the App goes in each topology: Where Each Package Goes. In a search head cluster, the App (and with it the ES content) is deployed through the SHC deployer, as usual.

    Setup checklist¶

    1. Check the prerequisites on the search head that runs ES.
    2. Install the LogServ App there and let SAP data arrive (Install the App and Seed the Dashboards).
    3. Check that SAP events reach the CIM data models: Verifying the integration is live.
    4. Load the asset and identity feeds and add them to ES: Customer wire-up.
    5. Optional: fill the three threat-intel lookups from your own threat-intel feed (Populating the lookups). Until you do, the three threat-intel searches find nothing.
    6. Review the severities, risk scores, schedules and the Risk Notable threshold: Customer-tunable surfaces.
    7. Confirm that notables reach Incident Review: How notables appear in ES Incident Review.
    8. On every other search head that runs the App without ES, turn the ES content off: Disabling or tuning the ES content.

    Disabling or tuning the ES content¶

    On a search head without ES, the scheduled ES searches use search capacity and add errors to _internal, and nothing reads their results. Turn them off there. On a search head with ES, use the same steps for any single search you do not want.

    13 of these searches also run AI Assistant prompts

    The AI Assistant’s Security pack runs 13 of these saved searches on demand: the 6 extended cross-stack searches, the 3 threat-intel searches and the 4 behavioral-anomaly searches. A disabled saved search cannot run, so its prompt then returns an error. If you use those prompts, turn off only the schedule of those 13 (option B below) and disable the other 9 (option A).

    The 9 searches that no prompt uses are the 6 base correlation searches (splunk_sap_logserv_es_hana_privilege_escalation, _cross_stack_auth_failure, _abap_gateway_anomalous_peer, _scc_access_denied_burst, _hana_failed_connect_spike, _oom_kill_burst), the Risk Notable (_risk_notable_threshold) and the 2 feeds (_asset_feed, _identity_feed).

    Option A: disable a search (Splunk Web; Splunk Cloud and Splunk Enterprise):

    1. Go to Settings → Searches, reports, and alerts.
    2. Set App to Splunk App for SAP LogServ and filter the names on splunk_sap_logserv_es_.
    3. For each search, choose Edit → Disable.

    A disabled search stays in the App, and Edit → Enable turns it back on.

    Option B: keep a search runnable, but stop its schedule (Splunk Web; Splunk Cloud and Splunk Enterprise):

    1. Go to Settings → Searches, reports, and alerts and find the search as above.
    2. Choose Edit → Advanced edit, set is_scheduled to off, and save.

    Splunk Enterprise only: a config override. Instead of the Splunk Web steps, add one stanza per search to $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/splunk_app_sap_logserv/local/savedsearches.conf (never edit default/), then restart Splunk:

    # Option A: disable the search
[splunk_sap_logserv_es_hana_privilege_escalation]
disabled = 1

# Option B: keep the search runnable on demand, without a schedule
[splunk_sap_logserv_es_lateral_movement]
enableSched = 0
# ... one stanza per splunk_sap_logserv_es_* search

    There are 22 ES searches: 19 detections, the Risk Notable and the 2 feeds. To keep some on a search head with ES, but cut the load, start with the anomaly searches below.

    The cost of the anomaly searches

    Two of the four behavioral-anomaly searches scan 30 days of raw events on each run: splunk_sap_logserv_es_anomaly_user_auth_volume (HANA audit and sapstartsrv authentication events) and splunk_sap_logserv_es_anomaly_after_hours_admin (HANA audit). They read the index directly, not a data model, so data model acceleration does not make them cheaper; they run once a day for that reason. The other two read the App’s own hourly KV Store rollups (logserv_web_timing_rollup, logserv_topology_edges), so their cost depends on the number of hosts and edges, not on event volume. See Behavioral & Anomaly Detections.

    The ES schedule (collision-free)¶

    All splunk_sap_logserv_es_* scheduled searches ship enabled on staggered crons, which run in the search head’s local time. They sit in minutes that the App’s other scheduled searches leave free, so no two of the App’s enabled scheduled searches share an (hour, minute). The other bands are the hourly rollup aggregates and the Data Doctor’s platform snapshot (:02–:28 every hour), the nightly retention and maintenance (00:30–00:58, 01:30–01:58 and 02:32–02:36), and the daily late-arrival check at 05:40. The full schedule is in Dashboard Data → Scheduled-search schedule.

    • The hourly searches (the 15 hourly correlation searches and the Risk Notable) run at :29 and the odd minutes :31–:59.
    • 2 Asset/Identity feeds run every 4 hours at :00 / :01.
    • 4 behavioral-anomaly searches run daily at :30 (hours 02–05), so the two heavy 30-day scans run once a day, not every hour. Each daily run evaluates every time bucket since the start of the previous day, so no bucket is skipped.

    What ships for ES integration¶

    Capability Count / Surface Source
    CIM data-model tagging Authentication, Change, Network_Sessions, Web, and Network_Resolution for DNS CIM Compliance
    Base correlation searches 6 (high-confidence SAP threat patterns) Correlation Searches
    Extended cross-stack correlation searches 6 (lateral movement, privilege chain, after-hours admin activity, service-account interactive, HANA user creation off-hours, HANA mass DROP) Correlation Searches → Extended cross-stack pack
    Threat-intel correlation searches 3 (DNS to malicious domain, proxy to malicious IP, compromised credential use) — joins against 3 customer-managed CSV lookups (ship empty) Threat Intelligence Integration
    Behavioral / anomaly detections 4 stats-based Z-score (per-user auth volume, per-host webdispatcher response time, per-edge topology call volume, per-admin off-hours activity); no MLTK dependency Behavioral & Anomaly Detections
    Tier-2 Risk Notable Critical-severity notable when accumulated risk on a single object ≥ 100 in 24h (aggregates risk from all 19 detection searches — base, extended, threat-intel, and anomaly) Correlation Searches
    Asset Inventory feed splunk_for_sap_logserv_assets.csv Asset & Identity Feed
    Identity Inventory feed splunk_for_sap_logserv_identities.csv Asset & Identity Feed

    Total: 19 detection correlation searches + 1 Risk Notable + 2 Asset/Identity feeds. The extended cross-stack, threat-intel, and behavioral searches can also be run on demand from the AI Assistant’s predefined-prompt browser (Security pack), once an admin has turned the AI Assistant on (Set Up the AI Assistant); the base correlation searches run on their schedule only.

    Verifying the integration is live¶

    Once SAP data arrives and the data models cover the LogServ index (see Prerequisites), SAP events appear in the CIM data models without further setup. Verify with:

    | datamodel Authentication search
| search sourcetype IN ("sap:hana:audit","sap:sapstartsrv","sap:scc:audit","linux:sudolog")
| stats count by sourcetype Authentication.action

    You should see rows for each populated SAP authentication source, with Authentication.action as success / failure.

    Same pattern for Change, Web, Network_Sessions — see CIM Compliance for full details.

    Customer-tunable surfaces¶

    Knob Default Where (Advanced edit attribute)
    Correlation-search schedules hourly (correlations) / daily (anomalies) / every 4h (feeds) cron_schedule
    Notable severity per search critical / high / medium action.notable.param.severity
    Risk scores per result 20–90 (varies per search and per risk object) action.risk.param._risk (JSON)
    Risk Notable threshold total_risk >= 100 in 24h search of splunk_sap_logserv_es_risk_notable_threshold: the \| where total_risk >= 100 clause
    Asset/Identity feed cadence every 4h cron_schedule of splunk_sap_logserv_es_asset_feed / _identity_feed

    Change these in Splunk Web, which works on Splunk Cloud and Splunk Enterprise alike: Settings → Searches, reports, and alerts, find the search, then Edit → Advanced edit. On Splunk Enterprise you can instead override the same attributes in local/savedsearches.conf; never edit default/. A new cron in a minute another App search already uses gives up the collision-free schedule above.

    The time windows of the 15 hourly correlation searches are set for an hourly cron. Eleven use a 60-minute window that ends 5 minutes before the run (dispatch.earliest_time = -65m@m, dispatch.latest_time = -5m@m), so their hourly runs follow on from each other without overlap. Four (the ABAP gateway peer, SCC ACCESS_DENIED, HANA failed-CONNECT and OOM-killer searches) set earliest=-1h@h latest=now in the search text, which takes the place of the dispatch window: each run searches from the start of the previous hour up to the run. If you change the cron of one of these searches, change its window to match: the dispatch.earliest_time / dispatch.latest_time attributes, or the earliest= / latest= in the search text where the search sets them. Run more often with the same window, a search reports the same events again (repeat notables, and risk counted again); run less often, it leaves events between its windows unsearched.

    Pages in this section¶

    • CIM Compliance — How SAP-side events get tagged into Splunk’s standard CIM data models so ES correlation searches can consume them.
    • Correlation Searches — The 6 base + 6 extended cross-stack correlation searches, the tier-2 Risk Notable, and the RBA risk-scoring scheme.
    • Asset & Identity Feed — How the App feeds ES asset and identity management with SAP system inventory + user identities.
    • Threat Intelligence Integration — The 3 customer-managed CSV lookups + the 3 TI-driven correlation searches that join against them. Customer populates the lookups from their own threat-intel feed.
    • Behavioral & Anomaly Detections — The 4 stats-based Z-score anomaly detections that complement the deterministic correlation searches by surfacing entities deviating from their own historical patterns. Optional MLTK upgrade path documented.

    CIM Compliance¶
