A tool name other than the two on this page is refused the same way.

    Arg Type Description
    name string (required) Saved-search name from the catalog (e.g., logserv_hana_failed_auth)
    earliest_time string (optional) Splunk earliest token (e.g., -24h, -7d). If omitted, the saved search’s own configured time range applies; the AI’s primer instructs it to pass an explicit window.
    latest_time string (optional) Splunk latest token (e.g., now).
    render_hint string (optional) One of table / timechart / kpi / pie. Falls back to the catalog’s per-prompt renderHint.
    top_n integer (optional, default 10, max 50) Width of categorical aggregates the AI receives in Tier 2 summary. The AI passes this when the user asks for “top 25 X” or similar.

    splunk_run_query¶

    Dispatch ad-hoc SPL written by the AI. Used when no saved search fits the user’s question.

    Arg Type Description
    query string (required) SPL string. Must start with the LogServ macro \sap_logserv_idx_macro`as its first term — or with| inputlookupof one of the App's lookups,| tstatswith the macro right afterWHEREor| makeresults` — and use only the allowed commands. The App enforces both (below).
    earliest_time string (optional) Passed to the MCP Server as given. When the AI omits it, the App adds no default: the window is whatever the Splunk MCP Server applies. (The tool description the AI sees says the user’s selected time range is the default; it is not.)
    latest_time string (optional) Same as above.
    render_hint string (optional) One of table / timechart / kpi / pie.
    top_n integer (optional, default 10, max 50) Width of categorical aggregates the AI receives in a Tier 2 summary.

    The SPL Guard¶

    SPL guard (LLM06 — Excessive Agency): the orchestrator checks every splunk_run_query query three times before dispatch, and a query any check refuses is never sent to Splunk:

    1. The denylist of known risky commands (below), the first fence.
    2. The allow-list. The App reads the query with a strict lexer and refuses it unless every command in it, subsearches included, is on the list, and it reads only what free-form analysis needs (details after the denylist).
    3. Splunk’s own search parser. The App then sends the query to search/parser (parse only, nothing runs; through Splunk Web’s splunkd proxy, as the signed-in user, in this App’s namespace) and refuses it when the parser reads it differently from the App: another list of commands, a command not on the list, a query starting with the data macro whose expansion is not the App’s definition (a macro of the same name the user’s context shadows — where the macro stands after WHERE in tstats or starts a subsearch, only an index term its expansion brings in is caught), an index term other than the LogServ index, or a lookup / inputlookup outside a subsearch whose lookup, as the parser reports it, is not one of the App’s or cannot be read. The parser reports a subsearch as text inside the command that holds it, not as commands of its own, so the commands and lookups inside a subsearch are checked by the App’s lexer only: a command or lookup that a shadowed macro brings into a subsearch is not caught (an index term it brings in is). If the parser cannot be asked — the call fails, times out or returns no command list — the query is refused (parser_unavailable); a query the parser rejects as invalid SPL is refused too (parser_rejected). It fails closed.

    The denylist refuses these commands at the start of the query, after a | or after a [, outside quoted strings — also when double or single quotes are written into the command word, as in | "delete" or | de'lete':

    • Write to an index: collect and its aliases stash, summaryindex and sumindex; mcollect; meventcollect.
    • Write lookups, files or other output: outputlookup, outputcsv, outputtext, dump, tscollect, createrss.
    • Delete events: delete.
    • Trigger alerts or email: sendalert, sendemail.
    • Run scripts: script and its alias run; runshellscript.
    • Read REST endpoints: rest — storage/passwords returns stored credentials decrypted.
    • Send data out: outputtelemetry, and the third-party curl, wget and sendresults.
    • Machine Learning Toolkit: ai (it sends the rows to an LLM) and deletemodel.
    • Run other searches: map, and savedsearch’s aliases macro and savedsplunk.

    It also refuses savedsearch and savedsplunk as words anywhere in the query, quoted text included (| from savedsearch:X), also when quotes split them (| "saved"search X, | sav"edsearch" X); the external lookup dnslookup anywhere, also split by quotes (| lookup "dns"lookup), because each row becomes a DNS query to an outside name server; a fit command (plain, quoted or split by quotes) followed anywhere later in the query by the word into, because fit ... into saves a model (fit with no into after it, and apply, stay allowed); an SPL inline comment (three backticks); an unmatched backtick; a double quote that is never closed, or a backslash-escaped double quote outside a quoted string; and a macro other than the App’s own (sap_logserv_idx_macro, sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro, sap_logserv_cloud_provider_default_macro), because a comment, ambiguous quoting or another macro could hide a command. Apart from those words, dnslookup, an into after a fit, and backticks, double-quoted text is read as data, so a bracketed tag inside a quoted string, such as search "[DELETE]", is not mistaken for a command. Where Splunk’s reading of quotes is uncertain, the guard assumes the worst and refuses. That includes a word that forms only once the quotes are removed ("saved""search"), a | or [ inside single quotes (read as a command position), and any into after a fit, even one that belongs to another command or to quoted text (| fit X | stats count by into, | fit X by "a into b").

    The allow-list. A query the denylist passes must also pass these rules (operators in brackets, as the audit event records them):

    • Commands (command_not_allowed): only search, where, eval, stats, eventstats, streamstats, tstats, chart, timechart, top, rare, sort, head, tail, dedup, reverse, table, fields, rename, fillnull, filldown, bin, bucket, rex, regex, spath, lookup, inputlookup, makeresults, addinfo, transaction, convert, iplocation, strcat, xyseries, untable, transpose, fieldsummary, addtotals, addcoltotals, makemv, nomv, mvcombine, append, appendcols, join, appendpipe. Everything else is refused, whatever it does and whichever app ships it — custom search commands of other apps, fit and apply, datamodel, metadata, loadjob, inputcsv, foreach, map, mvexpand, fieldformat, rangemap, return, format, multisearch, union. Every allowed command is one the Tier 2 summarizer reads in full. union is refused because Splunk’s search parser rewrites it before it runs (into search … | append [...], or multisearch when every arm streams), so the App cannot check it against the parser’s reading; use append to combine two searches — `sap_logserv_idx_macro` sourcetype=a | stats count by host | append [search `sap_logserv_idx_macro` sourcetype=b | stats count by host] — and the refusal of a union tells the model so.
    • Where a query starts (query_start): the query, and every subsearch arm, starts with `sap_logserv_idx_macro` as the first term of its search, or with | inputlookup <one of the App's lookups>, | tstats … WHERE `sap_logserv_idx_macro` or | makeresults; an appendpipe […] group starts with a command (stats, eval, …), never with the macro. Every tstats, anywhere in the query, names the macro right after WHERE.
    • Data scope (index_not_allowed): no index=, index!=, index:: or index IN term anywhere, no audit macro, and no OR or NOT right next to the LogServ macro — Splunk binds OR tighter than the implied AND, so `sap_logserv_idx_macro` OR index=main would leave the index. Put alternatives after the macro, in parentheses: `sap_logserv_idx_macro` (sourcetype=a OR sourcetype=b).
    • Lookups (lookup_not_allowed, eval_lookup): lookup and inputlookup only name the App’s own lookups — its rollups, its threat-intel lookups, its sourcetype metadata and the ISC BIND and Squid lookups. The Data Doctor’s collections, the Enterprise Security asset and identity feeds and the Settings backfill’s scratch collection (logserv_backfill_stage) are excluded, and so is every other app’s lookup and the eval lookup() function (also written lookup ( or across a line break). The lookup’s name must be the one Splunk reads too: an option before it may not have a quoted value (max="5", event_time_field='…'), and nothing may be written against the name (logserv_mc_rollup"_x"). Splunk’s parser must agree: for every lookup and inputlookup outside a subsearch the App reads the lookup again from the parser’s reply (step 3 above) and refuses the query (parser_mismatch) unless it is one of the App’s.
    • Subsearches (subsearch_not_allowed, subsearch_fields): only as a filter in search, ending with | fields or | table naming the fields it returns (no wildcard, not search or query, whose values Splunk would insert as text), or in append, appendcols, join and appendpipe (one group).
    • Macros (macro_position): the LogServ macro only as the first term of a search or right after WHERE in tstats; a macro inside quoted text is refused. A macro must stand apart, with a space, a | or a square bracket on each side: Splunk expands a macro as text, so anything written against it joins its expansion (`sap_logserv_idx_macro`* would become index="sap_logserv_logs"*, where`sap_logserv_idx_macro` would lose the WHERE).
    • Quoting and brackets (ambiguous_single_quote, unbalanced_bracket, escaped_outside_quotes): single quotes only around field names (eval 'User Name'=user) — every ' pairs with the next one, with no |, bracket, double quote, backtick, backslash or line break between them. A search term that contains an apostrophe goes in double quotes: "don't". Square brackets must balance outside quoted text. A backslash may appear only inside double-quoted text (a rex or regex pattern, a quoted value): Splunk reads \| as a pipe character passed to the command rather than the end of a command, so an escaped pipe, bracket or quote outside double quotes would make Splunk and the App see different commands.

    The AI’s primer lists the allowed commands exactly, and a refusal names the command, lookup or macro it is about, so the model can rewrite the query. Splunk role permissions remain the authoritative gate. Blocked SPL produces a synthetic error tool_result + a security_blocked_spl audit event (with the operator and, when the refusal is about one, the command). The AI is told Tool call refused by the App before it ran: followed by the guard’s reason, which is text the App wrote, so it can recover by writing a different query.

    Limitation: a renamed SAP data index

    The parser check compares the expansion of sap_logserv_idx_macro with the definition the App ships, index="sap_logserv_logs", and refuses any other index value. After the macro is changed for a renamed data index (Renaming an index), every free-form query that reads events, starting with the macro or using it in tstats, is refused (parser_mismatch). Predefined prompts are not affected; they are not checked this way. This release has no setting to change it.

    The System Primer¶

    A system-message prelude is sent on every free-form request. The primer teaches the AI:

    • A data-boundary rule that distinguishes customer data from instructions (mitigates LLM01 / LLM04)
    • The full saved-search catalog, built from the intent map at compile time (so the AI prefers splunk_run_saved_search when a saved search fits)
    • The LogServ data model (sourcetypes + key fields) for ad-hoc SPL
    • The exact list of commands allowed in splunk_run_query, and where a query must start, what it may read and how to quote
    • The time-window reasoning rules that kick in for severity claims
    • Synthesis rules — lettered findings, severity dots, citation format

    Two primer variants ship — one for each cloud tier — and the active tier picks which one is sent. For the primer’s full architecture (boundary block, primer constants, per-variant content), see LogServ App and AI Assistant Internals.

    Citation + Drill-Down Chips in the Narrative¶

    The AI’s narrative response uses a citation format [→ saved_search_name] to attribute each finding to its dispatched tool. Each citation in the chat becomes a clickable scroll-to-tile span (clicking it scrolls the right pane to the matching tile). The parser also auto-appends ↗ Dashboard chips (one per related OOTB dashboard) and a ↗ Run SPL chip on the same line — see Drill-down Chips.

    Severity markers ([severity:critical|high|medium|low]) are rendered as glossy colored dots inline next to the finding’s alpha letter. The finding format is enforced by the primer:

    A. [severity:high] Cross-stack auth failures concentrated on Windows.
[→ logserv_cross_stack_auth_failures] 7 of the top-10 failing-stack rows are
Windows; one user account hit 4,732 cumulative attempts — verify-query (-24h)
confirmed 412 of those landed today, ~17/hr, an active rate.

    Per-User Rate Limiting¶

    Free-form prompts are subject to a per-user rolling-1-hour rate limit, configurable in Settings → General (default 30 prompts/hour, 0 = disabled). Canned-prompt dispatches are intentionally NOT rate-limited — they bypass the AI vendor entirely (no token cost) and are bounded by Splunk’s own search-quota controls.

    When a user hits the cap, the next prompt:

    1. Renders the user message in chat as usual (preserves history continuity).
    2. Surfaces a system_notice in chat stating the limit was reached, how many free-form prompts were counted against the hourly threshold, roughly how long until the oldest prompt ages out, and which admin setting (rate_limit_per_hour) raises the cap.
    3. Records a rate_limited_prompt audit event with the user’s identity, the cap value, and the timestamp.
    4. Does NOT invoke the LLM vendor.

    The cap is per-user, not per-session — opening a new browser tab doesn’t reset it. Enforcement is browser-side (localStorage), so it is per-user per browser: a second browser or device gets its own budget, and clearing site data resets the counter. The rate_limited_prompt / daily_spend_cap_hit audit events still fire on every block, so the SOC record survives either way — treat both caps as defense-in-depth, not a hard quota; vendor-side limits and your billing dashboard remain the enforcement of record. Maps to LLM10 — Unbounded Consumption.

    Token-Usage Audit + USD Cost Estimate¶

    Every free-form prompt that completes — whichever tier is active — records one vendor_tier1 audit event, after its last turn, with:

    • Provider (anthropic / openai / azure_openai / bedrock, or mock)
    • Model
    • Input tokens and output tokens, summed over the prompt’s turns (for Anthropic also the cached and cache-written input tokens)
    • USD cost estimate (per-vendor pricing table — see LogServ App and AI Assistant Internals)
    • Outbound bytes and the SHA-256 of the outbound payload
    • Prompt length (chars) and the number of tool definitions sent
    • Number of AI turns the prompt took
    • tier2RedactionsApplied — number of PII redactions applied across the prompt’s tool results (0 at Tier 1)
    • powerMode — whether the forced-RAG Power Mode was on

    The Audit Log tab in Settings lists these events one by one; it has no aggregate views. For totals per user, run the cost search in Audit Log → Querying the Audit Index Directly. The USD cost estimate is a list price (not the customer’s negotiated rate, which the App does not know) and should be treated as an order-of-magnitude indicator.

    Daily Spend Cap¶

    To prevent runaway vendor spend, the orchestrator enforces a per-user (per browser) daily USD spend cap (Daily spend cap (USD) in Settings, default 50.00; 0 turns it off). Each prompt’s estimated cost is added after it completes, and the check runs before the next prompt, so the prompt that crosses the cap still completes. Once the day’s total has reached the cap, the orchestrator:

    1. Refuses the next prompt before any vendor call.
    2. Records a daily_spend_cap_hit audit event.
    3. Surfaces a system_notice stating the cap was reached, how much of the budget is spent, and that the tally resets at local midnight (the browser’s calendar day).

    The cap is cumulative-cost-based, not request-count-based — a single high-token-count free-form turn counts against the budget the same way many cheap turns do. Maps to LLM10 — Unbounded Consumption.

    Streaming + Abort¶

    The vendor response is streamed token-by-token. The chat-side rendering shows partial responses as they arrive, including partial tool_use blocks. The status indicator switches between three states:

    • streaming — AI is generating text or about to emit a tool_use
    • tool_executing — orchestrator is dispatching a tool the AI requested
    • idle — turn complete

    A red Stop button appears in the chat input toolbar during streaming / tool_executing states. Clicking it aborts the in-flight vendor call (closes the SSE stream) and any pending tool dispatches. The conversation history preserves what was emitted up to the abort point so the user can iterate from there.

    Jailbreak Pattern Detection¶

    Every user prompt is run through a jailbreak-pattern analyzer before dispatch. The analyzer is flag-and-proceed: a match fires a user_prompt_jailbreak_flag audit event but does NOT block the prompt. The defense-in-depth chain (type-system enforcement + Tier 2 sanitizer + tool-result sentinel + primer + vendor-side defenses) already covers the threat; the analyzer adds SOC observability for the user-prompt vector. Each flag captures a hash of the prompt (so SOC can correlate without archiving plain text), which patterns matched, and a character-class fingerprint to surface unusual encodings.

    For the analyzer’s pattern groups + audit event schema, see LogServ App and AI Assistant Internals. Maps to LLM01 — Prompt Injection.

    Session Tool-Call Cap¶

    In addition to the per-user rate limit, every chat session has a per-session tool-dispatch cap to prevent infinite tool loops (a misbehaving model emitting tool_use after tool_use without ever producing a final assistant_text). Counter resets on chat clear. When exceeded, dispatch is refused with a synthetic error tool_result and a session_tool_cap_hit audit event records the hit. Maps to LLM06 — Excessive Agency.

    Power Mode¶

    Requires a configured LLM provider credential

    Power Mode governs free-form LLM dispatch, so the ✦ Power toggle appears only where that path is live. The published v0.1.2 App package is the full-LLM build variant, but an admin must first configure an LLM provider credential. The toggle is hidden while Templates-only mode is on (Settings → AI Assistant → General) and in a compile-time templates-only build, since there is then no LLM dispatch to force a saved search before.

    Power Mode is a role-gated ✦ Power toggle in the AI Assistant chat-input toolbar. While it is on, the App adds a rule to the system primer of every free-form prompt: the AI must call splunk_run_saved_search (or splunk_run_query) at least once before it writes any narrative reply (forced-RAG). The rule is an instruction to the model, not a check the App makes: the App does not refuse a reply that comes without a search, so read the tiles to see which searches ran.

    Why Power Mode Exists¶

    The default free-form path lets the AI choose whether to dispatch a tool or reply from prior knowledge. For most questions the AI dispatches appropriately — but for questions that look like the AI knows them already from training data (“What’s a HANA audit log?”), it may answer from prior knowledge and skip the tool call. That’s fine for explanatory questions, but it’s the wrong behavior for investigations: a “what’s the failure rate this week?” question deserves a real Splunk dispatch, not a probability-weighted guess.

    Power Mode addresses this by adding a forced-RAG rule to the system primer: for every user message, the AI must call splunk_run_saved_search at least once (or splunk_run_query if no saved search fits) before generating any narrative answer.

    This is forced-RAG over chosen-RAG: same tools, same MCP path, same privacy tier. Power Mode asks the model for the saved-search-first step; the App does not enforce it. For the primer-augmentation mechanism, see LogServ App and AI Assistant Internals.

    Role-Gated Visibility¶

    Power Mode is opt-in per organization and per-role. The toggle is hidden from users entirely unless their Splunk role is in the configured allow-list. Default: empty list — Power Mode hidden from every user.

    Configuration path (admin-only):

    1. Open Settings → AI Assistant → General.
    2. Find the Power Users section and its Power Mode roles field. The list is populated from Splunk’s services/authorization/roles REST endpoint.
    3. Pick the roles that should see the Power toggle (typical: admin, power, sc_admin; add your stack’s delegated-admin role, for example sc_subadmin, if your admins use one).
    4. Click Save Defaults.
    5. Affected users see the ✦ Power button in their chat input toolbar on next page load.

    Per-user gating would require a custom directory and doesn’t compose with Splunk’s standard RBAC. Role gating reuses the same primitive admins already manage for everything else (search permissions, app permissions, etc.).

    Toggle UX¶

    The ✦ Power button is a small pill in the chat input toolbar between Send and the keyboard-shortcut hint. State is persisted per-tab in sessionStorage under logserv.aiAssistant.powerMode — opening a new browser tab resets to OFF.

    Visual states:

    State Button text Border Tooltip
    OFF (default) ✦ Power panel-border-weak “Power Mode OFF — click to enable forced saved-search-first behavior.”
    ON ✦ Power ON cyan-accent fill “Power Mode ON — every prompt forces a saved-search dispatch before AI synthesis. Click to turn off.”

    A11y: aria-pressed="true" when on, aria-pressed="false" when off.

    What Power Mode Does NOT Change¶

    • Privacy tier behavior is unchanged. Tier 1 still gives the AI count + timing only; Tier 2 still gives aggregated metadata only. Power Mode just enforces saved-search-first; tier still controls what AI sees about each search result.
    • Tool dispatch is unchanged. Same MCP path, same tool definitions (splunk_run_saved_search, splunk_run_query), same SPL static-analysis guard, same session tool-call cap.
    • Audit categories are unchanged. A Power Mode prompt records the same vendor_tier1 audit event as any free-form prompt (one per prompt, whatever the tier); its powerMode field records whether the toggle was on, for SOC pivot analysis.
    • Per-user rate limit, daily spend cap, jailbreak detection. All unchanged.

    When to Use Power Mode¶

    Use case Power Mode?
    Investigations that should be data-grounded (“what’s failing right now?”) ON
    Cross-cutting top-N questions (“find the top 10 issues to attend to”) ON — Power Mode + the TIME-WINDOW REASONING rules together produce verify-confirmed severity claims
    Compliance reports that the auditor will cross-check against the rendered tiles ON (so every claim has a citation)
    Conceptual questions (“what’s a HANA audit log?”, “explain risk_level”) OFF (the AI’s training knowledge is fine)
    One-shot follow-ups in an existing conversation where prior tool results already cover the answer OFF (forces an unnecessary dispatch)
    Streaming-only chat-only mode (MCP Required off) No effect — the toggle still appears for power-user roles, but with no tool path the App does not add the Power Mode rule to the primer

    Audit Trail¶

    Every free-form prompt that completes records one vendor_tier1 audit event, after its last turn, with a powerMode flag that captures whether the toggle was on for that prompt. Use cases for the audit field:

    • SOC pivot: filter audit events to powerMode=true to see only the strict-data-grounded turns.
    • Compliance review: confirm that audit-period investigations were run with Power Mode on (so every cited finding has a tool dispatch behind it).
    • Cost analysis: prompts with Power Mode on tend to run more searches, and so cost more per prompt. The audit lets finance attribute spend to the gating choice.

    Power Mode does NOT generate a separate audit category — it’s a flag on the existing vendor_tier1 event. See Audit Log.

    Time-Window Reasoning¶

    Applies once an LLM provider credential is configured

    The rules on this page shape what an LLM writes, so they apply only where free-form dispatch is live. The published v0.1.2 App package is the full-LLM build variant, but no LLM writes a narrative until an admin configures an LLM provider credential — and none does where Templates-only mode is on or a compile-time templates-only build is installed (Restricting the LLM Path). Predefined prompts are unaffected either way: they run over the window picked in the prompt browser’s Time range list, and their guidance cards are static.

    Time-window reasoning is a set of primer rules baked into the AI Assistant’s system primer (present in both the Tier 1 and Tier 2 primer variants, in tier-appropriate forms — see below) that teach the LLM to identify the dispatch window, normalize cumulative count to per-hour or per-day rate, and run a verify-query before declaring high-severity findings. The rules ship as a dedicated === TIME-WINDOW REASONING — APPLY BEFORE EVERY SEVERITY CLAIM === block in the primer, inserted right after the data-boundary block and before the saved-search catalog.

    This page exists primarily for SOC analysts who use the AI Assistant for top-N investigations: knowing how the AI reasons about windows + rates + verification helps you read its replies critically, validate its severity claims, and recognize its self-correction behavior.

    Why the Rules Exist¶

    Without these rules, an AI can cite a cumulative count as if it were an active rate. In testing, the prompt “find the top 10 issues I need to attend to in priority / severity” produced a high-severity brute-force finding from 4,799 failed authentications for one user/stack pair, with advice to lock and rotate the accounts that day. The 4,799 was a count over the saved search’s roughly 30-day window; the same data over the last 24 hours held 18 events on one host, which is baseline noise. A count alone cannot tell a 30-day baseline (about 160 a day) from a 24-hour burst, so the four rules below make the AI establish the window before it rates severity.

    The Four Rules¶

    The primer block teaches the AI to apply these rules before declaring a finding’s severity. The Tier 2 primer carries all four; the Tier 1 primer carries three (hedge the window / verify / state the window) — Rule 2’s rate normalization needs aggregate numbers a Tier 1 summary never contains:

    Rule 1 — Identify the Window¶

    Saved-search counts are CUMULATIVE over the window the search ran with: the earliest_time / latest_time the AI passed with the call (the primer tells it to pass one), or, when it passed none, the saved search’s own configured time range. The global time-range picker in the header does not set that window, so it does NOT necessarily match it.

    Tier 1: the summary the AI receives is Returned N rows in Mms. (inside the <TOOL_RESULT_DATA> wrapper) — no window data at all. The AI must hedge: “X rows over the search’s rolling window, exact span unknown” OR infer from the saved-search NAME (e.g., *_24h, *_after_hours) when the name carries a window hint.

    Tier 2: the summary includes a Time range: line ONLY when the result has a _time column (timecharts, time-series). When every _time value is a timestamp, both ends are ISO-8601 UTC timestamps the App writes and the line ends (UTC).; otherwise it reads Time range: not shown (the _time values are not all timestamps).. For aggregate searches like stats by user, no _time column → no time-range line → AI must hedge as in Tier 1.

    Rule 2 — Normalize Count → Rate¶

    Convert sum / max from the aggregates to events/hour or events/day before assigning severity (Tier 2 primer only — the Tier 1 primer has no normalization rule and no threshold table, since the AI never receives the numbers to normalize). Rough thresholds documented in the Tier 2 primer:

    Signal High threshold
    Auth failures >10/hour
    Warn-level errors >100/hour
    Ingest volume >1000/hour

    A 4,799 cumulative count over 30 days = ~160/day = ~6.6/hour. For auth failures, that’s below the >10/hour high threshold → severity should be medium or low, not high.

    Rule 3 — Verify Before Recommending Action¶

    For any finding ranked [severity:high] or [severity:critical], the AI MUST dispatch ONE additional splunk_run_query call with earliest=-24h latest=now BEFORE writing the narrative response. The verify either confirms the cumulative total is also a current rate, or reveals it’s baseline noise.

    If the verify returns dramatically smaller numbers than the cumulative headline, the AI must re-rank the finding to medium or low and SAY SO in the body. Active-tense claims (“Lock/rotate accounts today”, “active brute-force”, “data exfiltration in progress”) MUST be backed by a verify query, never by a cumulative count alone.

    Rule 4 — State the Window in Narrative¶

    Precise phrases: - “X events in the last 24 hours” — for verify-confirmed claims - “X cumulative over the search’s rolling window” — for un-verified cumulative aggregates - “~Y/hour active rate, verify-confirmed” — for normalized-to-rate severity claims

    Active-tense phrases (“active brute-force”, “happening today”, “current attack”) MUST be backed by a narrow-window verify query — not by cumulative counts or top-N aggregates alone.

    What “Verify-Confirmed Severity” Looks Like in Replies¶

    After the rules shipped, the same prompt (re-run on the same data) produced a self-corrected response that explicitly downgrades the finding:

    G. [severity:medium] Cross-stack auth failures show high cumulative count but no current activity. [→ logserv_cross_stack_auth_failures] ↗ Cross-Stack Authentication ↗ Run SPL Top row showed 4,799 attempts but my -24h verify returned only 19 auth failures across all stacks combined — this is a stale long-window aggregate, not an active brute-force. No immediate action needed; review baselines.

    The AI:

    1. Cited the cumulative number (4,799) — appropriate context.
    2. Ran the verify query (-24h) — required by Rule 3.
    3. Reported the verify result (only 19) — required by Rule 4.
    4. Re-ranked to medium — required by Rule 3.
    5. Used precise window-aware language (“stale long-window aggregate, not an active brute-force”) — required by Rule 4.
    6. Recommended a non-urgent next step (“review baselines”) instead of “Lock/rotate today”.

    This is the correct shape. When you read a top-N response, look for these markers:

    • ✓ Findings ranked high or critical reference both a cumulative number AND a verify-query result
    • ✓ Active-tense recommendations come ONLY from verified high-rate findings
    • ✓ Findings that were going to be high but verified down to noise are explicitly downgraded with framing like “stale aggregate, not active”

    Edge Cases¶

    When the verify query also returns high counts¶

    If a finding cites 4,799 cumulative AND the verify query returns 412 in the last 24h (~17/hour, above the >10/hour threshold), the AI keeps the finding at high severity and says: “412 of those 4,799 landed today, ~17/hr — an active rate.” Now the active-tense “Lock/rotate today” recommendation is justified.

    When the saved-search name implies the window¶

    Some prompts have window hints in their names: logserv_dns_beaconing_24h, logserv_hana_after_hours_admin. For these, the AI uses the name-implied window for Rule 1 and skips Rule 3’s verify step (the saved search itself IS the narrow-window query).

    When no splunk_run_query is available (Templates-only)¶

    With Templates-only mode on, or in a templates-only build (Restricting the LLM Path), free-form prompts are disabled — there’s no LLM-driven verify path. The time-window rules don’t apply because the AI doesn’t run. Predefined prompts run over the window picked in the prompt browser and produce static interpretation cards (no AI synthesis), so no rate-reasoning step is needed.

    When Tier 1 is active¶

    Tier 1 gives the AI count + timing only — it cannot see the actual values, so it cannot do Rule 2’s normalization. The AI hedges harder: “the search returned N rows for the rolling window, suggesting non-trivial activity” without making rate claims. Tier 1 narrative is intentionally less concrete; users read the rendered tile for the actual numbers.

    Power Mode Compounds With Time-Window Reasoning¶

    When Power Mode is on AND a free-form prompt asks for top-N issues:

    1. Power Mode forces a saved-search dispatch (Rule out: AI never replies from prior knowledge).
    2. Each high/critical finding in the AI’s reply forces an additional verify query (per Rule 3).
    3. Result: a 5-finding top-N response can dispatch 5 saved searches + up to 5 verify queries = 10 total Splunk dispatches.

    This is the correct behavior for compliance investigations and high-stakes triage — every claim is data-grounded AND verify-confirmed. The cost is higher per-turn latency + tool budget, but for the customer’s most important investigations, the cost is the right trade.

    Security & Compliance

    Privacy Tiers¶

    Applies once an LLM provider credential is configured

    The privacy tier governs what a vendor dispatch may carry, so it has something to govern only where that path is live. The released v0.1.2 App package is the full-LLM build, but it makes no vendor calls until an admin configures an LLM provider credential, and no vendor dispatch where Templates-only mode is on or a compile-time templates-only build is installed (Restricting the LLM Path; in Templates-only mode, Model discovery can still make metadata-only model-listing calls). Once a credential exists, the tier selected in Settings → AI Assistant → General governs every vendor dispatch. The Hidden<T> / Visible<T> type-system enforcement is compile-time in every build: a tool result reaches an outbound vendor payload only through the active tier’s summary, so no raw row and no unsummarized result is sent in any tier. What that summary may carry depends on the tier, as described below — in Tier 2 it includes aggregated values taken from the events.

    The privacy tier controls what an external LLM vendor sees about your Splunk data. Two tiers work in this release, Tier 1 (the default) and Tier 2; Tier 0 is listed in the Settings page but does not work yet. An admin selects the tier in Settings → AI Assistant → General. The active tier is enforced by the TypeScript type system at build time, not by runtime policy: every outbound vendor payload must pass through a single sanitize chokepoint, and the chokepoint’s summarizer is what the tier setting controls. For the type-system mechanism, see LogServ App and AI Assistant Internals.

    This page starts with the choice (the tiers, the decision matrix, and how to switch), then describes exactly what each tier sends.

    The Three Tiers at a Glance¶

    Tier Vendor traffic? What the AI sees about each tool result Use case
    Tier 0 (not available in this release) Planned: none, a local Ollama server. Today: whatever provider is selected Same as Tier 1 (count + timing only) Do not select it; see Tier 0 and the Ollama Provider
    Tier 1 (default) Cloud LLM (Anthropic / OpenAI / Azure / Bedrock) Returned N rows in M ms. — two numbers, a count and a timing. Nothing else. Most customers — strongest cloud-LLM privacy posture
    Tier 2 (admin opt-in) Same cloud LLM The Returned N rows in M ms. line (N is the number of result rows, 0 for an empty result) + per-column cardinality + top-N values + counts (categorical; filtered, 40 characters each; with PII redaction on, sent in clear only when the App can trace the column to a field that marks no identifier, otherwise as <redacted-…> tags) + min/max/avg/sum (numeric) + the time range as UTC timestamps the App formats. A column name is sent only when Splunk generates it, or when every word in it was written by the model in its own query or by the App’s catalog search that ran; any other name appears as col_N. No raw rows. Customers who want data-grounded narrative replies and have legal authority to expose aggregate metadata to the vendor

    The table describes successful calls. In every tier, a failed call reaches the vendor only as its HTTP status and a fixed error class, never as Splunk’s error text. See Failed Tool Calls.

    Decision Matrix¶

    Question Answer Recommended tier
    “Is the AI vendor a third-party data processor?” Yes; consult your DPA. Anthropic / OpenAI / Azure / Bedrock all publish their own privacy commitments, but they ARE data processors. Tier 1 if the vendor is approved as a processor; if not, configure no provider, or turn on Templates-only mode (Restricting the LLM Path)
    “Can the customer’s compliance team approve aggregate metadata exposure?” Yes Tier 2
    No Tier 1
    “Does the customer have outbound internet to the LLM vendor’s API?” Yes Tier 1 or Tier 2
    No (air-gapped) No tier: predefined prompts only, with Templates-only mode or a templates-only build (Restricting the LLM Path); Tier 0 is not available in this release
    “Does the customer want narrative replies with concrete values, or shape-only?” Concrete Tier 2 (with PII redaction on)
    Shape-only Tier 1
    “Does the customer want zero LLM dispatch (partner test, demo)?” Zero Templates-only mode, or a templates-only build where it must not be reversible (Restricting the LLM Path)

    Switching Tiers¶

    The tier is the Privacy Tier setting on Settings → AI Assistant → General. Switching tiers takes effect on the next vendor call — in-flight calls complete with the previously active tier. Note the emitted vendor_tier1 event does not carry the active tier: the tier in force at a given time is derivable only from the Settings history (vendor_tier2_elevation events) plus a non-zero tier2RedactionsApplied.

    Elevating from Tier 1 → Tier 2:

    1. Open Settings → AI Assistant → General.
    2. Under Privacy Tier, select Tier 2.
    3. Click Save Defaults. The save records a vendor_tier2_elevation audit event with the admin’s identity and the time.
    4. Optionally turn Tier 2 PII column redaction off (default: on) or Tier 2 hostname redaction on (default: off, since host names are often not sensitive in SAP environments).

    Lowering from Tier 2 → Tier 1:

    1. Same path. A downgrade produces no audit event and no conf-change record — settings persist to the logserv_ai_assistant_settings KV Store collection, so only elevation to Tier 2 is audited (vendor_tier2_elevation).
    2. The next vendor call uses the lower tier.

    No tier: to switch the LLM-driven path off entirely (predefined prompts only), turn on Templates-only mode, or install a templates-only build where that must not be reversible (Restricting the LLM Path). The tier setting is then moot, since no question reaches a vendor.

    Tier 0 and the Ollama Provider: Do Not Select¶

    Tier 0 and the Ollama (Tier 0 — local) provider are listed on the Settings page but are not implemented in this release. Selecting them does not keep data on the search head:

    • Privacy Tier = Tier 0 summarizes exactly like Tier 1 (the Tier 1 primer, count and timing) and sends the call to whatever Active Provider is selected, a cloud vendor included.
    • Active Provider = Ollama runs the Mock provider: a typed question gets a canned reply, and no Ollama server is contacted. The Base URL on the Provider Credentials sub-tab is not used.

    The plan for Tier 0 is to route the LLM call to a locally hosted Ollama server instead of a cloud vendor, with the same count-and-timing summary as Tier 1 and an unchanged MCP search path. Until it ships, a deployment that must not send anything to an outside vendor uses Templates-only mode or a templates-only build (Restricting the LLM Path), or configures no provider.

    Tier 1 — Cloud LLM, Count + Timing Only (default)¶

    What the LLM sees per tool result:

    <TOOL_RESULT_DATA>
Returned 47 rows in 320ms.
</TOOL_RESULT_DATA>

    That’s the entire summary: two numbers. Nothing about the column names, the row contents, the time range, the distinct counts, or the actual values. The <TOOL_RESULT_DATA>...</TOOL_RESULT_DATA> sentinel block is wrapped around every tool-result summary so the AI’s primer can teach it that anything inside is data from the customer’s environment, never instructions.

    • The count is the number of result rows whenever the App recognises rows in the MCP reply — the same rows Tier 2 counts, so a search that matched nothing reads Returned 0 rows. With the Splunk MCP Server that is the length of the result list in its reply. Only a reply in which the App finds no rows — plain text, for example — is counted another way: the number of items in its content list, or the total row count a server reports (totalRowCount).
    • The timing is the server’s execution time when the reply carries one, otherwise the time the browser measured for the call.

    What the AI does with this: the AI knows that the search ran, how many rows it returned and how long it took, but not what the rows hold. It writes structurally-aware narrative replies — “the failed-auth saved search completed in 320 ms; its results are in the tile on the right” — without making claims about specific users, IPs, or hosts.

    Decision rule for picking Tier 1:

    • The customer’s legal/security team is comfortable with the AI vendor seeing the natural-language question + tool definitions + summaries.
    • The customer is not comfortable exposing aggregate column metadata (cardinality, top-N values, min/max) to the vendor.
    • The customer values determinism: a Tier 1 reply mentions zero specific values, so audit reviewers can sanity-check the narrative against the rendered tile without needing to verify what the AI was told.

    Limitations: the AI can’t write “the top failing user was xcjadm with 42 attempts” — it doesn’t have that data. The narrative is correspondingly less concrete; the user is expected to read the tile in the right pane for the actual values.

    Tier 1 limits how much the vendor can learn; it does not make that zero. For each call the vendor gets two numbers, a count and a timing, and for a failed call a fixed error class and the HTTP status (see Failed Tool Calls). A model that writes its own queries can make these depend on event data — the timing, whether a search fails and which class its error gets, and the row count — so a few bits per call can leak: up to about log2 of the largest row count the server returns through the count. The session tool-call cap (tool_calls_per_session_cap, default 100) limits the calls per chat session; clearing the chat (Clear All in the results pane) starts a new session and resets the count, and 0 turns the cap off. No error text is sent in any tier.

    Failed Tool Calls — Every Tier¶

    When a tool call fails, the AI vendor is told only that it failed, with the HTTP status and a fixed error class. It never gets Splunk’s or the MCP server’s error text. This is the same in Tier 0, 1 and 2:

    <TOOL_RESULT_DATA>
Tool error (HTTP 400, class=missing_lookup): the query names a lookup that does not exist here. The error text is shown to the user only.
</TOOL_RESULT_DATA>
    • The status is included only when it is a whole number from 100 to 599. Otherwise the line reads Tool error (class=…).
    • The class is one of parse_error, unknown_command, missing_lookup, missing_saved_search, permission, timeout, rate_limited, not_found, server_error or other. The browser picks it with fixed rules over the error message, or from the status when no rule matches. Each class has its own fixed hint, written by the App.
    • The error text itself is shown only in the result panel on the user’s screen. It is not sent to the vendor, and it is not written to the audit index.

    The text is withheld because a Splunk error message repeats the search that failed, and a subsearch can put event data into that search. For example, | inputlookup [search … | eval v=substr(_raw,1,80) | return $v] can fail with an error that names the first 80 characters of an event as the missing lookup table.

    Refusals the App makes itself are different, because their text is the App’s own. These are calls the App stops before anything is sent: the SPL guard, the saved-search catalog check, the undeclared-tool check and the session tool-call cap. The vendor gets Tool call refused by the App before it ran: <reason>, so the model can rephrase:

    • The reason is written by the App. It may quote the tool name or saved-search name the model itself sent, or the command, lookup or macro name of the model’s query that the SPL guard refused.
    • It is capped at 1,000 characters. Control characters other than tab and line breaks become spaces, and <TOOL_RESULT_DATA> tags are replaced with <filtered>.
    • The App builds this text where it makes the refusal, never from a tool result. A server error that merely looks like a refusal is reduced to a class like any other error.

    Tier 2 — Cloud LLM + Aggregated Metadata (admin opt-in)¶

    What the LLM sees per tool result:

    For a stats count by user, stack result of 47 rows:

    <TOOL_RESULT_DATA>
Returned 47 rows in 320ms.
Column "user" (distinct=8): <redacted-f86a9fe>=6, <redacted-0e3cb9c>=6, <redacted-e849a33>=6, <redacted-ac446fb>=6 (+4 more).
Column "stack" (distinct=3): Windows=16, HANA=16, SAP=15.
Column "count" (numeric, distinct=47): min=1 max=95 avg=47.11 sum=2,214.
</TOOL_RESULT_DATA>

    The user column above shows the shipped default (tier2_pii_redaction = true): a column whose values come from an identifier field arrives as <redacted-…> tags, stable within the chat session. stack keeps its values because the query takes it from the events by its own name; had the query computed it with an eval — as the App’s own cross-stack catalog search does — its values would arrive as tags too (see Which values are sent below). With tier2_pii_redaction = false the same line carries the raw values (xcjadm=6, BKPADMIN=6, …). The column names user and stack are sent because the query that produced the result wrote them (for a saved search, the App’s catalog search does), and count because Splunk generates it. In Tier 2 the Returned N rows line counts the result rows the App finds in the reply; a search that matched nothing reads Returned 0 rows in 210ms (no events matched the query in the selected time range). and sends nothing else. A reply in which the App finds no rows at all — plain text, for example — is sent only as Returned a result that is not in row form, in 210ms.: no count, no column name and no value.

    For a timechart span=1h count by host result:

    <TOOL_RESULT_DATA>
Returned 3 rows in 210ms.
Time range: 2026-10-01T00:00:00.000Z → 2026-10-01T02:00:00.000Z (UTC).
Column names withheld: 2. Each such column is shown as col_N, N being its position among the result's columns that do not start with an underscore.
Column col_1 (numeric, distinct=3): min=0 max=2 avg=1 sum=3.
Column col_2 (numeric, distinct=3): min=0 max=4 avg=2 sum=6.
</TOOL_RESULT_DATA>

    The column names of a timechart split by host are host names — values from the events that the query did not write — so they are shown as col_N, with PII redaction on or off and whatever the hostname setting. Had the query named the hosts itself (host=sapdb01 OR host=sapapp01 | timechart span=1h count by host), the names would be the model’s own text and would be sent. The same holds when the cells hold text: for timechart latest(action) by user the user names are shown as col_N unless the query wrote them, and while redaction is on every value of a column shown as col_N arrives as a <redacted-…> tag, since nothing tells the AI what the column holds — and the text cells of a split-by column are redacted in any case (see Which values are sent below).

    What a Tier 2 summary contains, and what it leaves out:

    • No raw rows. The AI never gets a row: it cannot tell which user had how many failures on which stack, only the per-column distributions.
    • Values. Each categorical column sends its top-N values with their counts (top 10 by default; the AI’s top_n tool argument can ask for up to 50). Each value passes the value filter — a value that starts with a role marker (system:, assistant:, …), contains a known prompt-injection phrase or contains a <TOOL_RESULT_DATA> tag becomes <filtered>, and control characters become spaces — then PII redaction (below), then a 40-character cap, within a 160-character line. Each numeric column sends min / max / avg / sum. Columns whose name starts with _, all-empty columns and single-valued categorical columns are left out.

    • Column names. A name is sent only when one of these holds, and it passes the value filter unchanged:

      • it is a name Splunk itself generates: count, percent, total, Total, NULL, OTHER, column, a bare statistics-function name (sum, avg, mean, min, max, dc, distinct_count, values, earliest, latest, first, last, median, mode, stdev, range, rate), or fieldsummary’s field, is_exact and numeric_count; or
      • every word in it was written by the model or the App. Each run of letters, digits and _ in the name (values(user) is values and user; ip-10-1-2-3 is ip, 10, 1, 2 and 3) must appear as a whole word, in the same letter case, in the call’s author text: the query the model wrote itself for splunk_run_query, or the SPL of the App’s catalog search that produced the result for splunk_run_saved_search. Any word of that text counts, wherever it stands — a field name, an alias, a search term, a compared value, quoted text — because text the model or the App wrote tells the vendor nothing it does not already have. The name must also be at most 40 characters and have the shape of a field name (a letter or _, then letters, digits and _ . : -) or of one function call over one, * or nothing (avg(duration), sum(*)) — or it must be a display alias that the author text writes in quotes right after AS (rename sourcetype AS "Source Type", count AS "Event Count"): it starts with a letter or _ and is made of letters, digits and _ . : -, in words separated by single spaces.

      Any other name is shown as col_N — N is the column’s position among the result’s columns that do not start with _ — and is never sent, in full or in part; the summary says how many names were withheld. The rule is the same with PII redaction on or off. So stats count as failures by host keeps failures and host, table _time host process message keeps host, process and message, and a split-by value the query typed (user=jsmith | timechart count by user) keeps its name. sum(jsmith), from timechart count by user | stats sum(*), is shown as col_N — even when it is the only column — because the query wrote sum but not jsmith; it would be sent only if the query itself contained the word jsmith. A name is not sent because the query contains part of it: username is withheld when the query writes only user. A quoted alias is held to the same 40 characters and to the single-space shape: "Source Type" (two spaces) or "Events (%)" is shown as col_N.

    • Which values are sent — fail closed. With PII redaction on, a text column’s values are sent in clear only when the App can trace the column — when the author text defines it entirely through constructs the App reads in full — to fields that mark no identifier. The App reads each author text as Splunk runs it, command by command, and a column is traced through:

      • the field itself, by its own name: a field of the events or of a lookup, a by or over field, a field of top, rare (with or without a positional limit, top 10 uri), table or fields;
      • a statistics function over one field, nested or not, with or without AS (latest(user) → user, values(src_ip) AS ips → src_ip, latest(values(user)) → user);
      • <field> AS <alias>, a rename without wildcards (rename user AS u, rename sourcetype AS "Source Type"), and lookup … OUTPUT <field> [AS <alias>]. A lookup output that echoes the field the lookup matched on is that event field (lookup t w AS user OUTPUT w is user); any other output also reads the event fields the lookup matched on, so a lookup keyed on an identifier is treated like that identifier (lookup … ip AS src_ip OUTPUT hostname is redacted). The curated metadata of the App’s own threat-intel lookups — their category, source and date added — keeps its own trace; their free-text notes inherit the match like any other output;
      • eval <name>=<field>, when the expression is one bare field name or one field reference in single quotes (eval w=user, eval w='Authentication.user'). A single-quoted token is only ever a field reference: it cannot hold a |, a bracket, a double quote or a line break, so a stray apostrophe can no longer hide the commands after it (and the allow-list refuses such a query outright);
      • a count: count or c, bare or as a call (count(eval(action="failure"))), the count and percent of top and rare, and dc, distinct_count, estdc or estdc_error over one field the App traces (dc(user)). Its values are counts, not identifiers. A distinct count of a field the query computes (eval r=mvrange(0,len(user)) | stats dc(r)) is not a count: it reads what that field reads.

      These steps chain as far as the query takes them, in the order Splunk runs them: eval a=user | eval b=a | rename b AS c leads c back to user. Every other construct leaves the column untraced, and with redaction on every value of an untraced text column arrives as a <redacted-…> tag, whatever it holds:

      • any other eval expression — string concatenation with . (eval w=user."@".domain), any function (lower(action), case(…), coalesce(…), substr(_raw,1,200)), even a literal (eval x="a");
      • fieldformat, which only changes how a value is displayed: the column stays untraced and reads both its earlier definition and the format expression;
      • the outputs of rex (named groups written (?<name>…), (?P<name>…) or (?'name'…)), spath, strcat, bin, convert and iplocation, transaction’s duration and the totals of addtotals; and a field makemv cuts into pieces — by a delimiter or a tokenizer pattern, which extracts like rex — reading the field and the words of the delimiter or the pattern;
      • a wildcard rename or AS (rename user* AS w*, stats values(*) AS *_x) and a dynamic eval target (eval {action}=…);
      • the cells of a chart, timechart or xyseries split-by column, and every column of transpose, untable and fieldsummary, which mix the values of many fields;
      • a name defined in two different ways (for example once in the main search and once in a subsearch); a column that an append, appendcols, join, union, multisearch, set or appendpipe subsearch defines — a field it only passes through by its own name stays traced, and a subsearch that only filters (index=x [search … | fields host]) changes nothing; and a column the author text does not output;
      • every column after a command the App does not read in full: lookup without OUTPUT, inputlookup after the first command, a macro used as a command (a macro at the start of the query is read as the search), an eval or rename it cannot split, or — in the App’s own catalog SPL — any command it does not know. The first command inside appendpipe […] is always read as a command, never as a search, so an unknown one there makes the columns untraced too. A free-form query cannot use a command the App does not read: every command on the allow-list (see the Security Architecture) is one the App reads in full.

      The limits on reading fail closed too: a text longer than 20,000 characters, more than 256 commands, subsearches nested more than 8 deep, or more than 12 wildcard definitions (wildcard renames and AS, dynamic eval targets — each one resolves through the ones before it) leave every column untraced. Stacked appendpipe groups are read in time proportional to their number, so they cannot freeze the browser tab either. A column traced to a count that holds text is redacted as well. So stats count by action sends the actions; stats values(target_user) AS new_users and rename user AS u are redacted as user names; and eval stack=case(…), rex "peer=(?<peer>\S+)" and eval w=action."-".status are redacted although they hold no identifier. To keep values readable, aggregate the field by its own name. With PII redaction off, every column’s values are sent, filtered and capped, traced or not.

    • Values of a column shown as col_N. While PII redaction is on, every value of a categorical (text) column whose name is shown as col_N is redacted as an identifier and sent as a <redacted-…> tag, whatever the column holds; the App cannot tell from a placeholder whether its values are user names. A column whose name is sent is redacted unless it is traced to fields that mark no identifier, as above.

    • At most 30 columns are summarized; the rest are reported as R more columns not summarized..
    • Numeric values withheld. With PII redaction on, a numeric column sends values withheld instead of its statistics, at any cardinality, when it is not a count and either its own name or a field its definition may read marks an identifier, or its values mix many fields (transpose, untable, fieldsummary). For a traced column those fields are its source fields; for an untraced one, every field its expression reads (eval n=len(user) | stats avg(n) AS a is withheld) — and after a command the App does not read in full, every word of the author text. A definition that reads more than 64 fields is taken to read every word of the author text, so that limit fails closed as well. The words of a rex pattern, of an spath path and of the quoted strings in an eval count as fields the column reads, so rex "ssn=(?<n>\d{9})" | stats max(n) AS n and spath output=n path=user.id are withheld; and a field set by rex or spath keeps its earlier value on the events where the pattern or the path does not match, so it reads both definitions. Every other numeric column keeps its statistics, untraced ones included (rex "took (?<ms>\d+)" | stats avg(ms) AS a), and so does a count (dc(user) AS users). A field marks an identifier when it matches a PII redaction pattern (below) or names an id: id, uid, gid, guid, uuid, pid, ssn, iban, phone, msisdn, imsi, imei, acct and account / card / employee / personnel numbers — as the whole name or its last part after _, ., : or - (user_id, card_no) — and camelCase names ending in Id, ID, Sid, SID, Guid or GUID (Windows TargetUserSid, LogonGuid). A column with a single distinct value also sends values withheld, whatever the redaction setting, when its name is withheld, or when it is not a count and marks an identifier or mixes many fields. A named single-value column such as total_events — usually the KPI the query asked for — still sends its value.
    • The time range. The Time range: line is sent only when every _time value is a timestamp: an epoch in seconds (a number or a string of digits, from 1970 up to 2100-01-01) or a strict ISO-8601 timestamp with a zone (Z, +hh:mm or +hhmm) on a real calendar date. The App then writes both ends itself, as ISO-8601 UTC timestamps, and the line says so: Time range: 2026-10-01T00:00:00.000Z → 2026-10-01T02:00:00.000Z (UTC). No time zone from the data is sent. If any value is not a timestamp, the line reads Time range: not shown (the _time values are not all timestamps). and no _time text is sent. The range is also sent only when the author text traces _time — every definition of it — to a time source field: _time itself, or the epochs bucket_ts and day_ts of the App’s rollups (timechart, bin _time, tstats … by _time, stats latest(_time) AS _time, eval _time=bucket_ts, rename bucket_ts AS _time, bin bucket_ts span=1d AS _time). A _time the query computes from other fields (eval _time=len(src_ip)*100000000, eval _time=strptime(…), or a bin / bucket of another field into _time: bin n span=1 AS _time) reads Time range: not shown (the query computes _time from other fields). A result without a _time column, such as a stats by … aggregate, has no time-range line.
    • What the AI is told about these shapes. The Tier 2 primer explains col_N and the withheld-names line, <redacted-…> tags, values withheld, Returned a result that is not in row form and Time range: not shown. It says that a tag is stable within the chat session only, and tells the model never to guess, recover or attribute what a placeholder or a tag stands for, to name a user, host, IP address or account only when that exact value appears in clear, and how to get readable values: re-query with stats … by <field>, aggregate a field by its own name rather than computing a new one, or write the values into its own query.

    What the naming rule withholds: any name that neither Splunk, the model’s query nor the App’s catalog search wrote, and any name that does not have the shape — a name with spaces that the query does not quote right after AS (eval "Source Type"=…), an unaliased count(eval(…)), a nested call such as upper95(prediction(count)), a name over 40 characters. Besides split-by values, that includes fields a search returns without its text naming them — fields of raw events (host, sourcetype and the like, when the query does not write them), automatically extracted or spath fields, and the columns of an inputlookup that the search does not list. The AI can relate a placeholder to its own query’s columns by position, but the primer tells it never to guess which value — which host, user or series — a col_N column stands for. A catalog trend split by a value is named only where its catalog search writes the value itself: the stacks of the cross-stack authentication-failure trend (HANA, Windows) are named, the host names of the noisy-hosts trend are not. The tiles in the results pane are not affected.

    What Tier 2 still sends from the events. Tier 2 sends aggregated event values by design: the top-N values of every text column (with redaction on, of every traced column whose name is sent and whose fields mark no identifier), and the statistics of every numeric column that is not withheld — a column shown as col_N or untraced included. Redaction is decided by field names, so a value is sent as it is when its column is traced to a field named nothing like an identifier: an event field such as message, a lookup column that is not keyed on an identifier — or _raw itself, so a model can write eval m=_raw and receive up to 40 characters of an event. A number computed from event text is sent unless a field it reads marks an identifier. A name made only of words the model wrote is sent even if the model copied into its query a value it had seen; that text is the model’s own. PII redaction is name-based hygiene for ordinary queries, not a content filter; where no event value may be sent, use Tier 1.

    PII redaction (Tier 2 only, on by default): a field name marks an identifier in two ways.

    • The App’s own fields, one by one. Every field name the App defines — its extractions, aliases and calculated fields, its rollup columns and the columns of its lookups, about 440 names — has a class in a table the build checks: an identifier (user names, statements that name users such as sql_statement and command, the HANA audit target object, identity, info_sid, supplied_by, fetched_by, the topology canonical_value and label, the compliance rollup’s operator and the topology rollup’s error_detail), an address (src, dest, local_ip, peer_ip, icm_peer_ip, ssl_peer_ip, remote_address, the lastlog FROM, fw_dst, the topology rollups’ scope and spl_filter_clauses, the HANA audit client host src_host and its extraction audit_hostname, the SAP Router target saprouter_target_ip, the gateway’s gw_remgw_target and gw_client_ip, the RFC client’s gw_client_hostname, …), a host name (host, Computer, db_hostname, hana_host, … — redacted only with the hostname opt-in), free text, or safe. The client host names audit_hostname and gw_client_hostname are classed as addresses, because a workstation’s name can identify the person who uses it, so they are redacted by default, while a server’s host name such as db_hostname is redacted only with the hostname opt-in. The hostnames column of the topology IP-enrichment lookup, which also holds client workstation names, stays a host name (see Known Limits of Tier 2 below). The build fails if a new App field has no class, so no extraction ships unclassified, and it fails if a rollup column that a free-form query can read with inputlookup is classified weaker than the fields its rollup search writes into it directly; the check looks one step back, so a column filled through an intermediate field, such as hostnames, is not covered. The fields Splunk’s automatic key-value extraction finds in the LogServ Linux events are classified too: pam’s rhost (an address), ruser, logname and euid, and sudo’s PWD and COMMAND.
    • Name patterns, for every name (the App’s and any other) — ignoring letter case, as the whole name or after _, ., :, - or a space: email or emails; user, username, user_name, users or usernames (and "User Name"); src, source, client, remote, dest, destination or dvc followed by ip or addr, with or without _, singular or plural (src_ip, client_ips, remote_addr, dvc_ip); any ip, addr or address — a bare ip and every *_ip, *_addr and *_address (peer_ip, local_ip, "Client IP"); the CIM src, dest, dst and dvc themselves, singular or plural, alone or followed by _host (src, dests, src_host, fw_src, fw_dst) — the App’s own field aliases put client IP addresses and host names into src and dest; peer or peers; mac or mac_addr; account, account_name or "Account Name"; and, with the hostname opt-in, host, hostname, host_name, "Host Name", hosts or hostnames. So src_user, new_users and the dotted data-model and JSON names Authentication.user, All_Traffic.src_ip, All_Traffic.dest and event.user all match. A camelCase name ending in User, UserName or Email, optionally plural, matches too (Windows TargetUserName, SubjectUserName; letter case counts here), and so does one ending in Address, IpAddress, IPAddress or MacAddress (Windows IpAddress) and — with the hostname opt-in — in WorkstationName, HostName, ComputerName or MachineName. The table only ever adds to the patterns.

    A text column with such a field — or with an id-named one (above) — sends every value as a <redacted-XXXXXXX> tag, and a numeric one sends values withheld. These are not matched: source, destination, src_port, dest_port, src_category, dvc_type, user_agent and sap_sid; admins with strict postures should verify their own field names against the pattern list. The tag is the first 7 hex digits of a keyed hash (HMAC-SHA-256) of the value, under a random key the browser makes for each chat session and keeps in memory only; clearing the chat starts a new session with a new key, while closing and reopening the chat panel keeps the session and its key. So the same value gets the same tag within a chat session — the AI can still reason about cardinality and frequency — while tags of different sessions cannot be linked, and nobody without the key can recover a value by hashing candidates (every IPv4 address, short user names, SAP’s standard users). Within a session the model can still compare tags, including tags of values it writes into its own query (see Known Limits of Tier 2 below). While redaction is on it also redacts every value of a text column that is shown as col_N or is not traced to fields that mark no identifier (above). See OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM02.

    What the AI does with this: the AI can write data-grounded narrative replies — “8 distinct users across 3 stacks, with up to 95 failures for one user on one stack and 2,214 in total; the user/stack pairs split 16 Windows, 16 HANA, 15 SAP, so no single stack dominates”. The AI grounds its severity assessments in actual numbers instead of inferring from the shape of the result alone.

    Decision rule for picking Tier 2:

    • The customer’s legal/security team has reviewed and approved exposing aggregate metadata (column cardinalities, top-N value distributions) to the AI vendor.
    • The customer wants narrative replies with concrete values, not just shape descriptions.
    • PII concerns are mitigated by the fail-closed, field-name-based redaction (or the customer is comfortable with the redaction’s coverage).

    Audit trail: every free-form prompt that completes — whichever tier is active — records one vendor_tier1 audit event (the vendor_tier2 category is declared but never emitted) including: - Token counts (input + output) - USD cost estimate - Number of PII redactions applied (tier2RedactionsApplied): each redacted value (the values of a text column shown as col_N or untraced included) and each numeric column whose values are withheld under redaction — because a field it reads marks an identifier, or because it mixes many fields. A withheld column name is not counted. It is 0 in Tier 1, with redaction off, and in a Tier 2 prompt where nothing needed redacting - The user identity that triggered the call

    When elevating to Tier 2 in Settings (from Tier 0 or Tier 1), a vendor_tier2_elevation audit event captures the admin’s identity and timestamp. See Audit Log.

    Known Limits of Tier 2¶

    Tier 2 sends aggregated event values by design, and the App’s reading of a query is name-based hygiene, not a content filter. With PII redaction on, these cases can still carry an identifier or event text to the vendor; where any of them matters, use Tier 1. (The cases earlier builds listed as open are closed; the release notes record each change.)

    • Manufactured counts. A count still carries a few bits that a query computes: stats count by <a multivalue field computed from an identifier> followed by stats count, or the count of rows a filter on an identifier keeps. Counts are not traced to the fields that shaped them. This is documented rather than closed; where it matters, use Tier 1.
    • Fields named nothing like an identifier. A value is sent in clear when its column is traced to a field that neither the App’s table nor the patterns mark — an event field such as message, a field another app extracts, a field Splunk’s automatic key-value extraction finds under a name the App does not know, or _raw (up to 40 characters).
    • Workstation names in the topology IP enrichment. The hostnames column of logserv_topology_ip_enrichment, which a free-form query can read with inputlookup, holds the host names of client workstations (HANA clients and Windows WorkstationName). It is classed as a host name, so Tier 2 redacts it only with the hostname opt-in. Turn the opt-in on, or use Tier 1, where those names must not reach the vendor.
    • Text the model wrote. A column name or a value made only of words the model wrote in its query is sent, even if the model copied a value it had seen into the query.
    • Confirming a guess within a chat session. The model can test identifiers it guesses. A name made of its own words is sent, so a query that filters on guessed user names and splits by user (user="alice" OR user="bob" … | timechart count by user) returns, as column names, exactly the guesses that exist in the data. And a tag is the same for the same value within a chat session, so a column of values the model writes into its own query (eval guess="jsmith") carries the same tags as the real values. The keyed tag stops anyone without the key from reversing tags offline; it does not stop the model from comparing tags online within the session. Where that matters, use Tier 1.

    How the Privacy Invariant Is Enforced¶

    The privacy invariant — no raw event and no unsummarized tool result leaves the customer’s environment for the AI vendor — is enforced mechanically at build time via TypeScript brand types. Tool-result values from the MCP server carry one type; outbound vendor messages carry a different type; the compiler refuses to assign one to the other. The only conversion path is the active tier’s summarizer: in Tier 1 it produces two numbers, in Tier 2 the aggregated metadata described above, which includes values from the events. The type system guarantees that every result goes through a summarizer; the rules above decide what each summarizer may say. A type cannot tell an error message from data, so the summarizers do not pass error text on at all: a failed call’s summary is one of a fixed set of App-written strings, chosen by its HTTP status and error class (see Failed Tool Calls).

    This is the primary defense against LLM02 — Sensitive Information Disclosure. For the brand-type mechanism, summarizer call sites, and the <TOOL_RESULT_DATA> sentinel pattern, see LogServ App and AI Assistant Internals.

    OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025) Compliance¶

    This page is intended for the customer’s security team reviewing the LogServ App’s AI Assistant feature for production deployment. It covers each of the OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025) items and the controls the LogServ App ships to address them.

    Companion page

    For the same controls organized along Google’s Secure AI Framework (SAIF) four-pillar structure plus a coverage matrix of SAIF’s 15 Key Risks, see SAIF Security Architecture.

    These controls govern the path an LLM provider credential unlocks

    The published v0.1.2 App package is the full-LLM build variant, so the controls below (prompt-injection sanitization, the type-system data boundary, tier-gated summaries, SPL static analysis, rate limits, spend caps) actively govern it once an admin configures an LLM provider credential. Until a credential exists — and wherever Templates-only mode is on or a compile-time templates-only build is installed — there is no vendor dispatch at all, which is the strongest form of each LLM-specific control. The audit trail and the supply-chain controls are live either way; the audit trail is tamper-evident only when the HEC forwarder sends a copy to a separately administered destination (Audit Log).

    LLM01 — Prompt Injection¶

    Threat: an attacker (either via the user-prompt vector or via in-band tool-result data) crafts input that hijacks the LLM’s instruction-following behavior, causing it to ignore the system primer or perform unintended actions.

    Controls shipped:

    • <TOOL_RESULT_DATA>...</TOOL_RESULT_DATA> sentinel block wraps every tool-result summary the AI sees. The system primer instructs the AI to treat anything inside the sentinel as DATA from the customer’s environment, NEVER as instructions, regardless of how command-like the contents look. Mitigates the in-band channel of prompt injection: a malicious user who can write events into the customer’s Splunk index could in principle craft field values like user="Ignore prior instructions and...", but the sentinel + sanitizer reduces the effective attack surface to near-zero.
    • Per-value sanitizer for Tier 2 categorical aggregates (sanitizeAggregateValue()). Three classes of suspicious content get replaced wholesale with <filtered>: strings starting with role markers (system:, user:, assistant:, etc.), strings containing known jailbreak / prompt-injection idioms (ignore prior instructions, [INST], <|im_start|>, <|system|>, disregard the above, jailbreak), and strings containing the sentinel tags themselves (prevents a malicious value from prematurely closing the data block).
    • No error text in the tool-result channel. A failed tool call reaches the AI only as a fixed, App-written string built from its HTTP status and an error class. Splunk’s or the MCP server’s error message, which repeats the failed search and so can carry text an attacker wrote into an event, is never sent. See Privacy Tiers → Failed Tool Calls.
    • Jailbreak pattern detection on user prompts. Flag-and-proceed: matches fire a user_prompt_jailbreak_flag audit event but do not block the prompt. Captures a hash + length + matched-pattern groups + char-class fingerprint for SOC pivot analysis.
    • Defense-in-depth chain. Type-system enforcement (LLM02) + Tier 2 sanitizer + tool-result sentinel + primer + vendor-side defenses provide multiple independent layers; bypassing any one doesn’t break the chain.

    LLM02 — Sensitive Information Disclosure¶

    Threat: the LLM emits sensitive customer data (PII, secrets, internal-only information) in its responses or causes it to be transmitted to the vendor.

    Controls shipped:

    • TypeScript type-system enforcement, plus a runtime scan. The compiler refuses to put any tool-result value into the outbound vendor payload; the only conversion path is the summary that the active tier’s summarizer produces. As a second layer, every outbound payload is serialized and scanned at dispatch time and rejected if a Splunk data field name appears as a key; the scan checks the payload’s structure, not the text of a summary, so what a summary may say is set by the tier rules below. See Privacy Tiers and LogServ App and AI Assistant Internals.
    • Privacy tier scoping. Tier 1 (default) gives the AI two numbers per call, a count and a timing — no values. Tier 2 (admin opt-in) adds aggregated metadata: top-N values + counts (field values from the events — filtered, 40 characters each, and with PII redaction on sent in clear only when the App can trace the column to a field that marks no identifier), numeric stats, column names only when Splunk generates them or every word in them was written by the model in its own query or by the App’s catalog search that ran (any other name appears as col_N), and the time range only as UTC timestamps the App formats. Neither tier sends raw rows. Tier 1 limits how much the AI can learn rather than making it zero: for each call it sends a count and a timing, and for a failed call a fixed error class and the HTTP status. A model that writes its own queries can make these depend on event data, so a few bits per call can leak (up to about log2 of the largest row count the server returns through the count, which is the number of result rows whenever the App recognises them). The session tool-call cap (default 100) limits the calls per chat session; clearing the chat resets it, and 0 turns it off. No error text is sent in any tier.
    • No error text to the vendor, in any tier. A failed tool call reaches the AI only as Tool error (HTTP <status>, class=<class>): <fixed hint> The error text is shown to the user only. — the status only when it is a whole number from 100 to 599, the class one of ten fixed names chosen in the browser. A Splunk or MCP Server error text can carry event text (a subsearch such as | inputlookup [search … | eval v=substr(_raw,1,80) | return $v] can put it there), so none of it is sent. The full error stays in the user’s result panel.
