Refusals the App makes itself (the SPL guard, the saved-search catalog, an undeclared tool, the session tool-call cap) reach the AI as Tool call refused by the App before it ran: <reason>; the reason is App-written text, built where the App makes the refusal and never from a tool result.
    • PII redaction at Tier 2. Every field the App defines has a class in a table the build checks (identifier, address, host, free text, safe), and field-name patterns cover every other name: email(s), user(name)(s) and user_name, every *_ip, *_addr, *_address and a bare ip, the CIM src, dest, dst and dvc, peer, mac, account, camelCase …User / …UserName / …Email (TargetUserName), id names such as user_id (hostname opt-in) — also after ., :, - or a space, so data-model and JSON names such as Authentication.user, All_Traffic.src_ip and event.user and display names such as "User Name" match — before values are sent to the vendor. Per-value <redacted-XXXXXXX> tags — an HMAC-SHA-256 under a random per-chat-session key — let the AI reason about cardinality without seeing the actual identifier; they cannot be reversed by hashing candidates or linked across sessions. Redaction fails closed: a text column’s values are sent in clear only when the App traces the column through constructs it reads in full — the field’s own name, a statistics function over one field (values(user) → user), AS, a rename without wildcards, lookup … OUTPUT … AS, eval x=<one field> or a count — to fields that mark no identifier. Every other construct — an eval expression (. concatenation, functions), rex, spath, strcat, wildcard renames, a pivot’s cells, transpose / untable / fieldsummary, a column a subsearch defines, an unknown command, or a reading limit exceeded — leaves the column untraced and every value redacted; a pure count (dc(user)) keeps its numbers. While redaction is on, every value of a text column shown as col_N is redacted, and a numeric column whose name or a field it reads marks an identifier, or that mixes many fields, sends values withheld. Column names are withheld whatever the setting unless Splunk generates them or the model’s query or the App’s catalog search wrote every word of them. Redaction is name-based: a traced field named nothing like an identifier (an event field such as message, _raw under an eval alias) is sent as it is (see Security Architecture, gaps 10 and 11).
    • <TOOL_RESULT_DATA> sentinel (also LLM01) prevents the AI from accidentally treating sanitized data as instructions and echoing it back unsanitized.
    • Vendor-side commitments. Anthropic / OpenAI / Azure OpenAI / AWS Bedrock each publish their own data-usage commitments (no training on API traffic for Anthropic & OpenAI direct API by default). The customer’s DPA review should confirm vendor-side processor obligations.

    LLM03 — Supply Chain¶

    Threat: a compromised or vulnerable third-party dependency in the bundle introduces an attack vector or data-exfil channel.

    Controls shipped:

    • Dependency audit script. yarn audit:ci runs a dependency audit at the high advisory level and exits non-zero on high or critical advisories; yarn build:ci runs it before the build. It is not a gate on the release: the regular yarn build, which produces the release package, does not run it.
    • SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) shipped with every build. A bundled generator parses the package lock directly (no external tool dependency) and emits a SBOM.json in CycloneDX 1.4 format with purl (Package URL) + sha-512 hash per dependency. The SBOM enumerates every bundled dependency; reviewers can pin against this list.
    • Third-party notices. Every build also regenerates THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md from the same dependency tree, so the attribution matches the bundled code (Third-Party Software Licenses).

    LLM04 — Data and Model Poisoning¶

    Threat: an attacker with the ability to write events into the customer’s Splunk index could craft field values that, when surfaced to the AI as Tier 2 aggregates, hijack the AI’s downstream behavior (e.g., by appearing to be system instructions).

    Controls shipped:

    • <TOOL_RESULT_DATA> sentinel block (also LLM01).
    • Per-value sanitizer with role-marker + jailbreak-idiom + sentinel-tag filtering (also LLM01).
    • Fixed error strings (also LLM01, LLM02). A failed call’s error text, which can repeat values from the index, is not sent to the AI; it gets a fixed status-and-class string instead.
    • Truncation of categorical aggregate values to 40 chars to reduce the budget available for embedded jailbreak prompts.
    • Top-N capping of categorical aggregates at 10 by default (max 50) — bounds the volume of AI-visible value content per column.

    LLM05 — Improper Output Handling¶

    Threat: the LLM’s response contains content that, when rendered or executed, harms the user (e.g., XSS via injected HTML, command injection via shell-formatted output).

    Controls shipped:

    • React rendering uses JSX text nodes, not dangerouslySetInnerHTML. Strings are escaped by default; markdown is parsed via a controlled set of recognized markers (citation, severity, bold) — no general-purpose HTML rendering.
    • Drill-down URLs built via buildSplunkSearchUrl() use encodeURIComponent() for the SPL string and centralize the target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" security flags. The noopener flag breaks the window.opener reference for reverse-tabnabbing.
    • AI-authored SPL goes through a static-analysis guard before dispatch (see LLM06).

    LLM06 — Excessive Agency¶

    Threat: the AI is given the ability to perform actions whose consequences exceed the user’s intent (e.g., write/delete data, send emails, exfiltrate via output channels).

    Controls shipped:

    • Saved-search allow-list for splunk_run_saved_search. The AI can run only the saved searches in the App’s own prompt catalog, built from the App’s intent map — never a rollup aggregation, retention, backfill or Enterprise Security feed. The check runs where every saved-search call is sent to the MCP Server, for predefined prompts and free-form calls alike. A name the AI asks for that is not in the catalog is refused before dispatch, with a synthetic error tool_result and a security_blocked_spl audit event; predefined prompts take their names from the catalog itself, and a build gate checks that every one of them is allowed. The list is a copy of the catalog’s names taken when the App loads, and no code in the App can add to it while it runs. The App builds the MCP arguments itself (the vetted name, the App — app = splunk_app_sap_logserv — and the time range) instead of forwarding the model’s, and refuses any tool name other than the two it defines, with a security_blocked_spl audit event as well.
    • SPL guard for AI-authored splunk_run_query: a denylist, an allow-list and Splunk’s parser. Every query the AI writes is checked three times before it is sent, and a query any check refuses is never run. The first fence is a denylist of commands that write to an index, write lookups or files, delete events, alert, email, run scripts, read REST endpoints (rest returns stored credentials decrypted), send data out (outputtelemetry, curl, wget, sendresults, the external lookup dnslookup), save a model (fit ... into) or run another search (map, savedsearch and its aliases), with the quoting tricks that could hide them; it also refuses inline comments, ambiguous quoting and any macro other than the App’s own. The second fence is an allow-list read by a strict lexer: only the App’s list of read-only analytic commands (not union; append combines searches instead), only the LogServ index, only the App’s own lookups, and subsearches only where they cannot widen the search, so other apps’ custom commands and external lookups are refused too. Then Splunk’s own search parser reads the query, and the App refuses it when the two readings differ or when the parser cannot be asked (fail closed). A blocked query produces a synthetic error tool_result and a security_blocked_spl audit event; the AI is told Tool call refused by the App before it ran: with the App’s reason, and can write a different query. The full lists and rules are in Free-form Prompts → The SPL Guard.
    • Per-session tool-call cap prevents infinite tool loops. Maps to session_tool_cap_hit audit event on overflow.
    • Catalog saved searches are not run through the SPL guard — their SPL is reviewed at build time, and none of their searches contains a writing command. The guard scope is the AI-written ad-hoc path.
    • Scope. These controls protect this App’s AI Assistant. Other MCP clients holding a Splunk MCP Server token are governed by the Splunk MCP Server’s own controls and by Splunk permissions.

    LLM07 — System Prompt Leakage¶

    Threat: the system primer leaks to the user (or via the user back to the vendor’s prompt-logging) and exposes internal instructions, lookups, or configuration.

    Controls shipped:

    • No customer-secret content in the primer. The primer contains: tool definitions, the saved-search catalog (names + labels, public information), the LogServ data-model summary (sourcetypes + field names, public), the synthesis rules. No customer-specific identifiers, no API keys, no internal URLs.
    • Time-window reasoning rules are pedagogical (about how the AI should reason about its inputs) — leakage of these rules has no security impact.

    The customer’s DPA review should still confirm vendor-side prompt-logging policies (Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure, Bedrock all log prompts at varying retention; some offer enterprise tiers with no-logging guarantees).

    LLM08 — Vector and Embedding Weaknesses¶

    Threat: vector / embedding stores used for RAG can leak sensitive data if not access-controlled, can be poisoned by malicious indexed content, or can return chunks across security boundaries.

    Status: Not applicable. The LogServ App’s AI Assistant does NOT use vector embeddings or a separate RAG store. The “RAG” here is direct tool dispatch against the customer’s own Splunk index — every retrieval is an SPL search bounded by Splunk’s own RBAC (either a live event search or a read of one of the app’s own access-controlled KV-Store rollups; neither is an embedding store). There is no vector store to compromise.

    LLM09 — Misinformation¶

    Threat: the LLM produces confident-sounding but incorrect information that the user acts on.

    Controls shipped:

    • AI-generated — verify before acting disclaimer rendered as a small muted footer below every AI assistant_text bubble. Visible on every reply, never collapsed.
    • Time-window reasoning rules (Time-Window Reasoning) force the AI to verify high-severity claims with a narrow-window query before recommending action. Self-correction is observable in the response (the AI reports the cumulative number AND the verify-query result).
    • Citation chips ([→ saved_search_name]) link every claim back to the source tool_result tile, so users can sanity-check the narrative against the rendered data.
    • Predefined-prompt path (default for routine investigations) has zero AI-misinformation risk — the dispatch is deterministic and the interpretation card is pre-authored, not generated.

    LLM10 — Unbounded Consumption¶

    Threat: uncontrolled vendor calls drive arbitrary cost, latency, or denial-of-service on the user-facing experience.

    Controls shipped:

    • Per-user rolling-1-hour rate limit on free-form prompts. Configurable via rate_limit_per_hour in Settings (default 30, 0 = disabled). Records rate_limited_prompt audit event on hit.
    • Cumulative-cost daily spend cap in USD. Configurable via daily_spend_cap_usd in Settings. Resets at local midnight (the browser’s calendar day). Records daily_spend_cap_hit audit event on hit.
    • Per-session tool-call cap to prevent infinite tool loops. Records session_tool_cap_hit.
    • Token-usage observability in every vendor_tier1 audit event (emitted for every vendor call regardless of tier): input tokens, output tokens, total tokens, USD cost estimate. Lets finance attribute spend to specific users / sessions. The estimate uses an exact-id price table, which covers the Claude 5.x models at Anthropic’s published first-party rates (cache reads and writes included); an unpriced model reports $0 and does not count toward the daily spend cap.
    • Streaming + abort in the chat UI — users can cancel an in-flight expensive turn via the Stop button.
    • Canned prompts are NOT rate-limited — they bypass the AI vendor entirely and are bounded by Splunk’s own search-quota controls, not vendor cost.

    Enforcement of the rate limit and the spend cap is browser-side (localStorage keyed by Splunk username), so the caps bound good-faith use rather than a determined user with a second browser or cleared site data; every block still emits an audit event, which is the durable control. The session tool-call cap is likewise in-memory per tab. Server-side enforcement is a tracked follow-up.

    Compliance Posture Summary¶

    OWASP item Status Primary control
    LLM01 — Prompt Injection Mitigated TOOL_RESULT_DATA sentinel + per-value sanitizer + jailbreak detection + primer hardening
    LLM02 — Sensitive Information Disclosure Mitigated Hidden<T> type-system enforcement + Tier 1/2 sanitize chokepoint + fixed error strings (no error text to the vendor) + PII redaction
    LLM03 — Supply Chain Partly mitigated CycloneDX SBOM with sha-512 hashes in every build + a dependency-audit script (yarn audit:ci, high and above) that the release build does not run
    LLM04 — Data and Model Poisoning Mitigated TOOL_RESULT_DATA sentinel + per-value sanitizer + 40-char value truncation + top-N cap
    LLM05 — Improper Output Handling Mitigated React JSX text nodes + URL encoding + noopener + SPL static-analysis guard
    LLM06 — Excessive Agency Mitigated Saved-search allow-list (the App’s prompt catalog) + SPL guard (denylist, command / data-scope / lookup allow-list, search-parser cross-check) + session tool-call cap
    LLM07 — System Prompt Leakage Mitigated No customer-secret content in primer; vendor-side DPA review needed
    LLM08 — Vector and Embedding Weaknesses Not applicable No separate vector store; live SPL dispatch via Splunk RBAC
    LLM09 — Misinformation Mitigated AI-generated disclaimer + time-window reasoning + citation chips + predefined-prompt path
    LLM10 — Unbounded Consumption Mitigated Per-user rate limit + daily spend cap + session tool-call cap + token-usage audit

    When These Controls Are Live¶

    The published v0.1.2 App package is the full-LLM build variant: every control on this page actively governs its LLM path once an LLM provider credential is configured. Where no credential exists, or Templates-only mode is on, or a compile-time templates-only build is installed, the LLM-specific items above (LLM01/02/04/07/09/10) are moot by construction — there is no vendor dispatch to attack — while the audit trail, its forwarder, and the supply-chain controls remain live. Nothing about the controls themselves differs between builds beyond whether the path they protect is reachable.

    Security Architecture — SAIF Alignment¶

    This page is for customer security teams evaluating the LogServ App’s AI Assistant feature against Google’s Secure AI Framework (SAIF). It complements the OWASP LLM Top 10 Compliance page — same set of controls, organized along SAIF’s four-pillar structure and mapped to SAIF’s 15 Key Risks catalog.

    The AI-specific risk surface appears once an LLM provider credential is configured

    The published v0.1.2 App package is the full-LLM build variant, so the architecture described below is the one that governs it — but the vendor-dispatch path that architecture protects is inert until an admin configures an LLM provider credential. Until then, and wherever Templates-only mode is on or a compile-time templates-only build is installed, there is no vendor dispatch and the AI-specific surface does not exist. The audit trail and the type-system data boundary are live in every build.

    The Privacy Boundary¶

    The LogServ AI Assistant is designed around one flagship security property: no raw event and no unsummarized search result from your Splunk indexes is ever transmitted to any AI vendor; the vendor gets only the summary the active privacy tier allows. This isn’t a policy commitment — it’s enforced by the TypeScript type system at compile time.

    • Tool results returned from Splunk via MCP are typed as Hidden<T>.
    • The compiler refuses to put a Hidden<T> value into an outbound LLM payload.
    • The only conversion path is sanitize(hidden, summarizer) — which forces the caller to supply a summary string; the active tier picks the summarizer.
    • There is no runtime flag, no policy toggle, no override.

    What the AI sees:

    Privacy Tier What’s sent to the vendor LLM
    Tier 0 (Ollama, not available in this release) Planned: nothing, fully on-host. Today Tier 0 summarizes like Tier 1 and sends to the selected provider; do not select it (Privacy Tiers)
    Tier 1 (default) Two numbers per call: a count and a timing. No values.
    Tier 2 (admin opt-in) Tool result aggregated metadata: cardinality, top-N values + counts (field values from the events — filtered, 40 characters each, and with PII redaction on sent in clear only when the App can trace the column to a field that marks no identifier), numeric stats, and the time range as UTC timestamps the App formats. A column name only when Splunk generates it or every word in it was written by the model in its own query or by the App’s catalog search that ran; any other name appears as col_N. No raw rows.

    In every tier, a tool call that fails reaches the vendor only as its HTTP status and one of ten fixed error classes, with a hint the App writes (Tool error (HTTP 400, class=missing_lookup): …). Splunk’s or the MCP server’s error text is never sent: a Splunk error repeats the search that failed, and a subsearch can put event data into that search. The full error stays in the result panel on the user’s screen. A call the App refuses itself, before anything is sent, reaches the vendor as Tool call refused by the App before it ran: <reason>, with the App’s own reason.

    Detail: Privacy Tiers.

    SAIF Four-Pillar Mapping¶

    Google’s SAIF organizes AI security controls into four pillars. Here’s how the LogServ AI Assistant maps to each.

    Data¶

    SAIF’s Data pillar covers how AI systems handle training data, user data, and the data flowing between system boundaries.

    Training data — N/A. The LogServ AI Assistant does not train, fine-tune, or update any model. It uses third-party LLMs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock) through their public APIs. The data-poisoning, unauthorized-training-data, and training-data-sanitization controls in SAIF apply to those vendors, not to LogServ.

    User Data Management — fully enforced. The Privacy Boundary (above) is the core control:

    • Hidden<T> type system blocks raw event and unsummarized result egress at compile time.
    • Tier 1 (default) sends only count + timing.
    • Tier 2 sends aggregates only. A column name is sent only when Splunk generates it (count, percent, NULL, OTHER, …) or every word in it appears in the text the model or the App wrote for the call — the model’s own query, or the SPL of the App’s catalog search that ran; any other name, such as a split-by value (timechart … by user) or sum(jsmith) that the query did not type, is replaced with a col_N placeholder, with PII redaction on or off. With redaction on, the values of a text column shown as col_N are all redacted. A result the App finds no rows in is reported only as Returned a result that is not in row form. The _time range is sent only as UTC timestamps the App formats (see Privacy Tiers).
    • A failed tool call, in every tier, sends only its HTTP status and a fixed error class, never the error text (see Failed Tool Calls).
    • Tier 2 PII redaction replaces the values of identifier columns with a per-value pseudonym tag (<redacted-XXXXXXX>: 7 hex digits of an HMAC-SHA-256 under a random key made per chat session and kept in the browser’s memory only). The tag is stable within the chat session, so the LLM can still reason about cardinality, and it cannot be linked across sessions or reversed by hashing candidate values. Every field the App defines is classified one by one (identifier, address, host, free text, safe), checked by the build, and name patterns cover every other field. It fails closed: a text column’s values are sent in clear only when the App can trace the column, through constructs it reads in full, to fields that mark no identifier; any other column is redacted. Hostname redaction is opt-in via Settings. The exact patterns and tracing rules are in Privacy Tiers → Tier 2.
    • Every elevation from Tier 0/1 → Tier 2 is recorded in the audit log with the admin’s user identity, timestamp, and previous tier.

    Model¶

    SAIF’s Model pillar covers model integrity, exfiltration risk, and supply chain.

    Model Source Tampering — partial coverage:

    • Our supply chain: a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM.json, CycloneDX 1.4) ships in every release with per-dependency purl + sha-512 hashes; it enumerates every bundled dependency. A dependency-audit script (yarn audit:ci, high and critical advisories) exists, but the build that produces the release package does not run it.
    • Distribution integrity: each release package passes Splunk AppInspect in Splunk Cloud precert mode (--mode precert --included-tags cloud) with 0 errors and 0 failures before it is published; the results are published beside the packages. The packages are not published on Splunkbase. The Splunk Deployment Server delivers the Data TA to heavy forwarders over Splunk’s management port, encrypted with TLS; whether each side also verifies the other’s certificate depends on your Splunk TLS settings.
    • Vendor model weight integrity is the LLM vendor’s responsibility. The customer’s DPA review should confirm vendor-side controls.

    Model Exfiltration — N/A. The LogServ App does not host model weights. Cloud LLM models live in vendor infrastructure (Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure, Bedrock). Tier 0 Ollama (not available in this release) would run on the customer’s own host, with model weights under the customer’s existing storage controls.

    Model Reverse Engineering — N/A. The LogServ App exposes a known vendor LLM behind a thin wrapper. The system primer is publishable (see the free-form prompts documentation) — there’s no proprietary prompt engineering to reverse-engineer.

    Application¶

    SAIF’s Application pillar covers input validation, access management, and output handling for the AI-using application.

    Input Validation — multi-layered:

    • User-prompt anomaly detection. Five pattern groups (role redefinition, persona shift, system-prompt leak, control tokens, long base64 blobs) run on every user prompt before dispatch; prompt length and a character-class fingerprint are captured as recorded signals alongside the matched groups. Flag-and-proceed semantics: matches fire a user_prompt_jailbreak_flag audit event for SOC review but do not block the prompt — regex-based detection has false positives, and blocking would cripple legitimate investigative queries.
    • SPL static analysis on AI-authored queries. Every splunk_run_query call from the AI runs through two fences and a cross-check before it is sent. The first fence is a denylist of commands that write, delete, alert, email, run scripts, read REST endpoints, send data out or run other searches, plus the quoting tricks, inline comments and foreign macros that could hide one. The second fence is an allow-list read by a strict lexer: only the App’s read-only analytic commands, only the LogServ index, only the App’s own lookups, and subsearches only where they cannot widen the search, so other apps’ custom commands and external lookups are refused even when the denylist does not name them. Then Splunk’s own search parser reads the query (search/parser, parse only), and the App refuses it when the two readings differ or when the parser cannot be asked (fail closed). The AI can rephrase a refused query. Blocked queries surface as a security_blocked_spl audit event with the operator and the command. The full lists and rules: Free-form Prompts → The SPL Guard; the audit fields: Audit Log.
    • Saved-search allow-list. splunk_run_saved_search accepts only the names in the App’s own prompt catalog; any other name is refused before it reaches the MCP Server and recorded as a security_blocked_spl audit event. The list is a copy of the catalog’s names taken when the App loads, and it cannot be changed while the App runs.
    • Tool-result sanitization. AI-authored tool arguments are schema-validated. Tier 2 categorical aggregates pass through a per-value sanitizer that replaces strings matching known jailbreak idioms with <filtered>.
    • <TOOL_RESULT_DATA> sentinel block wraps every tool-result summary the AI sees. The system primer instructs the AI to treat anything inside the sentinel as data from the customer’s environment, never as instructions.

    Application Access Management:

    • Per-user prompt rate limit (configurable; default tunable in Settings) bounds free-form prompt volume per hour.
    • Per-user daily spend cap (default 50.00 USD; set to 0 to disable) bounds vendor cost per day. Tally resets at local midnight. Predefined-prompt executions don’t accumulate against the cap.
    • Per-chat-session MCP tool-dispatch cap is defense-in-depth above the per-message limit of at most 8 tool turns. Prevents runaway tool-loops in adversarial automation.
    • Feature toggle. The master enabled switch in Settings gates the entire feature; transitions from OFF to ON require admin acceptance of a liability acknowledgement modal (recorded with the admin’s user identity, timestamp, disclaimer hash, and version per Splunk’s standard opt-in pattern).

    Output Validation:

    • The LLM’s output is never executed. Tool calls are schema-validated against a closed catalog of MCP tools; a tool name outside it is refused, and a saved-search name outside the App’s prompt catalog is refused. There is no eval-style path from LLM output to system action.
    • React rendering uses JSX text nodes, not dangerouslySetInnerHTML. Strings are escaped by default. Citation markers, severity badges, and bold markdown are parsed via a controlled set of recognized patterns; no general-purpose HTML rendering.
    • Drill-down URLs are built via a centralized buildSplunkSearchUrl() helper that uses encodeURIComponent() and applies target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" flags to break reverse-tabnabbing attacks.

    Agent¶

    SAIF’s Agent pillar — newer in SAIF 2.0 — covers autonomous agent behavior, permissions, user control, and observability.

    Agent Permissions — a closed catalog. The AI is offered two MCP tools, and the App refuses any other tool name it emits:

    • splunk_run_query — dispatches an ad-hoc SPL query against the customer’s data, subject to the static-analysis guard (see Input Validation above).
    • splunk_run_saved_search — dispatches a saved search from the App’s own catalog only: the prompt library built from the App’s intent map. The check runs where every saved-search call is sent to the MCP Server, so a name outside the catalog is refused — never a rollup aggregation, retention, backfill or Enterprise Security feed — and recorded as a security_blocked_spl audit event. The App builds the MCP arguments itself (the vetted name, the App — app = splunk_app_sap_logserv — and the time range); other keys the model supplies are not forwarded.

    Free-form queries refuse the commands the guard knows to write, delete, alert, run scripts, read REST endpoints, send data out or run other searches — collect, outputlookup, outputcsv, delete, rest, curl, savedsearch, map, mcollect, meventcollect, runshellscript, dump and the rest of the guard’s list (see Input Validation above). Beyond Splunk searches, the AI has no config writes, no user creation, no permission changes, and no outbound network actions of any kind beyond the LLM API call. Within a search, the guard refuses the outbound commands and lookups it names (outputtelemetry, curl, wget, sendresults, dnslookup), and the allow-list refuses every command and lookup that is not on its list, including any another installed app adds.

    These controls protect this App’s AI Assistant. Another MCP client holding a Splunk MCP Server token is governed by the Splunk MCP Server’s own controls and by Splunk permissions, not by this App. Running MCP tools needs the MCP Server’s mcp_tool_execute capability, which it grants by default only to admin and sc_admin; every AI Assistant user needs it too (Splunk MCP Setup → Roles and Capabilities).

    Agent User Control:

    • Tier selection by an admin in Settings, at any time — Tier 1 (default) or Tier 2; Tier 0 is not available in this release.
    • Master enable toggle — admin-controlled, default OFF.
    • Per-prompt opt-in — every free-form prompt is user-initiated. There is no autonomous loop, no scheduled prompt execution, no background activity.
    • Power Mode is a per-browser-tab toggle, shown only to the roles an admin names. While it is on, the primer asks the model to run a saved search before answering; each prompt’s audit event records whether it was on.
    • Acknowledgement modals at Settings save time — an admin must answer a liability acknowledgement to (a) turn the feature on and (b) save with the audit forwarder off. A tier elevation needs no acknowledgement; it records a vendor_tier2_elevation audit event.

    Agent Observability:

    • Sequenced audit log. Every meaningful AI Assistant event (canned prompt execution, free-form vendor call, blocked SPL, rate-limit hit, spend-cap hit, prompt anomaly, tier elevation, legal acknowledgement, model discovery) lands in the logserv_ai_assistant_audit index with a stable per-tab session ID + monotonic per-session sequence number, so gaps and reordering are detectable. The browser writes the events as the signed-in user, which needs Splunk’s edit_tcp or edit_log_alert_event capability (by default admin holds both, power holds edit_log_alert_event and user neither); a user without either is not audited, and the chat panel says so (Who can write audit events); tamper-evidence comes from the optional HEC forwarder to a separately-administered destination. The chat panel surfaces “AI is generating response” status; the Audit Log viewer in Settings lets reviewers filter by category, user, and time range.
    • Who can read the audit index follows each role’s allowed indexes; Splunk’s default user role allows every non-internal index, so narrow it (Restricting who can read the audit index).
    • HEC audit forwarder. Admin can configure a Splunk HEC destination (e.g., a separate indexer, a SIEM, S3-with-Object-Lock owned by a different admin team) for tamper-evident off-host audit copies. Forwarder failures themselves are recorded locally so an off-host divergence is detectable.
    • Vendor token-usage audit events capture provider, model, input/output tokens, USD cost estimate (computed locally from list pricing), and turn count — letting SOC teams pivot on cost-anomaly indicators.

    SAIF 15 Key Risks — Coverage Matrix¶

    The table below maps each SAIF Key Risk to LogServ’s posture. Strong = flagship property of the architecture; Partial = mitigation in place with documented residual surface; N/A = out of scope because LogServ does not train or host models.

    # SAIF Risk LogServ Posture Key Controls
    1 Data Poisoning (DP) N/A LogServ does not train models.
    2 Unauthorized Training Data (UTD) N/A LogServ does not train models. No raw event or unsummarized result leaves the privacy boundary.
    3 Model Source Tampering (MST) Partial SBOM in every release; a dependency-audit script the release build does not run. AppInspect (Splunk Cloud precert mode) on every release package. Model weight integrity is vendor responsibility.
    4 Excessive Data Handling (EDH) Strong Hidden<T> privacy boundary, Tier 1 default, Tier 2 PII redaction.
    5 Model Exfiltration (MXF) N/A LogServ does not host models.
    6 Model Deployment Tampering (MDT) Partial AppInspect before release + DS-channel distribution. Tarball GPG signing is a known gap.
    7 Denial of ML Service (DMS) Partial Per-user prompt rate limit + per-user daily spend cap + per-session tool dispatch cap (browser-side enforcement — see Known Residual Gaps).
    8 Model Reverse Engineering (MRE) N/A Publishable system primer, no proprietary prompt engineering.
    9 Insecure Integrated Component (IIC) Strong Closed tool catalog, saved-search allow-list, schema-validated tool calls, SPL static-analysis guard.
    10 Prompt Injection (PIJ) Partial Tool-result vector physically blocked by Hidden<T> + sentinel + per-value sanitizer; a failed call’s error text is not sent at all (fixed error classes only). User-prompt vector flagged (five pattern groups), not blocked.
    11 Model Evasion (MEV) N/A LogServ has no classifiers to evade; ML-evasion is vendor-side.
    12 Sensitive Data Disclosure (SDD) Strong Same controls as EDH (privacy boundary + redaction).
    13 Inferred Sensitive Data (ISD) Partial Strong by construction (Tier 1 = no values; Tier 2 = redacted aggregates). Hostname redaction is opt-in — small inference surface for environment topology when off.
    14 Insecure Model Output (IMO) Strong LLM output never executed; no dangerouslySetInnerHTML; drill-down URLs encoded + tab-nabbing flags.
    15 Rogue Actions (RA) Strong Catalog-only saved searches + write-command guard on free-form SPL, no autonomous loop, sequenced audit log + off-host HEC forwarder.

    Summary: 5 Strong, 5 Partial, 5 N/A. Zero “Not covered” — every SAIF risk in scope for LogServ’s architecture has at least partial mitigation.

    Cross-Reference: SAIF ↔ OWASP LLM Top 10¶

    The OWASP LLM Top 10 Compliance page covers the same controls organized by attack pattern instead of structural pillar. Most LogServ controls map to both frameworks:

    SAIF Risk OWASP LLM Item
    EDH / SDD / ISD LLM02 — Sensitive Information Disclosure
    MST LLM03 — Supply Chain
    DP / UTD (N/A here) LLM04 — Data and Model Poisoning
    IMO LLM05 — Improper Output Handling
    IIC / RA LLM06 — Excessive Agency
    PIJ LLM01 — Prompt Injection
    MRE (N/A here) LLM07 — System Prompt Leakage (related)
    DMS LLM10 — Unbounded Consumption

    What’s Out of Scope¶

    Items in SAIF that don’t apply to LogServ’s architecture:

    • Model training, fine-tuning, RAG with embedded sensitive data — the AI Assistant does not train, fine-tune, embed, or persist any customer data into any model.
    • Vendor model integrity and vendor data handling — these are the LLM vendor’s responsibility. Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, and AWS Bedrock each publish their own data-usage commitments and security posture; the customer’s DPA review should confirm processor obligations.
    • Customer Splunk infrastructure security — Splunk’s own access controls, role-based ACLs, and indexer encryption apply normally. The AI Assistant inherits the security posture the customer has configured for Splunk Web access.

    Known Residual Gaps¶

    Honesty matters in a security architecture page. The following gaps are documented:

    1. User-prompt jailbreak detection is flag-and-proceed, not block. Regex pattern matching has false positives. Pattern coverage will grow as new attack patterns surface in the wild. The flag-and-proceed posture lets SOC teams review while preserving legitimate investigative use.
    2. Hostname redaction at Tier 2 is opt-in (default off). Hostname patterns can leak environment topology. Admins can flip the default in Settings if their threat model requires it. (Host names that become column names, as in timechart count by host, are shown as col_N whatever this setting, unless the query itself wrote them.)
    3. Tarball GPG signing is not yet implemented. AppInspect checks before release + DS-channel distribution cover most of the threat model, but a signed tarball would provide an additional integrity proof point. Tracked as a follow-up item.
    4. The rate limit and daily spend cap are enforced browser-side (localStorage keyed by Splunk username). They bound good-faith use; a user with a second browser or cleared storage can exceed them. Every block still writes an audit event, so attempts remain visible. Server-side enforcement is a tracked follow-up.
    5. The saved-search allow-list and the SPL guard protect this App’s assistant only. Other MCP clients holding a Splunk MCP Server token, and users of Splunk’s own search bar, can still run any saved search their Splunk permissions allow, the App’s rollup and retention searches included; Splunk roles and the Splunk MCP Server’s own settings govern them. The SPL guard matches command names in the query text, accepts only the App’s own macros and refuses inline comments; Splunk’s search parser, which expands the macros, cross-checks every free-form query (see gap 8).
    6. The saved-search allow-list matches names, not search text. A build gate proves that the shipped (default/) definitions of the catalog searches are read-only. A local/ edit of a catalog search, or a private saved search of the same name in this App, runs under its allowed name. Keeping such overrides read-only is the Splunk admin’s responsibility; to see which definition is in effect, run splunk btool savedsearches list <name> --app=splunk_app_sap_logserv --debug.
    7. The SPL guard’s command list is the App’s. Free-form queries may use only the commands and lookups on the App’s allow-list, and Splunk’s search parser cross-checks every query. What remains is what the allowed commands themselves do: they read the LogServ index and the App’s lookups, and a query can still be expensive (a wide transaction, a large join); the rate limit, the session tool-call cap and Splunk’s own search quotas bound that. Splunk role permissions remain the authoritative gate.
    8. Macro definitions are checked through Splunk’s own parser. Splunk expands whichever definition of a macro is in effect for the dispatching user and app: a local/macros.conf override in this App, the user’s own private macro of the same name, or another app’s globally exported macro of the same name can take precedence over the definition the App ships. The App has Splunk’s search parser expand every free-form query in the user’s context and refuses it when the parser finds a command not on the list, a different command list, a query starting with a data macro that does not expand to the App’s definition, an index other than the LogServ index, or a lookup outside a subsearch that is not one of the App’s. What remains: the definition is compared only where the query starts with the macro — where the macro stands after WHERE in tstats or starts a subsearch, a shadowing macro is caught only when its expansion names another index (Splunk’s parser reports a subsearch as text inside the command that holds it, so a command or lookup such a macro brings into a subsearch is not caught); the check relies on the parser being reachable (when it is not, every free-form query is refused, parser_unavailable), and catalog searches are not checked this way — keeping the three macros (sap_logserv_idx_macro, sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro, sap_logserv_cloud_provider_default_macro) unshadowed stays the Splunk admin’s responsibility. Catalog searches run in the LogServ App’s context; to see the definition a search there gets for a given user, run splunk btool macros list <name> --app=splunk_app_sap_logserv --user=<user> --debug (without --app and --user, btool shows the global merge, which is not what those searches use), or list every copy with | rest /servicesNS/-/-/configs/conf-macros splunk_server=local | search title=<name> | table eai:acl.app eai:acl.owner eai:acl.sharing definition. Both the LogServ App and the Data TA ship sap_logserv_idx_macro; where both are on the search head, keep the two copies the same (Renaming an index).
    9. Tier 1 limits what the vendor can learn; it does not make it zero. The vendor gets two numbers for each call, a count and a timing, and for a failed call a fixed error class and the HTTP status. A model that writes its own queries can make these depend on event data — the timing, whether a search fails and which class its error gets, and the count, which is the number of result rows whenever the App recognises them — so a few bits per call can leak, up to about log2 of the largest row count the server returns through the count. The session tool-call cap (default 100) limits the calls per chat session; clearing the chat resets it, and 0 turns it off. Error text, which could carry far more, is not sent in any tier (see Failed Tool Calls).
    10. Tier 2 sends aggregated event values by design. Its top-N values are field values from the events (filtered, 40 characters each, and with PII redaction on sent in clear only for columns the App traces to fields that mark no identifier), and a column shown as col_N keeps its numeric statistics. Redaction fails closed for anything the App cannot trace, but it is decided by field names: a value held by a field named nothing like an identifier (an event field such as message, a field another app extracts) is sent as it is, and so is _raw under a plain alias — eval m=_raw sends up to 40 characters of an event. A number computed from event text is sent unless a field it reads marks an identifier. A column name made only of words the model wrote in its own query is its own text and is sent even if it copies a value it has seen, and a count can still carry a few bits a query manufactures (stats count by <a multivalue field computed from an identifier> then stats count). Where no event value may be sent, use Tier 1, which sends no values (subject to gap 9).
    11. Tier 2’s reading of the query. The value rules of gap 10 depend on the App reading the model’s query. The cases earlier builds listed as read wrongly or not at all — a _time the query sets, a stray apostrophe, rex groups written (?'name'…), fieldformat, a lookup that echoes or maps the field it matches on, an unknown first command inside appendpipe, the App’s own identifier fields the patterns missed, rex patterns and spath paths in the numeric rule, and a redaction tag that could be reversed offline — are closed, and free-form queries are limited to commands the App reads in full. What remains is listed in Privacy Tiers — Known Limits of Tier 2: manufactured counts (documented, not traced), fields named nothing like an identifier, and text the model wrote itself.

    What Customers Can Do¶

    Concrete actions a customer’s security team can take to validate or strengthen the posture:

    • Review the audit log regularly. Open Settings → AI Assistant → Audit Log. Filter by category to investigate anomalies. Categories worth scheduled review: user_prompt_jailbreak_flag, security_blocked_spl, rate_limited_prompt, daily_spend_cap_hit, vendor_tier2_elevation.
    • Check what the AI’s searches can reach. Free-form queries read only the LogServ index and the App’s own lookups, with the commands of the App’s allow-list, and Splunk’s search parser cross-checks each one in the user’s context. Review which roles may use the AI Assistant and run searches, and confirm that the App’s three macros are not shadowed for the catalog searches: splunk btool macros list <name> --app=splunk_app_sap_logserv --user=<user> --debug (the user who runs them) for each of sap_logserv_idx_macro, sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro, sap_logserv_cloud_provider_default_macro. A steady stream of parser_unavailable refusals in the audit log means the App cannot reach the search parser.
    • Configure the HEC audit forwarder to a separate destination — a different Splunk indexer, a SIEM, an S3 bucket with Object Lock, or any HEC-compatible sink. The acceptance modal recorded when the forwarder is left disabled is a useful compliance artifact.
    • Pick the tier that matches your risk appetite. Tier 1 is the safest default (count + timing only). Tier 2 is more powerful but ships aggregated metadata to the vendor. Tier 0 (Ollama, local) is not available in this release; where nothing may reach a vendor, use Templates-only mode (Restricting the LLM Path).
    • Set the daily spend cap to a number that bounds your monthly liability. The cap can be raised or removed at any time via Settings.
    • Validate the SBOM against your organization’s vulnerability scanning. The SBOM.json ships at the root of the App tarball.

    Release Notes: 0.1.2¶

    This page lists what changed in each 0.1.2 build of the Splunk for SAP LogServ packages, newest first for each package. Read it before you upgrade, to see what a build changes and whom it affects; the steps an upgrade needs are in Upgrading to This Release. Earlier versions have their own pages: 0.1.1, 0.0.6 and 0.0.5 and earlier.

    Current Builds and How to Read Yours¶

    Package Splunk Web label App ID Current 0.1.2 build
    LogServ App Splunk App for SAP LogServ splunk_app_sap_logserv 394
    Data TA Splunk TA for SAP LogServ splunk_ta_sap_logserv 1792598960
    LogServ Azure add-on Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on Azure splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure 1792558069
    LogServ GCP add-on Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on GCP splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp 1792558072

    All four packages are version 0.1.2, so within 0.1.2 only the build number tells two builds of a package apart.

    • The LogServ App numbers its builds in sequence. The App and build pills in its header show the version and build, and About, at the bottom of the left navigation rail, shows the version, the build and the build date.
    • The Data TA and the Azure and GCP add-ons are built with Splunk’s UCC framework, whose build number is the time the package was built, in Unix seconds (UTC): build 1792598960 was built on 2026-10-21 at 16:09 UTC. A higher number is a later build. Their entries below give the date as well as the build.

    To read the installed build of each package, run this search in Splunk Web on the instance you check (the search head for the App; each heavy forwarder, or the single instance, for the add-ons), or read build in the package’s default/app.conf as Version Check shows:

    | rest /services/apps/local splunk_server=local
| search title=splunk_app_sap_logserv OR title=splunk_ta_sap_logserv*
| table title version build

    Some builds were made only for testing and never released. From build 380 on, the entry of such a build is merged with the released build that carried its changes, as in builds 387–388. Earlier test builds of the App (361, 364, 372 and 374) keep their entries, each marked as not released. The App builds released since build 379 are 383, 385, 386, 388, 390, 392, 393 and 394.

    Each entry says what changed, who is affected and what an upgrade needs; Upgrading to This Release lists every action by the build you are coming from. A statement that a later build changed carries Superseded by build N, and a statement found to be wrong carries a Correction.

    Compatibility¶
    Splunk platform versions 9.4.3 and later
    CIM 5.0.0 and later (per app.manifest)
    Supported OS for data collection Platform independent
    Vendor products SAP LogServ for SAP ECS in Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform (GCP)
    Published App artifact The full-LLM build variant. The AI Assistant ships turned off, and an admin turns it on in Settings. Predefined prompts need the Splunk MCP Server and no LLM credential; free-form chat also needs an LLM provider credential (see Restricting the LLM Path)
    AI Assistant prerequisite Splunk MCP Server (Splunkbase App 7931) v1.1.0 or later, on the search head where the LogServ App is installed. The predefined prompts run through its Run Saved Search tool, which first shipped in v1.1.0. The App’s health check blocks only versions below v1.0.3 (the CVE-2026-20205 fix) and has no upper bound since App build 393; the newest version verified is 2.0.0. v1.2.1 or later is recommended (SVD-2026-1004)
    AWS ingest The Splunk Add-on for AWS (SQS-Based S3 inputs) on the heavy forwarders (strongly recommended; a search head, Splunk Cloud included, is not blocked). No minimum version is enforced; 8.2.2 or later is recommended (SVD-2026-1005), and these docs were checked with 8.3.1. The Data TA’s AWS S3 Direct screen warns below 8.1.0 and has no upper bound
    Azure ingest A dedicated first-party add-on — Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on Azure (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure), installed on each heavy forwarder that runs the input (strongly recommended; a search head is not blocked: see Running the TAs on a search head)
    GCP ingest A dedicated first-party add-on — Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on GCP (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp), installed on each heavy forwarder that runs the input (strongly recommended; a search head is not blocked: see Running the TAs on a search head)

    v0.1.2 continues the v0.1.1 line

    v0.1.2 is the active line and carries everything in Release Notes: 0.1.1: the dashboard-performance data layer (tstats and KV Store rollups, the backfill panel, staggered schedules), the Azure and GCP ingest add-ons, the LogServ Data Doctor, the Environment Topology work and the LLM-driven AI Assistant. The published App artifact is the full-LLM build variant: the AI Assistant ships turned off, and once an admin turns it on, free-form chat also needs an LLM provider credential. No templates-only package is published for 0.1.2; it can be built from the same source (see Restricting the LLM Path). Entries for this release are added as work lands.

    LogServ App (splunk_app_sap_logserv)¶

    Builds of the Splunk App for SAP LogServ, which runs on the search head.

    The Audit Log’s user filter shows each name once (build 394)¶

    • With User contains set, Settings → AI Assistant → Audit Log showed each name twice in the User column (for example adminadmin). The filter makes Splunk extract user from the event to apply it, and the viewer’s spath then added the same value again. The viewer now reads user from the event’s JSON after spath, as it already did for category, so the column shows the name once with or without the filter.

    Who is affected: admins who read the Audit Log (Settings → AI Assistant → Audit Log) with User contains set.

    Upgrade action: none. No acknowledgement is asked again: the legal texts and their versions are unchanged.

    A newer Splunk MCP Server is no longer refused (build 393)¶

    • The AI Assistant no longer refuses a newer Splunk MCP Server. It used to refuse a version at or above an upper bound it had not been tested against (v3.0.0 since build 335), replacing the chat with an Uncertified version card. That bound is gone; the v1.0.3 security floor (CVE-2026-20205) stays, and the predefined prompts need v1.1.0 or later, the first version with the Run Saved Search tool they run through. A version reported in two parts, such as 3.0, now reads as 3.0.0; it used to be refused as too old. The newest version verified is 2.0.0 (the handshake, tools/list and tools/call); if a later version changed the protocol the AI Assistant depends on, that would show as failing tool calls in the chat rather than as a refusal to start.

    Who is affected: deployments whose Splunk MCP Server is version 3.0.0 or later, or reports its version in two parts.

    Upgrade action: none. No acknowledgement is asked again: the legal texts and their versions are unchanged.

    Audit events go where the settings in place when they were posted send them, and the dialog names both providers (builds 391–392)¶

    • The audit-forwarding acknowledgement’s audit event is posted as soon as the answer is recorded, for a Yes as for a No. A Yes’s event used to wait for the save, so a Yes followed by a failed save could leave the Yes recorded with no audit event, and the retry did not always ask again.
    • An audit event posted on its own goes where the audit settings in place at that moment send it. That covers the Settings page’s acknowledgement events, which are posted just before the save. Until now the forwarder setting was read only after the event’s local write, so that save could decide, while the event was being written, whether the event was also sent to the off-host forwarder. Now a Yes that turns forwarding off is also sent to the forwarder being turned off (an attempt with the forwarder settings the page has applied), and if that send fails, its failure record goes to the event’s audit index, even when the same save renames the index.
    • On a re-ask, the enablement dialog names the provider in effect, the one a No keeps; it named the provider selected on the page. When the same save also changes the LLM provider, it names both: the provider in effect, which a No keeps, and the one the save changes it to, which a Yes saves. When the AI Assistant is being turned on, it names the page’s provider.

    Build 391 was not released; its changes reached customers in build 392.

    Who is affected: admins who answer the AI Assistant’s acknowledgements in Settings, and whoever reviews the AI Assistant’s audit log.

    Upgrade action: none. No acknowledgement is asked again: the legal texts and their versions are unchanged.

    The Settings page waits for a No to be recorded, and the dialogs show their errors (builds 389–390)¶

    • The enablement dialog closes once a No has turned the AI Assistant off, before the No is recorded; until now it showed the turn-on wording and buttons for that moment. It also closes when an answer cannot be recorded, so the error shows on the page; it used to appear behind the dialog.
    • A No that turns the AI Assistant off keeps the Settings page busy until the No is recorded (the Save button reads Saving…); the page could be used again a moment too early.
    • The audit-forwarding dialog closes when its answer cannot be recorded, or when the save after a Yes fails, so the error shows on the page; it appeared behind the dialog.
    • A No’s audit event records the provider in effect, for both acknowledgements; it recorded the provider selected on the page, which a No does not save.

    Build 389 was not released; its changes reached customers in build 390.

    Who is affected: admins who answer the AI Assistant’s acknowledgements in Settings, and whoever reviews the AI Assistant’s audit log.

    Upgrade action: none. No acknowledgement is asked again: the legal texts and their versions are unchanged.

    Declining the AI Assistant terms turns the AI Assistant off, and the acknowledgements say where an answer is recorded (builds 387–388)¶

    • A No now does what the terms say. The enablement acknowledgement ends by saying that if Customer does not accept, the AI Assistant feature will remain disabled. That held when an admin was turning the AI Assistant on. When it was already on and the terms’ version rose, a No only cancelled that save: the AI Assistant stayed on, and the next save went through without asking. Now a No in that case turns the AI Assistant off. Only the Enable AI Assistant setting changes - nothing else in that save is applied - and it is written before the No is recorded, so if the write fails, the question is asked again at the next save. The dialog says so before the click, and its No button reads I do not accept (record No and turn off).
    • The enablement acknowledgement is at version 3. Two corrections raised it. Clause 7 said the administrator’s answer is recorded “via the standard Splunk telemetry endpoint”; the answer is recorded as an event in the AI Assistant audit log, with the administrator’s account name, network address and a timestamp, and, since build 240, stored with the acknowledged version in the KV Store, and the clause now says so. Its closing sentence now says the AI Assistant feature will then remain disabled or, if it is already enabled, be disabled. Turning the AI Assistant on asks every time, as before.
    • The note under both acknowledgements (outside their legal text) and the Settings page’s message when an answer cannot be recorded named the same telemetry endpoint. The note now names the audit log and the KV Store, and the message names the KV Store, the write that failed, without repeating itself.

    Build 387, which raised the enablement acknowledgement to version 2, was not released; its changes reached customers in build 388.

    Who is affected: deployments that run with the AI Assistant enabled.

    Upgrade action: nothing to rebuild. With the AI Assistant enabled, the next admin who saves the AI Assistant’s General settings (Save Defaults) is asked once to accept version 3 of the enablement acknowledgement; answering No turns the AI Assistant off. A local/ai_assistant_acks.conf that sets optInVersion under [logserv-ai-assistant-enable-tc] keeps the old version: remove that line. See Upgrading to This Release.

    The audit-log integrity acknowledgement names the audit index correctly (build 386)¶

    • The forwarder-disabled acknowledgement is at version 2. Its text named the audit index ai_assistant_audit, the index’s name before it was renamed logserv_ai_assistant_audit; it now reads the AI Assistant audit index (logserv_ai_assistant_audit, or the index set in Settings), so it stays correct where an admin named another index. Because the wording changed, its version rose from 1 to 2: on a deployment that runs with audit forwarding off, the next admin who saves the AI Assistant’s General settings (Save Defaults) is asked once to acknowledge the corrected text. With forwarding on nothing changes, and the AI Assistant enablement acknowledgement is unchanged.
    • Documentation. The add-ons’ urllib3 1.26.20 and the seven advisories scanners report against it are analysed in Third-Party Software Licenses: none affects the add-ons as shipped. The Application Settings page of this documentation now says an acknowledgement is recorded once per deployment.

    Who is affected: deployments that run with audit forwarding off.

    Upgrade action: nothing to rebuild. With audit forwarding off, the next admin who saves the AI Assistant’s General settings (Save Defaults) is asked once to acknowledge the corrected text. An optInVersion line under [logserv-ai-assistant-tc] in local/ai_assistant_acks.conf keeps the old version: remove it. See Upgrading to This Release.

    Dashboard data writable by admins only, and the audit warning names both capabilities Splunk accepts (builds 384–385)¶

    The App’s KV Store collections that hold dashboard data - the 24 rollups, the five Environment Topology collections and the Data Doctor’s platform snapshot - were writable by every role, so any signed-in user could alter or delete what the dashboards show through Splunk’s REST API. They are now writable by the admin, sc_admin and sc_subadmin roles only; every role can still read them. Their scheduled searches run as Splunk’s system user and the Settings → Dashboard Data backfill as the signed-in admin, so neither changes. Six collections stay writable by every role because ordinary users write them by design: the four per-user preferences (topology layouts, the default layout, the active layout mode, the dashboard refresh interval) and the Data Doctor’s saved reports and supplied ingest configuration.

    • Saved searches that write run as the requesting user. The 91 saved searches that write with outputlookup (the aggregate, backfill and retention searches of the rollups and topology collections, the Data Doctor’s platform-snapshot and report-retention searches, and the two ES feeds) now set dispatchAs = user. A user who starts one through Splunk’s REST API (saved/searches/<name>/dispatch) runs it with their own permissions, so a non-admin can no longer run a retention or a backfill that overwrites dashboard data. Their schedules run as before.
    • A stored refresh interval must be one the picker offers. The refresh-interval collection is writable by every role, so another user could store a one-second interval in your row and make every panel re-run each second; a stored value other than Never, 30s, 1m, 5m, 15m, 30m or 1hr is now ignored.
    • The Data Doctor says a supplier name is not verified. The name on a saved report and on a supplied ingest configuration is the one the browser sent, so the Data Doctor now shows it as (name not verified): the saved reports’ column reads By (not verified), and a re-downloaded saved report marks the name on its cover page, in the environment-fingerprint section’s Generated by, in the machine-readable appendix and in the JSON copy. The page’s note on saved reports no longer says every App collection is writable by every user. The platform snapshot’s provenance line now reads recorded by the hourly platform snapshot, a collection only Splunk administrators can write.
    • The AI Assistant’s audit warning names both capabilities. Splunk accepts the browser’s audit writes (receivers/simple) from a user who holds edit_tcp or edit_log_alert_event, and Splunk’s default power role holds edit_log_alert_event, so power users have been audited all along; only users whose sole role is user are refused. The warning (HTTP 403, or HTTP 401 after a reload) now names edit_log_alert_event, the narrower one to grant, and edit_tcp, and says Splunk’s default user role has neither; it no longer says power users lack them. See Audit Log.
    • The ingest-cutoff sentence gives the date first. The Data Doctor now says a range ends before the ingest cutoff of <date> (recorded as supplied by <name> (name not verified)), so the date no longer reads as the time the cutoff was supplied.
    • The Dashboard Data upgrade note names every panel a Backfill without the Clear inflates. Activity by SID / Instance on Work Process Performance counts the upgraded hours twice as well, and its WP Categories column counts each renamed component twice.

    Build 384 was not released; its changes reached customers in build 385.

    Who is affected: every deployment: non-admin users can no longer write the App’s dashboard data, and a scheduled search of your own that writes into one of these collections must be owned by an admin. Admins who read the AI Assistant’s audit warning (shown since build 383) now see both capabilities Splunk accepts.

    Upgrade action: nothing to rebuild. A metadata/local.meta stanza for one of these collections keeps its own ACL; remove it to take the new one. A scheduled search of your own that writes into one of these collections and is owned by a non-admin user stops writing. Start the App’s writing searches (a retention, a backfill, an ES feed) through the REST API only with an admin-tier account. See Upgrading to This Release.

    AI Assistant settings writable by admins only, a warning when audit events are not written, and SAP’s names for the trace components (build 383)¶

    Builds 380, 381 and 382 were not released; their changes reached customers in build 383.

    AI Assistant security

    • Only admins can change the AI Assistant’s settings. Its settings, its legal acknowledgements and its discovered-model cache live in three KV Store collections (logserv_ai_assistant_settings, logserv_ai_assistant_acks, logserv_ai_models) that every role could write. A signed-in user without admin rights could therefore change, through Splunk’s REST API, where an admin’s browser sends the audit forwarder’s HEC token (the forwarder URL) and the MCP bearer token (the MCP server URL), or the privacy tier. The three collections are now writable by the admin, sc_admin and sc_subadmin roles only; every role can still read them. The writes other users’ pages used to make there (a one-time move of conf-file values at page load, the model list’s refresh) were best-effort; they are now refused, quietly, and an admin’s page makes them.

    AI Assistant audit log

    • A warning when audit events are not written. The browser writes the AI Assistant’s audit events to logserv_ai_assistant_audit through Splunk’s receivers/simple endpoint, as the signed-in user, and that needs the edit_tcp or the edit_log_alert_event capability, which Splunk Enterprise’s default admin and power roles hold and user does not. (Correction: this entry first said admin only.) A refused write used to be dropped with a line in the browser console, so the activity of users without either capability went unaudited without a sign. While writes fail, the chat panel now shows an amber warning - on HTTP 403 it named edit_tcp (superseded by build 385, which names edit_log_alert_event and edit_tcp); on HTTP 401, which usually means the Splunk Web session has ended, it asks for a reload first - and the session’s audit list notes from when its events may be missing from the index. Which capability to grant, and what each allows, is in Audit Log.
    • The batch still buffered when a tab closes is sent. It went out as a browser beacon, which cannot carry Splunk Web’s CSRF header and was refused for every user; it is now a keep-alive request with the header, carrying the newest events that fit in 60 KB. Like every audit write, it still needs edit_tcp or edit_log_alert_event.
    • The audit index default is logserv_ai_assistant_audit in the App’s configuration fallbacks and the Audit Log viewer, which still named the retired ai_assistant_audit. The legal text of the forwarder acknowledgement still names it (superseded by build 386, which corrects it as version 2); changing that text would ask an admin to accept it again (it is accepted once per deployment, not per admin).

    SAP’s names for the work process trace components

    • The letter that starts each work process trace (dev_w*) line names SAP’s trace component, and ten of the App’s names change. Seven were wrong: C is the database-specific layer (C = Database (DBSL), not Communication), X extended memory (not RFC / CPIC), M the task handler (not memory management), S spool (not SQL / statistics), T the debug system (not the task handler), D the Diag processor (not the dispatcher), and N security - SNC, SSF, logon tickets (not the network interface); R reads R = Rolling and O is below. E (enqueue), G (language support), H (ICF / HTTP), I (IPC), J (VM container), L (background), P (paging) and W (WebGUI / ITS) get names, O and V, which SAP’s public lists do not name, are named from their lines (program buffer / PXA, coverage analyzer), and Q, which is not a trace component, reads Q = Other. The names come from SAP Help’s “Trace Components” list and SAP Note 112. They appear in wp_category_name and in the Work Process Performance, ABAP Operations and Host Details panels; searches, alerts or dashboards of your own that filter on the old wp_category_name values need the new ones.

    Environment Topology

    • The partner donuts and the hourly chart say what they count. A system’s “Partners calling this system” and “Partners this system calls” donuts name their unit from that side’s edge types - calls, connections (RFC and SAP Router edges count connections), or calls + connections, with “total” under a mixed donut’s centre - and the node’s hourly chart reads Count / hr, as the Live Activity chart does.

    AI Assistant

    • The sourcetype reference names fields that exist. The logserv_sourcetype_metadata_lookup the AI Assistant can read listed, for 30 of its 35 sourcetypes, fields the sourcetype does not have (sap_inst, severity and msg on the ABAP sourcetypes, for example), and 17 of its example searches returned nothing. Every row now names fields that the App, the Data TA or - for the Windows and Linux rows - Splunk’s Windows and *nix add-ons produce, and an example search that runs; the four Windows rows use the real sourcetype, XmlWinEventLog, and name their channel in source.

    Who is affected: deployments with ABAP work process trace data (Work Process Performance, ABAP Operations and Host Details), searches of your own that filter on wp_category_name, and every deployment for the AI Assistant settings’ write access.

    Upgrade action: coming from build 379 or earlier, Clear and then Backfill the Work Process Performance / ABAP Operations row in Settings → Dashboard Data once, over a window that covers its history; Upgrading to This Release has the details. To keep that row’s history older than the raw events your index still holds, use the narrower repair instead of the Clear.

    Host Details shows the work processes’ trace components, and the topology inventory takes each host’s most recent SID (build 379)¶

    Host Details

    • ABAP Work Process Trace Components replaces ABAP Work Process Mix. The old panel grouped the work process trace (dev_w*) by a work process type the logs do not record, so it never showed. The new one counts the lines by their trace component: the letter each line starts with, named the way wp_category_name names it (for example B = Database Interface; a letter without a name shows as <letter> = Other).

    Environment Topology

    • A host or address seen under two SAP systems takes its most recent one. The host-to-SID inventory recorded an endpoint only in an hour whose log lines all named one SID, and a row once written stayed, so an endpoint whose lines named two systems kept the SID of its last single-system hour, possibly a stale one, and one that had never had such an hour had no row. It now records each endpoint under the SID of its newest hour of activity; when that hour names two, the one with more events; an exact tie writes nothing and keeps the previous row. Endpoints left unattributed before can now fold into a system’s node, and an address that serves two systems at once is drawn under the one that logs more.
    • The totals that add up different edge types say so: Total calls + connections, Inbound calls + connections and Outbound calls + connections (RFC and SAP Router edges count connections, not calls), and the Live Activity table’s column reads Count.

    Smaller changes

    • The AI Assistant’s data-model hint names the fields the ABAP sourcetypes extract (sap_instance, the dispatcher’s dp_severity, dp_function and dp_reason, the work process’s wp_function, the enqueue server’s enq_function) instead of sap_inst, severity, message and error_code, which none of them extracts; sap:saphostexec and sap:sapstartsrv get a line of their own.
    • The upgrade hint on Settings → Dashboard Data no longer speaks of a 30-day backfill window: a Clear discards graph history older than the window you backfill, so pick one that covers it.
    • The documentation explains how to keep the AI Assistant’s audit index to its reviewers: Splunk’s default user role can search every index whose name does not start with _, the audit index among them (Audit Log).

    Who is affected: deployments that use Host Details or the Environment Topology.

    Upgrade action: coming from build 378 or earlier, click the row’s own Backfill, without Clear, on Host Role Activity (Host Details) and Environment Topology (graph) in Settings → Dashboard Data; see Upgrading to This Release.

    SAP Router and RFC connections in the topology, the HANA audit host, HANA trace lines read by their format, and the SAP client in the ICM trace — rebuild eleven rollups once (build 378)¶

    Environment Topology

    • SAP Router is a new integration type. Each router’s CONNECT TO lines become an edge from the router host — drawn as its own square, tagged SAP ROUTER, and never folded into an SAP system even when the same VM runs one — to the address it routed to, with the number of routed connections. A target named <ip>/sapms<SID> is that system’s message server, so its address is attributed to the SID and the edge ends on the system’s circle; targets reached by port or sapgw<NN> stay addresses until another source attributes them. The router’s failed server-side connections that name a target IPv4 address (NiBufReceive S… '<IPv4>' failed) count as the edge’s failed connections; client-side failures and failures that name a host are not counted. Loopback targets (127.0.0.0/8, such as a router’s port-3298 niping self-test) are left out. The edges have their own legend colour and filter checkbox, and the Edge Details pane shows routed and failed connections, the top target services (Operations, counted in routed connections) and the target role mix (Performance). New search-time fields on sap:saprouter: saprouter_target_addr, saprouter_target_ip, saprouter_target_service, saprouter_target_sid, saprouter_target_role (message server, gateway, gateway (secure), dispatcher, SAP Router, niping, other service), saprouter_target_instance and saprouter_fail_target_ip; ports 3298 (niping) and 3299 (SAP Router) carry no instance number. See SAP Router.
    • RFC edges count connections, in the direction they were made. The SAP gateway trace (dev_rd) records connections and their failures, not individual RFC calls. An RFC edge now counts the connections it saw: closed connections to remote gateways (outbound), closed client sessions (inbound) and broken connections, each broken connection once (before, each of its up to three trace lines counted as a call; two broken connections to the same remote gateway count as two). Errors are the broken connections, so an edge never shows more errors than connections, and the Edge Details pane says connections and broken connections where it said calls and errors. A connection made to a system’s gateway is now drawn from the caller to the system; until now every RFC edge pointed away from it. Clients and peers on a loopback address (127.0.0.0/8) are left out, so systems that each log a local client on 127.0.0.1 are not joined through one shared address node. Remote gateway hosts are named by the last hop of an SAP Router route and their short host name. The Operations tab of an RFC edge lists the remote gateway services and client programs, and the Performance tab the mix of connection records — both were empty for RFC edges before. The By app server table names the address of the gateway that recorded each connection; connection records name no local address and are grouped as (not recorded). New fields on sap:abap:gateway: gw_remgw_target, gw_remgw_service, gw_remgw_id, gw_client_ip, gw_client_hostname, gw_client_tp, gw_client_id, rfc_peer_port and rfc_local_port.
    • Saved layouts keep new types switched on. A layout records the integration types that were ticked, so a type added after it was saved used to load unticked. Layouts saved earlier now load with SAP Router enabled; layouts saved from now on also record which types existed, so a type you switch off stays off.
    • The health ring and the Edge Details error rate never exceed 100 %, and an edge whose only records in the window are failures counts as fully failed. HANA Tenant duration figures say that each hdbcons command’s duration is converted to milliseconds from the unit its trace line records.
    • HANA audit edges end on the HANA host that wrote each record (see HANA below), and node errors no longer list ICM sessions as HTTP errors (see ICM below).
    • Web Dispatcher events count toward their system. Web Dispatcher requests now also count toward their host’s node and toward the Hosts and Errors tabs of the system their log path names (a system’s Errors tab may now list Web Dispatcher HTTP 4xx / 5xx kinds; the tab shows the top 20). A Web Dispatcher’s own logs no longer attribute a host or an address to a system in the topology inventory: neither its access log nor its ICM trace (dev_icm), which LogServ files under webdispatcher/icm and the Data TA types sap:abap:icm, like an ABAP system’s ICM trace, so it carries the Web Dispatcher’s SID. A Web Dispatcher with its own SID on a host shared with another system therefore does not take that host, or the address its ICM listens on, over, and a host that runs only a Web Dispatcher stays a host square until another source names its system.
    • The Environment Topology (graph) backfill now adds up node counts across all of its searches. Settings › Dashboard Data rebuilds every rollup by running each of its component searches as its own job, so that no search is cut short at high event volumes. Two of the Environment Topology graph’s collections, however, combine those searches’ results: a node seen by several log sources (an IP address that is both a gateway address and an ICM address, or a Web Dispatcher client that also connects to the gateway) is one node whose event count is the sum of all of them, and an IP address or host is attributed to an SAP system only when every source names the same system. Until now each search wrote its own partial count to the same node row, so backfilled node counts were too low, and an address that two sources attribute to two different systems could be mapped to one of them. The backfill now collects those searches’ results in a scratch KV Store collection, logserv_backfill_stage, and writes each month’s node rows, and the inventory, only once every search for that month has finished and every result it collected reads back in full, so the rows match what the hourly aggregation writes. Keep the Settings page open until the Environment Topology (graph) row has finished. A month left unfinished, or one whose collected results do not all read back (as can happen while KV Store is still starting after a restart), is discarded rather than written in part: the row reads failed — re-run, and the next backfill rebuilds that month. Rows written by the hourly aggregation were always correct; history that an earlier backfill rebuilt for this row is repaired by the Clear and Backfill this upgrade asks for. See Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness.

    HANA

    • HANA audit events name the HANA host; the client gets its own field. Each HANA audit record names two machines: the HANA host that wrote it and the client that ran the action. Until this build the App put the client’s host name into host, so every panel and search that grouped HANA audit events by host listed client workstations and application servers, and the Host Details drilldown could open a host with no events of its own. host on sap:hana:audit is now the HANA host, the value the index stores for the event (as every tstats search already saw it), and the client’s host name is the new field src_host, beside src_ip (the client IP) and dest_host. On HANA Audit, Failed Operations by Host is now Failed Operations by HANA Host, and the High-Risk Events and After-Hours / Weekend Admin Activity tables show a HANA Host and a Client Host column; on Change & Configuration Activity, the HANA change table’s single Host column, which showed the client, becomes HANA Host and Client Host. Your own saved searches that group sap:hana:audit events by host now group by HANA host; use src_host where you meant the client. HANA audit records with no client (for example a GRANT PRIVILEGE or DDL statement; about 2 % of the records on the reference data) now parse fully, so they gain their action, category, severity and SID.
    • HANA trace lines are read by their own format.
